en: [1] The Section on the Accomplishment of Authority: The True Nature of the Duties of Śūdras.
Victorious are the garlands of dust from the feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Bliss, which, when worn upon the head, become garlands of glory for Mahendra and the other gods. (1)
Having bowed to Rāma, Kamalākara Śarman, the son of Rāmakṛṣṇa, sets forth the duties of the Śūdra. || 1 ||

In this context, *śūdratva* (the state of being a Śūdra) consists in being born from a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*) as the father, just like *vipratva* (the state of being a Brāhmaṇa) and so forth. Although this is not the case for Viśvāmitra and others at the time of the beginning of creation, nevertheless, in their case, *brāhmaṇatva* consists simply in having a body produced by a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit). In other cases, however, it is as previously stated. The same applies to the Śūdra; such is the general direction of the argument. Regarding this, there are scriptural passages such as those of the Bahvṛcas and Taittirīyas: "From his feet the Śūdra was born," and "The Śūdra is among men what the horse is among animals.
Furthermore: "The social classes were born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, respectively."
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, [he created them] from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.

“[The Creator] brought forth the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra” (Manusmṛti 1.31). Thus, even though the Śūdra is a member of a caste (*varṇa*) according to the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, the prohibition of [Vedic] rites for him is understood both from scriptural statements and from logical reasoning.

Accordingly, the *Śatapatha-śruti* states: “The Śūdra is indeed a walking cremation ground. The word *padyu* means that which is joined with feet; that is to say, it is mobile. Therefore, the *Taittirīya-śruti* says: “A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice, for the deities were not created after him” (TS 7.1.1).

The reasoning (*nyāya*), however, is found in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, specifically in the second and sixth [sub-sections]. To explain: in the first section, since the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" is understood through the gerundive suffix (*tavya*)—which denotes the object of the action—to mean that study has the Veda as its purpose, and because [the Veda] would thus serve a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) merely by the acquisition of the syllables, the requirement of the injunction is satisfied by that alone; consequently, there is no implication for further inquiry, and thus the *Mīmāṃsā* treatise is not commenced according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, one must return home after studying the Veda without performing inquiry, according to the Smṛti rule: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe. Consequently, since the knowledge required for the sacrificial rites is already established by the injunction for Vedic study, it follows that even a Śūdra—who like the twice-born would otherwise lack such knowledge—could acquire it by means of books and so forth; thus, it was argued that the Śūdra also possesses eligibility [for ritual acts].

[5] And in the sixth book, regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section on Śūdras: in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because study has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) insofar as it is the cause for the comprehension of meaning—just as the *sāman* chants have the purpose of hymns by way of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc* verses—the purpose of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is understood through the suffix *-tavya*. Since that comprehension of meaning is not possible without inquiry, the treatise (*śāstra*) must be commenced for that purpose. This was indicated in the *Śabara-bhāṣya* under the commentary on the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the aphorism "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*, PMS 1.1.1), specifically in the statement that the injunction to study has a visible purpose.

[7] Since the purpose of the injunction is not fulfilled without reflection (*vicāra*), there is a postponement of the *smārta* bath prescribed by the rule, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe. Consequently, from the injunction for study—"One should initiate him and then teach him"—it follows:
"Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should teach him the Veda preceded by the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), and he should instruct him in the rules of purity and so forth" (YDh 1.15).

Thus, based on the *smṛti*, because the initiation (*upanayana*) has a visible purpose and because its application is directed only toward those who have been initiated—and since initiation itself is prescribed for the three higher castes alone by the scriptural injunctions, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn," according to the principle of the second chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*], "Because it is subsidiary to all [rites] in the case of the fire-consecration" (*ādhāna*)—and because the injunctions for sacrifices, having their scope exhausted by referring to the three castes who possess the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study, do not imply the necessity of such knowledge (due to the absence of any other way to justify them), the Śūdra lacks qualification for ritual acts; this is also the result of the sixth [chapter’s] final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

[8] Regarding this, although in another Vedic text it says, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age; one should teach him," the mention of the initiated boy (*upanīta*) pertains to the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*) and not to the act of studying (*adhyayana*), nevertheless—because teaching is for the sake of livelihood and thus, like the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yājayet*), is unfit to be a primary injunction, and because it resides in the teacher and thus does not constitute a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for the student—the meaning should be understood through a syntactical modification (*vipariṇāma*) as: "The Brāhmaṇa should approach [the teacher]; he should study. This is the view of Vivaraṇa and others. Pārthasārathi, Rāṇaka, and others hold that, just as in the case of the rule "one should choose the *camasādhvaryu* priests by means of the *svādhyāya*," the student (*baṭu*), who is the recipient of the initiation sacrament, is also enjoined by this very text and is therefore an object to be taken up (*upādeya*). In that regard, since the initiation is already established by the rules concerning the spring season and so forth, the time of eight years is enjoined with reference to the initiation qualified by the Brāhmaṇa caste. Hemādri maintains that there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), because such a split occurs when the intended subject remains incomplete, whereas here there is no such split since the qualified subject is fully intended. However, the truth is that, due to the absence of a decisive factor and because they belong to different recensions (*śākhā*), there is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) in both cases. For this very reason, masculinity is intended to be significant as an object to be taken up. Otherwise, since the student is the recipient of the sacrament during initiation, masculinity would—as in the case of the singularity of the cup—not be intended, and who could prevent the application of initiation even to women?

As for what is stated in the *Tantraratna* regarding the passage "her [initiation] consists of the benediction and celibacy" (*āśīr brahmacaryam*) within the statement concerning the eight-year-old girl: although it is argued that—on the grounds of logical principle (*nyāya*)—the gender is not intended to be significant because she is the object of the rite denoted by the accusative case, and thus initiation would apply to a woman as well, yet initiation is nonetheless absent for her due to an explicit prohibition; that argument must be reconsidered. For, just as in the injunction "one should choose the Adhvaryu priest," the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is something to be undertaken (*upādeya*), and this applies equally to the injunctions concerning the spring season (*vasantādi-vākya*) and so forth. For this very reason, there is no initiation for a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*), as that would be a characteristic of a Śūdra. For this same reason, Devala states in the *Mitākṣarā*: [10] As for what is stated in the *Tantraratna* regarding the passage "her [initiation] consists of the benediction and celibacy" (*āśīr brahmacaryam*) within the statement concerning the eight-year-old girl: although it is argued that—on the grounds of logical principle (*nyāya*)—the gender is not intended to be significant because she is the object of the rite denoted by the accusative case, and thus initiation would apply to a woman as well, yet initiation is nonetheless absent for her due to an explicit prohibition; that argument must be reconsidered. For, just as in the injunction "one should choose the Adhvaryu priest," the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is something to be undertaken (*upādeya*), and this applies equally to the injunctions concerning the spring season (*vasantādi-vākya*) and so forth. For this very reason, there is no initiation for a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*), as that would be a characteristic of a Śūdra. For this same reason, Devala states in the *Mitākṣarā*:
One who is a *ṣaṇḍha* (impotent) possesses inferior sexual organs and is not at all fit for sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).
Yājñavalkya states: "But having killed a Brāhmaṇa who is a *ṣaṇḍha*, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra."

Thus he says. However, the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, and others state that there is an initiation (*upanayana*) for a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*) based on a specific scriptural injunction; this we shall explain further on. For this very reason, because they reside in the subject to be enjoined (*upādeyagatatvāt*), both the age of eight years and the singular number are intended to be significant. Now, one might object: "If the Śūdra’s lack of entitlement to perform rituals is established by logic alone (*nyāyataḥ*), then the prohibition, 'Therefore, a Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice,' is redundant."

The Bhāṭṭas maintain that this is a restatement of what is already established by logic (*nyāyaprāptānuvāda*). The Vedāntins, however, argue as follows: since the suffix *-tavya* indicates that the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic study) is the goal to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), and because it is the first thing to present itself, and because it is indispensable in cases such as the utterance of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, and for the sake of uniformity, the grasping of the syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*) alone must be the goal. Nor does it follow from the fact that sacrifices imply a knowledge of their meaning that a Śūdra would thereby gain the right to perform them by means of books and the like. Just as in the Bhāṭṭa view, once the acquisition of knowledge is established by the injunction to study, the sacrifices do not imply the acquisition of knowledge in the case of a Śūdra; likewise, the knowledge of the meaning—having its purpose fulfilled through the grasping of syllables by means of the injunction to study—is not compelled to imply the use of books and other means for a Śūdra. The situation is the same. Even if the Śūdra’s entitlement were reached through such implication, it is prohibited by the scriptural text: "Whether sitting or lying down. It is precisely because of this prohibition that the study has the purpose of grasping the syllables. Otherwise, since there would be no possibility of a Śūdra attaining it, the prohibition would be meaningless; so they say. In any case, the Śūdra’s lack of entitlement to ritual action is established.

However, the dispute regarding the "taking" (*grahaṇa*) arises from the term *upanīta*, derived from the root *nī*. This is because of Pāṇini’s rule: "The root *nī* takes the *ātmanepada* ending when it signifies honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*), knowledge, wages, counting, or expenditure" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.36). Since this rule prescribes the *ātmanepada* when "acting as a teacher" is the intended result (*bhāvya*), even though the act of initiation (*upanayana*) itself lacks an independent fruit by virtue of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*), it is said:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*."

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), the fruit of teaching itself is figuratively attributed to its subsidiary part (*aṅga*). This is similar to the statement: "The *prayāja* offerings are made as armor for the sacrifice. Therefore, although the injunction to study is prompted by the injunction to teach, because study resides in the student (*māṇavaka*) and is thus internal to him, it also has the purpose of understanding the meaning. Furthermore, since sacrifices depend upon the knowledge established thereby [by study], they do not imply any other means [of acquiring that knowledge]; thus, the Prābhākaras maintain that there is no entitlement for a *śūdra*.

That is incorrect. If the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇatva*) were intended for the benefit of the agent (*kartṛbhiprāya*), then because the root *ṇīj* is marked with the indicatory letter *ṇi*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be established by the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini 1.3.72). Consequently, the formulation of the rule beginning with *saṃmānana-* (Pāṇini 1.3.36) would be redundant. Therefore, this sūtra is intended to prescribe the middle voice even when the result is not intended for the agent. As stated in the Mahābhāṣya: "This undertaking is for the purpose of cases where the result is not intended for the agent. Thus, even though the fruit of the action exists, because it is not intended for the agent, the state of being made a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇatva*) is not that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). This is the general direction; the specific details, however, should be understood from the Vivaraṇa and the Tantraratna.
[13] In that regard, a Śūdra has no entitlement whatsoever to hear the Veda: "By drinking the milk of a brown cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Veda, a Śūdra becomes a Cāṇḍāla" (Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra 1.75).

Thus it is stated by Parāśara. Furthermore, in the Uttaramīmāṃsā, in the Vyāsasūtra, at the point stating "because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning" (1.3.38), as well as "and because of Smṛti," the Śūdra’s hearing of the Veda and so forth is forbidden. This was explained by Śaṅkarācārya: there is a prohibition against hearing [the Veda], such as: "Now, if he should overhear his Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac" (GDh 2.11); "A Śūdra is indeed a walking cremation ground" (GDh 2.10); and "In the case of reciting [it], there shall be the cutting of the tongue; in the case of retaining [it], the destruction of the body" (GDh 2.11). Likewise, there is also a prohibition against knowing the meaning of the Veda.

"One should not give instruction to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor the sacrificial oblation that has been soaked; nor should one teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him"—so says the *Padma Purāṇa*. (The term "instruction" [mati] refers to the teaching of the meaning of the Vedas. Furthermore, from the *Parāśara Purāṇa*: "One should not impart knowledge to a Śūdra by means of the Veda. Since the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is thus prohibited, the study of Mīmāṃsā and other such sciences is also forbidden.

[14] Likewise, the study of the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth is prohibited because they are rooted in the Vedas, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "The *Purāṇa* is the fifth Veda; the *Purāṇa* is equal to the Veda."
Therefore, this should be studied with diligence by those who know the Vedas,
and it should be taught to disciples who possess virtuous conduct, in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus, from the *Atri-smṛti* in the *Smṛtikaumudī*. Manu also says:

"He for whom the rites beginning with conception (*niṣeka*) and ending at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) are prescribed by means of mantras—his eligibility for this scripture is to be known, and not that of anyone else. (15)
The same applies to the hearing of the *Smṛtis* and other such texts.
This scripture must not be studied in the presence of a *vṛṣala*;
and that deluded soul who does study it shall go to many hells.
Thus it is stated in the Kūrma [Purāṇa]. Also in the Vāyu-saṃhitā:
"This jewel of a Purāṇa concerning the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) must not be told to those who do not know the Vedas."
For what is given to a disciple who is not devoted, or to atheists, indeed bestows hell.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O observer of noble vows, O best of Brahmins, I do not wish to hear these Dharmaśāstras that you have spoken, for they are indeed secrets, O twice-born one. (1)
These have been declared by the wise for the welfare of only the three social classes, but not for Śūdras; hear my words on this matter.
The Vedas are established among the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas;
likewise, the treatises of Manu and others, as well as all the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), are established therein.
In this context, there is a direct prohibition of listening to and reciting [the scriptures] for Śūdras primarily, but not by way of a Brāhmaṇa intermediary. As it is stated in the Mahābhārata:
"One should cause the four castes to hear [it], having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront.
And likewise in the Nāradīya:

"And those who are devoted to the Dharma, O King, and dedicated to the Vedas and the twice-born—among them, the twice-born should recite this in the presence of Hari. Thus it is said. Also in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa:
The three Vedas are not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the degraded twice-born;
for those deluded regarding the excellence of ritual action, this [other path] alone shall lead to their welfare in this world. || 1 ||

"Thus was the narrative known as the Bhārata composed by the sage out of compassion. (A son born of a Śūdra woman from a twice-born man is a *dvijabandhu* or a *vrātya*). In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O Indra among kings, O best of monarchs, listen to those treatises on Dharma which have been proclaimed for the welfare of all four castes."
In particular, the wise have declared that for Śūdras,
the eighteen Purāṇas and the life-story of Rāghava are purifying.
In the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"O tiger among kings, these treatises on dharma have been declared by the learned as common to all castes for their perpetual welfare. (1)
O King of kings, O observer of noble vows, you ought to hear these four [accounts] here from the Sūta-saṃhitā of the Skanda-purāṇa:
"And others, O Viṣṇu— namely Brāhmaṇas and likewise kings."
And Vaiśyas are qualified for the practice of knowledge according to their respective degrees of excellence. || 1 ||
Even for the wives of the twice-born, there is eligibility for the practice of knowledge derived from the Śrutis;
likewise, for the Śūdra, there is the duty of service and the acquisition of knowledge through the Purāṇas alone. (2)
Some learned men declare that women are equal to Śūdras; likewise,
the best of sages have stated that the hearing of established doctrines is for the twice-born.
And likewise for Śūdras who are dispassionate, as well as for women, O great sage. || 1 ||
The hearing of the *siddhānta* is declared by the wise to be the hearing of the *purāṇas*;
(*siddhānta* here means the meaning of the *smṛtis*). Also in the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"A twice-born man who recites [it] shall attain the state of being a bull among speakers."
A Kṣatriya might attain the status of a lord of the earth;
a merchant might attain the fruit of merit;
and even a Śūdra, by listening, might attain greatness. || 1 ||
This too [is to be heard] only through the medium of the Brahmins and others. As it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*:
"O best of kings, having placed the image of the deity and the Brahmins before him, the Śūdra, as well as the other twice-born classes, must certainly listen. (1)
Precisely because of the prescribed rule for listening to the Purāṇas, there is no fault even in hearing the Vedic mantras contained therein. As it is stated in the Vārttika:

"People employ those very same Vedic mantras that have been incorporated into the Mahābhārata and other texts, setting aside the restrictive rules for mantras and using them according to worldly understanding."

Although being a cause of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) does not exist apart from Vedic character, by that [fact], the existence of hymns (*stotra*) and so forth in the Veda is inferred in some cases. Nevertheless, there is no fault because of the explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*). Even though it is non-eternal, because its stream is beginningless, it falls within the scope of eternal injunctions, like the *Kalpasūtras* and similar texts. Regarding those [passages] where Śaṅkha, after enumerating the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), states: "The Brāhmaṇa is authorized for these, and he shows the means of livelihood (*vṛtti*) to others"—since the instruction of knowledge is through the medium of the Brāhmaṇa alone by virtue of the plural number, this indicates that the Śūdra is not qualified; yet even that [text] is solely concerned with the hearing [of the Purāṇas]. Here, the prescribed and prohibited duties of Śūdras should also be understood as applying to those equal to Śūdras—such as uninitiated twice-born women, *kuṇḍas*, *golakas*, and those born of mixed castes (*saṃkara*). These will be discussed further on. Thus it is established that knowledge is attained by a Śūdra through hearing the Purāṇas via the medium of a Brāhmaṇa.
[18] Now follows the consideration of the *mantra*s for the Śūdra. In this regard, because he lacks Vedic knowledge (*avidyatva*), he has no entitlement to the Vedic *mantra*s. Vyāsa also says:

"The Śūdra is the fourth caste; nevertheless, by virtue of being a member of a caste, he is entitled to the *dharma*, provided it is without the Vedic *mantra*s, the *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ* calls, and so forth. [1.6]
In the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*:
"One does not desire [to teach] the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajus, or Lakṣmī to a woman or a Śūdra.
It is likewise stated in the *Parāśarabhāṣya*. In the *Rāmatāpanīya*:

If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava, he goes to a lower state after death; for according to the Śruti, "In the case of pronouncing [these], there shall be the cutting off of the tongue. And in the *Tithitattva* of the *Gauḍanibandha*, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "A twice-born man who gives a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *Praṇava* to a Śūdra causes the Śūdra to attain hell and the Brāhmaṇa to fall into the state of a Śūdra."

Thus, there is likewise no entitlement for reciting the *Purāṇas*, the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*, the *Caṇḍīstotra*, and so forth; for while they possess the entitlement merely to hear them, there is no occasion for their recitation. This is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*: "Even a person of the Śūdra caste shall attain a good rebirth by hearing [it]. For this very reason, it is said in the *Bhārata* regarding the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*: "A Brāhmaṇa who studies the Vedānta shall become [so]; a Kṣatriya shall be victorious; a Vaiśya shall be enriched with wealth; and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness."

In this regard, Śaṅkarācārya has explained that for Śūdras, [the acquisition of knowledge] occurs through hearing alone. What more need be said? In rites such as bathing, giving gifts, and *śrāddha* performed by Śūdras, the recitation of the Puranic mantras belongs solely to the Brāhmaṇa; for the Śūdra, however, there is only hearing. This is because, according to the sense of the injunctions "one should cause the four castes to hear" and "one should cause the Niṣāda chief to sacrifice," the Śūdra is permitted to perform ritual acts only by means of the knowledge produced through hearing; furthermore, since there is no rule for the Śūdra to recite the Purāṇas, the question of reciting their mantras does not even arise. As it is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
This very same procedure is prescribed for Śūdras, excluding the mantras;
however, for a mantra-less Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa is employed to perform the rite with the mantra.

Even though this is recited within the section on *śrāddha*, it is a general rule (*paribhāṣā*). And since it is not in the form of a specific sentence, it cannot be restricted by the context of that particular section. Therefore, Śūlapāṇi maintains that in all cases—such as *śrāddhas* where the giver is a *śūdra*—the recitation of mantras must be performed by a Brahmin for the purpose of revealing the meaning. Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi holds that even Vedic mantras should be recited by the Brahmin; the same is stated in the *Mādhavīya*. Furthermore, the *Smṛtikaumudī* states that whichever recitation of mantras is prescribed for a Brahmin in a particular Vedic school (*śākhā*) during a *śrāddha*, that same recitation should indeed apply to a *śūdra’s* *śrāddha* as well. The commentary in the *Madanapārijāta*, however, is incorrect because its subject matter is absent [from the text]. Śūlapāṇi explains that because of the qualifying term "without mantras" (*amantrasya*), the rule applies to women and those equal to them. As for what he further stated—that the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction of mantras is achieved through a salutation alone, since Gautama declares that "for him, a salutation is authorized as the mantra"—that is to be considered with caution.

[21] For the attainment of that [result] occurs only through the door of direct perception (*dṛṣṭa*), not independently; nor is there the attainment of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) from a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the prohibition of mantras, since its accomplishment is achieved by the mere act of salutation (*namaskāra*). Indeed, that [salutation] is not a mantra; otherwise, even in the case of *nakhāvapūta* (grain purified by nails), that [act] would have to be performed for the sake of the unseen merit produced by threshing (*avaghāta*). The *Kalpataru*, however, states that because the Purāṇic rites are specifically prescribed for women and Śūdras, and because they are enjoined as being produced with mantras, the recitation of Purāṇic mantras certainly takes place for them. This is not correct, because it is set aside by the act of salutation and contradicts the *Vārāha-purāṇa*. Others hold that the word "namas" (*namaḥ*) occupies the place of Vedic mantras. But the truth is that this [use of *namaḥ*] applies only to those cases where there are no mantras at all. Therefore, in passages such as “by the name and lineage of the ancestors” (*pitṝṇāṃ nāmagotrataḥ*), where even for the twice-born (*dvija*) a mantra consisting of the name is mentioned, the rule of Gautama serves merely as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the Śūdra when a total prohibition of mantras has been established; it does not apply to the scattering of sesame seeds (*tilāvapana*) and other such acts. Others, however, [hold...]
Listen to how the invocation and other rites should be performed by a Śūdra:
for the gods, by their divine names; for the ancestors, by means of "namaḥ" and their lineage (gotra).

Thus, because of the statement in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* cited by Hemādri, they say that in all cases of rites for the gods (*daiva*), the name-mantra is "Salutation to the Gods" (*namo devebhyaḥ*), and in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), it is "Salutation to the Ancestors" (*namo pitṛbhyaḥ*). This refutes the assertion of Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi and Madanapārijāta that because a mere name is unfit for use, the mantra consists only of the word "namas. Haradatta and others hold that the salutation (*namaskāra*) applies only to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). That is not so, because the injunction of "namas" in the *śrāddha* and other rites serves a universal purpose through the avoidance of having to postulate a separate source (root-text). For this very reason, Vijñāneśvara has stated that the mantra "namas" is to be recited during the *kṛcchra* penance and others. Our venerable father, however, maintains that regarding Yājñavalkya’s statement—"One should not omit the five sacrifices with the mantra of salutation"—the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) prescribes the salutation with reference to the duties of Śūdras in general. If one were to qualify those sacrifices by specifying their number as five, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), similar to the case where the singular number of "cup" (*graha*) is intended to be restrictive. Therefore, he says that for a Śūdra performing meritorious works (*pūrta*) such as the gift of a balance (*tulādāna*), the mantra is "namas. There is no contradiction with the Purāṇic rule which specifies "of a Brāhmaṇa" (*viprasya*). By this, the assertion of Madanapārijāta—that because the salutation is prescribed only for the five sacrifices, a Śūdra does not have it in marriage-homas and the like—is refuted. This is also supported by the Vedic text, "He who [performs] his own sacrifice with salutation," and by the statement of Āśvalāyana: "Indeed, the gods do not accept salutation... for the sacrifice is indeed salutation," which constitutes a Brāhmaṇa passage. Furthermore, the fact that salutation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all ritual acts is set aside in various instances for the twice-born (*dvija*) by the recitation of Vedic mantras; however, it prevails in the case of *caityayajña* and similar rites.

[23] Likewise, even for a Śūdra, when the ritual action (*karman*) is prescribed and the mantra is not, one certainly proceeds with the rite. For this very reason, Harihara stated that the eight sacraments (*saṃskāra*) mentioned in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* as well as marriage apply to the Śūdra. Therefore, the rule from the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra*—"for him, the mantra is the salutation (*namaskāra*)"—is an exception (*pratiprasava*) granted even to the Śūdra. And although this [salutation] does not manifest the specific details of the performance, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is established by the scriptural statement and by the maxim: "In the absence of a specific rule, it should be like that of Indra" (*aidrī*). By this, the arguments of Vijñāneśvara, Madanapārijāta, and others—who claim that the mantra is either "to the gods and to the ancestors" or simply "salutation"—are refuted due to a lack of authoritative evidence. On this point, some maintain: "A Brāhmaṇa is characterized by the mantra" (*vipro mantreṇa gṛhyate*). Here, the Vedic mantra belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, whereas the Purāṇic mantra should be recited by Śūdras. For there is no qualification (*adhikāra*) for a Śūdra in the Vedas; rather, "my qualification here in the Purāṇas has been shown by the Brāhmaṇas," according to the *Padma-purāṇa* cited by Śūlapāṇi. Śrīdatta also holds this view. However, in the *Tithitattva*, the Smārta school maintains that a Śūdra has the right to recite mantras other than those of the Veda. The *Ācāracintāmaṇi* states: "For a Śūdra, [the rite is performed] excluding Vedic mantras. Furthermore, because of the word "Veda" as a qualifier in the *Chandogāhnika*, the prohibition—"it should only be heard by a Śūdra, never studied"—refers specifically to mantras other than the Purāṇas. Regarding the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), bathing, and *śrāddha*, even the Purāṇic mantra is not used with a salutation. As Yājñavalkya says regarding the five sacrifices: "Thus, for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, bathing with mantras is desired; for the Śūdra, it is considered to be silent, accompanied only by a salutation. This applies to the bath.

"This very same procedure is prescribed for Śūdras, excluding the mantras. He says this because it is stated specifically regarding the *śrāddha* in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*. Gautama also says, "A salutation is permitted as his mantra" (GDh 10.64), which refers to this [purāṇic] mantra and not to Vedic mantras. That is not so; for the Veda is far removed [from them] due to the prohibition in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*: "This scripture must not be studied in the presence of a *vṛṣala* (Śūdra)" (24). It is indeed to be studied by Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas.
A Śūdra may indeed listen, but he must never study [the Veda].
O best of kings, both the Śrauta and Smārta Dharma have been proclaimed herein;
therefore, Śūdras should never listen to it without a Brāhmaṇa present.

This is because of the statement in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* regarding the section on the *Śūlapāṇi*: "Therefore, a Brahmin does not receive the mantra"—thus Śūlapāṇi maintains that this applies to all purposes and refers specifically to the *śrāddha* alone. By this, the opinion of Śrīdatta and other Maithila scholars—that the prohibition "it should not be studied" (*nādhyetavyam*) refers to *purāṇas* other than those containing mantras—is refuted. Since it is stated "without a Brahmin," it is understood that listening [to the *purāṇa*] must be conducted through the medium of a Brahmin. The word *dharma* is neuter, as in the expression "those are the *dharmas*" (*tāni dharmāṇi*). The specific details, however, should be known from the *Nirṇayasindhu*.

Furthermore, just as in the injunction for the study of the Vedas by the twice-born (*dvija*), the recitation of mantras is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to ritual acts for the purpose of "one should produce the recollection of the meaning by means of the mantras already studied," and not the mere recollection itself—because mantras, being non-action (*akriyā*) in nature, cannot by themselves initiate a ritual act; just as in the injunction for Śūdras to "cause [them] to hear" (*śrāvayet*), where one should proceed by means of the heard injunctions and produce the recollection of the meaning by means of the heard mantras—for this reason, in the ritual acts of the Śūdra such as the great gifts (*mahādāna*) involving the balance-scale (*tulā*) and so forth, the hearing of the mantras is the auxiliary, not their recitation.

If it is argued that, since the injunction for hearing [the text] states, "One should cause the four castes to hear," even for the twice-born there would be only the hearing of the mantras during the *tulā* and other rites, and not their recitation—we reply to this as follows:

Because the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states, "It must be studied by the Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya," and because of such statements as, "The rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground [are performed through study]," study itself is a constituent part of the ritual acts.
This [text] must be studied with great effort by a learned Brāhmaṇa.
Thus it is stated in the *Manu-smṛti*. Otherwise [it is said]:

"One should recite the Vedas, the *Atharva-veda*, the *Purāṇas* along with the *Itihāsas*, according to one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), as well as the knowledge concerning the supreme self (*adhyātmikī vidyā*)."

[Otherwise, there would be the consequence of severing the injunction for the *brahmayajña* (Vedic study sacrifice), which includes] the *gāthās*, the *nārāśaṃsīs*, the *itihāsas*, the *purāṇas*, the *brāhmaṇas*, the *itihāsas*, the *purāṇas*, and the *kalpas*. As stated: "The Vedas, along with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of Dharma" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.3).
Thus it is stated in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*. Furthermore, because its purpose is for the sake of knowledge, the act of hearing is for the sake of a specific result:
"That man who would constantly hear this, and whoever would also recite it, shall encounter no inauspiciousness whatsoever, either here or in the hereafter."
Because the fruit [of the practice] is declared in such passages as those concerning the recitation of the Caṇḍī, Yājñavalkya also says:
"The wise man who causes the twice-born to hear this on every festival day obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; may you grant your approval of that."

Therefore, just as for the twice-born (*dvija*), the study of the Vedas has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*)—because it serves the purpose of ritual action (*karma*) by way of producing knowledge, and because it serves the purpose of mastering the text and grasping its syllables (for *pārāyaṇa* and so forth)—for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the status of the grasping of syllables as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is not abandoned; since it has a visible purpose by way of being for the sake of mastery (*pārāyaṇa*), yet its being for that alone is not accepted if every possible fruit is intended therein. Likewise, although both the study and the hearing of the Purāṇas and other texts are enjoined, study has a visible purpose because it serves ritual action by way of producing knowledge, whereas hearing has only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). For Śūdras, however, the opposite is the case: hearing has a visible purpose because it serves ritual action by way of producing knowledge, and it has an invisible purpose because it is for the sake of the fruit; but as for study, it simply does not exist for them.
For there is this statement: "A Śūdra may indeed listen, but must never study. Furthermore, as stated in the Vārtika and the Rāṇaka:
"In matters of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, O bull among the Bharatas..."

Thus, based on the statement in the *Bhārata*, it is said that through the words "dharma" and so forth, the knowledge of both dharma and adharma—which constitutes the fruit consisting in the components of adoption and rejection—is for a visible purpose alone; however, even that [statement] should be understood as referring exclusively to the Śūdra. For the twice-born (*dvija*), however, the mere recitation (*pāṭha*) itself serves the purpose of knowledge. Alternatively, let the hearing by the twice-born be for a visible purpose, since there is no restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) that either recitation or hearing must serve the purpose of knowledge; rather, the recitation of mantras is known to occur solely because of future declarations. Otherwise, if the injunction "he should cause [him] to hear" were intended only for the Śūdra, then—given that the Śūdra hears it with disregard according to the logic of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* regarding his lack of qualification for liberation—the mention of "liberation" (*mokṣa*) would be contradicted.

Indeed, in the first position, regarding the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa), there would be a lack of uniformity: for a Śūdra, it would be a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) because its purpose is a visible one—namely, the attainment of knowledge—whereas for the twice-born, it would be an original injunction (apūrvavidhi) because its purpose is the [attainment of] a result.

Not so. For, as stated in the Vārttika, since the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) applies to all [Vedic texts] by virtue of the connection with the word "what is to be recited" (*yac chakyate*), it is in fact an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) everywhere; its designation as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) and so forth is merely figurative. Furthermore, the entire logic of the injunction for study must be transferred to the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), which occupies its place. This has also been indicated in the Vārttika by the statement: "And thus, sentences from the *Mahābhārata* and other such works are also to be applied in this manner. Therefore, this point of mine should be clearly contemplated by the wise. Consequently, it is established that in rites such as *pūrta*, a Śūdra may recite only the Puranic mantras, while a Brāhmaṇa may recite only the Vedic ones.
Now, regarding the eligibility of a Śūdra for ritual action:

in that regard, since the Vedic injunctions concerning desires (*kāmaśruti*) refer to the twice-born who have acquired knowledge through the established rule of formal study, a Śūdra has no eligibility for Vedic rites by virtue of possessing such knowledge. Likewise, the rules for Smārta, Paurāṇic, planetary sacrifices (*grahayajña*), great gifts (*mahādāna*), works of public utility (*pūrta*), ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and so forth, apply to all four varṇas because they are intended for those desiring specific fruits and because the requisite knowledge is established through the rule of listening (*śravaṇa*). Thus, a Śūdra also has eligibility for these; however, this is not the case for Mlecchas and others, as they lack the acquisition of knowledge.

If it is argued that, in this case, a Śūdra would likewise have the entitlement for the *mahārudra-lakṣahoma* and other such rites mentioned therein, we say no. For in those cases, since Vedic mantras constitute essential auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the Śūdra lacks entitlement—just like the blind and others—due to the impossibility of performing all the required auxiliaries. Indeed, it was established in the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] that the application of the injunction for the primary rite (*pradhāna-vidhi*) occurs only when all the auxiliaries are performed. How then is there entitlement for a Śūdra in rites such as the *tulā-puruṣa*, which involve Vedic mantras and depend on the *kuśakaṇḍikā* (the ritual manual for fire-offerings) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*? [The answer follows: It is because these are not Vedic rituals, but rather Smārta rituals based on the authority of the *smṛtis*. Since they do not require the performance of all Vedic auxiliaries, the Śūdra is entitled to them. Furthermore, in the case of the *mahārudra-lakṣahoma* and similar rites, while the Vedic mantras are indeed auxiliaries, the entitlement is restricted by the specific scriptural injunction (*niyoga*) itself; thus, the Śūdra is excluded from those where the requirement for all auxiliaries is absolute. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

It is said that even though a qualification is prohibited by logic, it is restored for specific rituals by various scriptural injunctions, as in the case of the *niṣādasthapati* in the *raudreṣṭi*. Furthermore, there is no lack of qualification for a Śūdra due to a lack of knowledge of the three-fold cultivation (*tryaṃśabhāvanā*) arising from an absence of knowledge of the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*;
for [the rule states]: "Having studied the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or even one—in the proper order..."

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), under the view that one studies only a single Veda, the performance of the *hautra* (priestly duties of the Hotṛ) and *audgātra* (priestly duties of the Udgātṛ) and so forth belonging to other Vedas is possible through hearing, instruction, and the like; or, because these constitute the office of officiating priests (*ārtvijya*), they do not require the restrictive rules (*niyama*). However, the restriction applies only to the primary ritual itself. This has been stated by us at length in the *Dānakamalākara*, and it will also be explained here [in verse 29]. But where there is no auxiliary Vedic mantra, there is eligibility even in the absence of a specific injunction, because the knowledge required is established by the injunction for hearing and because the rite is performed for a desired result (*kāmya*), as in the case of the *Vināyaka-śānti* and similar rites; or where there is an option (*vikalpa*) for another mantra, as in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha* regarding the *Graha-yajña*.
"A wise man should perform the fire-oblation and other rites for a Śūdra using the Name-mantra (nāmamantra).
Regarding this, since all the constituent parts [of the rite] are included even by means of alternative mantras, it is now investigated where this [Name-mantra] exists and where it does not.
First, those [mantras] prescribed therein are set forth in the Agastyasaṃhitā:
Śūdras who are most pure in their vows, righteous, and servants of the twice-born;
women devoted to their husbands; and others born of both inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) unions.
In this regard, all people, even down to the *caṇḍālas*, are qualified for this Rāma-mantra. Likewise,
the Śruti states that Brahmā [taught] the six-syllabled [mantra], while the Smṛti speaks of that consisting of two syllables.
The six colors belong to the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, while those of two colors belong to the [remaining] three.
Therefore, the supreme *tāraka* [mantra] should be taught by the instructor to others;
in that very same [text it is said]:
"This mantra is to be imparted according to the suitability of the recipient, such as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth."
[31] In the *Brahmottarakhaṇḍa*, introducing the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva:
"This king of kings of mantras is the crest-jewel of all Vedāntas;
it is the treasury of all knowledge, and it is indeed this six-syllabled [mantra]."
This six-syllable mantra is the lamp on the path to liberation, the submarine fire for the ocean of ignorance, and the forest-fire for the great sins.
This very mantra, when devoid of the *praṇava*, is considered to be five-syllabled;
it is worn by women, Śūdras, and those of mixed caste who desire liberation.
For this [mantra], there is no initiation, no fire-oblation, no purificatory rite, and no libation;
nor is there any restriction regarding time—this mantra is to be recited by all.
This initiation is described in that very same [text] in the form of a ritual performed by another:
"Having bathed in the waters of a sacred pilgrimage site, the king, having fasted,
should sit facing east and bow before the lotus feet of Śiva."
Placing his hand upon his head, he imparted the mantra whose essence is Śiva;
thus it is stated in the *Smṛtikaumudī* according to the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the Pañcarātra is prescribed."
And it shall enter the path of the ears of the Śūdras and others as well.
Therefore, it was said further on:
"Now listen, O Mādhavī, regarding the Śūdra:
'The husband and wife are my devotees and are solely intent upon my service.'"
O Goddess, he who is established in the contemplation of salutation and constantly performs pure deeds—
even if he be a Śūdra— I shall indeed abandon thousands of sages and go to him alone.
[32] Likewise, in that very same work:
having begun with "Today I shall describe the glorious initiation for the four castes," and having explained the initiation for the twice-born, [he continues].
"And I shall also speak for the Śūdra who is my devotee, O fair-limbed lady"—by such words, the initiation of the Śūdra is declared. In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Then the Blessed One established the fourfold caste system for the worship of Hara."

Having said this, and having described the initiation of Śakti, the son of Vasiṣṭha, as well as his disciples and others, and having described the initiation of the Śūdra Ūrṇodara, it was stated: "Thus the Blessed Brahmā, having established the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) for the worship of Śiva, himself went to his own abode."
In the future as well,
one should initiate a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—
whether a man or a woman— into the solar orb.

Thus, wherever there is a specific statement, there the Śūdra has the right [to initiation]. However, in the *Smṛtikaumudī*, after citing the reading from the *Vārāha-purāṇa* stating that [the mantra] "will reach the range of the ears of Śūdras and others," the right to the mantras taught in the *Pañcarātra*—namely those of the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Saura, Śākta, and Vaināyaka traditions—is affirmed.
Thus ends the section on Mantra-initiation (mantradīkṣā).
Now, regarding the installation of a deity by a Śūdra,
the *Devīpurāṇa* in the *Kalpataru* states: "Deities should be installed according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), and not otherwise."
The Lord Brahmā, together with the Gāyatrī, should be installed by the Brāhmaṇas.
Likewise, Viṣṇu should be installed by members of the four castes who seek happiness;
Bhairava also is considered [suitable] for the four castes as well as for those of the lowest birth.
O best of gods, the Mothers should be installed and worshipped by all people;
whether a householder or an ascetic, one may dwell forever after having installed a linga.
In the *Tristhalīsetu*, the venerable grandfather (Vācaspati Miśra) states regarding the consecration of deities:
"O Lord of Men, women, those who have not received initiation, and Śūdras have no authority in the installation of Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara."
The man who bows to a linga consecrated by a Shudra, or even to Vishnu, experiences extreme sufferings in this world; what then need be said of the next?
Whether a Śūdra, one who has not been initiated, women, or even an outcaste—
by touching Keśava or Śiva, they fall into hell.

Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya*. Others say this is because of statements in the *Skanda-purāṇa* and other texts. Since the preceding statement mentions "by the four varṇas," it is more reasonable to hold that for a Śūdra there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the installation of Viṣṇu and other deities.
[34] Now, the worship of the gods by a Śūdra.
In the *Śivasarvasva* of the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Whoever— be they a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra— worships me, the Lord of the World, as the primordial deity within the *liṅga*, being solely devoted to me."
Being pleased with him, I shall grant him auspicious and unsurpassed worlds.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Gauḍanibandhatattva*:
"O beloved, that Śūdra who constantly performs his own duties..."
I accept her worship, she who is adorned with a crescent moon.
In the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "Then Rudra Mahādeva spoke concerning the mandala:
'I am sacred to the Brāhmaṇas, and especially so to the Kṣatriyas.'"
[35] Vaiśyas and Śūdras must serve and honor him;
likewise, women have the right to perform worship and other such rites—of this there is no doubt.
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and other castes—
having fully worshipped that best of gods who bears the form of Narasiṃha..."
And they are liberated from inauspicious states arising throughout ten million births.
In that very Purāṇa, it is said:
"One should be a giver of unasked-for gifts; one should resort to agriculture for the sake of a livelihood."
One should listen to the Purāṇa from Brahmins concerning the worship of Narasiṃha.
In the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, after describing worship with the five-syllabled mantra,
it says: "Whether a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller of firm vows,
one should thus worship the Lord, the husband of Ambikā, day by day."
Worship for women is prescribed by means of *namaḥ* alone;
and for detached Śūdras, worship is proclaimed to be performed in this same manner.

Although the word *namaḥ* comes first in the case of the five-syllable mantra, for women and *śūdras*, it must end with *namaḥ*. Others, however, say that the word *namaḥ* is distinct at the end [of each syllable].
O best of sages, for all other men as well, it is proclaimed that upon seeing a temple, one should perform prostration as an act of worship toward it.
Thus, for one by whom worship is performed in this manner, their life is fruitful.
As for that which Manu said:
"Recitation, austerity, visiting sacred fords, renunciation, and the accomplishment of mantras..."

"And the worship of deities [by one's own wife]—these six are the causes of downfall for women and Śūdras. This refers to something other than what is prescribed [in the scriptures], or rather, it refers to worship involving physical contact. Furthermore, this concerns the worship of ancient, worn-out *liṅgas* well-known in the Purāṇas. As for those [rules] in the *Nāradīya-purāṇa* within the *Tristhalīsetu*: "The man who bows down to a *liṅga* or Viṣṇu that has been worshipped by a Śūdra..."
No atonement for that is seen, even by means of ten thousand penances.
He who touches a Śūdra, or even Śaṅkara or Hari,
shall experience all manner of torments for as long as the moon and stars endure.
By bowing to a linga worshipped by heretics, one becomes a heretic;
by bowing to a linga worshipped by cowherds, one experiences hell.
Whoever bows down to a Linga worshipped by women, or even to Viṣṇu,
shall dwell in the Raurava hell for an entire Kalpa, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
These and other such passages refer to *liṅgas* that have been newly installed;
for when a *liṅga* has been consecrated by those learned in the mantras according to the prescribed rite,
from that time forward neither a Śūdra nor a woman should touch it.
Thus it is stated there.

[37] Others, however, have said: "Let there be fault for a Śūdra who pays homage to a *liṅga*, yet there is indeed fruit in his worship. However, in the case of the worship of a newly installed *liṅga* at places such as Śālagrāma and the like, the worship by Śūdras and others must be performed without physical contact:
'Whether he be a Śūdra, one uninitiated (*anupanīta*), a woman, or even an outcast (*patita*)..."
Or by touching Keśava or even Śiva, one experiences hell.
Even a Brāhmaṇa who desires his own welfare should not touch Hara or Viṣṇu;
yet she who worships either a Liṅga or Viṣṇu or Śiva [is to be honored].
Whether she has a protector or her protector is dead, there is no atonement for her here in this world,
O lord of men— this applies to women who have not been initiated and to Śūdras as well.
"There is no authority for Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara in touching [the image]," according to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"Four [deities] are to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas; three by those born of the Kṣatriya caste."
By Vaiśyas, only two should be honored; likewise, by those of the Śūdra caste, only one.
Thus it is stated in the *Skānda*. However, in the *Vārāha* [Purāṇa], it is said that the prohibition against touching applies specifically to the *śālagrāma*, and not to other images and such:
"O Vasundharā, a person of low caste must not touch the *śālagrāma*;
the touch of the hands of a woman or a *śūdra* is considered worse than the touch of a thunderbolt."
If a Śūdra or even a woman should ever touch [it] out of delusion,
he shall fall into a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
O Vasundharā, if there should be devotion toward it even on the part of women,
one who is well-composed should perform the worship from afar, without touching it.
"Images of all deities are to be worshipped by people of all castes;
likewise, lingas fashioned from jewels are also to be worshipped.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well.
O Lord of the Earth, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, one who is devoted to his own duty worships Viṣṇu; it is not otherwise for a Śūdra.
As for that which is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* within the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"A Brāhmaṇa should always worship either a Śālagrāma stone or likewise a stone marked with the discus; however, a Kṣatriya or others should not worship it."

Thus, this refers to worship accompanied by *sparśa* (touch). Others say it refers to those who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*). The specific details, however, should be known from my own work, the *Pūrtakamalākara*, and the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
[38] In this way, there is also eligibility for the worship of the earthen linga (*pārthivaliṅga*).
It may be made of clay, ashes, cow-dung, flour, copper, or bell-metal.
Having fashioned a linga and worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.
Thus it is stated in the *Tithitattva* based on the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*, and because there is an absence of Vedic mantras [for these acts]. That has been said in the same work, the *Skanda-purāṇa*:

"The fetching of clay, the kneading, as well as the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation (*sthāpana*), the worship (*pūjana*), and thereafter the dismissal (*visarjana*)."
Hara, Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, Pinākadhṛk,
Paśupati, Śiva, and Mahādeva— this is the sequence.

In the future: *Namaḥ* to Śarva, the earth-form; *namaḥ* to Bhava, the water-form; *namaḥ* to Rudra, the fire-form; *namaḥ* to Ugra, the wind-form; *namaḥ* to Bhīma, the ether-form; *namaḥ* to Paśupati, the sacrificer-form; *namaḥ* to Mahādeva, the moon-form; *namaḥ* to Īśāna, the sun-form.
These eight forms of Bhava are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east.
Having worshipped them in the southeast, one should conquer Śiva on the altar and in the linga.

In this regard, because of the prohibition in the *Rudrayāmala* stating, "the east is not [to be taken] as the front for Śambhu," the east is not an intermediate direction, but rather that which is universally established. This applies likewise to the worship of the Goddess during the Navarātra and similar rites. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* cited in the *Hemādri*: "Having begun with 'by those who fast during the Navarātra at Vindhyavāsinī,' it says: 'by Vaiśyas, by Śūdras endowed with devotion, by Mlecchas, and by other human beings. Likewise: "It is worshipped by various hosts of Mlecchas and by all Dasyus;
though without mantras, it is considered [suitable] even for the Kirātas, being of a *tāmasa* nature."
Thus, it is because of the statement in the *Rūpanārāyaṇīya* regarding what will happen in the future.
Likewise, a Śūdra also has the entitlement for vows, fasts, and so forth, because he possesses knowledge established through the rules of hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) and because he lacks Vedic mantras.
However, according to the Easterners, there is a prohibition against Vaiśyas and Śūdras fasting for more than two nights.
If Vaiśyas or Śūdras, out of delusion,
observe a fast for three nights or five nights, no spiritual merit (vyuṣṭi) accrues to them.
Thus they say, based on the statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* cited in the *Hemādri*.

However, the truth is that, according to the context, this prohibition concerns [fasting] during great austerities (*mahātapaḥ*). But in the case of the Navarātra, it certainly does occur; for after stating, "By means of fasting during Navarātra," it continues:
"By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other human beings."
And by women as well, O tiger among the Kurus; hear this rule regarding them.
Thus it is stated even for a Śūdra in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. Accordingly, penance should be prescribed for a Śūdra without the recitation of mantras (*japa*) or burnt offerings (*homa*).
Therefore: "Having approached a Śūdra who always stands on the path of dharma, penance should be granted, excluding *japa* and *homa*."

Thus, according to the statement of Aṅgiras in the *Mitākṣarā*: "In this context, regarding penance, giving, pilgrimage to holy places (*tīrthayātrā*), and so forth—excluding recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*)—there is no restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) of the rule concerning the Śūdra’s connection [to these acts]. For, as in the case of the 'twofold nature of the oblation' (*havir-ubhayatva*), a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would occur if a qualified object were intended; furthermore, it would result in the absence of such [penances] for the twice-born (*dvija*). Rather, the restriction that they exclude *japa* and *homa* is applied with reference to the penance connected to the Śūdra, because this is the simpler interpretation of the injunction."

[40] Regarding this, some say that the prohibition applies to *japa* and *homa* when they are the primary acts, but not when they are auxiliary (*aṅga*) elements. For this very reason, they state that in the *Mahārṇava*, for women and *śūdras*, the *vyāhṛti-homa* as an auxiliary to the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed to be performed through a Brahmin using a common fire (*laukikāgni*). That is not correct; for it is said:
"At the commencement of all *kṛcchra* penances, and especially at their conclusion..."
And one should offer oblations of clarified butter alone into the domestic fire, reciting each of the vyāhṛtis separately.
"At the conclusion of the vow, one should perform a *śrāddha* with gifts such as cows and gold;

however, for women, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is not to be performed, nor likewise the *pañcagavya* [rite]," because of this rule regarding the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) stated by Jābāli. Furthermore, it has been stated in the ninth [book] that there is no substitute for the sacred fire. Nor is there any mention of using a common worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). Therefore, since there is no distinction, both [types of fire] are prohibited; consequently, there is eligibility even for the great gifts (*mahādāna*). And so it is said in the *Mātsya-purāṇa* regarding the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha:

The *Madanaratna* and all other treatises state that there are eleven sacraments for a Śūdra and six for women, with the addition of the *namaḥ* mantra. This is also stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa* regarding great gifts (*mahādāna*).
O best of Brahmins, he who causes the sacrificial pits for women to be made in other shapes [is at fault].
Also in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"For Vaiśyas, the pit has the appearance of a half-moon, and for Śūdras, it is triangular."

Thus, because it is stated that the *kuṇḍa* belongs to Śūdras, and because women and Śūdras share the same religious duties (*sadharmatva*), for this very reason it is said in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, under the section on Hiraṇyagarbha: "Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever performs this great merit which originates from the Self of all Brahman— listen to the fruit of that as well."

Thus it has been stated. Also in the *Āgneya-purāṇa*, regarding the gift of the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*): "O King, [this rite] must be performed with great effort by Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Śūdras.
Likewise, in the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa*, regarding the gift of the plow and the furrow: [the same applies].
O protector of the earth, O best of kings, this gift should be given with great effort and devotion by either a woman or a man.
Regarding the gift of the seven islands within the Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa:
"Having thus performed this gift called the 'Seven Islands,' whether a woman or a man, one shall attain the world of Brahmā."
On the Mountain of Grain as well;
having ascended a divine celestial chariot, whether it be a woman or even a man—
there, on the Mountain of Cotton as well.
Having uttered this, a man or a woman should offer [the gift] according to the prescribed ritual,
even at a mountain of sesame seeds.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of merit, he becomes a righteous king.
Or his wife shall be a woman, fortunate and endowed with beauty.
Likewise, this gift was indeed given in former times by Māndhātṛ, by Kārtavīrya when he was young, and also by their wives.

Nor does eligibility [for knowledge] arise merely from such a statement, because it is a restatement (anuvāda) intended for the sake of a result. Although the general terms *narendra* (king) and *viprendra* (chief of Brahmins) refer to those who possess knowledge and thus appropriately denote the twice-born (*dvija*), nevertheless, there are instances where the four castes are mentioned, as well as references to the Śūdra and the woman. Since women and Śūdras share common duties, and since the Śūdra possesses the knowledge established by the injunction to listen (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) and has a desire [for liberation], the Śūdra also has eligibility. As it has been said: "The Śūdra may be eligible for the *pūrta* dharma, but not for the Vedic (*vaidika*) dharma.
This is also stated in the *Mokṣadharma*.
"They do not incur fault when performing rites for prosperity, provided they omit the mantras.
[43] Regarding the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), however, there is an option for women:
"For the purification of women and Śūdras, one should prescribe the *prājāpatya* penance."
One should prepare the five products of the cow; by bathing and drinking it, one becomes pure.

Thus it is stated by Parāśara. However, there is no prohibition regarding a Śūdra. As for that which Atri said: "If a Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and a Brāhmaṇa should drink liquor, both of them, having committed equal deeds, shall dwell in the Pumākha hell."

Thus, that [act] should be understood as requiring no expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The specific details regarding expiation should be sought in the *Prāyaścittaratna*. Likewise, even in the case of *pūrta* (acts of public utility), such as the consecration of reservoirs, the installation of temples, and great gifts (*mahādāna*), the Śūdra possesses the right to perform them. For it is stated by Vyāsa and Jātūkarṇya: "The Śūdra may be entitled to the *dharma* of *pūrta*, but not to the Vedic [dharma]. Regarding *pūrta*, Jātūkarṇya speaks in the *Hemādri* and the *Madanaratna*: [text follows].
The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as temples for the deities,
the gift of food, and gardens— this is designated as *pūrta*.
In that very regard, Nārada says:
"That gift which is given during an eclipse of a planet, at the sun's transits,
and outside the sacrificial altar— that is declared to be *pautika* (meritorious)."
By the ripening of that karma, one gains the qualification for giving and other such acts. Manu says:
"One should constantly practice the duty of giving, both *iṣṭika* (sacrificial) and *paurtika* (charitable).
Giving that is an auxiliary to the rites of the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires is indeed called *iṣṭa*; however, [giving] performed for the sake of the ancestors is *paurtika*."
Vyāsa also said: "O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding the four castes and the four stages of life within the system of the fourfold society,
I shall proclaim the duty of giving as it was spoken by Vyāsa."

The specific details, however, are to be understood from my own work, the *Dānakamalākara*. [44] In this regard, where eligibility for a Śūdra in acts such as giving or the consecration of a reservoir for great gifts (*mahādāna*)—which involve Vedic mantras—is stated on the basis of scriptural injunction (just as in the case of the chariot-maker), there are two possible courses. One position is that the act should be performed by Brāhmaṇas without Vedic mantras; for it is stated in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata* by Vyāsa: "Those performing rites for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*) do not incur fault when acting without mantras. Manu also says: "But those who desire merit, who know the Dharma, and who follow the path of the virtuous..."
Except for the recitation of mantras, they do not incur fault and even receive praise.

As for what Medhātithi stated—that those Śūdras who perform vows, fasts, and so forth that are devoid of mantras do not incur fault, but it is not the case that they do not incur fault when performing even those with mantras by omitting the mantras—[his argument being] that since the injunctions involving mantras do not apply to Śūdras, performing them while omitting the mantras would constitute a performance according to the word [of the injunction]; that is not correct. For, as in the case of the *sthapati-iṣṭi*, the exclusion of mantras is not enjoined through a direct prescription (*aṅgagrāhikayā*). Otherwise, since there would be no entitlement to vow-fasts and the like that are devoid of mantras, the injunction would be rendered futile. Therefore, this [exclusion of mantras] is solely for the purpose of the practical application (*saṃvidhāna*).

[46] Others, however, say that the *vipras* should perform the *homa* and other rites using only Vedic mantras, because of the statement by Parāśara to be cited below; and this is likewise held in the *Mādhavīya*. Regarding the Puranic mantras used by the officiating priest (*ācārya*), there is only recitation (*pāṭha*). Regarding those used by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), there is only recitation—so say the *Kalpataru*, the *Smārta-Gauḍas*, and others. But it is more reasonable that they should merely listen, due to the injunction for listening (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) and the aforementioned reasoning, since knowledge produced by listening alone is the required auxiliary (*aṅga*). In the case of the Vedic mantras used by the sacrificer, there is only a salutation (*namaskāra*), because of Gautama’s statement: "Salutation is permitted as his mantra. The Gauḍas and Maithilas hold this view. Thus, in the gift of a cow with two faces (*ubhayatomukhī*), the *homa* is performed with the mantra containing "namas," because of the Vedic text: "Sacrifice, indeed, is *namas*. By the use of the genitive case in the word "of him" (*asya*), the sacrificer is connected to it, just as in the case of the *yājyā*; therefore, the Puranic mantra belongs to the *vipra*. As for the *śūdra* who is without mantras, a *vipra* takes the place of the mantra, according to the previously cited statement of Varāha: "The *vipra* is taken as the mantra for the *śūdra*. As for what Rudradhara stated in the *Śuddhiviveka*—that because the *homa* accompanied by mantras is an auxiliary to the adoption of a son, and because women and *śūdras* lack the authority to recite mantras such as the *vyāhṛtis*, an adopted son cannot belong to them at all—that is their position.

That is not so, because it is stated that even a woman may perform an adoption with the permission of her husband. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “A woman shall neither give away nor adopt a son without the permission of her husband. This applies while he is alive; after his death, however, there is no need for permission due to her independence. Although Medhātithi has stated that, like the status of being a wife, the status of being an adopted son (*dattaka*) is of an invisible nature (*adṛṣṭa-rūpa*) and must be accomplished through a *homa* sacrifice, Harinātha and others maintain that since a woman cannot perform a *homa*, she should have the *homa* and other rites performed through a Brahmin, just as she does for vows and the like. The same is stated in the *Gauḍanibandhatattva*. Likewise, this applies to a Śūdra in the case of rites for pacifying extraordinary diseases, the ripening of karma, the balance-scale ordeal (*tulā*), and so forth, according to the Smṛti rule: “Women and Śūdras share the same religious duties (*sadharma*). For this very reason, Parāśara states that a *homa* performed by a Śūdra must be carried out through a Brahmin alone.
"But that Brahmin who offers oblations for the sake of a Śūdra’s sacrificial fee—the Brahmin shall become a Śūdra, and the Śūdra shall become a Brahmin. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, Mādhavācārya explains: "If a Brāhmaṇa, having accepted a fee from a Śūdra, offers his oblation with Vedic mantras for the sake of achieving peace, prosperity, and so forth, the fault belongs solely to the Brāhmaṇa; however, the Śūdra shall certainly obtain the fruit of the *homa*. This has been stated by us in detail in the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Consequently, in all cases of a Śūdra performing a *homa* with Vedic mantras, there are two options: either through a Brāhmaṇa with mantras, or without mantras, using only the name [of the deity]. [48] Now, the sacraments (*saṃskāras*) of the Śūdra.
Yama says: Even a Śūdra of such a kind should be consecrated with the rites, though without mantras;
Prajāpati did not create him with any Vedic verse.
"By means of *chandas* (Vedic meters) and *mantra* (sacred formulas). Vyāsa also says:

"Impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakriyā*), the first outing (*niṣkrama*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*vapanakriyā*)."
The piercing of the ears, the instruction in vows, the rite for commencing the Vedas,
the tonsure ceremony, the ritual bath, marriage, and the formal adoption of the nuptial fire;
"The maintenance of the three sacred fires and the sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are prescribed.
Having said this, he continued:
"These nine rites, ending with the piercing of the ears, are performed for women without the recitation of mantras."
Her marriage is performed with mantras; for a Śūdra, it is performed without mantras, up to ten [wives].
As for that which was stated by Madanapāla in the *Smṛtikaumudī*:

"For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), parting the hair (*sīmanta*), birth (*jātakarman*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), tonsure (*cūḍā*), initiation (*upanayana*), observance of vows (*vratacaryā*), study (*adhyayana*), graduation (*samāvartana*), marriage (*vivāha*), sacrifice (*yajña*), and giving (*dāna*) are common. This is because the *Sumantu-saṃhitā* specifies these only for the twice-born (*dvija*). Furthermore, from the *Brāhma-purāṇa*, it is said: "May even a Śūdra receive the sacrament of the marriage-mantra. Thus, there is no *jātakarman* and so forth for a Śūdra; likewise, there is an absence of the *caula*, for the *cūḍākarma* belongs to all the twice-born according to the Dharma.

Thus it is stated in the *Manu-smṛti*. This [interpretation] is to be reconsidered, because the statement of Somaṃtu is intended to establish parity with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and other rites; otherwise, it would follow that he lacks the entitlement even for giving gifts. Furthermore, since the word "according to dharma" is used in the *Mānava* [text], and since the *Manu-smṛti* prohibits *homa* and other such acts for a Śūdra, Manu says:
"By means of rites pertaining to the seed and the womb, by *homa*s, and by the tying of the crest-lock and the girdle..."
"The sin pertaining to seed and the sin pertaining to the womb are wiped away for the twice-born.
For this very reason, in the *Madanaratna* regarding the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha, it says:
"The *garbhādhāna*, the *puṃsavana*, and likewise the *sīmantonnayana*..."
Then those foremost of the twice-born should perform [the rites] for Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having said this, [the text continues]:
"One should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the other sixteen rites.
Thus it is stated here in the Mātsya Purāṇa.

For women, there are six sacraments (*saṃskāra*): birth-rite (*jātakarman*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), going out of the house (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), tonsure (*cūḍā*), and marriage (*vivāha*). For Śūdras, however, these six plus the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) make eleven;

so it has been stated. This is likewise the view in the commentaries of Rūpanārāyaṇa and Harihara. Jayapāla states that for Śūdras there are nine sacraments, beginning with conception (*garbhādāna*) and ending with marriage, excluding the initiation ceremony (*upavīta*). Śārṅgadhara, however, says: "The twice-born shall have sixteen, while Śūdras shall indeed have twelve."
There are exactly five types of mixed castes, according to the laws of their families.
"The Vedic vow, the initiation (*upanayana*), the *mahānāmnī*, and the *mahāvrata*—

these twelve sacraments for Śūdras are performed with names as mantras," so he said. [49] But Aparārka, however, says regarding the passage "The conception of a male occurs during the fertile period":

And this [rule] refers to all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), not merely to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). For if that were the case, it would have been necessary to state [the rule] after prescribing the initiation (*upanayana*). Therefore, according to his view, there are eight [sacraments]: *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *niṣkramaṇa*, *annaprāśana*, and what is called *caula*. However, in the *Kalpataru* based on the *Brahmapurāṇa*, it is stated:
"Even a Śūdra should always receive the sacrament of marriage alone."

Thus it has been stated. In this regard, the truth is that the determination [of the rules] is based either on the distinction of place or on the fact that the scope of "existent" and "non-existent" Śūdras differs.
As for Manu’s statement:
"A Śūdra incurs no sin whatsoever, nor is he entitled to any sacramental rite."
To that end, Medhātithi says:

"The sin incurred by one who transgresses general prohibitions such as theft and falsehood is not the same as that for the twice-born; furthermore, he does not deserve the sacrament consisting of initiation (*upanayana*). And those [rites] should be performed silently, according to the previously cited statement of Yama and others; such is the direction.

[51] Furthermore, for a Śūdra, there is no option for the five-crested (*pañcacūḍa*) arrangement at the time of the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), because that [arrangement] serves as a mark of one’s lineage (*gotra*), and such a mark is absent among Śūdras. Even though the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* scripture states, "Therefore they say: all creatures are descended from Kaśyapa," and Hemādri quotes Vyāghrapāda as saying that in the event of the loss of one's lineage, "Kaśyapa" [is used], and thus the Kaśyapa lineage does exist [for them]; for this very reason, it is said:
"O Hero, one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth according to the name and likewise according to the lineage."

Thus, this statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* regarding the *śrāddha* for Śūdras appears in Hemādri. Nevertheless, that [rule] applies only to the *śrāddha* ceremony; there is no authority for its application to the acquisition of a *pravara*, because [the Śūdra] lacks descent from a *ṛṣi*. For this very reason, Manu stated, "of the twice-born according to dharma. Medhātithi maintains that the shaving of the head for a Śūdra, which follows by implication, is not prohibited. Regarding the tonsure (*caula*), for Śūdras there is an option between total shaving or wearing a topknot (*śikhā*), because Vasiṣṭha declared, "for a Śūdra, hairstyles are unrestricted. For this same reason, Hārīta says:

"But a woman or a Śūdra, having cut off their top-knot out of anger or even out of detachment, should perform a *prājāpatya* penance; otherwise, there shall be no expiation. This states the penance for a Śūdra. For this very reason, the top-knot of widowed Gauḍa women is seen [to be worn]. As for that which is stated in the *Pādma*:
"One should not wear a topknot nor a sacred thread, nor should one utter refined (Sanskrit) speech;

one should not eat from the middle leaf of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, O beautiful lady. This refers to the position that accepts the shaving of the head; such is the general direction. For specific details, however, one should consult my *Nirṇayasindhu*.
[53] Likewise, for Śūdras there are the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña): devoted to his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and intent on the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha),
he should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation (namaskāra).
Thus it is stated by Yājñavalkya; and this is clear in the Mitākṣarā. In the Rājadharmas of the Mahābhārata:
"Therefore, a Śūdra, observing vows himself, should perform sacrifices with *pākayajñas*;
