gold is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for these *pākayajñas*."

And these [rites] should be performed according to the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, because Dakṣa states in the Gauḍa-nibandha: “The Śūdras are followers of the Vājasaneyins. This has also been stated thus in the section on marriage in the Hari-hara-bhāṣya. The rest will become clear in the practical application; this is the summary.
Thus ends the section on the sacraments for Śūdras in the *Śūdra-dharma* composed by Kamalākara, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of the venerable Jagadguru Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa Sūri.
Now follows the determination regarding the *śrāddha* for a *śūdra*.

In this regard, because it was previously stated that [the *śūdra*] is "devoted to the performance of *śrāddha*," his entitlement is established for the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites. The same applies to women:
likewise for their own three ancestors, beginning with their husband.
A widow, being diligent, should perform the śrāddha ceremony at the appropriate times.
Thus, according to the statement of Vṛddhamanu in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*: "That śrāddha for women and Śūdras is performed silently, without mantras;
the śrāddha for women and for the son of a Śūdra is without mantras. Furthermore, before the instruction of the vows (*vratādeśa*), the twice-born [sons] should perform it in that very same manner."
Thus, according to the statement of Marīci in the Hemādri:
"This very same procedure is prescribed for Śūdras, with the exception of mantras;
however, for a Śūdra who is without mantras, a Brāhmaṇa is employed to recite the mantra."

And thus it is stated by Bṛhaspati. Although this occurs within the section on *śrāddha*, because it is a general rule (*paribhāṣā*), in all cases such as bathing and giving gifts for a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa must perform the recitation of the mantras; moreover, that [recitation] must be from the Purāṇas alone. Śūlapāṇi says the same applies to women. Regarding the phrase "previously the twice-born," [this refers to those] who have not yet undergone the tonsure ceremony (*acūḍāḥ*) up to the age of three years. Even one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*) may perform the rites pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛmedhika*) with mantras, provided he has had his tonsure performed or has reached the age of three.

Thus says Sumantu. In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "Uninitiated persons, women, and Śūdras should have the Śrāddha performed by a priest, or they may perform it themselves without Vedic mantras. As for the wives of the twice-born, however, having made the mere formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) themselves, they should have everything else performed through a Brāhmaṇa using Vedic mantras"—so says the *Prayogapārijāta*. For this very reason, Hemādri states that the phrase "of women" refers specifically to married women. An uninitiated person, however, should perform everything himself, including the parts involving Vedic mantras. The specific details are to be known from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. As for the Śūdra, there is always only the *āma-śrāddha* (the Śrāddha with uncooked food).

"And for Śūdras, the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with uncooked food) is always prescribed," according to the statement of Sumantu. Also, in the *Mātsyapurāṇa* cited in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*: "In this same way, a Śūdra may also always perform the ordinary *śrāddha* and the *vṛddhiśrāddha*."
One should always perform [the offering] with the mantra "namaskāra," as if it were raw grain.
On that very point, Vṛddhaparāśara says:
"The worship of the twice-born for a Śūdra should be performed silently with uncooked food (āmanna). Having performed the āmaśrāddha, he should then feed his kinsmen."
It is that very same [rule]:

"The raw food of a Śūdra is called 'cooked' [impurity], and cooked food is called 'remnant' (ucchiṣṭa). On this basis, some maintain that there should be no fire-oblation (homa) in the house of a Śūdra. This is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa within the Hemādri.
But if Śūdras, desiring dharma and knowing dharma, perform [the rites],
the mantra for the *agnaukaraṇa* is prescribed as a mere salutation (*namaskāra*).
"Salutation to Agni Kavyavāhana; salutation to Soma accompanied by the ancestors"—this is the mantra.
Listen to how the invocation and other rites should be performed by a Śūdra:
for the gods, by their divine names, but for the ancestors, by their personal names and *gotras*.
O hero, one should offer the *piṇḍa* and other oblations according to name and *gotra*.

Regarding Śūdras, Hemādri states that their *gotra* is Kāśyapa; this should be understood to apply likewise to the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. Those who claim that because Śūdras lack descent from a *ṛṣi*, they have no *gotra* at all, are indeed fools. On that very point, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* says: "A Śūdra, moreover, should offer those *piṇḍas* with food cooked in his own household."
Its root, fruit, or flour-meal (saktu) is traditionally known as its food, or it may be milk-rice (pāyasa).

Therefore, the statement “cooked food is called *ucchiṣṭa*” refers either to that which is distinct from what has been prescribed, or it refers to the *śrāddha* rite. The Gauda Smārtas hold that it refers specifically to the *vaiśvadeva* performed by a Śūdra; otherwise, since cooked food would be prohibited everywhere, raw food (*āma*) would already be established for the *śrāddha* as well, making the injunction for a Śūdra to use raw food redundant. Consequently, when raw food is the general rule for the *śrāddha*, this [injunction] serves as an exception (*pratiprasava*) for items such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the case of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). Vijñāneśvara, Madanapāla, and others maintain that the mantra “To the deities and to the ancestors” is the mantra for the salutation (*namaskāra*). Hemādri, however, citing the *Matsya Purāṇa*—“A wise Śūdra should also perform [the rite] according to this procedure without mantras”—states that because of the prohibition of mantras, one should use the name-mantra (*nāmamantra*). Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*:
For one appointed to royal service, for one engaged in the restraint of prisoners,
and during all types of calamities, a Brahmin should cause the Śrāddha to be performed.

Thus, that [rule] applies equally even to a Śūdra; however, at a *śrāddha*, a Brāhmaṇa is not a substitute for a Śūdra. For a Brāhmaṇa should not perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for one of a lower caste, nor should a Śūdra perform them for a Brāhmaṇa, except in the case of a *pāraśava*.
Thus it is stated in that very same work by Pāraskara. A *pāraśava* is the son of a married *śūdra* woman. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "A *śūdra* may also give gifts or perform *pākayajña* sacrifices;
indeed, a *śūdra* should perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*) and so forth by means of those."
Because of that cooking, the Smārta-Gaudas say: "This is other than the Kali age. However, in the *Rājadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*, it says:
"The Yavanas, Irātas, Gāndhāras, Cīnas, Śabaras, Barbaras, Śakas, Tuṣāras, Kaṅkas, Palhavas, and Cāndra-Madrakas..."
Having said this:
"And how shall the men born of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes, as well as the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, all the inhabitants of the realm, practice their duties?"
And having said this:
"The performance of Vedic duties is indeed ordained as their dharma,
as well as ancestral sacrifices, wells, water-stations, and beds."
And one should always bestow gifts upon the twice-born at the appropriate times.
Likewise: A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given for all sacrifices by one who desires prosperity;
and even those of low birth must perform the Pākayajñas, which are worthy of great honor.
The ritual for *śrāddha* among the Mlecchas and others is also intended primarily for the giving of food and materials to those of their own kind. Viṣṇu and Uśanas state:
"A wise man should never feed cooked food even to a good Śūdra;
by feeding him, he would incur sin and would not obtain the fruit [of the rite]."
In that regard as well, there is a rule concerning cooking for the twice-born, as stated by Laghu-Hārīta:
"The Ekoddiṣṭa rite must always be performed by oneself using cooked food. Or as Gālava says in the Smṛtidarpaṇa:
On the anniversary of death, during the sapindikarana rite, at Gaya-shraddha, or during Mahalaya,
one should never perform a shraddha with raw food (ama), even if one is in distress.
Laukāxi says: "One should perform the annual rite with food alone, or with gold, but never with [the gift of] a cow.
Even in that case, for a Śūdra, it must be raw [food].

"And for Śūdras, the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with uncooked food) is prescribed at all times," according to the statement of Sumantu. Halāyudha maintains that for a Śūdra, the ten *piṇḍas* and so forth are performed with uncooked food alone;

however, that is not correct, because previous statements also prescribe milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other such items. Furthermore, this *āmaśrāddha* performed by a Śūdra takes place only in the afternoon, and not in the forenoon as is the case for the twice-born (*dvija*).
That period which is declared as Kutupa after midday—
only there is an offering of raw food (āmaśrāddha) given to the ancestors inexhaustible.

Thus it is stated in the *Aparārka* and the *Hemādri* based on the words of Sumantu. On the birth of a son, there is indeed a *hiraṇya-śrāddha* (an offering with gold). Regarding this, Saṃvarta says in the *Hemādri*:
"On the birth of a son, a wise man should perform the *śrāddha* with gold alone;
neither with cooked food nor with raw food, desiring the non-deprivation of anyone."
The specific details regarding the *āmāśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) and others should be understood from my *Nirṇayasindhu*. Vyāsa states in the *Kriyānibandha*:
"Gold obtained from a Kṣatriya for the purpose of an *āmāśrāddha*..."

It may be employed as one desires; one may eat it oneself, or give it to Brāhmaṇas. Regarding what is obtained from a Vaiśya or others, there is the freedom to employ it as desired. However, even with that, one must not perform the *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, and so forth. Devayājñika maintains that this is because it is impossible to relinquish what has already been offered to the gods for the sake of other deities or men. As for what is obtained from a Śūdra, it has already been stated. Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Whatever raw food (*āma*) belonging to a *śrāddha* is accepted from a Śūdra..."
All of that is sufficient for eating, but not for the obligatory and occasional rites.
In the Gauḍaśuddhitattva, Aṅgiras states:
"If a Brahmin has turned away from a Śūdra's house, he must not consume milk or curd;
that too is recorded as 'Śūdra-food' (śūdrānna)."
Food from a Śūdra that has entered the houses of Brahmins is always pure; so says Parāśara:
"The food of a Śūdra remains [impure] only as long as a twice-born man does not touch it."
Everything touched by the hand of a twice-born man is not inconsistent with that [purity].
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Having sprinkled it with water, one may accept the food of a Śūdra that has come to one's house. Thus says Aṅgiras.

Milk that has come to one’s own house should be accepted when it has been poured into another vessel. Likewise, for those who have not undergone initiation—such as women and Śūdras—the *uttarīya* (upper garment) should be understood as being worn over both the left (*savya*) and right (*apasavya*) shoulders. In the absence of a cloth for an upper garment, that *uttarīya* should be circular, measuring two, three, or four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). It should be known, as stated by Jātūkarṇya, to be ninety-six finger-breadths in length. In its absence, even a mere upper covering (*uparivāsa*) will suffice. Having arranged the cloth in the *apasavya* manner in due order, some kinsman of the same lineage (*sagotraja*) [should perform the rite].

Thus says the Lord of Mithila, citing the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]. In the *Smṛtikaumudī*, Baudhāyana, beginning with the words "Of Śūdras," states: "The sacred thread (*upavīta*) is formed by the arrangement of the cloth. Śaṅkha states:
"The purifier (*pavitraka*) for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four blades of *darbha* grass; for each successive caste, one blade is prescribed to be fewer in order."

Regarding the mandala, it should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu* that for a Śūdra, sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) is prescribed, and so forth. The procedure for the *tilaka* of a Śūdra is stated in the *Parāśara Purāṇa*:

"One devoted to the Vedas should not wear the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the triple horizontal mark (*tripuṇḍra*), the circular, the square, the half-moon, or any such sectarian signs (*liṅga*)."
By the statement "one who is devoted to the Vedas," the permission for Śūdras is granted. In the *Brāhma* section of the *Madanapārijāta*:
"A twice-born man should make the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*); a Kṣatriya, however, a triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*);
a Vaiśya, a half-moon; and among the Śūdra castes, a circular mark."
Viṣṇu and Āśvalāyana state:
"The marking of the body with the conch, discus, and so forth, as well as singing, dancing, and the like—
this is the duty of the single-born (Śūdra) and should never belong to the twice-born."
However, in works such as the *Puruṣārthaprabodha* and the *Śivasarvasva*, the wearing of sacred ash (*vibhūti*) by women and Śūdras is also mentioned.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the Śrāddha for Śūdras, composed by Kamalākara, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa.
[61] Now, the minor Parāśara [Smṛti] concerning the prescribed and prohibited duties of Śūdras.

By selling liquor, meat, and the like; by eating what is forbidden to eat; or by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment.
By drinking the milk of a brown cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Vedas, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
As for that very point:
salt, honey, liquor, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not cause defilement for those of the Śūdra caste; he may sell them among all [castes].

Thus, the *Smṛtikaumudī* states that this should be understood as applying to times of distress (*āpad*). This is said with reference to unworthy Śūdras (*asac-chūdra*). Likewise, there is no fault even in the consumption of liquor and meat by unworthy Śūdras, provided it is not prohibited meat. Therefore, there is no fault in association with a Śūdra who drinks liquor. For that [penalty] applies to association with an outcast (*patita*), and this [Śūdra] is not such. However, for the twice-born (*dvija*), such association results in loss of caste (*pātitya*) due to the prohibition; whereas for the Śūdra, association with them is indeed a fault, but avoiding them leads to spiritual progress (*abhyudaya*). As Manu says: "There is no fault in eating meat, nor in [drinking] liquor, nor in sexual intercourse."

"This is the way of beings in worldly engagement, but withdrawal bears great fruit. Thus it is said; therefore, this [selling] must indeed be avoided by virtuous Śūdras. As for that which is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"A Śūdra who engages in the sale of all goods incurs no fault."
“Having consumed honey, leather, liquor, lac, and fifthly, meat.
Regarding this, the *Kalpataru* states: “This is a prohibition against honey and the other items except in times of distress. This is also stated in the *Parāśara Purāṇa*:
“Oil-cake, fermented liquor, oil, and likewise cow’s products such as buttermilk and the like...”
It must be accepted only from a Śūdra, and never from the twice-born.

In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* of the *Skānda-purāṇa*: "A Śūdra should not pull up *darbha* grass, nor should he drink the milk of a tawny cow (*kāpila*). O beautiful lady, he should not eat from the middle leaf of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree."
He should not recite the Praṇava mantra, nor should he eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). He should neither wear a topknot nor a sacred thread, nor should he utter refined speech.
One should not recite the words of the Vedas, nor should one perform the three daily ablutions;
by means of the mantra of salutation alone, the accomplishment of all rites will surely come to pass.
One who practices what is forbidden sinks into hell along with his ancestors.
[63] Other forbidden acts as well are described in the *Mātsya Purāṇa* among the characteristics of the Kali age:
"From that time forth, this entire world will suffer greatly."
Having begun thus:
"Brahmins born from the womb of Śūdras, and Śūdras born from the womb of mantras—
desiring wealth, they shall wait upon those Brahmins."
Also in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"In that Kali age, there occurs for Śūdras a connection with Brāhmaṇas through the source of mantras, as well as through sharing beds, seats, and meals."
Kings, for the most part consisting of Śūdras, oppress the Brāhmaṇas;
and Śūdras adopt the conduct of Brāhmaṇas, while Brāhmaṇas adopt the conduct of Śūdras.
There will be kings who are not Kṣatriyas, Brahmins who live off Śūdras,
and all those who salute Śūdras being saluted by Brahmins.
Seeing the twice-born seated, those of small intellect do not move;
indeed, Śūdras of very limited understanding strike the best of the twice-born.
O twice-born ones, placing their hand upon the mouth and ear of a Śūdra or a low-born person,
they then speak words with humility.
Likewise, Śūdras who are experts in the meaning of the Dharma study the Vedas;
and kings born of Śūdra lineage perform the horse sacrifice.
Therefore, having reached the Kali age, lifespan, strength, and beauty decline;
yet at that time, human beings attain accomplishment in a short period of time.
"Blessed are those who will practice the Dharma when the end of the age has arrived," having said, "In the Tretā age, the Dharma lasts for a year."
In the Kali age, that is attained in a single day.
Thus it has been said.
[64] These same verses also appear in the *Kūrma-purāṇa* with variant readings. In the *Kūrma*:
"Those with white teeth, with conquered faces, shaven-headed, and clad in saffron robes..."
When the end of the age has arrived, Śūdras will desire dharma.
O scorcher of enemies, Śūdras who live off the king beat the best of the twice-born,
and they place Śūdras on high seats in the midst of the twice-born.
O twice-born ones, those endowed with little learning, meager fortune, and weak power worship Śūdras with flowers, ornaments, and other such decorations.
O King, even when the best of the twice-born were worshipping, the Śūdras did not look upon them;
and the twice-born stood at the door, waiting for an opportunity to serve.
In the Kali age, having surrounded themselves with Śūdras and those who live off Śūdras while standing upon their vehicles, they serve Brāhmaṇas and praise them with hymns of praise.
Those who subsist on Śūdras indeed teach the Vedas to Śūdras;
they recite Vedic mantras while having resorted to terrible atheism.

In this regard, it is prohibited by the statement, "Therefore, one should not act in such a manner. This is stated in the *Skānda* and *Kaurma* Purāṇas concerning the characteristics of the Kali age: "Where Umā is the speaker and there is a dialogue with Nārada, therein [are found] the Buddhist, Jaina, Śākta, Śaiva, and Vaiṣṇava [teachings]."
O Brahmin, the doctrine of the knowledge of Yoga is erroneous and contradicts the Vedic scriptures;
in the Kali age, O Brahmin, the twice-born will conduct themselves according to that doctrine.
Women [should perform] service to their husbands, Śūdras to Brāhmaṇas,
and sons to their parents, setting aside the practice of recitation, fire-offerings, and other such means.
Those who perform rites for specific desires for the sake of visible results fall downward;
however, that worship of the deity which is performed with worldly names and songs [is different].
This dharma belongs to the Śūdras and others, never to the twice-born;
for Śūdras, in the Kali age, [worship] before the deity with composed songs.
Brahmins and others perform dances for the sake of those who disregard the Vedas, as prescribed by the scriptures;
widows sing songs that bring sin even upon their listeners.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Those who, abandoning their own duties, dwell crying 'Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa,' are sinners who merely seek the appearance of Hari; for the birth of Hari is for the sake of dharma."
In that very same place:
"By the mere service of the twice-born, this Śūdra becomes entitled to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he attains his own worlds, and for that reason, he is more blessed than [the other castes]."
Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
indeed, a man of the Śūdra caste may perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors and so forth.

The *pākayajñas* are the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); for the word *pāka* has the sense of "excellence," as in the expression "with a *pāka* [refined] mind" (*taṃ pākena manasā*), or else it has the sense of "smallness," as in the phrase "one who is more *pāka* than we" (*yo 'smatpākataraḥ*). Bṛhaspati states in the *Madanapārijāta*: "Purity, service to Brahmins, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—these are the duties of a Śūdra; likewise, the use of the mantra 'namas' (reverence) is prescribed for him."
In the Anuśāsana Parva of the Mahābhārata,
having seen that the Śūdra was overwhelmed by qualities of darkness (tamas),
the Grandfather (Brahmā) prescribed service to the twice-born as the duty of Śūdras.
The qualities of darkness (tāmasa) perish for the Śūdra through devotion to the twice-born;
by serving the twice-born, the Śūdra attains the highest good.
Non-violent, of virtuous conduct, and a worshiper of the deities and the twice-born.
A Śūdra is joined with the desired fruits of dharma through his own specific duty alone. Likewise:
"The two mantras consisting of the utterance of 'svāhā' and the salutation 'namas' are prescribed for the Śūdra."
A Śūdra who possesses the Veda should himself perform sacrifices with cooked offerings (pākayajña) by means of those two.
The Vedic mantra is for him.
A Śūdra should never, under any circumstances, engage in the accumulation of wealth;
for having acquired riches, he might become more wicked and even oppress those who are superior.
Or, with the king’s permission, he may act according to his desire in accordance with the Dharma.
Āpastamba says: Service to the other castes is the duty of the Śūdra; among them, as each preceding one is mentioned, the spiritual benefit (niḥśreyasa) is greater.

Baudhāyana states: "For Śūdras under the supervision of Āryas, there is shaving every month; the rule for sipping water (ācamana) is purposeful, as is the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta), provided by the arrangement of a garment.
Here, "Ārya" refers to a Vaiśya; for Pāṇini says, "The word *arya* denotes both a master and a Vaiśya. Manu also [says the same].
For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving should be performed monthly;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born.

Purification, ritual sipping (ācamana), and the rules regarding birth and death impurity (sūta-sūtaka) are to be observed by him as for a Vaiśya; however, the meaning is that he is not subject to the threefold sipping of water nor the fifteen-night period of impurity regarding the remains of food left in a vessel. As for what Yājñavalkya says:

"A woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that has merely touched the extremities [of their mouths]"—Madanapāla maintains that this refers specifically to an *asat-śūdra* (a Śūdra who is not a true follower of the Vedic path). "Extremities" means reaching the palate; for women and Śūdras, there is no wiping of the lips or touching of the nostrils and so forth.
One should sip water three times, wipe the mouth twice, and touch the cavities of the head with water.

Some say that because Yājñavalkya stated this in reference specifically to the threefold consumption [of the water], it applies only to those three. Others, however, maintain that because it is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), it applies to women and Śūdras as well; for this very reason, they say that in the passage "And the woman and the Śūdra," only a specific rule regarding the Śūdra was mentioned. Gautama states: "The Śūdra is the fourth caste, having but one birth. His duties are truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity; some say that for him there is merely the washing of the feet instead of the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). He may perform the *śrāddha* rite, support his dependents, and live with his own wife. The mantra permitted for him is 'namas' (reverence). Some say he may himself sacrifice with *pākayajñas*. Thus.

Regarding the statement, "One should perform the *pākayajñas*, such as the *aṣṭakā* rites, oneself and not through officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and so forth," Lakṣmīdhara explains in his commentary that the word "oneself" is intended to exclude the wife and others. This is because it has been stated elsewhere that for rites such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), one may act even through a Brahmin, due to the mention of the singular form. Jayapāla states that one who is capable should perform them himself, while one who is incapable may do so through a Brahmin; likewise, a virtuous Śūdra may perform them himself, whereas an unvirtuous Śūdra must do so through a Brahmin. In the *Bhārata* cited by Hemādri:
"The performance of *śrāddha*, justice, truthfulness, and freedom from anger..."
Contentment with one's own wife, purity, and constant freedom from malice.

"Self-knowledge and forbearance, O King, are the common dharma for the four castes"—this is the remainder [of the statement]. For Śūdras, self-knowledge is attained through listening to the Purāṇas. However, Hemādri, citing the *Vrata* section, states that the restrictive rule "it must be heard" applies specifically to the twice-born. As it says in the *Bhagavadgītā*:
"O son of Kuntī, even those who may be of low birth, by taking refuge in Me..."
Women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—even they go to the supreme goal.
In the Hemādri, Viṣṇu says: "Forgiveness, purity, self-restraint, charity, control of the senses, truthfulness, self-discipline,
non-violence, service to the guru, devotion to sacred fords, and compassion."
Straightforwardness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise absence of malice— this is called the common dharma.
Manu and Parāśara declare his duty:
"Service alone is the dharma of the Śūdra, the supreme means to the highest good;
he should be pure, devoted to serving those superior to him, gentle in speech, and free from egoism."
One who constantly takes refuge in a Brāhmaṇa attains a superior birth;
however, if a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya, [he likewise attains it].
A Śūdra desiring to live should serve either a wealthy Vaiśya or a Brāhmaṇa;
for the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should indeed propitiate Brāhmaṇas alone.
Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs, that becomes fruitless for him.

Even if performed without serving a Brahmin, acts such as ritual bathing and giving gifts are considered as if they were not done at all; this is the meaning. Regarding the one who is to be served, he says:

"They must provide for his livelihood from their own family according to what is appropriate, having regard for both their own capacity and the skill of their dependents in the matter of gathering [attendants]."
"He should be protected like a son by those twice-born ones," said Medhātithi.
"He should be given leftover food, worn-out garments,
the chaff of grain, and old household utensils."

"Pulāka" refers to grain-husks. Medhātithi states that "ucchiṣṭa" (remnants) refers to what remains after eating and stays in the vessel. Gautama says: "He should seek his livelihood from them [the Śūdras]. Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, clothing, mats, and so forth, as well as the eating of remnants, crafts, and service—if an Ārya should resort to these, he must be supported by him; even if impoverished, the Śūdra must support the latter, and he should maintain a store of goods for that purpose. "Impoverished" means deprived of a livelihood; he must be supported by that Ārya, and the meaning is that the latter Ārya must be supported by that Śūdra. The giving of remnants is intended for slaves. Others, however, [hold otherwise].
Food that has been left over from a meal should be given to a Śūdra who is a householder;
however, food itself should be given day after day to one who is a householder.

Thus, regarding the prohibition of leftovers mentioned by Vyāghra, they say it refers to the householder; the same is stated in the *Madanaratna*. Likewise, for a Śūdra, austerity consists of service. Yājñavalkya says:
"The Śūdra’s duty is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born."
In the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*: "One should be a giver of what is unasked; one should resort to agriculture for the sake of livelihood;
one should constantly listen to the Purāṇas and perform the worship of Narasiṃha."
Uśanas says: Service to the twice-born and all crafts,
as well as the sale of all commodities— this is declared to be the duty of the Śūdra.

Devala says: "The duty of the Śūdra consists of service to the three [higher] castes, the maintenance of his wife and others, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in merchandise, manual crafts, dancing, singing, and playing the flute and the mṛdaṅga drum. Thus says Manu.
But if a Śūdra is unable to perform service for the twice-born,
he may live by the work of craftsmen when a crisis involving his sons or wife has arisen.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the duties of artisans.
The word "should do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"A Brāhmaṇa, blazing like fire, should be served by a Śūdra from a distance. Regarding such practice of dharma, Paiṭhīnasi says: "The station of a Śūdra is that of a Gāndharva"—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on the prescribed and prohibited duties for Śūdras in the *Śūdradharma-tattva* composed by Kamalākara, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa.

Now, regarding the performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for a Śūdra: first, because it is a constituent part of all rituals, the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is described here according to traditional practice. Vyāsa says:
"Having honored the Brāhmaṇas with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should have them pronounce a blessing (*svasti*)."
In rites performed for specific desires, in auspicious ceremonies, and in witnessing battles or wonders;
Yama says:

One should utter the syllable *oṃ* when addressing a Brāhmaṇa, omit the *oṃ* when addressing a king; one should speak in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) to a Vaiśya, and one should pronounce "svasti" for a Śūdra.

The performer, having sipped water (ācamya) and recited "sumukhaś caikadantaś ca," etc., or having heard it, shall announce the place and time, resolving: "I shall perform such-and-such a rite; as an ancillary part of that, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana). Having thus resolved, he should worship Gaṇeśa.
As follows: "O Heramba, come, come! O son of Ambikā and Tryambaka!
O you endowed with Siddhi and Buddhi, O three-eyed one, O father of all the worlds, O father!"
O Nāgāsya, O Nāgahāra, O Lord of the Gaṇas, four-armed one,
you are adorned with divine weapons— the noose, the goad, and the battle-axe.
I invoke you for the sake of worship and for the protection of my sacrifice;
having come here, accept this worship and protect my sacrifice.
Having thus invoked and worshipped with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and having taken the arghya-water together with fruit in the vessel:
"Protect, protect, O Lord of the Gaṇas! O Three-eyed One, protector of the three worlds!
Be the granter of fearlessness to your devotees and their savior from the ocean of worldly existence."
O Lord, son of two mothers, ocean of compassion, elder brother of the six-faced one;
you are the granter of boons—grant me a boon and become the source of my desired object.
"O Lord, by this offering of fruit, become the bestower of fruit upon me. Having made this request, one should pray: "O Vakratuṇḍa, O Mahākāya! Or alternatively:
"To Vighneśvara, the giver of boons, beloved of the gods, the pot-bellied one, the all-encompassing, the benefactor of the world."
Obeisance, obeisance to you, the elephant-faced one, adorned with white serpents, the son of Gaurī, the Lord of Gaṇas!
Obeisance to the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Lord of all, the bestower of auspiciousness, the Lord of the gods, who is intent on destroying the suffering of his devotees!
Obeisance, obeisance to you, the bearer of knowledge, the formidable one, the dwarf, who is pleased by devotion and grants boons!
Salutations to you who are the form of Brahmā; salutations to you who are the form of Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you who are the form of Rudra; salutations to you who are the form of an elephant.

Thus is the prayer. Then, having placed two jars upon two heaps of grain before oneself, and having cast into them fragrances, *dūrvā* grass, five types of sprouts, fruits, gold, the five gems, and so forth, and having set down two vessels filled with grain, one should say:
"I invoke Varuṇa, the Lord and Master of the Waters, who holds a noose in his hand, into this sacrifice; may he accept this worship."

Having thus invoked and worshipped Varuṇa, and having prayed to the jar with the verses beginning "Viṣṇu is at the mouth of the jar," they pray for blessings: "Be one to whom the mother is a god; be one to whom the father is a god; be one to whom the teacher is a god; be one to whom the guest is a god. (The prayer is stated: "May these blessings be true. With his knees placed upon the ground, placing his hands—joined like a lotus bud—at his head, and holding a jar filled with gold in his right hand, he says: "As long as the serpents, the rivers, the mountains, and the three strides of Viṣṇu endure, by that measure of time may there be a holy day and long life. May the waters be auspicious. May there be goodwill. May there be well-being and freedom from misfortune. May the perfumes protect us. May there be auspiciousness. May the unbroken grains protect us. May there be longevity. May the flowers protect us. May there be much to give. Having said this, he places [the grains] into the hands of the Brahmins. "Having bowed to Him, by whose performance all undertakings of divine worship, sacrifice, and ritual actions become auspicious and beautiful, I, permitted by you, shall cause the declaration of the holy day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited. When they say, "Let it be recited," [he continues]:
May there be no obstacle, may there be no evil for me, and may there be no adversaries.
May all beings be gentle and happy, bringing happiness to the world.
Thus the performer should say. The Brahmins, having said "So be it," [should respond]:
"May Brahmā grant you well-being, and may the twice-born also grant you well-being;
and from those who are the best of reptiles, may there always be well-being for you."
Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Dhundhumāra, and Bhagīratha—
all these royal sages constantly wish you well.
May there be well-being for you from those with two feet and from those with four feet;
may there be well-being from all those without feet, and may there be well-being at all times.
May Svāhā, Svadhā, and Śacī always grant you well-being;
may Lakṣmī and Arundhatī likewise bestow auspiciousness upon you, O sinless one.
May Asita Devala, Viśvāmitra, Aṅgiras,
and the six-faced Kārttikeya grant you well-being this day.
May the blessed Vivasvat grant you well-being in every way;
and may the four elephants of the quarters, the earth, the sky, and the planets likewise do so.
May that Nāga named Śeṣa, the best of serpents, who always supports the earth from below,
grant you well-being.
Thus they should say. Then the performer [should act].

"O Brahmins, let your minds be composed. "Our minds are composed," they reply. "May you be gracious. "We are gracious," they say. Having said this, while pouring water from the jar, he should say: "May there be peace (*śānti*). May there be nourishment (*puṣṭi*). May there be contentment (*tuṣṭi*). May there be growth (*vṛddhi*). May there be freedom from obstacles (*avighna*). May there be long life (*āyuṣya*). May there be health (*ārogya*). May the rite be auspicious (*śiva-karma*). May there be success in the rite (*karma-samṛddhi*). May there be success in [obtaining] sons (*putra-samṛddhi*). May there be success in wealth and grain (*dhana-dhānya-samṛddhi*). May there be the attainment of what is desired (*iṣṭa-sampad*). May there be the removal of misfortune (*ariṣṭa-nirasana*). May whatever is evil be warded off (*pratihata*). May whatever is auspicious prevail (*śreyaḥ*). May there be no obstacle in the subsequent rites (*uttare karmaṇi*). May there be daily increase in each succeeding day (*ahar-ahaḥ*). May each succeeding action be auspicious and beautiful. May there be the excellence of the lunar day (*tithi*), the *karana*, the moment (*muhūrta*), and the asterism (*nakṣatra*). May the deities presiding over the lunar day, the *karana*, the moment, the asterism, the planets, the ascendant (*lagna*), and so forth, be pleased. May Durgā and Pāñcālī be pleased. May the Viśvedevas, led by Agni, be pleased. May the hosts of Maruts, led by Indra, be pleased. May all the Vedas, led by the Brahman, be pleased. May the hosts of Sages (*ṛṣi-gaṇa*), led by Vasiṣṭha, be pleased. May the wives devoted to a single husband (*ekapatnī*), led by Arundhatī, be pleased. May the Brahman and the Brahmins be pleased. May Śrī and Sarasvatī be pleased. May Faith (*Śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*Medhā*) be pleased. May the blessed Kātyāyanī be pleased. May the blessed Māheśvarī be pleased. May the blessed Puṣṭikarī be pleased. May the blessed Tuṣṭikarī be pleased. May the blessed Vṛddhikarī be pleased. May the blessed Ṛddhikarī be pleased. May the blessed Vighna and Vināyaka be pleased. May the blessed Lord Mahāsena, together with his wife, his sons, his attendants, and residing in all places, be pleased. May Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha be pleased. May all the village deities (*grāma-devatā*) be pleased. May all the chosen deities (*iṣṭa-devatā*) be pleased. May those who hate the Veda be slain. May the adversaries be slain. May the obstructors of this rite be slain. May enemies meet with defeat. May the terrible things be pacified. May sins be pacified. May calamities be pacified. May auspicious things increase. May the waters be auspicious. May the seasons be auspicious. May the fires be auspicious. May the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) be auspicious. May the trees (*vanaspati*) be auspicious. May guests (*atithi*) be auspicious. May day and night be auspicious. May all the planets—Venus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the Moon—together with the Sun as their leader, be pleased. May the blessed Nārāyaṇa be pleased. May the blessed Parjanya be pleased. May the blessed Lord Mahāsena be pleased. I shall cause the proclamation of the auspicious time (*puṇyāha-vācana*)."
Let them be proclaimed!
Let them declare for us that auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), which is the merit of Brahmā, which brings about well-being,
and which eternally arises from the tree of the Vedas.
May that day always be auspicious for me, wherein gifts are given, the twice-born are honored, and auspiciousness is beheld.
"May you, sirs, declare an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) for this rite in my house! "Auspiciousness! An auspicious day! the Brahmins reply three times. Then:
"O sirs, may you proclaim for us that *svasti* which is called 'indestructible,' which bestows merit, prosperity, and increase, and which is eternally dear to Vināyaka."

"May there be well-being in my home; let them say, 'May there be well-being for the long-lived one,' O Brahmins! O sirs, speak to us of that prosperity which was produced by Mahālakṣmī and others in the ocean, or like the fullness of the full moon."
"May you, O Brahmins, declare prosperity for my house! May it prosper!"—thus they say three times.
"Whatever auspiciousness was performed of old when the earth was lifted up by the ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Gandharvas—may they declare that auspiciousness for us!"
"May there be auspiciousness in my house; may you, O Brahmins, proclaim 'Auspiciousness! "Auspiciousness!"—thus three times the Brahmins [should say].
Then: "O sages, proclaim that Śrī to us—she who was born from the Ocean of Milk when the great ocean was being churned, and who is eternally the beloved of Viṣṇu."

"May prosperity be in my home," [the patron] should say; when they have replied, "May there be prosperity," [he should say], "May a full hundred years be granted; may there be auspiciousness; may there be the increase of the lineage; may Prajāpati be pleased. Then the Brahmins [recite]:
"May the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you;
as well as Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, and the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa."
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha be for your victory!
So too may Ākhaṇḍala, the lord Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.
May Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth, and likewise Śiva—
may all these guardians of the directions, together with Brahmā, protect you always.
Fame, Fortune, Fortitude, Intelligence, Nourishment, Faith, Action,
Intellect, Modesty, Form, Peace, Splendor, and Contentment are the Mothers.
May these wives of the gods, assembled here, as well as the seers, the sages, the cows, and the divine mothers, consecrate you.
The wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, the hosts of apsarases,
all weapons and missiles, as well as kings and vehicles.
Medicines and gems, the divisions of time,
rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams.

"May these [deities] consecrate you for the fulfillment of all desires and aims"—with these and other previously mentioned verses, they should perform the consecration. Therein, the wife stands on the left. Then, with the previously mentioned verses beginning "May Brahmā grant you well-being," the patron (yajamāna) shall receive the lustration (*nīrājana*), the *tilaka*, and the benediction (*āśīrvāda*). This applies everywhere.
Thus ends the *Puṇyāhavācana* for a Śūdra, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
The Section on Formations and so forth.
[80] There is a great divergence between the two texts.
Then the performer [should place offerings] upon heaps of rice:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā— the Mothers, the Mothers of the World.
Fortitude, Nourishment, and Contentment are the family deities of the self;
these sixteen, being superior even to Gaṇeśa, should be worshipped during rites for prosperity.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.

Thus, having invoked the Mothers—beginning with Gaṇeśa, followed by the sixteen beginning with Gaurī, and the seven beginning with Brāhmī—by their names; having drawn five or seven lines on the wall with ghee; having invoked them with "Obeisance to Vastudhārā"; and having worshipped them with the sixteen services (upacāras), one should perform the Nāndīśrāddha.
[81] Now, the Nāndīśrāddha.

As follows: All [rites] are performed with the left hand using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods), and with barley grains even in the ancestral (*pitrya*) rites. In the place of the three maternal ancestors (mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother), the three paternal ancestors (father, grandfather, and great-grandfather), and the three maternal grandfathers (maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather), along with their wives—the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors known as the Viśvedevas named Satyavasu and Bhava—you two should accept the invitation (*kṣaṇa*). Having placed two Brahmins or two bundles of *kuśa* grass for the divine (*daiva*) rite, saying "May you two accept" or "We two accept," [one says]: "For the mothers, Amukadevīs, the female servants"—so says Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi. For the two [seats] in the place of the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors starting with the mother, etc.; for the two in the place of the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors starting with the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; and for the two in the place of the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors starting with the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, together with their wives. However, according to the followers of the Kokila school, the sequence is mother, maternal grandfather, and maternal great-grandfather; thus the *śrāddha* for the mother is performed together with the maternal grandfather. In that case, there are only two *pārvaṇas*. Here, there is no mention of name or lineage (*nāmagotra*). The source for this should be sought in the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Then: "O Viśvedevas named Satyavasu and Bhava, this is your water for washing the feet (*pādya*); this is your *arghya* offering. Likewise for the mothers and so forth, the fathers and so forth, and the maternal grandfathers and so forth: "This is your *pādya*. Then: "O Viśvedevas, here is a seat; please sit down, obeisance (*namaḥ*). Likewise for the mothers and so forth. In the place of the *arghya*, one says: "May there be the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṃkalpasiddhi*). "O Viśvedevas, this is your fragrance (*gandha*). Likewise for the mothers and so forth. Similarly: these flowers; incense (*dhūpa*); lamp (*dīpa*); clothing (*ācchādana*). All these services, ending with the clothing, are offered to those named [Amuka]. Then, having drawn a half-moon mandala or sprinkled water, and having placed double or equal amounts of uncooked rice (*āmānna*) in the vessels, having sprinkled them, touched the vessel, scattered barley grains, and pressed the thumb into the food, one says: "O Viśvedevas named Satyavasu and Bhava, the *Nāndīmukhas*, I offer this—sufficient for the meal of a pair of Brahmins, doubled, consisting of uncooked rice with its accessories, or gold representing the value of the uncooked rice according to my ability—*svāhā namaḥ*. Likewise for the mothers, grandmothers, and great-grandmothers, the *Nāndīmukhīs*: "This is for you, a pair... and so forth. For the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, the *Nāndīmukhas*: "This is for you, a pair... and so forth. Likewise for the maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers, together with their wives, the *Nāndīmukhas*: "This is for you... and so forth. In this rite, the *piṇḍas* (rice balls) may or may not be made. If the *piṇḍa* rite is performed, having prepared an altar (*vedi*), drawn three lines facing east, and spread *darbha* grass, one says: "O Mother, *Nāndīmukhī*, wash yourself (*avanenikṣva*)," giving water. Likewise: "O Grandmother, wash yourself"; "O Great-grandmother, wash yourself. Likewise: "O Father, *Nāndīmukha*, wash yourself," and so forth. Then, having made *piṇḍas* mixed with roasted flour (*saktu*), molasses, curd, jujube (*badara*), and barley, one gives one *piṇḍa* while saying: "This is for you, O Mother, *Nāndīmukhī*; this is your *piṇḍa*; this is the food, *svāhā namaḥ*. After giving one *piṇḍa*, one gives a second silently. Thus, giving two to each ancestor, one again performs the secondary rinsing (*pratyavanejana*) as before, saying "Wash yourself again," and offers ointment, collyrium, and garments. Having smelled the remainder and sprinkled the water remaining in the vessel, and having performed the rites beginning with "May the waters be auspicious," one gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to each person, saying: "For the sake of the successful completion of this *Nāndīśrāddha* rite, I give to you this gift of grapes, myrobalans, and barley, or the money equivalent thereof, *svāhā namaḥ*. Finally: "By this *Nāndīśrāddha*, may the *Nāndīmukha* deities be pleased."
The mother, the paternal grandmother, and likewise the paternal great-grandmother;
the father, the paternal grandfather, and likewise the paternal great-grandfather.
May my maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather, and the others—
may these be pleased with me and grant me auspiciousness.
Having thus made this prayer, one should release the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
Thus concludes the *vṛddhiśrāddha*.

This incidental [discussion] concludes here; it is the same for all ritual preparations (*saṃskāras*). However, where there is the selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*)—as in the case of the *grahayajña* or the *tulā* ceremony—it is according to custom that [the materials] are placed in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*):
water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, curd, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
"Mustard seeds and saffron—this is proclaimed as the eightfold *argha*.
Having thus prepared the eightfold *argha* and offered it, [he says]:
"Welcome, O best of the twice-born, you who act for my benefit!"
Please accept this water for honor and this water for the feet.

Having thus offered water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya) according to tradition, and having performed the formal selection of the preceptor, the Brahmins, and the officiating priests, he should entreat the Brahmins:
"May the Brahmins be my benefactors; may they, being composed, protect me from evil.
May they be the givers of the Vedas and the protectors of all embodied beings."
Furthermore, for the sake of satisfying the gods and the ancestors through recitations, sacrifices, oblations, and various kinds of gifts, priests were appointed.
May those in whose bodies the Vedas reside and purify the three worlds—
may they, established in the sacrifice of recitation, protect me constantly.
Brahmins are renowned throughout the three worlds as a moving sanctuary;
by the water of their very words, defiled people are purified.
The Brahmins, who are the very embodiment of Brahman, are the purifiers of all social classes;
they are constantly engaged in every righteous duty and are experts in the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras.
Versed in the Vedas, truthful in speech, and always devoted to meditation on the gods,
the human trees attain prosperity when sprinkled by the nectar of their words.
May those whose blessings are like the wish-fulfilling tree, who are endowed with the prescribed observances and whose intellects are firm in the meaning of the mantra, undertake this rite.
May all supernatural powers attain increase through the glance of your compassion;
may you, endowed with self-restraint, be honored by me in my sacrifice and recitation.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy,
constantly intent on meditation upon the Divine, they are ever serene in mind.
May they be speakers of no ill-will, and may they not be revilers of others;
may these same vows belong to me as well as to you.
Let this incidental matter rest.
Now, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).

In that regard, regarding the first appearance of menstruation, if it occurs on an inauspicious day, weekday, lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or lunar day (*tithi*), one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to the procedure stated in my own *Śāntiratna*. Then, avoiding the first four nights, during even-numbered nights at the time prescribed in my *Nirṇayasindhu*, the following should be performed. The performer, together with his wife, having remembered the place and time, should say: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*), by means of removing the sins arising from the seed and the womb for all future embryos to be conceived in this wife of mine, I shall perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite). Having said this, and having performed as a part of that ritual the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *nāndīśrāddha* as previously described, he—being adorned and wearing new garments—should sprinkle the juice of *aśvagandhā* and the juice of *dūrvā* into the right nostril of his wife. Having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*), he should bow to the Sun. Then, at night, upon the bed, he should touch the vulva while reciting: "Salutation to Viṣṇu; likewise, salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ; salutation to Prajāpati; salutation to Dhātṛ; salutation to Sinīvālī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to the two Aśvins; salutation to Parjanya. Having thus touched her and approached the woman, he should bathe after the period (*ṛtu*). The woman does not bathe. If it is not the period, purification and sipping of water (*ācamana*) are required as in the case of passing urine.
Thus ends the rite of conception (garbhādhāna). Now follows the rite for ensuring the birth of a male child (puṃsavana).

In the second, third, or fourth month, under an auspicious lunar mansion (*puṇyanakṣatra*), the husband, having performed an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) and being mindful of the place and time, should make this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of attaining a male form for the fetus about to be born in this my wife, for the removal of sins arising from the seed and the womb, and for the pleasure of the Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall perform the *Puṃsavana* rite. Having thus resolved, and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the *Puṇyāha*, the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *Nāndīśrāddha*, he should place curd from a cow of the same color as the calf into the right hand of his wife. Placing a barley grain with its tip pointing eastward in the middle and two black gram (*māṣa*) beans on either side, he asks her three times, "What do you drink? and she, having replied three times, "The production of a male (*puṃsavanaṃ puṃsavanam*"), should consume it. He should perform this in this manner three times.
Thus ends the Puṃsavana rite. Now follows the Sīmantonnayana.

In the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, or even before the birth, under an auspicious constellation (nakṣatra), the husband, having announced the place and time, shall say: "For the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall perform the *Sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) for the sake of removing the sins arising from the seed and the womb of all future children to be born of this wife of mine, and by means of the excellence of the sacramental refinement for each subsequent pregnancy. Having said this, and having performed as ancillary rites the worship of Gaṇeśa (*gaṇeśapūjā*), the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *Nāndī-śrāddha*, he—adorned and wearing new garments—should pour the juice of *dūrvā* grass onto the right side of his wife's hair with the formulas: "Obeisance to Agni" and "Obeisance to King Varuṇa. Then, standing behind her, taking three white thorns of the *śalalī* plant together with three blades of *kuśa* grass and a cluster of *udumbara* fruits, and saying "Obeisance to Prajāpati," he should part the hair into two sections starting from between the eyebrows up to the crown of the head, and thus create the *sīmanta* (parting) three times. Then, having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) and placed fruit, sweets, and other offerings in her lap, he should give ten measures of cooked rice and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins. Thus says Nārada.
One should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite for a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya during the day;
however, for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, some authorities maintain that it may be performed either by day or at night.
Regarding this, the specific details and the duties of the pregnant woman and her husband are to be known from my work, the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
[91] Thus concludes the *sīmanta* ceremony.
Now, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
Kārṣṇājini states in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*:
"Upon the birth of a son or a daughter, as well as during an eclipse of the moon or the sun..."
Immediately after bathing, one should satisfy one's own ancestors with a śrāddha offering.

When a son is born, before the umbilical cord is cut, the father shall bathe with his clothes on, announce the place and time, and make the following formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of removing the defects arising from drinking the water of the womb, for the destruction of the sins produced by the seed and the womb, and for the increase of strength, longevity, and luster—and for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*), I shall perform the *jātakarma* rite. Having thus resolved, he shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *nāndī-śrāddha* with gold. Then, having rubbed clarified butter and honey together with gold and having the child taste them with gold, he shall place [the gold] upon the child's ears and say: "Obeisance to the god Savitṛ; obeisance to Sarasvatī; obeisance to the two Aśvins. Having touched the child's shoulders and said, "Obeisance to Indra," he shall honor the Brahmins.
Thus concludes the birth-rite (jātakarman).
[92] Now follows the worship on the sixth day (ṣaṣṭhīpūjā).
In the Mitākṣarā, Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"Likewise, the sixth night must be guarded with special care;
a vigil should be performed at night, as well as an offering to the Mothers (Janmadās)."
Men with a thousand hands and women with dance and song should keep a vigil at night during the period of birth-impurity on the tenth day as well.
Vyāsa says:
The deities named Janmadās reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of sacrificing to them, purification at birth is prescribed.
On the first day, the sixth, and always on the tenth—
on these three days, one should never observe birth-impurity (sūtaka) upon the birth of a son.
In the *Aparārka* [commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti], the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa] states:
"The four *kanyās* beginning with *rākā*, and *vātaghnī* as the fifth;
the sixth is for the play of children, and she is the protector of the ears."
Indeed, the sword should be worshipped by Vaiśyas, by Vrātyas, and by the twice-born.

*Rākā*, *Anumati*, *Sinīvālī*, and *Kuhū*—these are the four daughters; this is the meaning. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Remembering the place and time, for the sake of pacifying all misfortunes and for the attainment of long life and health for this child of mine, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, Janmadā, Jīvantikā, Rākā, and the others," one should set up the water-pot (*kalaśa*). Upon a cloth placed over a full vessel therein, one should invoke the images of Gaṇeśa, Janmadā, Jīvantikā, Skanda, Rākā, Anumati, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Vātaghnī. On a sword, one should invoke Śiśurakṣiṇī, and on a wall, one should invoke Ṣaṣṭhī. Having worshipped them with the sixteen types of offerings (*upacāra*), and having offered an oblation (*bali*) of black-gram and rice, one should pray as follows:
"Just as Skanda, the son of Gaurī, was protected in his childhood in the past, so too, O Ṣaṣṭhikā, may this child of mine be protected; salutations to you!

Thus ends the worship of the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhīpūjā*). Now, the procedure for an adopted son (*dattakaputra*): Since the oblation (*homa*) consisting of the *vyāhṛti*s and other mantras is an ancillary part of the formal adoption of a son, and since women and Śūdras lack the entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to perform it, Rudradhara and others maintain that an adopted son cannot belong to them at all. Vardhamāna, Harinātha, and other Gauḍa scholars hold that one should have the oblation and other rites performed through the mediation of a Brāhmaṇa. The same is stated in the *Saṃbandhatattva*. Śaunaka states this in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
A man who is childless or whose children have died, having observed the fast for the sake of obtaining a son,
should give two garments, two earrings, a turban, and a ring.
Having fed his relatives, and especially the Brāhmaṇas with food,
he should perform the ritual procedure beginning with the *anvādhāna* and ending with the purification (*utpavana*) of the clarified butter.
Having gone before the donor, one should entreat him, saying, "Give me a son," and,
taking [the child] with both hands while reciting the mantra *devasya tvā*.
Having recited the verse "aṅgād aṅgāt" and smelled the child's head,
he should place him in the middle of the house and offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the prescribed rule.
With the verse beginning "yas tvā hṛdā," with the single verse "tubhyam agre," and likewise with the five verses beginning "somo dadat," he offers oblations verse by verse.
Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent oblations, one should complete the remainder of the rite.

In the *Mitākṣarā* and other texts, however, Vasiṣṭha has prescribed an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*; this must be performed through a Brahmin priest. The specific details should be understood from my own work, the *Nirṇayasindhu* [94]. Furthermore, that adopted son (*dattaka*) should be taken within five years, not after; for the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states: "O King, sons such as the *datta* and others are not [to be taken] after the fifth year. After that age, the giving occurs only if the child himself desires to be given away. Regarding both sale and giving, those who do not wish to be given away should not be surrendered.
One should indeed unite one's wife, sons, and all one's possessions with oneself alone.
Thus it is stated by Vyāsa in the Hemādri. As for Yājñavalkya’s statement:

"One may give from one's own family property without detriment to one's dependents, except for one's wife and son," that refers specifically to a son who is unwilling to give his own share; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
Thus concludes the rule regarding the adopted son.
[95] Now follows the ritual bathing for a woman who has given birth.

The lords of astrology declare that for men, on days when the asterisms are Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Maghā, Svātī, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Aśvinī, and Dhruva (Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-āsāḍhā, and Uttarā-bhādrapadā),
and on lunar dates that are not *riktā*, the procedure for the ceremonial bath after childbirth is auspicious.
Now, regarding the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*): Bṛhaspati states in the *Madanaratna*:
"On the twelfth or tenth day from birth, or even on the thirteenth."
In the sixteenth, the twentieth, and the thirty-second [syllables], according to their sequence, they are [distinguished] by color.
In the Nāradīya:
At the end of the period of birth-impurity, the naming ceremony (nāmakarma) should be performed according to the custom of one's own family;
the name of the child should first be auspicious and composed of well-selected syllables.
On that very point, Gārgya says:
"The father should indeed give the child a name derived from the month;
[the names] are Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Acyuta, Cakrī, Vaikuṇṭha, and Janārdana."
Upendra, Yajñapuruṣa, Vāsudeva, Hari, Yogīśa, and Puṇḍarīkākṣa are the names of the months in their respective order.

In this regard, the *Madanaratna* states that the sequence [of names] may begin with Mārgaśīrṣa or with Caitra. Furthermore, it should not be based on a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), for in that same work, Śaṅkha declares: "The father should give a name connected with the family deity and the lunar mansion. This is also stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"That name, beginning with a syllable, [should correspond to] whichever syllable belongs to whichever lunar mansion (*dhiṣṇya*)."

Manu states: "The Śūdra’s [duty] is connected with service. Regarding this, at the end of his own period of impurity, or on the twenty-second day, the father—having remembered the place and time and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, by means of removing the defects arising from seed and womb, and by means of establishing the usage of a name for this boy, I shall perform the naming ceremony"—and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*; and having written the name of Gaṇeśa with gold in a vessel of bell-metal or similar material filled with rice, followed by the name of the family deity, then the name of the month, then the lunar mansion name (*nākṣatra*), and then the conventional name such as "Śivadāsa" and so forth; and having worshipped the deities of the names; and having spoken the names beginning with "You are a devotee of [deity], you are named [Name]" into the right ear of the child; and then, with palms joined above, addressing all the Brāhmaṇas: "Obeisance to you all, O [Name]dāsa, descendant of the family deity! The Brāhmaṇas respond: "May [Name]dāsa be long-lived! In the same manner, one should speak using the name of the month, the lunar mansion name, and the conventional name, and so forth. Then, having given a hundred or ten cows or other gifts to the Brāhmaṇas, he should receive their blessings.
Thus concludes the naming ceremony.
Now follows the ritual of ascending the swing.
Bṛhaspati says in the Pārijāta:
"The mounting of the bed (khaṭvāroha) should be performed in the tenth or even the twelfth [month].
This is stated in the Jyotirnibandha.
For a man, the twelfth day is auspicious for swinging and sleeping;
for a woman, the thirteenth day is so; there is no need for consideration of the lunar mansions.

O King, one should likewise perform the swinging of children and monarchs during the three *Kara* nakṣatras, in *Revatī*, in the two *Diti* nakṣatras, and in the two sets of *Aśvinakā*; thus they shall become happy.
[98] Now, the piercing of the ears.
In the *Jyotirnibandha*, Garga states:
"They praise the piercing of the ears in the sixth, seventh, or eighth month, or even in the year, for the increase of merit, longevity, and prosperity."
Vasiṣṭha states in the Madanaratna:
"The ears should be pierced in the sixth, seventh, or eighth month, or on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight. Vyāsa states in the Hemādri:
They praise the piercing of the ears in the month of Kārttika, or Pauṣa, or Caitra, or even Phālguna, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day.

And that [act] should be performed under the asterisms of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Ārdrā, Hastā, Citrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Revatī, on a lunar day excluding the *ṛkta* (the first, sixth, and eleventh) and *parvan* days. As stated in the *Madanaratna*:
"The needle for a prince should be made of gold, for a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya of silver, and for a Śūdra of iron; it should be eight finger-breadths in length and of medium thickness."
Now, regarding the consumption of betel leaf (*tāmbūla*). Caṇḍeśvara states:
"One should give betel leaf to an infant for the first time after two and a half months."
Now, regarding the rite of going out [of the house]: Yama states in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"The going out should take place in the third or the fourth month."
Manu says: "In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family."
In this context, it is the statement of Śūkti and not that of the twice-born (dvija); therefore, Medhātithi maintains that this applies to the Śūdra as well. Bṛhaspati states in the Madanaratna:
"Or one may perform the rite of Niṣkramaṇa at the time of the first feeding of solid food.
[The Viṣṇudharmottara says:]
O twice-born one, on that day, one should likewise perform the worship of the lords of the directions, as well as of the moon and the sun,
of Vāsudeva, and of the sky.
One should cause him to be led out from the house to the outside amidst the sounds of conch shells and auspicious drums.

The father, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Recalling the place and time, for the sake of increasing the strength, longevity, and luster of this child by means of removing the impurities arising from the seed and the womb, I shall perform the *niṣkramaṇa* ceremony," and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*, he should perform the worship—including invocation—of Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions, as well as the Moon, the Sun, Vāsudeva, and the Sky, using their names over images or heaps of unbroken rice (*akṣata*). Then, accompanied by the auspicious sounds of conchs and trumpets, he should cause the child to behold the Sun, the Moon, and a cow, and recite [the following]:
For the sake of entrusting this to you, I give it to the Moon and the Sun, to the lords of the directions, to the quarters, and to the sky; may they protect you at all times.
Then the Brahmins should bestow blessings, beginning with "May Brahmā grant you well-being.
This concludes the departure;
now follows the seating.
In the *Prayogapārijāta* and the *Pādmapurāṇa*, it is stated:
"And likewise in the fifth month, one should seat him upon the ground;
all planets are auspicious for that occasion, but Mars especially so."
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"One should worship the god Vārāha, as well as the Earth and the twice-born."

The father, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—“Recalling the place and time, I shall perform the ceremony of seating this boy for the sake of pacifying all misfortunes and for the attainment of long life, health, and well-being”—and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), he should worship Vārāha and Pṛthivī by name with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) upon an image on a pedestal. Having arranged five or seven heaps of grain before that, and having seated the child upon a cloth on the ground in their midst while the sound of musical instruments plays, reciting “May Brahmā grant you well-being,” and so forth; then, having meditated upon Mṛtyuñjaya and performed a protective rite (*rakṣā*) with sacred ash, he should recite [the following].
O Goddess Earth, O auspicious one, always protect him who is omnipresent;
O beloved of Hari, deposit his entire lifespan within yourself.
But whatever obstacles there may be to his short life— concerning his vitality, health, and wealth— consume them all without delay.
You are the sustainer of all beings without exception, their mother, and the fulfiller of desires;
you are ageless, immeasurable, and saluted by all living creatures.
"For you are indeed the imperishable foundation of all beings, both moving and unmoving.
O Mother, protect the boy; may Brahmā grant his approval.

At this very point, the tying of the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*) takes place. However, other authorities perform the rite of going out (*niṣkramaṇa*) and the rite of sitting down (*upaveśana*) on the very day of the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
Thus ends the section on seating and so forth. Now follows the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*). Nārada states in the *Madanaratna*:
In the sixth or eighth month for males, but in the fifth or seventh month for females,
the auspicious ceremony of first feeding with new food (navānnaprāśana) should be performed.
Laugākṣi states: "The first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place in the sixth month, or when the teeth have appeared. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

"Having worshipped Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, the Moon and Sun, and the lords of the directions, as well as the earth and the quarters, and having likewise offered the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) into the fire..."
In the presence of the deities, while he is seated on the lap of his nurse and adorned with ornaments, the golden food-vessel should be presented to him.
One should cause him to consume milk-rice mixed with honey, clarified butter, and curd, or simply milk-rice.

The general rule and its specific exceptions regarding my [the author's] work are to be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Remembering the father, the place, and the time, I shall perform the *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) for this child, by way of destroying the afflictions arising from the seed and the womb, and for the sake of increasing strength, longevity, and luster," and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*; and having worshipped Brahmā and the other deities either in their images or in heaps of rice; and having offered oblations (*homa*) into the fire with their respective names; and having fed [the child] rice-milk (*pāyasa*) mixed with clarified butter, curd, and honey, or simply rice-milk; and having given betel-leaf; and having placed gems, gold, jewels, vessels, and so forth before [the child], one should examine which [item] the child touches, for that shall be his means of livelihood.
Thus concludes the ceremony of first feeding solid food (annaprāśana).
Now follows the completion of the first year (abdapūrti),
according to the determination of Gauḍa practice.
Having put on new garments, a man should worship Mārkaṇḍeya, who possesses long life;
likewise, he should worship him with devotion and self-restraint.
Then one should worship the long-lived Vyāsa, Rāma, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), Kṛpa, Bali, Prahlāda, Hanumān, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having reached his own natal asterism and birth-day,
a man should worship [the deity] year after year with curd-rice, again and again.
In the *Tilatatva*, an oblation of sesame seeds under that name is also prescribed. In the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"On the day of birth, all who have bathed with auspicious waters should diligently worship the preceptor, the gods, the sacred fire, and the brahmins."
The ancestors, as well as the god Prajāpati, [reside] under one's own constellation;
therefore, a great festival must be performed with diligence every year.
In the *Kṛtyacintāmaṇi*:
One should offer jaggery, milk, and sesame seeds, and tie them to the hand and the knot.
[One should also apply] guggulu, nimba, white mustard, dūrvā grass, gorocanā, and so forth.
Having worshipped the Sun and Vighneśa, one should pray thus to the Great Sage:
"The birth-day (janmatithi) should be taken as that which occurs at sunrise. This is stated in the *Kṛtyatattvārṇava*, citing the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The beginnings of the Yugas, the anniversary of the year, and the seventh lunar day dear to Pārvatī [are to be observed as such]."
"They behold the rising of the sun; there, no pair of lunar days (tithis) is recognized. Thus it is said.

The father, having bathed with his child, anointed himself, and put on new clothes, should remember the place and time and say: "For the sake of this child’s long life and health, I shall perform the annual rite. Having spoken thus, he should worship Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Vyāsa, Paraśurāma, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Bali, Prahlāda, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa, Ṣaṣṭhī, his own birth-star (nakṣatra), the two parents, Prajāpati, the Guru, and Agni—either before images or upon heaps of unbroken rice (akṣata)—and having performed an oblation of sesame seeds in their names according to the lunar fortnight, he should tie a bundle of guggulu, nimba, mustard, dūrvā grass, gorocana, and guḍūcī to his hand and pray to Mārkaṇḍeya.
O Sage, may I become long-lived just as you are,
and likewise endowed with beauty, wealth, and prosperity at all times.
O Mārkaṇḍeya, salutations be unto you, who lives through the end of seven kalpas;
O venerable sage, be gracious for the sake of attaining long life and health.
O twice-born one, foremost among sages, just as you are long-lived,
O tiger among munis, so do you make me long-lived as well.
O illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya, who lives through the end of seven kalpas,
grant us your boon for the sake of attaining long life and health.
The father, however, should say: "This [is for you]. Then, taking milk mixed with jaggery and sesame seeds—one half-anjali measure of milk mixed with sesame and jaggery—he should say:
"Having obtained the boon from Mārkaṇḍeya, I drink this for the increase of my lifespan."
Having thus drunk [the wine], the gods and brahmins should then be honored. In the *Gauḍatithitattva* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"One should avoid clipping the nails or hair, sexual intercourse, traveling on a road, meat, quarreling, and violence during the celebration of the New Year."
In that very same [text]:
"If one's birth-day falls on the day of Saturn or Mars,
and there is the occurrence of a *narkṣa-yoga*, there will be obstacles for him at every step."

*Kṛtānta* is Saturn (*śani*). There is no fault [in performing the rite] when it coincides with one's birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*). For that [person], there should be a bath with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*) and worship of the Guru, the deities, and the Fire. The specific details should be known from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Now, regarding the specific procedure for the *vardhāpana* (birthday celebration) as found in the *Hemādri*: [as stated] in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, for the benefit of children—
and especially for kings— please describe the ritual for celebrating a birthday.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Thus questioned by Vyāsa at Prayāga, Sanatkumāra replied:
"When the first month has arrived, the wise should perform the rite of hair-cutting for the child."
Or, O best of sages, that [rite] is prescribed for kings at the end of their term of office.
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Pārvatī,
Umā, Kālī, Sarasvatī, and Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā.
Satī, Saṃjñā, Tathā, Medhā, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi;
endowed with these, she who protects the children of kings is the sixteenth, named Jīvantī.
Having drawn [the deities] within the center of the sun, they should be worshipped with effort;
one may draw them either with a paste of turmeric or with saffron.
Having established them individually, Kumuda and the others are to be worshipped with fragrant perfumes and flowers, as well as with lamps, garments, and food offerings.
O Sage, having worshipped those [goddesses] with their names, one should then worship the infant king, adorned with all ornaments.
When the birth-anniversary ceremony for a child takes place, one should honor the mother and father;
O Brahmin, in the ritual for the king’s birth-anniversary, the domestic priest should perform the worship.
Having designated the Kumuda and the others, one should prepare bamboo vessels;
a wealthy person should give sixteen to each of them.
Half of that, half of that again, two, or even one each;
they should be provided with many cooked foods and many flowers and fruits.
One should offer [these] with devotion to the wives of the Brahmins, saying:
"May Kumudā and the others, who increase the lifespan of children, be pleased with me."
May they indeed cause my child to grow in strength, fame, and contentment;
and may they always grant him health, happiness, and good fortune.
