With the mantra "Śrīś ca te," one should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented to them;
on that day, one should provide garments, betel, flowers, and other such items.
"To the married women (suvāsinīs), however, one should give [gifts] with the words, 'May Kumudā be pleased'. Regarding this, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In this manner, O child, at the end of the year on the birthday, there is indeed the *vardhāpana* (congratulatory ceremony)."
And when the months had passed, for the sake of increasing the strength of the children.
Neither childhood diseases nor Skanda-diseases, nor those from Śākinīs, shall prevail over him;
nor shall they arise from existence itself, nor from water, fire, or the cardinal directions.
And especially because of the child's possession by spirits and the like.
Having attained the kingdom at the end of the year, the king should perform this great festival of peace (śāntimahotsava),
as well as worship the planets and Vināyaka.
And with devotion, [one should worship] Durgā and the goddesses Kumudā and the others.
He who indeed worships with devotion shall be filled with gold and endowed with strength and prosperity.
Thus it is stated in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.

Desiring to increase the king in longevity, luster, splendor, fame, glory, victory, and renown, he should sprinkle him with purifying and auspicious waters, honor him with gold, prepare the *māhendra* oblation, and cook for the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) while reciting, "The great Indra, who by his might... Having worshipped the world-protectors, he should take hold of the king and offer oblations with the three verses beginning with "Indra hitherward," "Indra the protector," and "Make him grow. Having performed the protection, he should adorn him with the *rocanā* ointment while reciting, "They sit upon the very heavy seat. Having performed the *sampāta* rite with the hymn "For the sake of progeny, the thread... and having recited "This is your creator," he should say, "May you prosper!"
Thus ends the section on the completion of the year in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by the venerable Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa. Now begins the section on the tonsure ceremony (*caula*).
Bṛhaspati says:
On the day of the malefic planets and so forth, the Sun brings auspiciousness to Brahmins;
on the day of Mars, it is auspicious for Kṣatriyas; and on the day of Saturn, there is good fortune for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.

The determination of the proper time for this rite—namely, that it should not be performed during the mother’s pregnancy or when her menses are occurring—and other such specific details equal to those for the twice-born (*dvija*), should be understood from my *Nirṇayasindhu*. Only the specific particulars for the Śūdra are stated here: In the first, second, third, or fifth year, according to family custom and at the prescribed time, the father, having remembered the place and time, should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): “For the sake of destroying the defects arising from the seed and the womb, and for the increase of strength, longevity, and luster, I shall perform the *caula-karma* (tonsure ceremony) for this child. Then, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the *puṇyāha*, the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjā*), the *vasordhārā*, and the *nāndī-śrāddha*, he should seat the child on an auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*). He should then either preserve one lock of hair or a row of locks, or perform a complete shaving of the head according to local custom. Thereafter, the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) and other rites should be performed.
Thus concludes the tonsure ceremony.
Now begins the commencement of learning.
In the Madanaratna, Nṛsiṃha states:
"One should perform the formal adoption of the alphabet when the fifth year has arrived;
this should be done while the sun is in its northern course, avoiding the month of Kumbha."
Now, in the *Dhanurvidyādīpikā*:
[The asterisms] Aditi, Guru, Yama, Arka, Svāti, Citrā, Agni, Pitrya, the Dhruva group, Hari, Vasu, Mūla, Indubhāga, and Antyabha;

On Saturdays, Mondays, or Wednesdays, during the awakening of Viṣṇu in the month of Pauṣa, and when there is an auspicious conjunction of time and lunar day, the imparting of the science of archery [should take place].
Having worshipped Hari, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī there, one should perform the ritual:
"O great master of all weapons, O destroyer of the enemies of all gods,
protect me here in battle along with your excellent arrows."
I bow to the Lord who has taken the form of the Three Vedas— the bow for protection by Kṛṣṇa and the arrow for destruction by Hara.

Having worshipped with this mantra and bowed, and having discharged the arrow toward the east, one should worship the Brahmins. Next is the binding of the dagger (churikā). Nārada says in the Jyotirnibandha:
I shall now describe the binding of the sword for kings prior to their taking of the hand [in marriage],
during the months prescribed for marriage, in the bright fortnight, and when the sun has not yet set.
When Jupiter and Venus are strong, and Mars is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
on days corresponding to the asterisms and lunar dates for the investiture with the sacred thread (mauñjībandha), and on days other than Tuesday;
In the *Saṃgraha*: For Śūdras and princes, in the absence of the girdle of muñja grass, there is the binding of a sword.
This should be performed on the lunar day and other times prescribed for the muñja-girdle ceremony, avoiding Tuesday.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "Having worshipped Hari, Lakṣmī, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī,
as well as the authors of one's own sciences and sūtras, and especially one's own science..."
One should offer clarified butter with the names of these very deities;
furthermore, the honoring of the best of the twice-born should be performed here with sacrificial fees.
As for the mantras:
"O you who were fashioned first among all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
having been extracted from his trident weapon and grasped firmly in a beautiful fist."
You have been bestowed upon Caṇḍikā as the destroyer of all that is wicked;
likewise, you have been expanded and presented to the gods.
You have become the very limb of all sentient beings; you are the eradicator of all that is unwholesome.
O Churikā, protect me always, grant me peace—homage be to you!

Having thus worshipped and bowed, one should tie [the thread] on the right side of the waist. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states in the *Aparārka*: "Sprinkling with water is prescribed for an infant; sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed for a young child; however, in the case of contact with water, land, or other such things, a full bath is required for a boy."
A child (*bāla*) is one prior to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*); an infant (*śiśu*) is one prior to the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*);
he is to be known as a youth (*kumāra*) until the girdle of muñja grass is bound.
Regarding the statement, "One should prescribe purification for the sake of protecting the child from the fifth year onwards," and so forth, this should be understood from my *Nirṇayasindhu*.
[109] Now, marriage (*vivāha*).

Regarding this, Vijñāneśvara maintains that for Śūdras, the sapinda relationship (*sāpiṇḍya*) is exactly as for the twice-born (*dvija*), because the continuity of bodily parts exists in all cases. That has been explained by me in the *Nirṇayasindhu*, so it is not discussed here. In that regard, there are eight forms of marriage: Brāhma, Ārṣa, Daiva, Prājāpatya, Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca. Yājñavalkya states them as follows:
The Brāhma marriage consists of giving away a girl, adorned according to one's means, after inviting her;
the Daiva marriage consists of giving her to the officiating priest at a sacrifice; and the Ārṣa marriage consists of taking two cows in exchange.

Having said this, that body born from such an act performed by one practicing the Dharma together with his wife when she is given to a supplicant shall purify six, six, and six lineages along with himself.

"The Āsura [form] is from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement; the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden. Among these, for a Śūdra, the Prājāpatya is the primary; the Āsura and Gāndharva are middling; and the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca are the lowest. Thus said Manu.
The Āsura rite is for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra.
Of these six in order, four are for the Brāhmaṇa, and four excluding the last are for the Kṣatriya;
one should know that those same [four], excluding the Rākṣasa, are lawful for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra.

The four [forms of marriage] are those of the Asuras, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and Paiśācas. Of these four, excluding the Rākṣasa form, the *Kalpataru* states that after describing the *brahma*-marriage, "this is the duty of virtuous Brāhmaṇas"; thus, the *brāhma* and *daiva* forms belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. The other three are common to all three [higher castes]. In the *Hemādri*, Paiṭhīnasi says: "The *paiśāca* belongs to those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). Kāśyapa says:
"Those who, deluded by greed, give away their own daughters for a bride-price (*śulka*)—they are sellers of themselves, sinful, and perpetrators of great transgression."
They fall into a terrible hell or destroy the seventh generation of their lineage.

A gift should be given with affection by a Śūdra for the sake of achieving the status of an Asura marriage, but not for a price; therefore, there is no fault. For this very reason, the fruit of the Gāndharva and Āsura marriages is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "He who gives away his daughter in the Gāndharva form of marriage..."
He goes to the world of the Gandharvas and is honored by the Gandharvas.
He who gives his daughter to a suitable suitor for a bride-price shall be sung of by the Kinnaras and goes to the world of the Gandharvas.

Hārīta says: Others declare that a woman wedded according to any one of these [forms] is a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). The specific details should be understood from Medhātithi and the Kalpataru. In that regard, with the exception of the Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca forms, the giving [of the bride] preceded by the pouring of water is mandatory in all cases. Vasiṣṭha says:
A girl’s husband is not designated by water alone, nor by mere words;
husbandhood arises from the sacramental rite of taking the hand at the seventh step.

Even in the Gāndharva and other forms of marriage, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites is indeed required; for it is said: "The Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa marriages—among these, the formal acceptance of the bride occurs first, and the fire-oblation is prescribed to follow afterwards."

Thus it is stated by Vasiṣṭha in the *Aparārka*. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana, in that same context, have declared that in the absence of the *homa* and other rites, she may be given to another:
"If a maiden has been forcibly abducted but not consecrated with mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; as was the maiden [before], so is she [now]."
This [mantra] is for the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca [forms of marriage], because in those two cases the bride is taken away by force. For a Śūdra, however, the mantra is simply "namas. Manu also says:
"The mantras recited at the time of taking the hand are invariably the defining characteristic of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the learned to occur at the seventh step."

In that regard, the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is common to all castes, because Yājñavalkya stated without distinction: "The hand of those of the same caste (*savarṇā*) should be grasped. Regarding the giving of a maiden preceded by water (*udakapūrva*), there is an option for the Śūdra. This is stated in the *Smṛtikaumudī* under the *Brāhma* marriage:
"Grasping the hand is appropriate for all castes in every way;
however, for Brāhmaṇas it is preceded by water, and for others as well, it may be done according to their desire."

[110] Others, however, maintain that by this [definition] the *brāhma* form also occurs, because Āśvalāyana states that the *brāhma* alone involves water first: "Having adorned the maiden, one should give her away preceded by water; such is the *brāhma* marriage. Other particulars should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Regarding the *brāhma* form in the *Smṛtikaumudī*:
"Having performed the *vaināyakī* sacrifice and the auspicious *śacīyāga*..."
And for the accomplishment of one's goals, a Śrāddha rite should be performed for the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
In the Varāhasaṃhitā: "A maiden [should worship] the consort of Puruhūta (Indra) situated in her home during the morning, midday, evening, and at sunset."
"One should worship with garlands, perfumes, and incense that woman who has arrived for the taking of the hand.
Now follows the formal application (prayoga).

"In the case of a Śūdra marrying a Śūdra woman, only the ritual action (kriyā) devoid of mantras should be performed," so it is stated in the *Hariharabhāṣya*. By this, the Kāṭhaka rite is intended. Therein, at the auspicious moment (muhūrta) prescribed for the marriage, the girl’s father, brother, or another relative goes to the groom's house, performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and after proclaiming the place and time, makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) as a constituent part of the marriage to be performed. Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and Varuṇa, and having performed the washing of the groom’s feet and his worship with perfumes, garments, and other offerings, he takes betel nuts, coconuts, saffron, and cloth dyed [with these], and says: "To you, the groom named So-and-so—the great-grandson of So-and-so, the grandson of So-and-so, and the son of So-and-so—I shall give, at the auspicious moment declared by the astrologer, this maiden named So-and-so—the great-granddaughter of So-and-so, the granddaughter of So-and-so, and the daughter of So-and-so."
"Your father will give his daughter to you—one who is free from physical defects, not fallen [from caste], not impotent, and devoid of the ten faults—when she is available at that time.
To this, the father should say, "I shall give her, without a doubt. [The reading may also be: "to one who has bathed, or to one who is healthy."
Some, however, having gone to the girl's house and honored her,
say: "To one who is free from physical defects, not fallen [from caste], not impotent, and devoid of the ten faults—
to such a one I shall give this daughter in the presence of the gods, the fire, and the twice-born."
Thus, having placed [the bride] into the hand of the groom’s kinsman, the father of the girl said:
"The girl has been given by you in word; she has been accepted by me for the sake of the groom.
You have been chosen for the rite of viewing the bride; may you be happy."
Thus says the father of the bride:
"The girl has been given by you in word, and she has been accepted by me for the sake of a groom.
It is said that the father of the groom should speak thus with the understanding that "the rite of beholding the groom has taken place."

Thereafter, the mutual honoring and worship of the Brahmins and other rites should be performed. According to custom, turmeric, sandalwood, and so forth should be applied during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) prescribed for the marriage.
Thus concludes the betrothal (vāgdāna).

Then, on the day prior to the wedding or on the wedding day itself, in the morning, the father of the bride and the groom shall perform an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*). Having performed the propitiatory rites for the planets and Vināyaka (*grahavināyakaśānti*), and having announced the place and time (*deśakāla*), he shall say: "I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjā*), the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*), the worship of Śacī, and the *Nāndīmukha* Śrāddhas as ancillaries to the marriage of [Name]. Having performed these as previously described, he shall place two jars filled with rice upon two bamboo poles (*vaṃśapātra*) among the branches, saying: "For the removal of obstacles: Nandinī, Nalinī, Maitrā, Umā, and Paśuvardhinī."

Having installed the Goddess (Bhagavatī) and the Mother (Mātṛ) in front of the sacrificial post (*śastra*), one should worship the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) on the fourth day. Having tied a bracelet with a yellow thread, one should construct an altar (*vedi*) with five or seven steps, measured by seven or five handspans of the girl; Harihara says the altar should be four cubits square. Having performed the *sīmānta-pūjā* for the groom, one should seat the groom who has arrived at the house with due honor. Then the officiant (*ācārya*), having swept a space of one cubit on the altar with *darbha* grass, smeared it with cow dung, drawn three lines with the tips pointing east using sacrificial wood, removed the earth three times, sprinkled it, and established the fire, should perform the *madhuparka* worship for the groom facing east. As follows: The father of the girl, having offered a seat, says to the groom standing behind him, "Be seated, sir; we shall honor you. The groom replies, "Honor me. Then, while the giver stands facing west and says "The mat" (*viṣṭaraḥ*) three times, he should offer a mat made of twenty-five *kuśa* blades, saying "May it be accepted. The groom, standing behind the seat, takes it and sits down after placing it on the seat with the words "Salutation to the mat" (*viṣṭarāya namaḥ*). Then, when another says "The water for the feet" (*pādya*) three times, the giver should offer the *pādya*—consisting of sandalwood paste, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains—saying "May it be accepted. With that, the groom should wash his feet, first the left, then the right. Then the giver should take another mat offered three times by another and place it under the groom's feet. Then, taking the *arghya*—consisting of sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken rice, *kuśa*, sesame, mustard, curds, and *dūrvā*—when another says "The *arghya*" three times, the giver should offer it, saying "May it be accepted. The groom should take it in his joined palms, saying "Salutation to the waters" (*adbhyo namaḥ*), bow his head, and cast it on the ground. Then, when another says "The water for sipping" (*ācamanīya*) three times, he should accept what is given, sip it once, and rinse his mouth. Then, when another says "The *madhuparka*," the groom should open the vessel of bell-metal containing curds, honey, and clarified butter—which was given by the giver and covered by the same—while it remains in the giver's hand; looking at it, saying "Salutation to Savitṛ," accepting it, saying "Salutation to Savitṛ," and placing it on his left, he should stir it with his ring finger, saying "Salutation to the *madhuparka*," and throw some out with his ring finger and thumb. Having done this twice more, he should eat from it three times with those same two fingers. Or he may say "Salutation to the *madhuparka*. According to the *Smṛtikaumudī*, he should take the second portion with the thumb and ring finger, and the third with the thumb and middle finger; however, this should be considered. Then, having poured the remainder away where there is no passage, having sipped water twice and rinsed again, he should touch his face saying "Salutation to Speech" (*vāce namaḥ*), his nostrils saying "Salutation to Breath" (*prāṇāya namaḥ*), his eyes saying "Salutation to the Eyes" (*cakṣurbhyāṃ namaḥ*), his ears saying "Salutation to the Ears" (*śrotābhyāṃ namaḥ*), his arms saying "Salutation to Strength" (*balāya namaḥ*), his thighs saying "Salutation to Vitality" (*ojase namaḥ*), and his limbs saying "Salutation to the Limbs" (*aṅgebhyo namaḥ*). Then, when another says "The cow" (*gauḥ*) three times, he should accept her and release her, whispering "Salutation to the Cow, mother of the Rudras, daughter of the Vasus, sister of the Ādityas; may the sin of my worshipper be destroyed," and aloud saying "Go forth, eat the grass. Then the giver should honor the groom with garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth. Then, at an auspicious moment, having held a curtain between them, he should look upon the face [of the bride].

Others, however, desire the taking of the hand at the moment of the *lagna*. Then, having removed the inner curtain (*antaḥpaṭa*), the groom should gaze upon the face of the bride. Having established the fire here and placed grass, fruit, or a mat behind the fire, one should give two of the four garments provided by the father of the girl, repeating: "O long-lived one, put on this garment. And she should put it on, repeating: "Salutation to the garment" (*vāsase namaḥ*). Then, being prompted by the giver with the words, "Behold the bride," he should gaze upon her. Following that is the giving away of the girl (*kanyādāna*); thus says Harihara.

Others, however, state that [the giving of] garments and so forth occurs after the formal gift of the girl (*kanyādāna*). Then, [the father] should perform the rite beginning with "May Brahmā grant you well-being" and ending with the scattering of unbroken rice grains (*akṣatāropaṇa*). Facing north, the father of the girl seats his wife to his right; holding *kuśa* grass in his hand and having sipped water (*ācamana*), he announces the place and time, and says: "For the attainment of the fruits described in the ritual manual for the gift of a daughter—namely, the attainment of the unsurpassed blissful world of Brahmā and so forth for all my ancestors; and for the sake of purifying twelve generations of ancestors and twelve generations of descendants through the lineage to be produced by this bridegroom in this girl (or, in the *prājāpatya* case, eight generations of ancestors and eight generations of descendants)—and for the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa myself, I shall perform the gift of this girl according to the *brāhma* marriage rite or the *prājāpatya* rite, after having adorned her. Having said this, he should recite [the following].
Desiring to conquer the world of Brahmā, I shall give to you, O Viṣṇu, a maiden endowed with gold and adorned with the ornaments of a young girl.
"O Viśvambhara, O all-pervading Being, O witnesses, O all deities!
I shall give this maiden so that she may bring about the liberation of my ancestors. Thus [he says].

Then, having placed his own hand upon the bride’s hand—which is over the groom’s hand on a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*)—he says over the groom’s hand: "May it be well-sprinkled! May the waters be auspicious! May there be goodwill! Having said this, he continues: "May the maiden cross over [to the other shore]; may merit increase; may there be peace, nourishment, and contentment; may there be the excellence of the lunar day, the *karaṇa*, the hour, and the asterism; may you, sirs, declare it a holy day (*puṇyāha*). The Brahmins say, "A holy day! He says, "May you, sirs, declare it a blessing (*svasti*); may you, sirs, declare prosperity (*ṛddhi*); may you, sirs, declare 'May there be fortune (*śrī*)'! I am the servant of such-and-such [name]. For all my ancestors... and so forth, up to "...for the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa," as stated previously. Then he says: "To the groom Devadattadāsa, of the Kāśyapa lineage, grandson of Viṣṇudāsa, and son of Śivadāsa; [and to] the maiden named Amukapreṣyā (or by her name), of the Kāśyapa lineage, great-granddaughter of Caitradāsa, granddaughter of Maitradāsa, and mother of my father Bhojadāsa, who has Prajāpati as her deity, adorned according to my ability. Having spoken thus, and having repeated it a second time in the same way, saying: "Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit of a hundred *Jyotiṣṭoma-atirātra* sacrifices, for the sake of procreating offspring and for the practice of common duty, I give you, in the *Prājāpatya* rite, as a wife to be shared in dharma"—with these words, he should pour water mixed with *kuśa* grass and barley, along with the bride's hand, into the groom's hand. According to some, the mother should also say, "It is given by me. According to others, the recitation of the lineage names (*gotra*) is not required. The groom says, "I accept."
Take refuge in this which has been given to you, to Gotra and to Dāsa;
O maiden, may you be before me, O goddess, and on my two sides.
"O daughter, may you remain behind me; through your gift, may I attain heaven.
Born into my own lineage and nurtured for eight years, [you are my daughter]."
O servant, this woman, who shall increase your sons and grandsons, has been given to you by me.

Thus he should recite. Then, for the sake of the bridegroom’s non-establishment [of the marriage], he should give, saying: "I offer this gold and a pair of cattle as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thereafter, if he is able, he should give vessels of copper or bell-metal, cows, horses, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth. The relatives of the bride should also give a dowry (*yautaka*). Some say that the groom and his father and others should also give. Some say that the dowry is given at the end of the *homa*. Then, having wrapped the bride and groom three times with a thread four or five times each, and having passed the upper [end] through the lower [loop] and the lower [end] through the upper, and having made it triple and yellow, he should tie the lower [end] as a bracelet on the groom's hand and the upper [end] on the bride's hand.

"By that [bond] with which the powerful King, the lord of the Dānavas, possessed of great strength, was bound—by that I bind you, O Rakṣas; do not move, do not move! Thus [he speaks]. Then follows the scattering of rice grains moistened with milk by the bride and groom. This should first be performed by the bride, and then by the groom. The mantras are: "Obeisance to Bhaga; obeisance to Yajña; obeisance to Śrī; obeisance to Dharma; obeisance to Prajā; obeisance to Yaśas. Then, having sat down facing the east, he should give a garment to the girl. She, for her part, should put it on with the words, "Obeisance to the garments. Then the groom...
With this auspicious thread, which is the cause of my husband’s long life, I bind you around your neck, O fortunate one; may you live for a hundred autumns.

He should tie this "thread of good fortune" (*saubhāgyatantu*) around the bride’s neck. Then, he should look at the bride, saying: "Salutation to the Viśvedevas, Āyu, Mātariśvan, and Dhātṛ. At this point, a bracelet may also be tied with a safflower-dyed thread (*kausumbhasūtra*). Then, on the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), having sat down behind the fire facing east upon a mat of *tejana* or *vīraṇa* grass, someone should stand holding an auspicious water-pot (*maṅgalakumbha*) on his shoulder, either to the south or in the northeast, until the bride has taken her final step. To the north, having placed the decorated grinding stones (*dṛṣad-upala*), it is the custom that the groom should say the name of the girl while offering food. Then, when it is said by the bride’s father, "They should look at each other," they should gaze at one another.
With eyes free from fierceness, non-hostile, auspicious, and well-disposed;
radiant, a mother of sons, devoted to the gods—be a bestower of happiness.

Thus the bridegroom should say: "Salutation to Soma, Gandharva, Agni, and Pūṣan. Madanapāla maintains that for Śūdras, there is no *homa* at all in the marriage ceremony because they lack the study of the *Gṛhyasūtras*, lack knowledge of the collection of ritual accessories prescribed therein, and lack the capacity for performance. Others, however, state that since eligibility is established in the principal act (*pradhāna*), knowledge of the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) is possible through oral instruction and so forth—just as in the case of the *Sthapati-iṣṭi* sacrifice—and thus they maintain that the *homa* should be performed. The procedure is as follows: Having given the seat of Brahmā to the Guru on the south, he should have him sit down. Having placed *kuśa* grass in a clay vessel filled with water and having set it to the north upon *kuśa* grass, he should surround the fire with *darbha* blades starting from the east and perform the *āsādana* (placing of materials). These are: three blades of grass, two *pavitra* strainers, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pot), the *carusthālī* (gruel pot), *saṃmārgakuśāḥ* (cleansing *kuśa* blades), *upayamanakuśāḥ* (supporting *kuśa* blades), three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), the *sruva* ladle, clarified butter, rice grains, parched grain (*lāja*), a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), a vessel for the scrapings (*saṃsrāvapātra*), a stone, the hide of a bull, a cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then, having cut two *pavitra* strainers a span long and having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, he should purify it with the two *pavitra* strainers, place them therein, and holding the right hand over the left, kindle the fire. Having sprinkled the vessels and set them down, he should pour the clarified butter into the pot, heat it over the fire on the south, and perform the *paryagni-karaṇa* (circumambulation with fire) using a fire-brand together with the parched grain. Having heated the *sruva* ladle, wiped it with *kuśa* blades, sprinkled it with *prokṣaṇī* water, heated it again, and placed it on the south, he should take out the clarified butter, purify it, inspect it, discard the husks, purify the *prokṣaṇī* water again, inspect it, take up the supporting *kuśa* blades, stand up, and place three fuel-sticks into the fire. Having sprinkled around the fire with *prokṣaṇī* water, the Guru, touched by the bridegroom, should bend his right knee and, touched by the right hand of the Brahmā priest, offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle: "To Prajāpati, salutation! "To Indra, salutation!"—these are the two *āghāra* offerings. The bridegroom should everywhere perform the renunciation (*tyāga*) saying, "This is for Prajāpati, not mine," and so forth. "To Agni, salutation! "To Soma, salutation!"—these are the two *ājyabhāga* portions. "To Agni, salutation! "To Vāyu, salutation! "To Sūrya, salutation! "To Agni and Varuṇa, salutation! (twice) "To Agni, salutation! "To Varuṇa, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, Maruts, and Svarke, salutation! "To Varuṇa, Āditya, Aditi, and Prajāpati, salutation!"—or this may be omitted. Then he should offer three times to Agni and Mṛtyu—or this may be omitted. Then, having spread an under-layer of clarified butter in the bride's joined palms, her brother or someone else acting in his stead, should twice throw parched grain mixed with *śamī* leaves from the winnowing basket into her hands. Then, having poured clarified butter over it while she stands, she should offer it three times, saying, "To Agni, salutation! The mantra belongs to the bridegroom alone. Then the bridegroom should grasp the bride’s raised right hand, including the thumb, with his own raised hand. Therein the mantra is: "To Bhaga, Aryaman, and Savitṛ, salutation!"
"Endowed with the virtues of wealth and gentleness, be a mother of heroes and a mother of living sons; may you always follow my heart as the sovereign queen in my lineage. Thus [he spoke].

Then, having taken hold of the bride, he makes her step upon a stone with her right foot to the north of the fire, saying: "Homage to the Maiden. Then: "Homage to Sarasvatī. They sing verses. Then: "Homage to Agni. Having circumambulated the fire, and having performed the sequence beginning with the parched grains (*lāja*) and ending with the circumambulation twice more, on the fourth occasion the bride's brother pours all the parched grains from the winnowing basket into the bride's joined palms. Standing, she offers them into the fire, saying: "Homage to Bhaga. Then, having circumambulated the fire for the fourth time and sat down, while the *brahmán* priest holds his hand, he offers an oblation saying: "Homage to Prajāpati. Then, having made seven heaps of rice grains arranged toward the north, the groom leads the bride in seven steps with her right foot, saying: "Homage to Viṣṇu. [He says: "Homage to *iṣ* (food); homage to Viṣṇu; everywhere, homage to *ūrj* (strength); homage to the increase of wealth; homage to the state of being a wife; homage to offspring; homage to the seasons"—some say these are the formulas. Then, at the seventh step, the teacher places the heads of the two together. The groom should sprinkle them with water from the eastern jar using mango sprouts. Having been told by the groom, "Behold the Sun," she should look at the sun, saying: "Homage to the Sun. Placing his hand over the bride's right shoulder and touching her heart, he says: "Homage to my mind and your speech. Seating the bride to the north, he consecrates her, saying: "Homage to the Bride. Having applied vermilion to the parting of her hair, either another person or the groom raises the bride and seats her upon the red hide of a bull, saying: "Homage to cows, horses, and men. He then offers an oblation saying: "Homage to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," consumes the remnants of the offering, purifies himself with the *praṇītā* water using the two strainers, and throws the strainers into the fire. He gives a cow to the teacher, releases the *praṇītā* vessel, gives a full vessel to the *brahmán*, and prepares raw food for the Brahmins. If the wedding occurs during the day, at night the bride, sent by the groom, should look at the Pole Star (*dhruva*), saying: "Homage to the Pole Star. Then, for one year, twelve nights, six nights, or three nights, the couple should remain celibate, avoiding pungent and salty foods, not wearing ornaments, and sleeping on the ground. They may use oil, unbroken rice, sandalwood, and so forth according to custom. On the fourth day, in the latter part of the night, having performed the five purificatory rites of the site and established the marriage fire, he should perform the rites from the seating of the *brahmán* until the placing of the fuel sticks as before. There, having set out clarified butter in a pot, having silently poured out four portions, having sprinkled and washed them three times each, and having cooked them, he adds fuel sticks, sprinkles the fire, and at the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers: "Homage to Agni Prāyaścitta. Likewise: "Homage to Vāyu Prāyaścitta; homage to Sūrya Prāyaścitta; homage to Candra Prāyaścitta; homage to Gandharva Prāyaścitta. At the end of the nine oblations, having offered the *caru* with "Homage to Prajāpati," and taking the remnants from the water-pitcher, he applies them to the bride's head, saying: "Homage to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candra, Nakṣatra, Gandharva, and Prajāpati. Saying, "Be one who follows my vows," he feeds the bride the remainder of the *caru* from the northern side of the fire, saying: "Homage to the vital breaths; homage to the bones; homage to the flesh; homage to the skin. Having had her rinse her mouth, he offers an oblation of clarified butter to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. These are the nine oblations from Agni to Prajāpati. The remnants for consumption are placed in a separate vessel. The consumption of the remnants, the purification, the disposal of the strainers, the gift of a fee to the teacher, a full vessel to the *brahmán*, and the giving of raw food are prescribed. However, in the *Smṛtikaumudī*, it is stated that there is no *homa* for a Śūdra at all. That is incorrect, because the principle—"even when dead, she has attained unity with him through mantra-oblations and vows"—applies without distinction even to a Śūdra. Then, some say that the father of the girl should honor the groom and his party, and give a bamboo vessel to the groom alone. For example, having worshipped Umā and Maheśvara in a bamboo vessel containing sixteen small winnowing baskets, he should pray.
You are Airiṇī, the goddess Umā; Maheśa is the Lord of Girijā.
Therefore, I shall worship you, Airiṇī, the granter of all desires.
I shall give [this] together with clothing and a lamp, joined with sixteen winnowing baskets, to the bridegroom’s mother for the successful completion of the gift of the daughter.

Having said this, and in order to obtain the full fruit of the gift of the maiden that has been performed, one should recite while saying: "I give this bamboo vessel to the bridegroom alone, and not to myself. "The bamboo is the best maker of lineage; the bamboo increases the lineage. May you, being pleased by this gift of the bamboo, grant me prosperity."
"This bamboo vessel is meritorious, produced from that which grows on a bamboo stalk;
it is the supreme gift among all gifts. Therefore, grant me peace.
Some do not perform this [recitation]. Then, the father of the girl—
"This girl, who has been eight years old, was raised by me like a son;
now she is given by me to you—please protect her with affection. Thus [he spoke].

He should cause the bride to sit upon the lap of the groom. Then the groom, having gone to the house with the bride by means of a vehicle, should worship Śrī there, perform the worship of the installed Mothers and the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and after dismissing them, he should untie the knots of the garments and the *kaṅkaṇa* bracelet and honor the Brahmins. Regarding the bride’s entry into the house and the time of the dismantling of the pavilion (*maṇḍapodvāsana*), other specific details should be understood from my *Nirṇayasindhu*. These sacraments (*saṃskāras*) apply to virtuous Śūdras (*sacchūdra*). Likewise, the daily observances (*āhnika*) and so forth to be described hereafter are also mandatory for them; however, for virtuous Śūdras, only marriage is [required].
Thus ends the procedure for the marriage of a Śūdra and the performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by the venerable Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
This second section is completed.
[128] Now, the daily observance (*āhnika*) of the *śūdra* is described.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: “Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*... (Viṣṇudharma).
Whoever, having risen from his bed, should glorify Madhusūdana,
by that glorification his sins go to destruction without remainder.
There, having sipped water for purification and bowed to one's parents and the chosen deity,
one recites: "At dawn, I remember Nārāyaṇa, whose navel is a lotus, who has Garuḍa as his vehicle, for the sake of pacifying the great agony of the fear of worldly existence."
The wielder of the discus weapon, whose eyes are like the petals of a fresh lotus, is the cause of liberation for the noble elephant seized by the crocodile.
At dawn, I bow with my mind, my speech, and my head to the pair of lotus feet of the Supreme Person,
Nārāyaṇa, who delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Of him who is devoted to the Brahmins intent upon the study of the Pārāyaṇa.
In the morning, I worship Him, the bestower of fearlessness to those who seek refuge, for the sake of removing the fear of sins committed throughout all previous births—
He who [rescued] the lordly elephant whose foot had fallen into the mouth of a crocodile.
Bearing the conch and the discus, he brought about the destruction of sorrow.
To whoever recites these three meritorious verses every morning,
Hari, the teacher of the three worlds, shall grant his own abode.
Having recited, according to one's inclination, "In the morning I remember Śiva, the one, the infinite, the primordial," and so forth, [one should recite]:
"King Nala is of virtuous fame; Yudhiṣṭhira is of virtuous fame;
Vaidehī is of virtuous fame; and Janārdana is of virtuous fame."
Having spoken thus and paid homage to the earth, he disappeared; covering the ground with grass, he veiled his head with his garment,
and restraining his speech with effort, he remained free from spitting and exhaling.
One should void urine and feces in a clean place with a concentrated mind,
according to the rule stated by Aṅgiras:
"During the day and at the twilights, one should face north."
But if one must void urine or feces at night, one should do so facing south.
One should walk one hundred paces from a village, and four times that distance from a city.
Having voided urine and feces in a place prescribed by Yājñavalkya, Parāśara, and others, and having removed the excrement and urine with wood, clods of earth, grass, or the like—
as stated by Bhāradvāja— one should wipe the anus with the left hand using a clod of earth or similar object.
Having risen with his penis still held [in the hand],
he should untiringly perform purification that removes odor and residue, using earth and water drawn from a source.

One should perform purification according to this statement of Yājñavalkya. Regarding that, Śātātapa says concerning urine: "One application [of earth] on the penis, three on the left hand, and two on both hands—this is declared to be the purification for urine; for semen, it should be double that."
Regarding excrement, Dakṣa says:
"Two applications of clay should be given to the penis; five to the anus; ten to the hands;
and seven applications of clay should be given to both [hands] for the sake of purification."
Śaṅkha says: Seven applications of clay are prescribed for the penis, two for the male organ;
twenty are to be known for one hand, and fourteen for both hands.
One cloth [is required]; three applications of earth should be given for the cleaning of the nails by the performer;
and three applications on the feet are always to be known as necessary for one desiring purity.

In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: One application of clay should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to the left hand, and seven to both hands; these are the applications of clay that effect purification.

In this matter, the determination is made according to the deficiency or excess of the paste, or based on the status of the householder and so forth. Dakṣa states the quantity of clay for the urine: "But for the penis, the clay is said to be that amount by which three joints are filled. Regarding the anus, Manu says:
The first clay is prescribed as being the measure of half a prasṛti;
the second and the third are declared to be half of that [respectively].
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "For women and Śūdras, half the measure of purification has been declared by the wise.
Devala, however, states that purification according to what has been prescribed occurs when the odor has departed.
Purification is prescribed for as long as one considers it sufficient. Dakṣa states: "That purification which is prescribed for the day is ordained to be half as much at night."
Half of that is prescribed for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey.
Vṛddhaparāśara says:
He who, having sat down to void excrement or urine, does not find a place to do so,
should always perform half of his usual purification.
In the *Brāhma* [Smṛti]: "For a child who has not been initiated, it serves to remove odors and stains;
however, until he has been initiated, a Brahmin is no more than a Śūdra, and likewise a woman."
For them, purification is prescribed as that which removes odor and stains.
"Neither the measure nor the number of purifications has been prescribed by the learned.

Thus it is for a Śūdra prior to marriage. However, in the absence of marriage, all religious duties (*dharma*) become obligatory after twelve years or after sixteen years, but not before. This we shall explain later. Regarding the discharge of feces while eating, Bṛhaspati says: "If the anus of a Brāhmaṇa should ever discharge [feces] while he is eating..."
Having first performed purification, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet).
Then, having observed a fast, one is purified by means of the *pañcagavya*.

The meaning is that after washing the hands and performing the purification (*śauca*), one should observe a fast following the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*). The mention of "the Brahmin" is illustrative (and applies to others as well).
Thus ends the rule for purification in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by the venerable Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Sitting in a clean place, facing either east or north, with his hands between his knees and formed like a cow’s ear, he should sip pure water that reaches the palate once; or thrice, according to the *Smṛtikaumudī*. The Bhaṭṭas maintain that one should touch the lips with the thumb. Thereafter, he should wipe the lips twice with the base of the thumb; touch the nostrils with the thumb and forefinger; the eyes with the thumb and middle finger; the ears with the thumb and ring finger; the navel with the thumb and little finger; the heart with the palm of the hand; and touch the head and the shoulders with all the fingers.
Now, regarding the tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*):

The wise declare that for a Brāhmaṇa, the tooth-stick should be made of *badara*, *udumbara*, *āpāmārga*, *panasa*, *kadamba*, *āmra*, *jātī*, *bilva*, or *priyaṅgu*, or from thorny trees and milky trees, and it should be twelve finger-breadths long. For those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it should be nine, six, and four finger-breadths long respectively; thus it is stated by Viṣṇu in the *Madanapārijāta*. It should be as thick as the little finger, with its tip fashioned into a brush-like end; having washed this tooth-stick, [one should use it].
O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence.

Having eaten [the betel] while facing east with this mantra, having cleansed the teeth, and likewise having scraped the tongue, one should discard it toward the east or the north and perform sixteen or twelve mouthfuls of water-rinses (*gaṇḍūṣa*). This should not be done on the first, ninth, sixth, new moon, full moon, fourteenth, eighth, the day of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or on days of *śrāddha*, vows (*vrata*), or festivals. On those occasions, there should be twelve rinses. Then, having groomed the hair, one should bathe.
Now, regarding the bath, [it is stated] in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
Just as during the day, so too in the morning, one who is not ill should bathe daily;
having cleansed his teeth at a river or similar place, or at home, if it be there, he should do so without reciting mantras.
In the *Smṛtikaumudī*, Yogiyājñavalkya states:
"Being self-restrained and pure, one should bring earth, sesame seeds, cow dung, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers at the time of bathing for the purpose of the bath."
Having gone to the edge of the Ganges water and set this down separately upon the ground,
the wise man should divide that clay and the cow dung into three parts.
One should indeed perform the cleansing of the lower, upper, and middle parts separately with distinct portions; for in cleansing, there must be no mixing of earth.
Having washed his feet with water and earth and having sipped water, he becomes pure;
he should then wash his limbs in sequence with water and earth.
Having washed the head with one [portion], and likewise the area above the navel with two;
then the waist, bladder, thighs, shanks, and feet with three portions each.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should pay homage to that water;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he should bow down to it with this mantra: "Whatever [impurity] there may be in this..."
Then, having described the bath according to the ritual of Kātyāyana, he says:
"In this manner, the bath accompanied by mantras is prescribed for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
however, for a Śūdra, it is considered to be performed silently with a salutation."

Therefore, for Śūdras, the ritual of bathing without mantras belongs specifically to the Kāṭhaka school. However, Śrīdatta of Mithilā has stated that the bath described in the *Padma Purāṇa* is common to all castes, as follows: "A wise person who knows the mantras should perform the bath with waters either drawn up or not drawn up; the knower of mantras should designate the sacred site (*tīrtha*) by means of the root mantra."
"Salutation to Nārāyaṇa"—this is declared to be the root mantra.
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, having sipped water according to the rule, being self-controlled and pure;
Having fashioned a square measuring four cubits on all sides,
the wise practitioner should invoke the Gaṅgā with these mantras:
You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, you belong to Viṣṇu, and you are worshipped by Viṣṇu;
protect us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death.
"Three and a half crores of sacred fords," Vāyu said,
"are yours, O Jāhnavī, in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space."
Your name is indeed Nandinī, and among the gods you are known as Nalinī;
you are Vṛndā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, and Sitā.
Vidyādharī is well-pleased, as is Lokaprasādinī;
Veṇyā and Jāhnavī, Śāntā and Śāntipradāyinī.
One should recite these names of merit at the time of bathing;
there, the Gaṅgā that flows through the three paths becomes present.
Or this should be recited by a Brahmin;
it means that [the mantra] previously mentioned as the root-mantra (mūlamantra) should be joined with the hollowed palms after being consecrated seven times.
One should again pour water upon the head three, four, five, or seven times.
One should perform the bath with clay afterwards, having invoked it according to the rule:
"O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!"
I shall bear you upon my head; may you protect me at every step.
You were raised up by the boar, by Kṛṣṇa of the hundred arms.
"O Earth, remove my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me;
salutations to you, O source of all worlds, O you of excellent vows.

Regarding this, it should be considered that since there is no specific mention of the *śūdra* in the previously cited statement, and because the *śūdra* lacks the qualification for reciting Purāṇic mantras, [the application of this verse] is doubtful. Even if such qualification exists, the truth is that for all [castes], this [verse] is to be used in conjunction with what was stated before. Thus it is said in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*.
A twice-born man should bathe in rivers and streams standing against the current;
in waters such as those of tanks and the like, he should perform his bath facing the sun.
According to the followers of Kātyāyana, even for one facing the sun, bathing in a river is prescribed. To that effect, it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"A twice-born man (Brāhmaṇa) should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*; a Kṣatriya, however, the *tripuṇḍra*;
a Vaiśya, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); and among the Śūdra castes, the circular mark (*vartula*)."

Thus it has been said: having applied a *tilaka* mark on the forehead, head, throat, arms, heart, navel, back, and both sides, and being seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, one should mutter "namo namaḥ" three times.
[133] Now follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Vyāsa says:
The gods deserve one handful [of water] each; Sanaka and the others, two each;
the ancestors, three each; but women, one handful each.
For each member of the group of mothers, three *añjali*s [of water] are offered. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"One should also offer three [libations] below for the sake of pleasing the gods. Thus, three are prescribed for the divine ancestors (*daiva*). In the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
One should satisfy all the gods and the brahmin seers with water mixed with unbroken grains;
one should satisfy the ancestors with devotion using water, sesame seeds, and sandalwood paste.

Śaṅkha says: One should offer water while touching the *pitṛtīrtha* [the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors], using either a vessel made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood, or a horn-vessel, or even with *kuśa* grass. Yogayājñavalkya says:
If even sesame seeds are unavailable, [one should sprinkle] with gold and silver;
in their absence, one should sprinkle with *darbha* grass or else with the mantra.
Having uttered either "May they be satisfied" or "Let them be satisfied," one who knows the ritual rule should pour water for the gods and all others without exception.

Furthermore, because it has been stated by that very [author], "then, having bent the left knee, facing south with water and sesame," the practice of falling on the right knee before the gods and sages (*devarṣi*) is established. Yama says:
"Having joined both hands together, one should fill them with a handful (*añjali*) of water;
lifting [the water] to the height of a cow's horn, one should pour the water into the midst of the [other] water."

The skillful one [should satisfy]: the gods with the tips of the kuśa grass, humans from the middle of the kuśa, and the ancestors with the roots and tips of the kuśa; such is the rule for kusha grass according to the sequence.
Yogayājñavalkya states:
One should first satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati;
then the gods, the meters, the Vedas, and the eternal sages.
The Gandharvas who are teachers, as well as the sons of teachers,
the year with its constituent parts, and likewise the goddesses and the Apsarases.
Likewise, [he saw] the gods, the followers of the gods, the nāgas, the oceans, and even the mountains;
as well as the rivers, human beings, yakṣas, and indeed rākṣasas.
The Piśācas, the Suparṇas, the Bhūtas, as well as the animals,
the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the fourfold collection of living beings.
Viṣṇu says: Then, having adjusted the sacrificial thread so that it hangs around the neck (nivīta), one should, being unwearied,
separately gratify the human beings with the prājāpatya tīrtha.
Kārṣṇājini says:
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, immediately following this [passage], it says: "Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada."
Yogayājñavalkya states:
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and facing the direction of the ancestors,
one should satisfy the divine and non-divine ancestors with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.

The eight Vasus, such as Divya, Dhara, Dhruva, and so forth; the Rudras, such as Ajaikapād and others; and the Ādityas, such as Indra, Dhātṛ, and so forth—whether individually or collectively—it is he alone.
Likewise, Kavyavāla, Nala, Soma, Yama, Aryaman, as well as the Agniṣvāttas, the Somapas, and the Barhiṣads.

If one has a living father, then he should know these [ancestors] as the *pitaras* during the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Although many methods have been stated in the *Smṛtikaumudī*, the *Padma Purāṇa*, and other texts, nevertheless—due to the agreement with the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*, the statement by Gauḍa that "Śūdras are followers of the Vājasaneya school," and because this method is seen in the context of bathing and other rites—the truth is that this very method taught by Yogayājñavalkya applies to Śūdras. Likewise, the *Vaiśvadeva* and other rites should also follow the *Kātyāyana* tradition.

[136] Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): Having taken clay, cow dung, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one goes to a river or similar place, washes one's hands and feet, holds two *pavitra* strainers made from a single *kuśa* leaf between the ring fingers, and takes hold of *kuśa* grass.
O you with upraised hair, O three-eyed one, O eater of flesh and blood!
Stay, O Goddess Śikhābaddhā Cāmuṇḍā, the unconquered!

Having said this, [33] having tied his topknot, sipped water, and recollected the place and time, he should say: "For the sake of destroying all my sins and for the pleasure of the glorious Supreme Lord (Śrī Parameśvara), I shall perform the morning bath. As for the sacred site (tīrtha):
"O you whose roar is like the sound of the ocean, who hold a staff in hand, O Sutāraka!
O Creator of the world, O Destroyer of the world, I bow to you, O Lord of the gods! [34]
O you with sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, homage to you, Bhairava; you should grant me your permission.

Having thus prayed, [one should proceed as follows]: Saying "Salutation to Varuṇa" (*varuṇāya namaḥ*), one should turn back the stream of water with that same [mantra]. Then, saying "Salutation to the waters; may my sin depart" (*namo ’dbhyo mama pāpaṃ yātu*), one should cast the *añjali* (handful) of water outside. Saying "Salutation to such-and-such holy ford" (*amukatīrthāya namaḥ*), one should offer an *añjali*. Taking clay, one should smear it three times on the hips, the abdomen, the thighs, the calves, and the feet, and then wash them. Placing one foot in the water and the other on the ground, one should smear the entire body with clay, saying "Salutation to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇave namaḥ*). Facing the sun, one should submerge oneself two, three, or twelve times. Wiping oneself while saying "Salutation to the waters" (*adbhyo namaḥ*), and having submerged and wiped oneself, one should sip water (*ācamana*). In the same manner, one should smear oneself with cow dung, saying "Salutation to Rudra" (*rudrāya namaḥ*), bathe, sip water, and purify oneself with *kuśa* grass. One should recite "Salutation to Varuṇa" eight times, and "Salutation to the Supreme Self" (*paramātmane namaḥ*). Then: "Salutation to Agni," "Salutation to Vāyu," "Salutation to Sūrya," "Salutation to Savitṛ," "Salutation to Yajña. Having submerged oneself, one should recite "Salutation to the waters" twenty-two times. Alternatively, one may recite "Salutation to Agni" three times, and "Salutation to Jātavedas, Savitṛ, Cit, etc. Having purified oneself from the navel down to the navel with *darbha* grass using these mantras beginning with "Salutation to Savitṛ," and having purified oneself again with the mantras ending in "Salutation to Savitṛ" and "Salutation to the Supreme Self," one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite by reciting "Salutation" three times, or "Salutation to the Supreme Self. Having bathed and remembered "Salutation to Viṣṇu," one should satisfy the gods beginning with Brahmā, saying "May the gods be satisfied; salutation" (*devās tṛpyantāṃ namaḥ*), three times with the right hand using the *devatīrtha* part of the hand. Saying "May the sages beginning with Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana be satisfied," one should satisfy the sages two by two with the left hand (*apasavya*). Saying "May the ancestors beginning with Soma, Pitṛmat, and Mada be satisfied," one should offer three *añjali*s three times. Having put on two washed garments, washed the hands and feet gently, and sipped water, one should apply a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) shaped like a bamboo leaf, a half-moon, or a circle. Having made or worn the ritual hand-gestures (*mudrā*), one should offer handfuls of water and flowers to each of the following: "Salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, the Directions, and the deities of the directions"—thus says Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi. Then, having worshipped the risen sun upon an eight-petaled mandala with red sandalwood, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers, one should offer the *arghya* water, as stated in the *Kalpataru*: "Salutation to you, O Vivasvat, the radiant one, the splendor of Viṣṇu; salutation to Savitṛ, the pure one, the progenitor, the giver of action. Then, offering the *arghya* again to the Supreme Self residing in the solar orb, saying "Salutation to the Supreme Self," one should repeat the names of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others according to one's ability, or offer salutation with: "Salutation to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, who consists of the three Vedas, who bears the nature of the three qualities (*guṇa*), and whose essence is Viriñci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara. This bath should be performed in the morning and at midday. If unable, it should be done only at midday. If bathing with hot water at home, the procedure is the same. For those who are ill or otherwise unable to bathe, one should perform purification with *kuśa* grass, a bath with ashes, or a bath with the dust of a cow, or wipe the limbs with a wet cloth.
Jābāli says:
For those engaged in ritual acts who are unable to perform a full bath, the bath shall be headless;
they know that the cleansing of the body may also be accomplished by wiping it with a wet cloth.

They know the *sārasvata* bath to be that which is attained through the Sarasvatī of the learned; the meaning is that it is performed by means of the speech of a Brahmin. Alternatively, a mental bath (*mārjana*) or purification should be performed. For example:
"One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who resembles the sun and has four arms."
Adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, and a forest garland.
One should contemplate that stream born from the water of His feet falling upon one’s own head,
entering one’s own body through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
By means of that [mudrā], one should wash away all impurity located within the body.
Likewise: "Whether impure or pure, even if one has reached every possible state,"
"Whoever should remember the Lotus-Eyed One [Viṣṇu] becomes pure both internally and externally.
Then, having observed the reflection in the clarified butter (ājya) within a bronze vessel:
"Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is remembered as the remover of sin."
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
Born from the wish-fulfilling cows and present in all sacrifices, you are the clarified butter, the food of the gods; therefore, grant me peace.
Having thus given [the gift] to the Brahmin, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is clearly stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

[139] Then, at midday, having bathed as before, one should perform the *brahmayajña*. Regarding that, according to the Vedic revelation: "The Brāhmaṇas, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Kalpas," and:
"The Vedas, the Atharva, the Purāṇas, together with the Itihāsas, according to one's ability."

And because of the statement by Yājñavalkya: "For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), one should recite the knowledge pertaining to the self (*adhyātmikī vidyā*)," and because even though there is an injunction for the recitation of the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, and so forth, it is impossible for a Śūdra to perform such recitation—since hearing alone constitutes a constituent part of the ritual—some maintain that the hearing of the Purāṇas itself is the *brahmayajña*. That is not correct, because [the text says]:
"One should not omit the five sacrifices with a mantra consisting of a salutation."

Because of the statement of Yājñavalkya, "Thus," there is a sublation [of other mantras] by that [mantra of salutation]. In this regard, since the Śruti says, "He who [performs] with salutation his own sacrifice," and because the Brāhmaṇa states, "Salutation (namaḥ) is indeed sacrifice (yajñaḥ)," it is appropriate that it should end with that; thus, one should perform the rite with words ending in "namaḥ. For example: having sat upon a seat of Darbha grass, having sipped water (ācamana), and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the Brahmayajña for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord," one should place the hands in the *brahmāñjali* position over the lap, hold Darbha grass within them, and mutter, "namo namo namaḥ. Alternatively, one may mutter there: "Obeisance to the Ṛgveda; likewise obeisance to the Yajurveda; obeisance to the Sāmaveda; obeisance to the Atharvaveda; obeisance to the Śikhā; obeisance to the Kalpas; obeisance to Grammar (Vyākaraṇa); obeisance to Etymology (Nirukta); obeisance to Astronomy (Jyotiṣa); obeisance to Prosody (Chandoviciti); obeisance to the Science of the Self (Adhyātmavidyā); obeisance to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; obeisance to the Science of Logic (Tarkavidyā); obeisance to the Pūrvamīmāṃsā; obeisance to the Uttaramīmāṃsā. Having thus muttered these, [one completes the rite].
Salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and indeed to the great yogis; salutation to Svāhā and to Svadhā, always salutation, salutation!

Having thus recited this three times: "May Janārdana, the praised Viṣṇu, whose source is the sacrifice of knowledge and austerity, who is himself without origin, and who is the God worshipped by the sacrifice of speech, be pleased with me."
Having said this, one should touch that water.
[140] Now follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

Some say that this [libation] should be performed with mantras ending in "namaḥ" (such as *brahmaṇe namaḥ*), because the word "namaḥ" is explicitly mentioned therein. Others, however, maintain that they should end with the word "tṛpyatām," preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, because there is no authority for omitting the word "tṛpyatām" from the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* which states: "preceded by *oṃ*, [the words] 'may they be satisfied' (*tṛpyatām*). Having bent the right knee upon the seat, one should offer libations with both hands using *darbha* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) through the *devatīrtha*. This procedure, as taught by Yājñavalkya the Yogin in the *Madanapārijāta*, is stated here in accordance with the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "May Brahmā be satisfied; may Viṣṇu be satisfied; may the Vedas be satisfied; may the Ṛṣis be satisfied; may the teachers of the Purāṇas be satisfied; may the Gandharvas be satisfied; may the other teachers be satisfied; may the Year (*saṃvatsara*) be satisfied; may the Year with its parts be satisfied; may the goddesses be satisfied; may the Apsarases be satisfied; may the attendants of the gods be satisfied; may the Nāgas be satisfied; may the oceans be satisfied; may the mountains be satisfied; may the rivers be satisfied; may human beings be satisfied; may the Yakṣas be satisfied; may the Rakṣases be satisfied; may the Piśācas be satisfied; may the Suparṇas be satisfied; may all beings (*bhūta*) be satisfied; may animals be satisfied; may the lords of the forest (*vanaspati*) be satisfied; may medicinal herbs be satisfied; may the fourfold assembly of beings be satisfied. In the *Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi*, however, [the list ends] after Prajāpati.
Gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
cruel serpents, suparṇas, trees, jambhakas, and birds.
The Vidyādharas, the clouds, and likewise those who travel through the sky;
those living beings who subsist on nothing, and those who delight in sinful dharma.
"This water is given by me for their nourishment"—
thus, according to the *Matsya-purāṇa*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is prescribed.
Then, for the sages (*ṛṣis*):

having arranged the *nivīta* [sacred thread], one should offer two handfuls (*añjali*) at a time, mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, through the middle of the darbha grass blades with their tips pointing north, using the *prajāpati-tīrtha*, while repeating the mantra for each. "May Sanaka be satisfied; may Sanandana be satisfied; may Sanātana be satisfied; may Kapila be satisfied; may Āsuri be satisfied; may Voḍhu be satisfied; may Pañcaśikha be satisfied.
Then follows the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*).

Facing south, having bent his left knee, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should offer three handfuls each with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* and double-folded *darbha* grass mixed with sesame seeds, saying: "May the Vasus be satisfied; may the Rudras be satisfied; may the Ādityas be satisfied; may the Maruts be satisfied; may the Aśvins be satisfied; may Kavyavāḍ-Anala be satisfied; may Soma be satisfied; may Yama be satisfied; may Aryaman be satisfied; may the Agniṣvāttas be satisfied; may the Somapas be satisfied; may the Barhiṣads be satisfied; may Yama be satisfied; may Dharmarāja be satisfied; may Mṛtyu be satisfied; may Antaka be satisfied; may Vaivasvata be satisfied; may Kāla be satisfied; may Sarvabhūtakṣaya be satisfied; may Audumbara be satisfied; may Dadhna be satisfied; may Nīla be satisfied; may Parameṣṭhin be satisfied; may Vṛkodara be satisfied; may Citra be satisfied; may Citragupta be satisfied. Even one whose father is living should satisfy all these up to this point. Then follows the libation for one's own ancestors (*svapitṛtarpaṇa*). Having invoked them with "Obeisance to the Pitṛs," he should say: "May our father, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named Mukadāsa, be satisfied. Thus three times. Likewise: "May the grandfather be satisfied; may the great-grandfather be satisfied. With "Obeisance to the Pitṛs," he should pour out the handful either three times or with the word "Madhu. "May our mother, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named Amukadevīdā, be satisfied. Likewise: "May the grandmother be satisfied; may the great-grandmother be satisfied; may the stepmother be satisfied. Having invoked them with "Obeisance to the Pitṛs," he should say: "May the maternal grandfather be satisfied; may the maternal great-grandfather be satisfied; may the maternal great-great-grandfather be satisfied. Likewise: "May the maternal grandmother be satisfied; may the maternal great-grandmother be satisfied; may the maternal great-great-grandmother be satisfied. Likewise: "May my wife, named Amukadevīdā, be satisfied. [Then]: son, daughter, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, one’s own brother, sisters other than the wife, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, one’s own sister—these three along with their children and their husbands. Father-in-law, teacher, friend, and those who have become friends. Or else:
May all the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, up to the praises of Brahmā,
as well as all the paternal ancestors, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.
"May this water with sesame seeds reach the millions of ancestors of past generations who dwelt in the seven continents, up to the world of Brahmā.
As for that which Hārīta states in the *Madanapārijāta*:
Having put on clean clothing upon a dry spot strewn with sacrificial grass,
one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), but never in a vessel.

Thus, that [rule] refers to libation performed at a water-source from which water has not been drawn; when water has been drawn, that same [rule applies]. Or, having taken water from a vessel, one should pour it oneself into another vessel.
It should be done in a pit filled with water, neither on dry ground nor on sacrificial grass (barhis). Thus says Yogayājñavalkya.
If one should sprinkle with water drawn up [from a vessel], one should mix sesame seeds into the water;
otherwise, the wise should take the sesame seeds with the left hand.
Moreover, this should not be performed at home by one who has sons;
on the seventh lunar day, on Sundays, at home, or likewise on one's birthday,
one who desires servants, sons, or a wife should not perform the libation with sesame seeds.
Thus, according to the *Marīci-smṛti*: "Therefore,
whatever members of our lineage who have died childless— those kinsmen of the same *gotra*—
may they accept this water squeezed from the cloth offered by me."
Thus, one should wring out the garment on the bank or on dry land. However, in the *Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi*, it is said:
"May those who are relatives or non-relatives, and those who were relatives at birth—may they all attain satisfaction, as well as those who have expectations from us."
"Salutation, salutation"—thus the pressing of the *śāṭhī* is described. Thereafter, one should perform the libations with the left hand according to the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The gods, asuras, and likewise the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas;
the piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, trees, and birds."
May all creatures— those that move in water, those that dwell on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain satisfaction by this water given by me.
This water is offered by me for the nourishment of those who abide in all the hells and amidst the various torments.
"Whether they be kinsmen or non-kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen in another birth—may they all attain satisfaction through these sesame-water offerings given by me. Thus [it is said].

The summary is as follows: With one handful of water (*añjali*), one should say, "May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied. Then, having worshipped in the water with: "Salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Savitṛ; salutation to Mitra; salutation to Varuṇa," and again with the hand: "Salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Agni; salutation to Earth; salutation to the Herbs; salutation to Vācaspati; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to the Great Ones; salutation to the Waters; salutation to the Lord of Waters; salutation to Varuṇa"—thus one performs the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having worshipped the mouth [of the deity], one should dismiss [the deities] with "Obeisance to the gods.
Thus ends the section on the bathing, libations, and other rites for a Śūdra in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
Now, regarding the worship of the deity:

in the case of the worship of ancient *liṅgas* such as those of Viśveśvara, or of earthen *liṅgas* (*pārthivaliṅga*) consecrated by oneself, the worship should be performed from a distance without physical contact. In the case of the worship of *śālagrāma*, crystal, or *liṅgas* consecrated by Brahmins, it should likewise be performed from a distance without physical contact, provided that the *liṅga* was installed according to the prescribed rules by those learned in the mantras.
From that time forward, neither a Śūdra nor a woman should touch it.

Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya, and this has been mentioned previously. And she [the image] should be made according to her name. Likewise for a woman: "The worship of Viṣṇu must be performed with the thought that He is one's husband, and not otherwise," as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa regarding the duties of a widow in the Madanapārijāta. In that same work, the Padma Purāṇa states:
One should worship Āditya, Gaṇanātha, and Devendra in their proper order,
followed by Nārāyaṇa known as Viśuddha, and finally the family deity (kuladevatā).
The Nigama states: One should worship daily Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Īśa; or Sūrya, Agni, or Gaṇādhipa; or Durgā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, or Gaurī.
As for that which Manu said:
"Muttering prayers, austerity, visiting sacred fords, renunciation, the practice of mantras,
and the propitiation of deities— these six lead to the downfall of women and Śūdras."
Thus, that [statement] refers to something other than what has been prescribed. In the *Mātsya*:
"It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of jewels;
it may also be made of stone, wood, or even of an alloy of metals."
An image of a deity made of iron, or of the five metallic essences,
or joined with the ore of bell-metal, or consisting of copper or bronze,
or even made of auspicious wood, is highly praised.
Starting from the size of a thumb-joint up to a span, an image should be made for domestic shrines; a larger one is not recommended by the wise.
In the Bhāgavata: "My sacrifice is threefold: Vaidika, Tāntrika, and Miśra.
And in the Śivārcanacandrikā, from the Pādma [Purāṇa]:
The Vedic or the mixed [form] is prescribed for Brahmins and the other [twice-born];
the Tantric is proclaimed for even a Śūdra who is devoted to a Brahmin.
In that regard, various types of ritual services (*upacāra*) have been described by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in the *Padārthādarśa*. In the *Ācāracintāmaṇi*, it is said:

"Various forms of worship (*saparyā*) have been taught; one should resort to one among them. Worship beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) and ending with the food offering (*nivedya*) is the five-fold service (*pañcopacārikā*)."
Now, the ten services (daśopacāra):

the water for honor (argha), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the seats (āsana), and the five beginning with fragrance (gandha)— these are declared to be the ten services.
[146] Now, the sixteen services:
the seat, welcome, the water of honor (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and likewise water for sipping (*ācamana*).
The honey-mixture, water for sipping, the bath, garments, and ornaments.
Incense and flowers, incense-sticks and lamps, food offerings, and likewise sandalwood paste.
Now, the eighteen services (upacāras):
the seat, the invocation, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana),
as well as the bath, the garment, the sacred thread, and all kinds of ornaments.
Likewise, [one should offer] perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps,
and food offerings, as well as garlands, ointments, prostrations, and the ritual dismissal.
Now, the thirty-six services:
the seat, the unguent, likewise the rubbing powder and the drying powder,
the sweeping, the clarified butter and other offerings, the bath, and then the invocation.

Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), water for bathing, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), again water for sipping, as well as a garment and a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, and likewise lamps;
betel leaves, food offerings, and likewise flower garlands.
Anointing ointment, a bed, a fly-whisk, a fan,
as well as the sight of a mirror, a parasol, prostration, and then circumambulation.
Then there are gifts of song and instrumental music, praise, fire-offerings, circumambulation,
the offering of tooth-sticks, and finally, the dismissal of the deity.
These thirty-six modes of worship are to be known for the propitiation of the gods;
there are also sixty-four other modes of worship, which are used for optional (kāmya) worship. These alternatives are to be adopted according to one's means.
Now, regarding circumambulations and prostrations:
in the *Bahvṛca-Pariśiṣṭa* it is said:
"One should perform one circumambulation for Vināyaka, two for Sūrya, and three for Śaṅkara."
One should offer four [prostrations] to Keśava and perform seven circumambulations around the Aśvattha tree.
But elsewhere it is said: "One circumambulation should be performed for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka,
four should be offered for Viṣṇu, and half a circumambulation for Śiva."
Vṛṣa, Caṇḍa, and Vṛṣa again; Soma and Sūtra, and Vṛṣa once more;
Caṇḍa and Soma and Sūtra, and again Caṇḍa, and Vṛṣa again.
For ascetics it is counter-clockwise, for students it is clockwise, and for householders it is both clockwise and counter-clockwise; such is the circumambulation of Śambhu.
Likewise, in the Āgneya Purāṇa:
"A wise person should perform three circumambulations in the temple of Śiva. In the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
One should proceed to the right and then to the left, never stepping over the drain. Likewise:
with chest, head, mind, and speech as well.
Prostration with the two feet, the two hands, and the two knees is called the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga).
Now, the application of the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering).

This worship (*pūjā*) should be performed using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the deity), because Hārīta has stated: "Washing, worship, the *bali* offering, and feeding [the deity] are to be done with the *devatīrtha*. [This is also stated] in the *Brāhma*.
That which has touched the limb of Brahmā should be given to the Brahmins; that which has touched the limb of Viṣṇu should likewise be given;
but that which has touched the limb of Rudra should be burned in fire, and all of it [is purified] in that very instant.
