Then, one should cast what has been given to the remaining deities into the waters on those days.
As stated in the *Madanapārijāta* and the *Gāruḍa*:
"Whatever merit is gained by the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree through fasting on the *jayantī* day..."
O Lord of Birds, that mortal may obtain all that through the worship of Tulasī.
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"Śatapuṣpa, bilva leaves, campaka, tagara,
as well as karavīra, white [flowers], pālāśa, and kuśa flowers."
Vanamālā, Aśoka, Sevantī, Kuñjamālatī,
as well as Śveta, Kunda, and Śatapatraka [worship] at the three junctions of the day.
The *mallikā* and the *jātī* are superior to all flowers; their leaves as well are likewise [superior]. Also, the *apāmārga*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *śamī* leaf, and *khādira* [are to be used].
Dūrvā grass, kuśa blades, damana, and likewise maruka;
Therefore, the bilva leaf is the most excellent, and the tulasī is even better;
the sprouts of these as well are recommended for the ritual worship of Hari.
Those who worship the Lord of Gods with black and white flowers produced from the agasti tree shall indeed attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Likewise:
"Viṣṇu, when worshipped with a garland of tulasī or even with a ketakī flower,
becomes well-pleased for a thousand years, O Madhusūdana."
Regarding things to be avoided for Śiva, it is stated in that very same source:
"The *japā* flower, the *bandhūka*, vermilion (*sindūra*), as well as both [types of] *trisandhika*,
the *nadantī*, *ketakī*, *yūthī*, *mālatī*, or *kuṭaja* flowers."
One should not offer saffron or Kumāra even through negligence, nor barbarī, sarja, parā, or the two types of kumuda.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*: "Water that has stood overnight should be discarded, as should leaves and flowers—
with the exception of *tulasī*, *agastya*, and *bilva*— and water from the Gaṅgā does not become defiled."

The specific details, however, should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu* and the *Pūrtakamalākara*, both composed by me. Now, regarding the greatness of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), [it is said] in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
Where the deity originating from Śālagrāma and the one originating from Dvāravatī exist,
the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted by the water used for bathing both of them.
In the *Lakṣaṇakāṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the *Hemādri*: "Saffron, sandalwood, betel leaves, food offerings, and pure water—
when they come into contact with a *śālagrāma* stone, they become superior to hundreds of millions of sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "He who performs an ablution with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices."
The rivers Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, and Revā, which bestow liberation,
all dwell here everywhere within the water of the Śālagrāma stone.
In the dialogue between Gautama and Ambarīṣa:
"I am always a servant under the control of those in the house of Ambarīṣa whose limbs have been washed with the water from the feet of Hari."
Having bowed deeply to Ambarīṣa, whose belly contains the water remaining from Hari’s bath, let the dust of his feet be taken up.
Other sacred fords in the three worlds may indeed roar with renown,
so long as the sacred ford of the Śālagrāma ablution has not been attained.
If you desire expiation for the sins committed since birth,
let the water from the Śālagrāma stone, which removes all evil, be resorted to.
In the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*: "The Gaṅgā, Prayāga, Gayā, Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and those holy places such as Kurujāṅgala and the Yamunā..."
The water of a sacred ford destroys sin over time,
but the water from the feet of the Blessed One purifies instantly.
He who has the water from Viṣṇu’s feet in his mouth, upon his head, and throughout his body is a celibate student, one who observes vows, a dweller in a sacred stage of life, and is ever pure.
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"The body and the self are purified by drinking the water from the feet of Hari;
having drunk it or eaten after [performing] obligatory, occasional, or optional rites, one does not incur sin."

Having drunk the water from Viṣṇu’s feet at the beginning of a vow (*vrata*) and having subsequently eaten, one does not incur fault. Regarding the reading *kṛtvā* (having performed): whether it be a compulsory (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*) rite such as the Ekādaśī vow, or an occasional (*naimittika*) rite such as the annual *śrāddha*, having drunk the water from his feet and performed that ritual act, one does not incur fault. Now, an objection:
"O best of men, even in the case of water, except for medicinal purposes, the performance of obligatory rites—along with optional and occasional ones—should be suspended after drinking it."

From the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "But the meaning is not that one does not incur sin after having performed that ritual act. If it is asked, "How can this [water] be offered when there is a prohibition against drinking before eating, as in the verse: 'This [is for one who has] not eaten, [and] for one who has eaten'?"—it is not so; for a general rule is set aside by a specific exception, and because this is a prohibition regarding what is obtained through worldly desire (*rāga*). Furthermore, from the observation of faults [in the following passage]: "Regarding an image of Viṣṇu, one should have the notion of stone; regarding gurus, the notion of a mere man; regarding a Vaiṣṇava, the notion of belonging to a particular caste; regarding the foot-water of Viṣṇu—which washes away the impurities of the Kali age—the notion of ordinary water; regarding the name of Viṣṇu, which destroys all defilements, the notion of a mere common word; and regarding Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, the notion of being equal to others—he who possesses such [notions] is a *vāraka* (one who must be avoided). Moreover, that [water] is to be drunk at the conclusion of the worship, as it is a subsequent part (*uttarāṅga*) of the rite. Those, however, who do not drink on the day of fasting or before the ritual act are deluded. For it is said: "Water is both eaten and uneaten; one should satisfy oneself with water alone."
Thus, according to the *Viṣṇuvājapeyin* school, it is stated in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Those who do not have water mixed with *tulasī*,
nor the water from the feet [of the Lord] arising from the *cakrāṅka* stone..."
O Lord of Birds, those men who have turned away from the Dharma do not float at the three junctions of the day, even though their bodies are constantly [in water].
In the *Āhnikapradīpa*:
"Whether during birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*),
no impurity exists for those who place the water from [the Guru’s] feet upon their heads and consume it."
Even at the time of death, he who here offers water at the feet of [the Guru] attains a good rebirth, even if he has been cast out for his sinful conduct.
Having eaten and drunk, one becomes purified by drinking the water used for washing the feet of Hari.
This is the word of Śiva in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That water which has been purified by the gaze of the all-powerful Viṣṇu..."
O son, that indeed removes sin; how much more so the water from the feet!
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Having drunk the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, if one subsequently suspects it is impure,
or later, due to delusion of mind, he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "One should daily drink the water from the feet [of the Lord] and eat the food offering (naivedya) of Hari;
the remains should also be worn upon the head—such is the instruction of the Vedas."
He who, without drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, merely pours it upon his head,
is declared to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.

One should drink the water from a Śālagrāma stone using the cupped palm (somakara). If done unknowingly, it is said that one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; if knowingly, one should observe it for a year.
Having drunk the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, which destroys the sins of ten million births,
one incurs eightfold sin by letting even a single drop fall upon the ground.
In the *Baktracandrodaya*: "If one has touched iron, bronze, wood, or a wooden mortar, one should declare that water from which the foot has been washed is equal to liquor."
Having taken the water from the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu in one's hand, one should pour it into one's mouth;
even if one does not offer the water during a vow, one shall dwell in the Raurava hell.
"Without having given [the water] to Viṣvaksena and the others"—this is the ellipsis. The mantra for receiving it is from Halāyudha:
"Having drunk the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, which removes untimely death and wards off all diseases, I bear it upon my head. Thus.
Now, regarding the acceptance of the favor (*prasādagrahaṇa*): in the *Skanda-purāṇa*, as cited in Hemādri’s *Mādhavīya*, it is said:
"Furthermore, he who, having fasted on the eleventh day, eats on the twelfth day..."
An offering mixed with Tulasī destroys ten million sins of killing.

As for what is stated in the *Ācārādarśa* by Śrīdatta: "If it is argued that 'having pressed the *sātvatī* [liquor] and offered it, they consume it,' this is because the consumption is mentioned as having the same agent as the offering; because of the prohibition, 'Since one has no ownership over what has been offered by another, one should carefully avoid the property of the gods and the property of the guru';
and because of the prohibition, 'Having touched a *devalaka*, one should enter the water along with one's clothes.'"
Having touched a sacrificial post, a bard, or one who subsists on the property of the gods,
one becomes pure by entering the water with one's clothes on and consuming clarified butter.
And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*). The specific details regarding me should be known from the *Ācāradīpa*.
Now, the *vaiśvadeva* rite for a *śūdra*. Śaṅkha says:
A householder should never neglect the performance of the five sacrifices.
Yama says: "The sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to the gods, and likewise the sacrifice to the ancestors..."
The sacrifice to beings and the sacrifice to men are proclaimed as the five sacrifices.

And that [rite] should be performed in a worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). Vijñāneśvara states: "In the wedding fire, so says the Teacher. For this very reason, the *Sthapatīṣṭi* is prescribed in the *Tantraratna* as being performed in a worldly fire. Those who claim that it does not even take place in a worldly fire for a Śūdra are indeed fools. Vijñāneśvara, Aparārka, and Medhātithi also say the same. In that case as well, it should be performed in the cooking fire; for it is said: "One should cook food in the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), or always in a worldly fire.
In whichever fire one cooks food, in that [fire] the oblation (*homa*) is ordained."
Thus it is stated in the *Manu-smṛti* [153]. Regarding the impossibility [of performing the rite at home], Śātātapa says:
"Whether in common or Vedic water, or in water offered after a libation, or on the ground, the Vaiśvadeva must be performed for the removal of the five slaughter-houses (*pañcasūnā*)."

And that [offering] must be made with cooked food, as in the *Sthapati-iṣṭi*; otherwise, some maintain that even there it would have to be raw. However, because it is stated that "cooked food is called *ucchiṣṭa*," the Smārta-Gaudas hold that it should be performed by the agent himself using only raw food. Regarding the Vaiśvadeva, various methods have been described by Manu and others; among these, the one stated by Manu refers to twice-born men who are without sacred fires (*niragni*), because, according to the author of the *Smṛtikaumudī*, such a person lacks the qualification for the *Gṛhya-agni* mentioned in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*. That is not so, because for one without sacred fires, the performance of oblations and other rites is prescribed by means of the *Śākala-mantras*. To this effect, Vasiṣṭha says in the *Madanapārijāta*:
But that Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire should himself offer the food with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *śākala* mantras,
and from the remainder he should present the *bhūtabali*.

The *Śākala-mantras* are six, beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ. For a Śūdra as well, according to the previously mentioned method, the *Kāṭhaka-karman* prescribes that the oblation (*homa*) be performed using the names of these deities; however, that which is stated by Manu is not applicable. This is because a Śūdra lacks the qualification for those rites due to the absence of hearing the *Śruti*. Therefore, for those belonging to the branches (*śākhā*) of Kaṭha and others in whose tradition the Vaiśvadeva is not mentioned, the rite stated by Manu applies. Alternatively, since Śūdras have the qualification to hear the Purāṇas, they should perform the Vaiśvadeva as described therein. Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Then he should worship the Fire-god and offer oblations in the proper sequence."
One should give the first [oblation] to Brahmā, and then to Prajāpati.
One should offer the third portion to the Gṛhyās, and likewise another to Kaśyapa;
thereafter, one should present an offering to Anumati, and then give the domestic oblation (gṛhabali).
One should offer three [libations] at the water-jar for Parjanya, the Cloud, and the Earth;
and [one each] for Vāyu, for the intermediate directions, and for the cardinal directions, starting from the east in due order.
To Brahmā, to the intermediate space, and to Sūrya in due order;
and likewise to all the gods and to all beings.
Then one should give to Uṣas and Bhūtapati in the north;
and having said "Svadhā, obeisance," one should also offer to the Pitṛs in the south.
"Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, [one says] 'O Yakṣman, this is your water for washing' (avanejana) toward the northwest;
then, taking water, one should pour it on the ground while pronouncing their names.
Thus, having described the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the same way in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, a specific rule regarding the food-offering (*bali*) is stated:
Then he should pour that remainder into the water-jar for Earth and Parjanya;
thereafter, he should pour [water] at the door for Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and in the middle for Brahmā.
A wise person should offer the bali consisting of the remnants of the oblation to Indra, Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, and likewise to Indu, in the eastern and other directions.
In the north-eastern direction, they know the offering to Dhanvantari is performed;
then, in the north-west and all the other directions, [the offerings] for the quarters [are made].
One should offer the bali-oblation to Brahmā, to the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and to Bhānu;
then to the Viśvedevas, to all beings (viśvabhūta), and to the ancestors who are the lords of all (viśvapati).
O Lord of Men, one should offer a bali-oblation intended for the Yakṣas.

In the Kāṭhaka Sūtra as well, this very same offering of the bali is prescribed with only slight variations. Therefore, this same [offering] applies even to a Śūdra. In that case, for a Śūdra, the mantra is prescribed as "svāhā" or a salutation (namaskāra).
Thus, according to the statement in the *Bhārata*, the word *svāhā* is used in the *homa* and the word *namaḥ* in the *bali*; so says the *Smṛtikaumudī*.
That is not correct, because it contradicts the rule: "with the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*). Furthermore, that *balidāna* should be performed in the areas of the house or behind the fire.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and either silently restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) or otherwise, having recollected the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the removal of the five slaughtering grounds (*pañcasūnā*) and for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord, I shall perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Then, having swept the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), smeared it with cow-dung, and drawn lines upon it, one should remove the soil with the thumb and ring finger, sprinkle it with water, and establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*). [One should worship it with: "Obeisance to Agni!
He who is the mouth of all the gods, the eater of offerings to the gods (*havyabhuj*), and likewise the eater of offerings to the ancestors (*kavyabhuj*)."
And salutation to that Viṣṇu, the soul of the fire, who is the father of the ancestors.

Having thus performed worship and sprinkled water around the fire, one should prepare a *caru* (cooked sacrificial rice) in the fire using either household food, rice grains soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*), or fruits. Having placed that substance in the fire, removed it, and sprinkled it with water, one should offer it by hand, saturated with clarified butter. An oblation (*āhuti*) should fill twelve finger-joints or be the size of an *āmalaka* fruit. For example: "Salutation to Agni; this is for Agni, not mine"—this is the renunciation (*tyāga*). The same applies to the following: "Salutation to Vāyu," "Salutation to Sūrya," "Salutation to Prajāpati," "Salutation to Agni," and "Salutation to Brahmā. These are the six. This concludes the *Śākala-homa*. Then: "Salutation to Anumati," "Salutation to the Viśvedevas," and "Salutation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Thereafter, having sprinkled water around the fire and applied sacred ash (*vibhūti*), one should pay obeisance. According to the opinion of Vijñāneśvara:
"To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;

salutation to Svāhā, to Svadhā—always salutation, salutation. With this [formula], the oblation is offered once. Some say that the oblation is offered with the mantra "Salutation" alone. In the *Pariśiṣṭa* of the *Madanapārijāta*:
"Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit..."
Whatever one intends regarding food, with that one should also offer oblations into the fire.
Vyāsa says: One should offer oblations smeared with clarified butter, avoiding oil and alkaline substances;
or smeared with curd, or smeared with milk; or, in the absence of these, even with water.

In the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "If [the proper materials] are unavailable, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva with whatever is at hand— such as fruits, vegetables, water, and so forth— or with milk, curd, and ghee, using a *sruva* ladle."
"One should perform [the offering] with water from the palms using the *hastena* and other mantras while in the water.
Thus is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).
Now follows the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña).

In the center: *namaḥ* to Parjanya; *namaḥ* to the Waters; *namaḥ* to the Earth. On the two door-posts: *namaḥ* to Dhātṛ. The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This is for Dhātṛ, not for me. The same applies hereafter. *Namaḥ* to Vidhātṛ. In every direction: *namaḥ* to Vāyu; *namaḥ* to the Quarters (*diś*). To Indra; *namaḥ* to Dharmarāja; *namaḥ* to Varuṇa; *namaḥ* to Indu. In the northeast (*īśānī*), *namaḥ* to Dhanvantari. In the northwest (*vāyavī*), *namaḥ* to Vāyu. *Namaḥ* to Brahmā; *namaḥ* to the Atmosphere (*antarikṣa*); *namaḥ* to Sūrya. In the north, *namaḥ* to the Viśvedevas; *namaḥ* to the Viśvebhūtas; *namaḥ* to Bhūtānāṃpati. Then, on the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*): *svāhā namaḥ* to the Pitṛs. "This is for the Pitṛs. Touching water. This is the Kāṭhaka tradition and the Paurāṇika tradition. Some say there is no word *svadhā*. Having washed the vessel, one should pour out [the remainder] toward the northwest with the words, "O Yakṣman, this is for you. "This is for Yakṣman. Or else, the *bali* offering on the ground is made simply with the words, "To the deities and to the Pitṛs. Some say that by this alone the *pitṛyajña* is accomplished. In the *Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi*, however, when the Brahmin says, "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā," one should oneself offer the oblation saying, "namo namaḥ. Thus both separately and collectively. Then, when the Brahmin says, "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā," one should perform the homa oneself saying "namaḥ. That is not correct, because the Vedic formula is set aside by the salutation (*namaskāra*). To Agni, "this" [is the offering]; thus six [offerings]. Then to Yama as Sviṣṭakṛt. On the ground: *namaḥ* to the Viśvedevas; *namaḥ* to all beings (*sarvabhūta*); *namaḥ* to the Pitṛs—thus on the south. In the northeast, "O Yakṣman, this is for you"—thus one [offering] according to the Paurāṇikas. To the Cāṇḍālas and others, and to the crows. It is said that one should give [the offering] to Dharmarāja and Citragupta on the south. Then, taking the remainder and sprinkling it in the courtyard of the house: 16. *namaḥ* to Dhanvantari; 10. *namaḥ* to the eastern quarter; 5. *namaḥ* to Vidhātṛ; 6. *namaḥ* to Vāyu; 27. *namaḥ* to Viśvapati; 21. *namaḥ* to Antarikṣa; 4. *namaḥ* to Dhātṛ; 17. *namaḥ* to Indu; 26. *namaḥ* to Bhūpati; 20. *namaḥ* to Brahmā; 11. *namaḥ* to the southern quarter; 18. *namaḥ* to Vāyu; 25. *namaḥ* to the Viśvebhūtas; 3. *namaḥ* to Pṛthivī; 7. *namaḥ* to Vāyu; 24. *namaḥ* to Yakṣman; 23. *namaḥ* to the Viśvebhūtas; 2. *Atyaḥ*; 15. *namaḥ* to Dharmarāja; 12. *namaḥ* to the western quarter; 1. *namaḥ* to Parjanya; 2. *svadhā* to the Pitṛs; 8. *namaḥ* to Vāyu; 15. *namaḥ* to Varuṇa.
There are two dogs, one black and one brindled, born from the lineage of Vaivasvata;
to them I shall offer this funeral cake—may these two be free from violence.
"Salutation to the two dogs. Having said this and having taken [the offering] again, [he says]:
"May the crows belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise to Nirṛti, accept the ball offered by me upon the ground."
Having thus offered the *kākabali* and said, "This for the crows," he should take it up again and offer the oblations with the mantras spoken in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*,
as follows: "The gods, humans, animals, birds, the Siddhas, along with the hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas..."
Pretas, piśācas, trees, and all others who desire food—may it be granted by me. || 1 ||
This is for the gods and others;
and for the ants, insects, moths, and the like,
who are hungry and bound by the fetters of karma.
May they attain satisfaction; this food has been offered by me to them—may they be happy. (2)
This [is for] ants and the like—
those who have neither mother nor father, neither kinsman nor means of preparing food, and likewise no food at all.
May this food given on the earth for their satisfaction reach them;
may they attain contentment and be joyful. || 3 ||
This is for those who have no protector;
likewise, all beings, this food,
and I am Viṣṇu— for there is nothing other than this.
Therefore, I offer food, which is the very essence of the multitude of beings, for their sustenance. || 4 ||
This [is offered] to the spirits:
to this fourteenfold host of spirits, and indeed to those multitudes of spirits who dwell therein.
For this food has been released by me for the sake of their satisfaction; may they be joyful with it. || 5 ||
Having recited, "This [is for] the hosts of spirits and others," a person endowed with faith should offer food upon the ground for the benefit of those beings,
since the householder is the refuge of all.
Then the man should give [the food] on the ground to dogs, outcastes, and birds,
as well as to any other fallen men on earth who are childless.

"Then he should remain in the courtyard of the house for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow. Thus it is stated. Furthermore, in the *Nāgadevahnikā* and the *Haribhāṣya* of Hariharā, it is said that one should then give [food] to those fallen from their caste due to worms and the like, to those afflicted by sinful diseases, to outcastes (*śvapaca*), and so forth. Although this *vaiśvadeva* rite has been prescribed for the twice-born both morning and evening, nevertheless, for *śūdras*, it is to be performed only during the day and not in the evening. This is because of the mention of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) [for them], and because there is no specific injunction for a *vaiśvadeva* rite [in the evening]. Regarding this, Jamadagni states in the *Madanapārijāta*:
"One should perform the *vaiśvadeva* during the day, and likewise the offering of the *bali* at night."
The knower of dharma has declared that one should perform the five great sacrifices only during the day.
Therefore, because it is distinct from the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), the *vaiśvadeva* rite does not apply to a *śūdra*; this is the summary. Thus concludes the *vaiśvadeva*.
[159] Now follows the daily ancestral offering (*nityaśrāddha*).
Is that [offering] to be performed separately, or not?
For the *Chandoga-praiṣiṣṭa* states: "The *śrāddha* may be the *pitṛyajña*, or it may be the *pitrya bali*. Thus says Manu.
A householder, always composed, should feed even a single Brahmin; [so says] Pracetas:
there is no formal invitation, no fire-oblation, and no rites of invocation or dismissal.
The best of the twice-born should not offer funeral cakes nor consume wine at the daily rites.

Vyāsa states: There is no invocation (āvāhana), no utterance of "svadhā," no offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), no pouring into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and so forth; likewise, there are no rules regarding celibacy and the like, nor are there the Viśvedevas.
That [rite] should be known as involving six persons, excluding the *piṇḍa* offerings to the south.
Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there is an option, because of the statement by Pracetas: "Having given something, one should dismiss [the Brahmins].
Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

Having sipped water (ācamana) and recollected the place and time, and having declared, "I shall perform the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*)," he should offer the invitation (*kṣaṇa*) by saying: "In the place of my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of the lineage of Kāśyapa, named so-and-so-dāsa, and likewise of my maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, together with their wives, let the moment of invitation be granted. Having given the invitation, and having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) to the ancestors and maternal ancestors, saying, "This is your *pādya*," and having sipped water again, he should sit facing north on a seat of *kuśa* grass. He says: "This is the seat for the ancestors and maternal ancestors. Let the moment of invitation be made for the ancestral rite (*pitrye*). May you accept it; I accept it. When this has been said, he offers to the ancestors and maternal ancestors: "This is your fragrance; these are flowers; incense, a lamp, and clothing. Having caused [the guests] to declare the completion of the rite, he prepares double the amount of raw rice (*āmānna*), sprinkles it, touches the vessel, scatters sesame seeds, and places his thumb in the food. He says: "O ancestors, this is your raw rice, doubled or equal in measure, along with its accompaniments. This land is Gayā; the Brahmin is Gadādhara; this is the form of Brahmā. To the ancestors of the Kāśyapa lineage, named so-and-so-dāsa, who are of the nature of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, and likewise to the maternal grandfather and others—may this raw offering be accomplished as *svadhā*. Salutations! What is given may become inexhaustible! May it be an offering to Brahmā! Having recited "Madhu" three times, he says: "May the sprinkling be auspicious; may the waters be propitious; may there be joy; may there be well-being and freedom from misfortune. O ancestors, grant long life, prosperity, and well-being! What is given to the ancestors may be inexhaustible. He may or may not give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). If one is unable to do all this, the daily *śrāddha* is accomplished by the ancestral offering (*pitryabali*) alone.
Thus concludes the daily śrāddha; now follows the sacrifice to human beings (manuṣyayajña).
Hārīta says:
All the deities come to the house of that man to whose home a learned Brāhmaṇa thus approaches. The vital deities wait upon him;
[so does] Bṛhaspati.
Agni is pleased by a welcome; Śatakratu by a seat;
the ancestors by the washing of the feet; and Prajāpati by the food.
Yājñavalkya says: A traveler on the road is to be known as a guest, as is a learned Vedic scholar who has mastered the Vedas;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman.
One should follow a learned guest who has been satisfied as far as the boundary of one's own dwelling.
Yama says: One should not inquire about his lineage, Vedic school, country, name, family, or sacred learning.
A Brahmin who has arrived from afar and stands before one seeking food.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Whatever sin belongs to men when a lunar day (tithi) has passed while the moon is turned away,
that very same sin becomes eightfold for men when the sun has also passed while turned away."

The meaning is "at sunset. Then, having waited for a guest, washed his feet, honored him, and offered food, one should give [the remainder] to some brahmin or to human beings such as Sanaka and others, saying, "This is not mine. Hari and Hara state that this occurs prior to the *nityaśrāddha*. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Whether he is a friend or a foe, a fool or even a scholar, a guest who arrives at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is a bridge to heaven."
Then follows the feeding of cows. In the *Madanapārijāta*, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "One should always, with a concentrated mind, offer morsels of food to the cows."
Scratching the cows, touching them, feeding them, and likewise attending to their daily needs.
The mantras, however, are: "O daughters of Surabhi, benefactors of all, pure, destroyers of sin— may you,
the mothers of the three worlds, accept this morsel."

"O Surabhi, O Mother of the World, O Goddess, you who abide in the foot of Viṣṇu; accept this morsel given by me, for you, O Mother of Cows, ought to protect us. Thus [it is said] in the *Śrīdattīya-bhaviṣya*.
If one provides the daily fodder for cows consisting of grass and water, one should know that this yields the fruit of giving a hundred Kapila cows; of this there is no doubt.
*Gavāhnika* refers to fodder for a cow sufficient for one day and night. The mantra is as follows:
"O daughter of Surabhi, auspicious, meritorious, pure, and born of the sun; in these five elements, accept this which has been given by me. Homage be unto you!"

Now, regarding the meal: having fed children, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, female friends, kinsmen, and others, and having washed one's hands and feet and sipped water twice, one should, in a clean and secluded place,
[draw] a square, a triangle, a circle, and a half-moon.
The mandala should be constructed in the proper sequence among the Brahmins and the other castes.
Having performed either the *ardhacandra* rite as stated by Vyāsa, or the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) as stated by Śaṅkha— “sprinkling is prescribed for the Śūdra”—
the householders should always use a bronze vessel weighing fifty palas and two more for eating, in the absence of gold or silver.

Thus, in the *Hemādri*, it is stated by Atri: Having seated oneself facing east, remaining silent, and having sprinkled with ghee the food served in a vessel of bell-metal or similar material, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the south, saying: "Salutation to Dharmarāja; salutation to Citra; salutation to Citragupta; salutation to the departed spirits (*pretas*). Then, having offered water, sipped water, and silently partaken of five mouthfuls with the thumb using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods), or simply saying "Salutation," one should eat at ease. In the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "One should not cause [another] to take the clarified butter while still impure from eating; nor should one discard what remains after burning [it]. Pulastya says:
A wise person should never finish their meal entirely,
except in the case of curd, milk, honey, and roasted grain flour.
Vṛddha-Manu:
"One should not drink water offered by a Śūdra with only one hand," and so forth; such rules for Śūdras should be understood to be the same as those for the twice-born. Devala: [continues].
Having taken a little from all the remnants of the meal, he should sip water;
he should then offer water with those remnants upon the ground for those who are entitled to the remains.
At the end of the meal, having again sipped water, one should sprinkle the remainder [on the ground]. The mantra is as follows:
"May this water, given to those who dwell in the hundreds of millions of lotuses in Raurava, the abode of merit, reach those who seek it and become inexhaustible."
Then, having washed his face, hands, and feet, sipped water twice, touched his knees, and sipped water again:
"May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest the food eaten by me in its entirety."
May this happiness of mine arise from its full maturation, and may my body be free from disease.
For the sake of digesting food, I call upon Agastya, Kumbhakarṇa, Śani, and the submarine fire,
as well as Vṛkodara.

Thus, having touched his abdomen and consumed betel leaf, he should spend the remainder of the day listening to ancient scriptures and other such activities. Then, at night—provided it is a night distinct from those of a solar eclipse, a lunar parvan, a *saṃkrānti*, a *vyatīpāta*, a *vaighṛti* yoga, a *śrāddha*, or the day preceding a *śrāddha*—and having eaten a second meal, he should sleep after one watch (*yāma*) has passed. Having bowed with the mantras: "Obeisance to Agasti; obeisance to Mādhava; obeisance to Mucakuṇḍa; obeisance to Kapila; obeisance to Āstika," he should sleep placing his head toward the east or the south. In that regard, for a woman during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), within the first four days—excluding the twelfth and thirteenth days—and specifically on the sixteenth day, she should engage in union on a night distinct from the fourth, sixth, eighth, fourteenth, the two *parvan* days, a *śrāddha*, or the day preceding a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, avoiding Saturdays, Sundays, and Tuesdays, as well as the constellations (*nakṣatra*) of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Maghā, Pūrvā-phalgunī, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvā-āṣāḍhā, and Pūrvā-bhādrapada, and avoiding the three birth-stars (*trijanman*), a *saṃkrānti*, a *pāta*, or a *vaighṛti* yoga, she should engage in union during an equal night. She should then perform purification three times that of urination and take a bath. This is as previously stated: having performed this except for the bath during the non-fertile period, she should sleep. One should perform this daily ritual every day.

Thus ends the section on the Daily Duties (*Āhnika*) of Śūdras in the *Śūdradharmakamalākara*, composed by Kamalākara, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of the illustrious Jagadguru Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Now follows the procedure for the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha for a Śūdra. (In this regard, the duties of the preceding day:)

Madanapāla maintains that this rite may be performed according to any branch (*śākhā*) at the discretion of the officiating Brāhmaṇa. This is not correct, because that which is indeterminate cannot constitute *dharma*. Therefore, based on the statement of Dakṣa in the Gauḍa texts—"Śūdras are followers of the Vājasaneyins"—which is corroborated by the *Harihara-bhāṣya* and other works, as well as by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is performed according to the Mādhyandina branch. The performer, having eaten only once the day before without meat, should go to the house of a twice-born man either at nightfall or the following morning. Having seated him within a ritual circle (*maṇḍala*), he should bend his right knee with his left hand. According to the injunction, "The Śūdra [should act] preceded by a prostration," he should bow down, remember the place and time, and say: "For the sake of the three ancestors beginning with the father, the three maternal grandfathers beginning with the maternal grandfather, and the Viśvedevas, I invite you for the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha to be performed tomorrow. Alternatively, after giving a moment [of attention], he should say, "May you show me favor. Having given fruit or betel-leaf, he should invite one or two Brāhmaṇas. When the invited one has replied, "I am so invited," [The text continues with the subsequent rites.]
In the performance of the śrāddha rite, you as well as I must remain free from anger, devoted to purity, and constantly observant of celibacy.
On the preceding day,
you must remain free from all exertion and devoid of desire and anger,
as the śrāddha rite is to take place on the following day.

Thus he should either recite this mantra or listen to it. Then, in the same manner, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), and bending the left knee, he should say: "I invite you for the place of the *pitṛ*s in the *śrāddha* to be performed tomorrow. "I am invited. In the same way for the place of the grandfather and the great-grandfather. Likewise for the three places beginning with the maternal grandfather—thus six. For the *vaiśvadeva* portion, there are four; thus ten in total. In that regard, in the *vaiśvadeva* case, there are eight; or one for the *daiva* (divine) rite performed in common (*tantra*) for the *pitṛ*s and so on, and one for the maternal grandfather and so on—thus three; or else, one for the six [ancestors] and one for the *daiva*—thus two. Having divided that raw rice (*āmānna*) into six portions, although it is stated that on the new moon day (*darśa*) the *śrāddha* may have nine deities with the mother in the middle, or twelve deities including the maternal grandmothers, nevertheless, the arrangement follows local custom. However, the six-deity version alone is widely accepted. In every case, if Brahmins are unavailable, even after placing them in the form of *darbha* grass, having performed the *śrāddha* preceded by the ritual calls and responses, he should give that raw rice to a Brahmin or cast it into the fire. In all instances, the response is "I am invited," and the injunction is "by those free from anger. [166] Then, on the following day at dawn, having smeared the site and bathed with his clothes on, he should prepare the materials for the *śrāddha*. After six *muhūrtas* of the day have passed, he should summon the twice-born (*dvija*s). On a day not forbidden for shaving, he should have them undergo the shaving of their beards and have bathing water, oil, *āmalaka*, and ointments sent to them. At midday, standing with palms joined, he asks those who have arrived after bathing, "Are you welcome? When they reply, "We are very welcome," he performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice, recalls the place and time, and makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall immediately perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the Kāśyapa gotra, named So-and-so, who are of the nature of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, together with the *daiva* rite and the *sapiṇḍana*, according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure, using *āmānna* and non-meat offerings. Then, having made a square and a circular mandala, each a span in size, at the door to the north and south respectively, using cow urine and cow dung, therein—
One should scatter kuśa grass for the rite of the gods and barley and sesame seeds for the rite of the ancestors.

Thus says Madanapāla. However, the true principle is that sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) is prescribed for a Śūdra; therefore, having performed the sprinkling, facing north with his upper body turned toward the north, he asks with his left hand, "O Viśvedevas named Purūravas and Ārdrava, welcome! When the other replies, "A very warm welcome," he himself—because of the rule "for a Śūdra [the worship is] with perfumes and flowers"—first worships the left foot and then the right, saying, "O Viśvedevas named Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is for you: water for the feet (*pādya*) and the guest-offering (*arghya*), obeisance. Having thus given it to the two Brahmins representing the gods, he then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), gives it to the Brahmin representing the ancestors, saying: "O our father, Kāśyapa-gotra, Amukadāsa, in the form of Vasu, this is for you: water for the feet and the guest-offering, obeisance. It should be understood that the same applies to the grandfather and great-grandfather, using the forms of Rudra and Āditya respectively. Likewise for the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather. Then, after they have sipped water twice, he himself sips water; for the two representing the gods, facing east, he touches the seat with his left hand and seats the Brahmins with his right, saying, "Obeisance to the gods; here is the seat, please sit. In the same way, for the ancestors, facing north with the sacred thread over the right shoulder. Then, in the east, for the maternal grandfathers.
At the conclusion of the *śrāddha* water-offering, during the washing of the feet, as well as during the worship,
the scattering of food (*vikira*), and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), double sipping of water (*dvir-ācamana*) is prescribed.
Then, having filled the ritual vessel with water using the left hand and having cast into it perfumes, flowers, and *kuśa* grass,
[one should recite]: "Whether impure or pure, or even if one has reached any state whatsoever,
whoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*) is pure both externally and internally."
Having sprinkled the materials for the *śrāddha* with the words, "Homage to the lotus-eyed one (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*)," [he says]:
"May the sesame seeds protect against the *asuras*; may the *darbha* grass protect against the *rākṣasas*;
may the learned *śrotriya* protect the row; the guest is the protector of all."

Having thus scattered sesame seeds, one should offer lamps to each brāhmaṇa. However, the sanctifiers for the raw rice offerings (*āmānna*) and so forth are as follows: some [recite], "The seven hunters in the Daśārṇa forest, the deer on Mount Kālañjara, the cakravāka birds on Śaradvīpa, and the swans in Lake Mānasa."
They too were born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
renowned for a long time, why do you despair?
I always pay homage to those who are beyond the sun, who possess embodied forms and blazing splendor, who are ever-meditating and endowed with the eye of yoga.
Having meditated upon Gayā, the ground of the śrāddha, having meditated upon the god Janārdana,
and having meditated upon the ancestors beginning with the Vasus, I shall then perform the śrāddha.
Thus they mutter. Then, having tied the knot of the lower garment and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), [they say]:
"To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis;
salutation to Svāhā and to Svadhā; eternal salutation, salutation indeed."

Having recited this three times and recalled the place and time, [he says]: "I shall perform this commenced *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, of the Kāśyapa *gotra*; and likewise for our maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, named so-and-so, of the Kāśyapa *gotra*. When they have replied, "Do so," he should bend his right knee and, saying, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, who are connected to the triad of ancestors beginning with the father and the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather, this seat is for you; *namaḥ*," he should place two straight blades of *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing east upon the seat. According to the *Ḍhondupaddhati*, the use of the genitive case is appropriate. Having offered *kuśa* grass and said, "May the moment (*kṣaṇa*) be made for the gods," and when he has replied, "So be it," [the performer] says, "May you receive it," and the Brahmin says, "I shall receive it. The same applies to the second deity. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), bending his left knee, and saying, "O our father, named so-and-so, of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, in the form of Vasu, this seat is for you; *svadhā namaḥ*," he should offer twice-bent *kuśa* grass along with sesame seeds. For the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), he should say, "May the moment be made," as before. Likewise for the grandfather and others, and the maternal grandfather and others. With the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), having asked, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," and being permitted with the words "Invoke them," he should take hold of the thumb of the hand of each divine Brahmin.
May the illustrious Viśvedevas of great power come;
may those who are invited here to this śrāddha be attentive.

Having thus [168] praised [them] (60), and having said, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdravasu, come," one should scatter sesame seeds from the feet to the head; so says Karka. Others say "sesame seeds" based on the Smṛti rule, "having scattered with barley. Then, water for the hands. Thus for each item. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), having been asked, "I invite the ancestors of our lineage, beginning with our father, named So-and-so Dāsa, and likewise the maternal grandfathers and others," and being authorized by the reply "Invite them," one should scatter sesame seeds from the head to the feet, saying: "O our father, So-and-so Dāsa, of the Kāśyapa gotra, in the form of Vasu, come! Likewise for the grandfather in the form of Rudra, and the great-grandfather in the form of Āditya; and likewise for the maternal grandfathers. Then, in front of the gods, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), having placed two *kuśa* blades in a single vessel, one should pour water with the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods) while saying "Salutation to the gods," and likewise drop barley, sandalwood paste, and flowers while saying "Salutation. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, for the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), having placed two *pavitra* blades (grass rings) with their tips pointing south into six vessels—made of silver, copper, iron, *palāśa* wood, or clay, or all of the same material—one should pour water while saying "Salutation to the waters," barley while saying "Salutation to the sesame seeds," and drop sandalwood paste and flowers. Having said, "The *arghya* vessels are ready," and being told, "They are well-prepared," one should place the *pavitra* blades in the hands of the gods with the left hand. Then, using the vessel held in the right hand, one should offer the *arghya* to the three ancestors starting with the father and the three maternal grandfathers, along with the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdravasu, saying: "This is your *arghya*, salutation," or "This *arghya* is for you, salutation. Having consecrated the flowing water with "Salutation to the waters" and offered it in the second vessel, and having placed the *pavitra* blades in the vessel, one should turn it face down to the north, saying "You are the place for the gods. Some do not desire this for the gods. Ḍhondu says there should be no turning face down. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, having placed a *pavitra* blade with its tip pointing south in the hand of the ancestor, one should offer it through the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) while saying: "O our father, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named So-and-so Dāsa, this is your *arghya*, *svadhā* and salutation. Having consecrated the flowing water with "Salutation to the waters" and kept the *pavitra* blades there, one should give in the same manner to the grandfather and great-grandfather, and to the maternal grandfathers and others. Then, having collected the flowing water into the first vessel, one should turn it face down to the north of the ancestors and to the south of the performer, saying "You are the place for the ancestors," and must not move it until the end of the rite. Then, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having given water, one should offer sandalwood paste to the Viśvedevas, saying "This sandalwood paste is for you, salutation," and flowers, saying "These flowers are for you, salutation. Likewise, one should offer incense, lamps, clothing, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), ornaments, and betel. Having given water, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should offer to the father: "O our father, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named So-and-so Dāsa, this sandalwood paste is for you, salutation," and likewise flowers, incense, lamps, clothing, ornaments. One should give in the same way to the grandfather and great-grandfather, and likewise to the maternal grandfathers and others. Then, having had the completion of the worship announced, one should sweep the ground in front of the twice-born (*dvija*), arrange rows of *palāśa* leaves and other leaves, and draw a mandala with white earth, ash, or other materials. Taking a portion of the raw rice (*āmānna*) from the *śrāddha* food, one should ask the head of the row, "I shall perform the *agnau-karaṇa* (offering into the fire). When told, "Do so," one should sprinkle water on the hand of the first twice-born with the sacred thread over the left shoulder, spread *darbha* grass, and taking two portions according to the rule of *avadāna* (cutting off portions), one should offer into the fire while saying: "Salutation to Agni Kavyavāhana," and recite: "This is for Agni Kavyavāhana. Taking again, one offers: "Salutation to Soma Pitṛmat," and "This is for Soma Pitṛmat. In the case of the *apasavya* method, the offering to Soma comes first and the offering to Agni comes after. Having offered thus, one should set aside the remnants of the offering for the sake of the *piṇḍas*. One should silently place [the remainder] into the vessels of the grandfather and great-grandfather, and the maternal grandfathers and others. Then, having given other raw food to the gods and sprinkled the vessels, one should give fourfold, twofold, or equal amounts of raw food starting with the gods, and having sprinkled it, with the right knee bent and the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should touch the vessel with the right hand raised and the left lowered, and place the thumb of the twice-born while saying: "Salutation to Viṣṇu" or "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering (*havya*). In the same way, for the ancestral rite, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should touch the vessel, place the thumb, scatter sesame seeds, and touch water. Having done this for each vessel, holding the divine vessel with the left hand and taking *kuśa* grass, barley, and water in the right, one should say: "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdravasu, connected to the *śrāddha* of the three ancestors starting with the father and the three maternal grandfathers, this raw food with its accompaniments is for you. This is the land of Gayā; Gadādhara is the eater; I am Brahmā, the receiver; the raw food is Brahmā, the form of Brahman, situated in a golden vessel imagined by the mind, under the shade of the imperishable banyan tree. I bestow this upon the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdravasu for the sake of imperishable satisfaction, *svāhā*, not mine. May this raw food with its accessories become nectar. [169] Salutation to the offering (*havya*). What is given at Kāśī at the feet of Viśveśvara, may it be imperishable. May Gadādhara of Gayā be pleased. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, taking double-folded *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, and holding the vessel with the left hand, bending the left knee, one should say: "O our father, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named So-and-so Dāsa, this raw food with its accompaniments is for you. This is the land of Gayā... and so on, ending with: "Situated in a silver vessel under the shade of the imperishable banyan tree, I bestow this raw food with its accessories upon our father, of the Kāśyapa gotra, named So-and-so Dāsa, in the form of Vasu, for the sake of imperishable satisfaction, *svadhā* and salutation. May it become nectar. Salutation to the offering (*kavya*). At Kāśī... and so on, as before. One should give in the same way to the grandfather and great-grandfather, and to the maternal grandfathers and others. Having given the scattering (*vikira*) with the words "This is the *piṇḍa* for those who died without sacraments," and taking the raw food, one should give the *ucchiṣṭa-piṇḍa* (remnant ball) with water
Now follows the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍadāna).

That [offering] should be prepared with cooked rice, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), barley meal (*saktu*), roots, or fruits. Having formed a mound (*vedi*) for the purpose of the *piṇḍas*, he should bend his left knee, and with the *apasavya* (sacred thread over the right shoulder) and the root-end of a *darbha* grass, draw a line toward the south; having drawn a second [line] in the same manner, he should touch water, place a firebrand (*ulmuka*) at the tip of the lines, and with a vessel of water, offer libations (*avanejana*) at the root, middle, and tip of the first line, saying: "O *Kāśyapa*-gotra, our father, *Amukadāsa*, in the form of Vasu, accept this water. Having offered thus for the grandfather and great-grandfather, and having offered on the second line to the three beginning with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), he should cast *sakṛdācchinna* *kuśa* grasses toward the south on both lines. Having placed in a vessel food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and all seasonings, together with the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering, and having made six *piṇḍas*, he should offer them by the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), saying: "O *Kāśyapa*-gotra, our father, *Amukadāsa*, this food is for you, *svadhā*; this *piṇḍa* is for you, not mine," or simply "This is for the father. Then, having placed *kuśa* grass between [the hands], he offers to the three beginning with the grandfather, saying: "O *Kāśyapa*-gotra, our grandfather... and so forth. Having wiped his hands at the roots of the *darbhas* for those who partake of the smears (*lepabhuj*), and having offered similarly to the three beginning with the maternal grandfather, he should wash his hands, sip water, turn toward the north, and restrain his breath. He should pay homage to the six seasons, saying: "Homage to Spring! Homage to Summer! and so on. With the *apasavya* [arrangement], he should join his palms in *añjali* and say: "Homage to the Fathers! and likewise, "Homage to the Maternal Grandfathers! Then, turning counter-clockwise and facing north, restraining his breath, and turning back again, he bows, saying: "Homage to the Fathers! Homage to the Maternal Grandfathers! He should then offer the secondary libation (*pratyavanejana*) on the six *piṇḍas* as before, saying: "O *Kāśyapa*-gotra, our father, *Amukadāsa*, accept this water," and so on. Having loosened the knot of his lower garment (*nīvī*), he bows, saying: "Homage to the Fathers! Homage to the Maternal Grandfathers! He should give threads upon each *piṇḍa*, saying: "Homage to the Fathers! Homage to the Maternal Grandfathers! He should pour the remainder of the libation water, or the water used for washing the *piṇḍa*-vessel, clockwise over the *piṇḍas* of the fathers, saying: "Homage to the Fathers! Homage to the Maternal Grandfathers! Then, having muttered three times: "To the Devas and to the Pitṛs," he should present perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, fruit, and betel-leaf upon the *piṇḍas* under the names of the father and others, and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He should then offer the water from the ritual vessel (*karmapātra*), saying: "May it be well-sprinkled (*suprokṣita*); may the waters be auspicious (*śivā*). For the deities, he says: "May there be mental satisfaction (*saumanasya*)," and offers flowers. For the ancestors, with the *apasavya* arrangement, he says: "May there be no harm (*akṣata*) and prosperity (*ariṣṭa*)," and offers unbroken grains (*akṣata*). Having given [these] to the fathers and maternal grandfathers, he says over his own head: "May there be long life; may there be nourishment; may there be increase; may that which is auspicious be ours; may that which is evil be averted; may there be peace for bipeds and quadrupeds on the earth. The twice-born respond: "So be it. Then he says: "For the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, may what has been given—raw grain and so forth—be inexhaustible (*akṣayya*). Likewise for the *Kāśyapa*-gotra father *Amukadāsa*, and so on. Similarly for the grandfather and maternal grandfather, the Brahmins respond: "May it be inexhaustible. He says: "May the fathers be non-terrible (*aghora*); likewise the maternal grandfathers; may our lineage increase; may our givers increase; may our progeny increase; may our faith not depart; may we have much to give; may we have much food; may we obtain guests; may there be those who ask of us; and may we not have to ask anyone. The Brahmins respond: "So be it. Then he says: "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the fathers and maternal grandfathers. The Brahmins respond: "Let there be *svadhā*. Having placed *kuśa* grass on the *piṇḍas* and turned the *arghya*-vessels face up, he gives a sacrificial fee: gold for the gods and silver for the fathers. Having given raw grain and gold to those of various names and lineages, and having removed the *piṇḍas* and smelled them, he causes [the Brahmins] to recite: "May the Viśvedevas be pleased. Having performed the rites for the ancestors in this way, with the *savya* [arrangement], he says: "May there be well-being; let them speak of well-being. When they have said "Well-being," he causes them to recite: "May there be completion. Having dismissed them with *kuśa* grass, saying: "May the fathers rise together with the Viśvedevas," and having circumambulated the mandala clockwise and bowed, he should bid them farewell.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* of Śūdras, composed by the venerable Kamalākara.
Having described the duties of Śūdras, Kamalākara Śramaṇa, the son of Rāmakṛṣṇa,
now describes their impurity (*āśauca*).

In this regard, although everything has been stated in our *Nirṇayasindhu*, nevertheless, something concerning Śūdras is briefly stated here from that very work; the source, however, should be sought therein. First, the impurity due to miscarriage (*garbhāśauca*) is described:
until the end of the fourth month it is a miscarriage (*srāva*); in the fifth and sixth months it is a fall (*pāta*); from the seventh month onwards it is a full birth (*pūrṇaprasava*). Manu says:

In the case of a miscarriage, one is purified in as many nights as there were months [of gestation]. This rule applies up to the fourth month; for within the first three months, purification by three nights is established simply by virtue of being menstruating. Marīci states: "In the event of a miscarriage, purification is according to the number of months; however, if it occurs shortly after, even in the best case, it takes three [nights]."
For a Kṣatriya, however, it is four nights; for a Vaiśya, it is five days.
But for a Śūdra, this purification is proclaimed to take eight days.

"Within three months" means during the middle of the third month. "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa" [is mentioned]. Its meaning is explained in the *Smṛtikaumudī*: In the case of a miscarriage (*garbhasrāva*) after the third month, the four days equivalent to the fourth month apply equally to all castes (*varṇa*). Within the first three months, even the three days apply equally to all castes. For a Brāhmaṇa within the first three months, three additional days are added at the end of the three-night period. The repetition of the word "three" (*traya*) and the formation of a collective compound (*ekaśeṣa*) imply that for a Brāhmaṇa within the first three months, there is a three-day period at the end of the three-night period; for Kṣatriyas and others, there is a four-day period and so forth. However, some say that even in the first and subsequent months, after one night and so on, there is a three-night period and so forth for the various castes. Otherwise, in the fifth month and beyond, there would be a five-day period and so forth for Vaiśyas and others, and a four-day period and so forth within the first three months, which would be improper. Regarding miscarriage, bathing is prescribed for the *sapiṇḍa* relatives; for the father and mother, it lasts according to the month; and for the father and other relatives, it is three days. This applies to those lacking qualities (*nirguṇa*). Madanapāla states that for those possessing qualities (*saguṇa*), it is only one day. This applies equally to all castes, because Vyāghra stated: "When the age is equal, it is the same for all; likewise when it has passed."
[176] Now, regarding impurity due to childbirth: Saṃvarta says:
Upon the birth of a son, the father’s bath with his clothes on is prescribed;
by the word "son," a daughter is also included. As for that which is stated in the *Hāralatā*:
"But upon the birth [of a child], having seen the face of the newborn, the father [then...]"
By performing a bath with his clothes on, a Śūdra becomes [purified] at that very moment.

The statement that one must bathe again after seeing the face of a Brāhmaṇa following the announcement [of birth] has been refuted; for the act of "seeing" (dṛśi) implies knowledge, and since the source [of the news] is the same, [the impurity is already removed]. The Gauḍas, however, maintain that the stepmother (*sāpatnamātṛ*) is untouchable before the bath, and other mothers likewise do not enter her house until then, provided they have not done so previously; this is stated by the *Brāhmaṇa* [Smṛti]. Aṅgiras says:
"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth (*sūtaka*) if he does not come into contact [with the source of impurity];
in that case, it is the menstrual flow (*rajas*) that should be known as the impure element, and that is not found in a man."

Mādhava states that "contact" refers to sexual intercourse, lying on the same bed, sitting together, and so forth; the Gauḍas, however, say it means physical touch. That is not correct, because Aṅgiras has stated: "In the case of contact with a woman who has recently given birth, bathing alone is prescribed. By the use of the word "alone" (*eva*), there is no fault in touching a child. Vyāsa says:
On the first day, the sixth, and always on the tenth—
on these three days, one should never observe impurity (*sūtaka*) upon the birth of a son.

In this regard, the specific details concerning the worship on the sixth day and so forth have been stated previously. However, in the *Prayogapārijāta*, it is said: "Upon the birth of a male, [impurity lasts for] ten days; but upon the birth of a female, for three days.
O best of the twice-born, in the case of the birth of a female, both the *sapiṇḍas* and the *sodakas* become pure after three days;
the status of being a *sapiṇḍa* among women should be understood as extending to three generations."
Thus he says, "according to the Smṛti of Agni. However, the Gauḍas say that this refers to a maiden who was betrothed but remains unmarried (*kānīna*). Now follows the impurity on account of death.

Hārīta states: “In the case of ‘born-dead’ or ‘dead-born,’ the period of impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts ten days. The meaning is that the child is considered “dead” after the cutting of the umbilical cord (*nālaccheda*), as he himself has stated: “Impurity [occurs] once the umbilical cord is severed. According to the *Śuddhitattva*, before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the mother is not untouchable. However, regarding death occurring before the cutting of the umbilical cord, Bṛhan-Manu says:
“If one born alive should then die, that is indeed *sūtaka* (birth-impurity);
the full period of *sūtaka* applies to the mother, while for the father and others it is three nights.”

Bathing alone suffices for the occasion of a death during the *śāva* period, according to the statement of Śaṅkha: “Until the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*)”; furthermore, Medhātithi, Haradatta, Gauḍa, and others hold that the naming ceremony and the first tonsure (*caula*) serve as markers of time. Mādhava and others, however, say this is not so. After the naming but before the eruption of teeth, if cremation occurs, the impurity for *sapiṇḍas* lasts one day; in the absence of cremation, bathing alone is required, based on the statement of Yājñavalkya: “Until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate. From the eruption of teeth until the third year, if the tonsure has not been performed, the impurity lasts one day; regarding this, Mādhava states that if the fire is applied (cremation), it lasts three days. Whether before or after the third year, if the tonsure has been performed, it lasts exactly three days. After one year, even if the tonsure has not been performed, it lasts three days. This applies to *sapiṇḍas*; however, for the parents, if the child dies after ten days, there is always a three-night period of impurity. For children who have not yet erupted teeth, purification occurs after three nights, according to the statement of Kaśyapa.
"Due to the connection through the seed, one should observe impurity for three days," according to the statement of Manu;

thus say the Mitākṣarā, Mādhava, and others. However, the Gauḍas, such as those following the Śuddhitattva, maintain that this three-night period refers to Śūdras, whereas for the twice-born (the *dvijas*): if the child has not yet cut its teeth, there is one day of impurity; if the teeth have cut, it is three nights. In the case of the death of a child whose teeth have not yet emerged, one day of impurity is prescribed for the parents.
If the two [parents] are devoid of merit, there shall be a three-night period of impurity once the teeth have appeared.
Thus, from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"But for unmarried girls and likewise for those born of the Śūdra caste," as stated by Śaṅkha in the context of the three-day [impurity] rule.
"However, for a Śūdra, it shall be three nights even if a child dies within six months," according to the *Matsyasūkta*. But for a Śūdra whose teeth have emerged, it is five days. As Aṅgiras said:
"When a Śūdra child who has reached its third year dies, purification is achieved in five [days]."
After this, in the case of the death of a Śūdra, a period of twelve days is prescribed.
"If a Śūdra who has passed the age of six years dies, the purification shall be monthly; so it was declared by Aṅgiras."

Therefore, in the case of a *śūdra* who is unmarried and devoid of merit, if he dies after three years [of age], the impurity lasts for twelve days; after six years, it lasts for one month. As for the statement by Śaṅkha, "But a *śūdra* who is unmarried," which prescribes a month of impurity after sixteen years, that refers specifically to a virtuous and well-born *śūdra*. However, once he has been married, in all cases there is a month's impurity even before six years have passed. As for the claim that there is a lesser period of impurity for a *śūdra* based on Vyāghra’s statement, "For all, it is equal according to age," that refers only to the people of the South (*dākṣiṇātya*). They say that in other regions, the rule is that which was previously stated by Kūrma. Vijñāneśvara, Madanapārijāta, and others maintain that the rules of Aṅgiras and others should not be respected because they contradict the rule "For all, it is equal according to age" and because they involve the disagreement of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). If there is no marriage within sixteen years, the impurity is three nights; if there is marriage, it is a month. After that, even in the absence of marriage, it is a month—so say Aparārka, Madanapāla, and others. For girls, however, if death occurs before the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), purification is by bathing.

"However, in the case of a girl who has not yet reached the age of puberty (*acūḍā*), immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) is prescribed," according to the statement of Āpastamba. This [refers to] within three generations (*tripuruṣa*). After the tonsure (*caula*) but before the betrothal (*vāgdāna*), there is one day's impurity for all castes (*varṇa*) without distinction, prior to the sacramental rites (*saṃskārakarma*).
Purification occurs after three nights [in the case of other women], but for daughters, it is ordained to take place in a single day.

Because Aṅgiras has prescribed a three-night period regarding unmarried girls, stating, "But [the impurity lasts for] one day in the case of unmarried girls," and because Vasiṣṭha has stated, "For unmarried women, the sapinda relationship is understood to extend through three generations," this [three-day rule] applies within the context of three generations. However, the Gauḍas say that this applies after the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), based on the statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Likewise, for unmarried women, the sapinda relationship extends through seven generations. Thus, in the event of death prior to marriage but after the verbal betrothal, there is a three-night period of impurity extending up to seven generations in both the husband's family and the father's family.

But she who was promised before the water-ceremony yet not actually bestowed is to be known as "unconsecrated" (asaṃskṛtā); for her, a period of three nights is prescribed for both [the groom and the bride).
Thus it is stated by Marīci.
Now, there is a specific rule regarding an uninitiated Śūdra who has died.
In the *Mādhavīya-Brāhma*:
"The fetus of women that has fallen, whether born alive or dead,
or one who has died outside before the eruption of teeth, or after six months have passed," is considered fallen.
Having adorned him with garments and other ornaments, one should place him like a piece of wood;
having slowly dug a pit in the ground, immediate purification is prescribed.
Viṣṇu:
But if one passes away within ten days [of impurity], purification occurs immediately; there is neither the rite for the deceased nor the water libation.
Yama states: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years old outside [the village], smeared with clarified butter;

by that [act], burial alone is performed prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). After that, but before three years have passed, if the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has not been performed, there is an option between fire and water [rites]."

As stated by Manu: "They may perform [the rite] once teeth have appeared, or even when the naming ceremony has been performed. Thus, the offering of fire (agnidāna) after the tonsure (cūḍā) is mandatory either before or after the third year.
One should perform the water-libation silently, and likewise the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) itself silently.
For all those who have had their tonsure ceremony performed, the two [rites] may also be performed elsewhere according to one's wish.

Thus says the *Laugākṣismṛti*. Otherwise, an option is stated for one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has been performed, depending on one's wish. After the tonsure, the ten funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) must also be offered. This is because of the statement of Pracetas: "For those who have not undergone sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), one should offer the rice-ball on the ground; for those who have undergone them, on *kuśa* grass. Furthermore, when the death of a child occurs before the twelfth year, there shall be no *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; rather, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites alone.
And because of the statement of Devala cited by Haradatta: "After twelve days... this refers specifically to an unmarried Śūdra. Marīci says:
"One should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) outside, devoid of Darbha grass and mantras.
Vijñāneśvara states that this refers to one who has not undergone the purificatory rites (asaṃskṛta). Pāraskara says there are ten rice-balls during the three-night period.
On the first day, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered by those composed in mind;
on the second day, one should offer four, and likewise perform the collection of the bones.

One should give three [garments] even on the third day, and thereafter one should wash the clothes and other items. The collection of bones (asthisaṃcayana) is performed only after the formal consecration (saṃskṛta), and not otherwise. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Kriyānibandha* composed by Devayājñika; it is stated in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*:
One is called a *śiśu* (infant) until the eruption of teeth, and a *bāla* (child) as long as the hair reaches the crown;
according to all the scriptures, one is called a *kumāra* (youth) from the tying of the *mauñjī* grass girdle.
Likewise: "If the fetus is lost, there is no ritual; if the infant dies, milk should be given. Furthermore, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and milk following the death of a child."
On the eleventh or twelfth day, the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) is performed without [the usual] ritual procedure. Likewise: "Wherever a child dies, there generally [a bull] is offered."
Having honored those of similar age, he should offer food according to the prescribed rule.
Food to be chewed and food to be swallowed, as well as sweetmeats, should be given; likewise, garments along with sandals should be bestowed upon those who are equal to him.
The food and clothing for the young princes,
as well as whatever is used by the children— all that is given to the Brahmin.
Likewise:
"The casting of the body upon the ground for a child up to two years of age is done with the hair intact;
beyond that, O best of birds, cremation of the body is performed according to the prescribed rite."

The phrase "up to two years" is intended to exclude digging further upward even for one who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*). The phrase "up to the crest" is intended to exclude that [digging] for one who has already had the tonsure performed previously. Furthermore: "But when death should occur once the tonsure ceremony has been performed, then the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) must be performed at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*)."
In that case, cremation must be performed, and water libations are certainly required there;
furthermore, all sixteen śrāddhas should be offered, excluding the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
This refers to the period beyond five years.

One enjoys for five years from birth what has been given [as an inheritance] without [the child] being consecrated by rites. If death should occur when the child is over five years old, [the parents must give a portion].
The rite of releasing a bull and other such ceremonies should be performed, followed by the offering of water;
then, as each day arrives, one should perform the sixteen śrāddhas.
One should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in due order with milk-rice and molasses; likewise, one should perform the offering of the water-pot and whatever offerings of footprints are prescribed.

O best of birds, whatever offerings of lamps are made, they should always be performed before the completion of the vow for the satisfaction of the deceased, provided the person is more than five years old.
[The rite] should be performed with straight *darbha* grass and white sesame seeds by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).
However, the annual [śrāddha] does not occur at all in the absence of *sapiṇḍana*, because in its absence there is no status as a *pitṛ*. Thus it is said in the *Divodāsīya*:
"When a Brahmin or other [twice-born] dies before completing his vows, he is treated like a member of the Śūdra caste."
All ritual acts have been fully described, with the exception of the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
The offering of water and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) are prescribed for one whose tonsure ceremony has been performed.
Regarding unmarried girls, there is an option regarding the funeral cake, based on the statement of Gautama: "And for some, [the rite is performed] for women who have been given away in marriage.
Now, regarding the impurity due to birth for a Śūdra:
in that regard, Manu, Parāśara, Gautama, and others have stated a period of exactly one month, saying, "A Śūdra is purified after a month. Yājñavalkya, however, says:
"The [impurity] for a Śūdra is thirty days; half of that for one who lives according to the law."

Thus, he has stated a period of fifteen days for virtuous Śūdras who are devoted to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other duties. However, Aṅgiras says: "For all castes alike, in the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) as well as death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), purification occurs after ten days; so said Śātātapa."
Thus he said. Devala also, in the *Śuddhitattva*, states:
"Others know that the period of impurity for all is ten nights, perceiving the fruit of ritual action in both death and birth."

According to the author of the *Hāralatā*, for a Śūdra who has lost an extremely superior member of his family and is thus afflicted with grief, the period of impurity lasts ten nights while he is intent on serving Brāhmaṇas. As for that which Dakṣa stated:
"Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days, four days, six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month..."
"Likewise, there is another [period] ending at death; however, in the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), there are ten fortnights.

Here, following death, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) and so forth, which is distinct from birth-impurity and the like. That which lasts up to six days pertains to the *Yāyāvara* and others.
"In whose house there may be a wife who has had a previous husband, for him [there is impurity] constantly."
Impurity always resides in the body with respect to all activities.

Thus, Aparārka and others maintain that this is the settled rule based on the statement of Brāhmaṇa. In that regard, after marriage, full impurity applies to a Śūdra in all cases. Even in the absence of marriage, the Gauḍas hold that for those lacking qualities (*nirguṇa*), there is one month’s impurity after six years have passed. Aparārka holds that for those possessing qualities (*saguṇa*), even in the absence of marriage, there is one month’s impurity after sixteen years have passed. Here, the arrangement depends on whether there is a time of distress (*āpad*) or no distress, or whether the individuals possess qualities or lack them, or it may vary according to different regions. However, for the slaves of the twice-born and others, the impurity is precisely that of their master; for "the female slave and the male slave of whatever caste [their master] may be, [they share his status]."
The purification for that [slave] shall be according to his caste, but for a female slave, the period of impurity lasts one month.

Thus says Āṅgirasa. Śātātapa states: "One who depends on that [person] shall be like him. This means one who has taken refuge with that twice-born man. For others—such as the *kuṇḍas*, *golakas*, and so forth, as well as the *sūtas* and other offspring of inverse unions (*pratiloma*)—the period of impurity lasts for one month, because of Manu’s statement: "All those born of transgression (*apadhvaṃsaja*) are declared to have the same status as Śūdras. Those born of transgression are those born of illicit union (*vyabhicāra*).

"Those of mixed caste (varṇasaṃkara) should perform rites of purification and impurity like Śūdras," according to the *Śuddhitattva* and the *Brāhma-purāṇa*.
