However, for Mlecchas and others, there is no period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*); rather, there is merely a cleansing for the removal of physical filth, like that for urine and feces—so says Vijñāneśvara. In that regard, during childbirth (*sūtaka*), there is no state of untouchability except for the mother;
during childbirth, contact with everyone except the woman who has recently given birth is not prohibited.

Thus says the *Āṅgirasa* [Smṛti]. Regarding the father as well, after the bath [on the eleventh day], the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the touching of the father occurs immediately upon the bath; so says the *Smṛti*. As for purification, Devala says:

"Touching [the corpse] should be understood to occur after one-third of one's own period of impurity has passed; this applies when the period is short. But regarding a full period of impurity, Aṅgiras says:
'When the collection of bones (saṃcayana) has been performed in sequence after one-third of the ten-day period and so forth has elapsed...'"
Those who perceive reality desire the touching of the limbs of the social classes.

This is prohibited in the Kali age, for it is stated in the *Ādi-purāṇa* within the section on things to be avoided in the Kali age as found in the *Hemādri*: "Furthermore, touching the body after the collection of the bones [has occurred]. However, in the case of a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), [the prohibition lasts] for ten days only.
"A woman who has given birth becomes pure after ten nights among all castes;
and during the menstrual period, there is no separate purification—this is the rule for all castes," according to the statement of Pracetas. As for that which is in the Brāhma [Smṛti]:
A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā becomes touchable after ten days have passed since giving birth;
a Śūdrā becomes touchable after thirteen days.
Thus, that [passage] refers to unworthy Śūdras. However, Paiṭhīnasi speaks of their eligibility for ritual acts:
"One should have a woman who has given birth to a son perform her rites after twenty nights;
one who has given birth to a daughter, after a month."

And this [period] is to be understood as occurring after the twenty-day period of impurity (*āśauca*). Otherwise, it would be improper for her to be eligible for ritual acts while the *sapiṇḍas* are still in a state of one-month impurity; furthermore, there would be an inconsistency in the rule regarding the ten-day period. Āpastamba states:

"Regarding those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes who have undergone death or birth-impurity, their purity is determined by the father's [caste]; however, for those who are divided [from the family property], it is determined by the mother's [caste]."
Manu:
"Impurity on account of death (śāva-āśauca) is ordained for ten days among sapindas.
The term "ten days" refers to one's own specific period of impurity. Likewise:
"Those who touch a corpse are purified after three days, as are those who offer water; this means those who offer the water-libations (*sodaka*). In the *Agnipurāṇa*:
'But for all [relatives], the sapinda-relationship extends through seven generations on the basis of lineage.'"
And the status of being a *samānodaka* (a sapinda beyond the seventh degree) ceases up to the fourteenth generation.
Some say that for those who do not remember their birth names, the lineage (gotra) beyond them is what is meant;
however, for those related by the water-offering (samānodaka), the impurity lasts three days, while for those born of the same lineage (gotraja), it is declared to be one day.
In the *Agnismṛti* within the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"Upon the birth of a female child, both the *sapiṇḍas* and the *sodakas* become pure after three days.
O best of the twice-born, among women, the status of *sapiṇḍa* is to be understood as extending through three generations."

Vasiṣṭha states: "For unmarried women, it is known that the impurity extends through three generations. This period of impurity applies only to the biological son (*aurasa*). In the case of birth or death among the eleven types of sons, such as the *dattaka* (given son) and others, there is only a three-night period for both parents. This is stated in the *Brāhma* section of the *Smṛtikaumudī*.

If there is neither a legitimate son (aurasa) nor a son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta), then those such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and others are to be recognized as belonging to them.
Beginning with "The adopted son, the one given by himself, the made son, and the purchased son," [it continues]:
"These eleven are of separate lineages, but they merely continue the family line."
They all constantly perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other duties for them, like servants.
In both cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), those who share a three-day period of impurity are affected;
this is likewise stated in the *Śuddhitattva*. Similarly for the biological father:
"Due to the connection through the seed (*baijika*), one should follow the impurity for three days."

Thus it is stated in the *Manu-smṛti*. Accordingly, when the biological father, the protector (*pālaka*), or the paternal or maternal parents die, the adopted sons (*dattaka*) must observe impurity for exactly three days. And these three days refer specifically to Brāhmaṇas; however, for Śūdras in this case, the period is twelve days.
Where a three-night period of impurity is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, there it is twelve days for a Śūdra, and six or nine days for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas respectively.

"Thus it is from the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga," says Madanapāla. Where, without specifying a particular caste, a three-night period is prescribed—as in the case of *sodaka* relations, adopted sons (*dattaka*), and so forth—there the period for a Śūdra is twelve days; however, this does not apply to [impurity] caused by age-stages, for in that regard, "for all [castes], when [the age] is equal, and likewise when it has passed... [the rule remains the same].

Thus says Vyāghrapāda. Vijñāneśvara and others maintain that the statements of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others are not to be respected because they contradict the consensus of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Madanapāla holds that the rule is determined by the distinction of regions. Likewise, in the case of the birth or death of women who have committed adultery, or of *dattaka* (adopted) sons and others, there is a period of three nights for the former and latter husbands, as well as for the fathers. And so Viṣṇu states regarding the persistence of the three-night period:
"In the case of non-aurasa sons being born or having died, and in the case of wives who previously belonged to another being delivered of a child or having died."
Marīci says:
In the case of birth or death involving women who previously belonged to another family, the impurity lasts for three nights;
however, for their *sapiṇḍa* relatives it lasts one day, whereas for the father it lasts three nights.

As for Yājñavalkya’s statement, "In the case of non-aurasa sons and wives who have gone to others," which prescribes [impurity] for a day and night—that refers either to sapinda relatives or to those residing in another country. "Sons of other men's wives" refers to adopted sons (datta) and the rest. Bṛhaspati [says]:
If those wives who depend on others, or those wives of others,
or those persons themselves die, the best of the twice-born becomes pure by bathing and observing a three-night fast.

In the Mādhavīya, Hārīta states: "When wives who have had previous husbands or sons born of such wives die, there shall be a three-night period of impurity for the husband and the father; however, for those who are *sapiṇḍa* relatives, it is but one day."

In the case of a Śūdra woman, however, the period of twelve nights has been stated previously. A "woman previously married to another" (parapūrvā) is one who was herself taken as a wife by another man. This [rule] applies to women of the same caste (savarṇā). But in the case of women of lower castes, there is no impurity (āśauca); however, it is certain that for those of equal caste, the impurity shall be three nights, according to the statement of Brāhma: "It is determined that among those of equal caste, the impurity shall be three nights. Regarding the two sons born of a woman from her previous and subsequent husbands, Marīci says:

When two brothers have different fathers but share the same mother and belong to different gotras, there is one day of impurity (sūtaka) for them on that occasion; however, in the case of death (mṛtaka), the impurity for those two lasts three nights.
Regarding a Śūdra, however, some maintain that in the absence of marriage, the impurity according to caste (jātyāśauca) applies after six years have passed. To this effect, Kāśyapa and Aṅgiras state:
"If a Śūdra dies before three years [of age], purification occurs in five days;
if a Śūdra dies after that, a period of twelve days is prescribed."
If a Śūdra who has passed the age of six years dies, the purification shall be one month; thus is the statement of Āṅgirasa.

Medhātithi also states: "One is declared pure before the eighth year, but by others, a child [is so] until the sixteenth. Even for those who say that childhood ceases at sixteen, purification is indeed monthly after the eighth year. Regarding the period beyond six years, the Smṛti says: "For a Śūdra, purification is monthly. He notes that elsewhere it is stated that for an eight-year-old, the period is one month. However, Aparārka records that Śaṅkha prescribes a month's purification after the sixteenth year in the absence of marriage.
If a Śūdra who has not yet married a wife should meet his death after the sixteenth year, his kinsmen [must perform the rites] after one month.
"They attain purity; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
As for that which Hārīta states in the *Madanapārijāta*:
"A Brahmin [is purified] until the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, and a Kṣatriya until the taking up of the bow..."
A Vaiśya [is purified] by the seizing of the goad, and a Śūdra by the seizing of two garments.

Thus it is said; even in that case, the two garments [worn by the bride] must be at most sixteen years old. As for Madana’s statement that there are two garments at twelve, that is without foundation. Here, the legal arrangement regarding the presence or absence of impurity depends on whether the Śūdra is worthy or unworthy, and on whether it is a time of distress or not. Regarding daughters married in their father's house, Vijñāneśvara and Aparārka state that if a birth occurs, the impurity lasts one night, and if a death occurs, it lasts three nights. Mādhava, however, maintains that even upon a birth, the parents' impurity lasts three nights and that of the circle of kinsmen lasts one night, as in the verse: "If a daughter who has been given away in marriage should give birth or die in her father's house..."
But his circle of kinsmen shall be purified by one [day], and his father by three.

Thus he says, "because of the statement of Brahmā. It is stated in the *Kalpataru*, the *Śuddhitattva*, and the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "When a woman who has been given away [in marriage] gives birth or dies while in her father's principal house, then her father shall be purified after three days."

In the case of childbirth within the paternal household, there is no impurity for the father and others; however, in the event of death, there is indeed a three-night period of impurity for both parents, whether the daughters have been given in marriage or not, and whether they have been consecrated or not.
For the mother and father, it shall be three nights; for others, it shall be according to the rule.

Thus, from the *Kārṣṇājinismṛti* in Mādhava’s work. Regarding the impurity for brothers upon the death of a sister, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states in the *Śuddhitattva*: "In the case of a uterine brother, [impurity lasts] until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), it is one night;
until marriage (*pradāna*), it is three nights; and beyond that, it is ten nights."
Bṛhaspati, however, said regarding the *pakṣiṇī* [impurity]:
"One should spend the night as a *pakṣiṇī* for the parents-in-law, for a sister, for a maternal aunt, for a maternal uncle, and likewise for a paternal aunt."
Regarding the death of parents, Vṛddha-Manu states in the Mādhavīya:
"When both parents have passed away, what shall be the case for married women?
Purification occurs after three nights alone; thus said the venerable Yama."

For a brother and a sister, there is a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) of impurity for each other. According to the *Brāhma* [Smṛti], "In the case of the death of one another, there shall be a *pakṣiṇī* for a brother and a sister. The same applies in the *Ṣaḍaśīti* and the *Triṃśacchlokī*. Regarding those who have died: for the teacher (*ācārya*), maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), daughter’s son (*duhitṛsuta*), a learned *śrotriya*, officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a person for whom one sacrifices (*sayājya*), and a sister’s son (*svasrīya*), one remains impure for three nights (*trirātra*). However, for a *sodaka* (a relative connected by the offering of water), the impurity lasts for three days in both cases. The *pakṣiṇī* impurity applies upon the death of: an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a daughter’s son, a co-student (*sahādhyāyin*), three types of kinsmen (*bandhu*), a pupil (*antevāsī*), mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*), a good friend (*sumitra*), father-in-law (*śvaśura*), sister (*bhaginī*), sister’s son (*bhāgineya*), maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*), a paternal aunt (*pitṛsvasṛ*), a maternal uncle (*mātula*), and a maternal aunt (*mātulānī*). Furthermore, it lasts as long as the sun or stars shine (*sajyotis*) upon the death of the king of one's own territory or the head of one's village. Upon the death of a pupil (*śiṣya*), sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), three types of kinsmen, the son of a guru, the wife of a teacher (*ācāryabhāryā*), a member of the same lineage (*sagotra*), a Vedic scholar (*anūcāna*), or a *śrotriya*—if their death occurs within one's own house—the impurity lasts for one night (*ekarātra*) for a maternal uncle. If it concerns a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) or someone with only a slight connection, there should be a bath with clothes on (*vāsoyuta-snāna*). All of this is equal for all castes (*sarvavarṇa*). The source for this should be sought in the *Mādhavīya* and the *Mitākṣarā*. For an unmarried daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) or sister’s son (*bhāgineya*), the impurity is a *pakṣiṇī*; for married ones, it is three nights (*trirātra*).
When a daughter's son has died, the impurity lasts for three nights;
however, if he has been consecrated [with initiatory rites], it shall last for three nights—thus the law is settled.

Thus it is stated in the *Vṛddhamanu*. The Gauḍas maintain that [the impurity lasts] for three days when cremation has taken place; however, that is incorrect because the specific qualification would then be redundant. Where one-day or two-day periods are prescribed for a single maternal uncle or similar relative, the determination depends on whether he was present or in a distant location. For the Smṛti states: "If a Śrotriya dies in one's own house, there is three nights of impurity; likewise, if a Śrotriya who is well-versed [in the Vedas] has died, one shall remain impure for three nights. But if he resides in the same village, it is one day. Three types of kinsmen have been described in the *Mitākṣarā*.
The sons of one's father's sister, the sons of one's mother's sister,
and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father's paternal aunt, the sons of one's father's maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father's maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother's paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother's maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's mother's maternal uncle are to be known as maternal kinsmen (mātṛbandhu).
On this point, the *Pakṣiṇī* states: "The Gauḍas, however, declare that for those related by water (samānodaka), the impurity lasts three days; for those born of the same lineage (gotraja), one day;
and likewise for a maternal relative, a guru, a friend, and a regional ruler."
Thus, based on the statement of Jābāla, they say that for maternal relatives there is one day of impurity. However, as for what Pracetas says in the Mādhavīya:
"Upon the death of a mother’s sister, a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, a father-in-law, a teacher, or a sacrificial priest (ṛtvij) or a patron (yājya), one becomes pure after three nights."
Thus, this should be understood to apply when the death occurs in one's own home; but elsewhere, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"In the case of a paternal or maternal aunt, one should likewise spend the night with its two flanking days (a *pakṣiṇī*)."

In the presence of one's parents-in-law, the impurity lasts for three nights; in their absence, for a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night); and in another country, for one night. Regarding a *śālaka* (brother-in-law) who resides in the same country, it is one day; if he is in another country, it is merely a bath. According to Viṣṇu as cited in the *Mādhavīya*: "In the case of the wife or son of the teacher (*ācārya*), the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the maternal uncle (*mātula*), father-in-law (*śvaśura*), mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*), brother-in-law (*śvaśurya*), fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*), or pupil (*śiṣya*), there is likewise one night. Haradatta says the same; he explains that *śvaśurya* refers to the *śālaka*. The Gauḍas also hold this view. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaḍaśīti*:
"Likewise, [the period of impurity applies] to the sisters of one's parents, and those who are the [sisters] of one's grandfathers."
And those who are the sisters of both maternal grandfathers, as well as their offspring.

The wives of one's maternal uncles and of one's own parents, as well as their offspring, are to be regarded as mothers; thus, for all these, one must observe the *pakṣiṇī* period of impurity for three days in one's own home.

In this manner, it is recorded that [the period of impurity applies] upon the death of a father-in-law, a son-in-law, or a daughter’s son. Regarding the phrase "grandmother and grandfather," the compound is formed by the elision of one member (*ekaśeṣa*). As for what Vṛddha-Manu stated: "When a sister has been consecrated [by marriage], when a brother has been consecrated, when a friend, a son-in-law, a daughter’s son, or a sister’s son has died..."

"In the case of a maternal uncle and his son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing"—this [rule] should be understood to apply when the brother and others die in another country, while the maternal uncle's son and the son-in-law die in one's own country. In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "If a person who is not a sapinda dies in one's own house, there is impurity for one night."
Mādhava states that in the case of the death of a principal member of the household, the impurity lasts for three nights. In the *Śuddhitattva*, Bṛhan-Manu says:
"If Śvapacas, Śūdras, outcasts, or Antyajas die in the house of a twice-born man...
Here, the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is either an elliptical expression or a form of address.
In this regard, I shall declare the rules of purification as they were spoken by Manu in the past.
If a dog dies, one becomes pure after ten nights; if a Śūdra dies, one becomes pure after a month;
if a fallen person (patita) dies in the house, after two months; and if an outcaste (antyaja) dies, after four months.
"One should avoid the house of an outcaste (antyaja); thus Manu has declared.
Vācaspati states that an *antya* is a Mleccha, while an *antyaja* is a dog or a crow. Manu says:
"Upon the death of a twice-born person, the house becomes pure after three days."
Saṃvarta says: I shall now declare the purification of a house defiled by a corpse within it:
one should discard earthenware vessels as well as prepared food.
Then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should cause a goat to sniff it;
thereafter, [one should purify it] with gold, kuśa grass, and water, consecrated by Brahmins with mantras.
One should sprinkle the entire house with water; then it becomes pure without a doubt.
However, even in the absence of payment, the performer of the rite must observe full impurity.
But when a *sapiṇḍa* relative has died without any remaining property, one who is moved by compassion [should perform the rites].
Having first observed that period of impurity, he should perform the rites for the ancestors as his father did.
Thus it is stated in the *Mādhavīya* based on the *Brāhma-purāṇa*. In the *Divodāsīya*:
"Whether he be of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or a different lineage (*asagotra*), that man who offers the fire to a friend should also perform the *navaśrāddha*; he becomes pure on the tenth day."

But regarding one killed in battle, Manu says: "For one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya by weapons raised in combat, the sacrifice is immediately completed, and so too is ritual purity; such is the settled rule."

The sacrifice is the funeral rite; the meaning is that all of it is indeed that [sacrifice]. As for the statement that there is one night of impurity even for those killed in battle, that should be understood to apply to one who dies at a later time from a wound sustained in combat. Mādhava states that if the relative is absent, there is purification by bathing; if present, there is one day of impurity. Furthermore, in the *Rājadharmas* of the *Mahābhārata*:
"A hero killed in battle is not to be mourned, for he is glorified in the heavenly world;
for him there is no need for food or water, nor bathing, nor any ritual of impurity."

Thus, the prohibition regarding *śrāddha* and other rites refers to those who lack sons and other heirs; for this very reason, the performance of *śrāddha* and other ceremonies is prescribed there for such individuals. Others, however, maintain that—as in the case of an ascetic (*yati*)—there is a prohibition against the offering of the ten *piṇḍas*. In the *Agnipurāṇa*, within the *Śuddhitattva*, it is stated: "O King, those killed by fanged or horned animals, or by barbarians (*mleccha*) and thieves, and those killed for the sake of their master, go to heaven without a doubt."
This applies to all castes, but especially to the Kṣatriya;
as Bṛhaspati has stated: "In a riotous battle, by lightning, or while protecting cows and Brahmins by the king..."
Some great seers declare that purification from death occurs immediately, while others say it takes three days.

In that regard, if someone is killed by a weapon other than that [specific one] or by him [the assailant] while turning away from battle, the impurity lasts for three nights. If someone is killed by a king when he ought to be executed, there is immediate purification; otherwise, it is three nights. On this very point, Vyāghra says: "For one who dies from a wound, the impurity shall be of two kinds:
up to seven days it shall be three nights, and beyond that, ten nights."
If anyone dies more than three days after being struck by a weapon,
the standard period of impurity applies there for all castes at all times.

In the absence of wounds from weapons, touching a corpse, carrying it out for burial, residing in its house, or eating its food, one incurs the full period of impurity (pūrṇāśauca) corresponding to the caste of the deceased. Merely residing in that house entails three days; if neither of these two conditions applies, it is one day. If one carries out the corpse for wages, the impurity lasts for a full month. For carrying out a corpse of a different caste, the impurity is that of the deceased's caste; if for wages, it is doubled. In times of distress, it is equal [to the deceased's caste]. For carrying out a relative connected by water (sodaka), the impurity is full. If one knowingly decorates a corpse, there is a quarter-kṛcchra penance; if unknowingly, a fast. In carrying out a helpless person of one’s own caste or in providing the funeral fire, the fruit is infinite. Purity is attained merely by bathing.

"The one who carries [the corpse] and the one who provides the fire becomes pure immediately after bathing"—so says Vṛddha-Parāśara as cited in the *Aparārka*. In cases of relationship such as that of a maternal uncle or out of affection, the impurity lasts for three nights. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Atri states in his commentary on Gautama:
"Impurity due to birth is double that of death; impurity due to death is double that of menstruation."
Impurity due to menstruation lasts for two nights; that for a birth is twice as long, and for one who burns a corpse, it is even longer than that.

However, there is no fault in following [the corpse] if the person is a *sapiṇḍa*. But if the person is not a *sapiṇḍa* and is of the same caste (*samavarṇa*), there is bathing, the consumption of ghee, and a period of impurity lasting for two days and the intervening night (*pakṣiṇī*). If the person is of a higher caste, there is merely bathing. Regarding weeping, Mādhava states that for a *śūdra* [weeping for] a *śūdra*, there is one day of impurity before the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*), provided there is no physical contact; after that, it lasts as long as the light [of the sun or moon] remains. Pāraskara says in the *Śuddhitattva*: "For twice-born persons, until the month [following the death], they become pure in a single day and by the washing of their clothes, once the collection of the bones has taken place."
For those of the same caste (*sajāti*), there is no fault for the *sapiṇḍas* after one day; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it is after three days. In the *Mitākṣarā*, Pāraskara states:
"Having performed lamentation together with the kinsmen of the deceased, one should avoid that day and night, as well as acts such as giving gifts and performing *śrāddha*."

Thus, he states that in all cases there is one [rule]. However, regarding the eating of food belonging to one in a state of impurity (*āśauca*), if it is done unknowingly, the penance lasts until the food is digested; if done knowingly, for a Śūdra, it is merely bathing. [193] Now, the impurity of servants (*dāsa*).

In that regard, when a slave born of one's own [wife] dies, he becomes fit for the master’s work immediately after bathing, even during the period of impurity following the death of a sapinda relative of his own. For a *bhaktadāsa* (slave by food), this occurs after three days; for it is stated in another Smṛti cited in the *Mitākṣarā*: "A *garbhadāsa* (slave from birth) is immediately touchable, while a *bhaktadāsa* becomes pure after three days. Furthermore: "Laborers who have been paid their wages, as well as Śūdra female and male slaves, are not defiled in matters of bathing, personal grooming, or household chores."

And because of this statement by Śātātapa: "In this very context, for the thirteen types of slaves beginning with those given [in marriage], once the period of impurity corresponding to the number of days of their master's impurity has passed, they attain touchability for the sake of their master's business even while they themselves remain in a state of impurity for a month or longer. 'Slaves, apprentices, those who have died, and pupils living together—these are purified by an impurity equal to that of their master during both death and birth.'"

Thus, according to the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti*: "In the case of one's own impurity regarding rites for unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is indeed a period of impurity (*āśauca*) of one month and so forth for all [servants]. The same applies to a female slave (*dāsī*). However, upon her giving birth, even in the service of her master, her impurity lasts for only one month: 'Whichever caste a male or female slave may belong to, their purification shall be that of that caste; but for a female slave, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts for one month.'"
Thus it is stated by Aṅgiras. Also in the *Ṣaḍaśīti*:
"By the purification of the master, servants and others become touchable after one month; they become fit for ritual acts after one month.
But if a female servant has given birth, she attains touchability after two months."
The types of slaves are stated by Nārada:
one born in the house, one purchased, one obtained as a gift, one received through inheritance,
one maintained during a famine, and likewise one pledged by his master.
Rescued from great bondage, won as a prize in battle,
approached saying "I am yours," and made one who has completed his period of exile— such a person is ordained.
The slave by gift, as well as the one acquired from a mare,
and the one who sells himself— these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen types of slaves.
The meaning is that a female slave (*vaḍavā-dāsī*) gives birth to a male slave out of greed for wealth. Regarding the death of a master or his *sapiṇḍas* by a slave and others, Viṣṇu states:

"For wives and slaves who follow the natural order (*ānulomyena*), the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is equal to that of the master; when the master has died, they observe their own [period]. There is no impurity for slaves born of the inverse order (*pratiloma*), because Yājñavalkya says: "Slavery exists for the castes in the natural order, not in the inverse order. Even if slavery is entered into by transgressing the scriptures, there is still no impurity, because Viṣṇu says: "In the natural order, there is no impurity. [75]
[194] Now, regarding impurity that has elapsed:

if it becomes known while one is in the midst of an impurity, only the remainder of that period applies. This is because of the statement of Yājñavalkya: "In the case of one who has gone abroad, there shall be no further period beyond what remains. In the case of birth, there is no such thing as impurity that has elapsed.

"There is no impurity even when the days [of the period] following birth have passed," according to the statement of Devala. Even in that case, bathing for the father certainly occurs. However, if it is known after the period of impurity has ended, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"In the case of [the death of a child] within three months, there shall be a three-night [impurity]; likewise, within six months, a pakṣiṇī [day]."
But if it occurs before the ninth day, one becomes pure by bathing after that time.

This [rule] applies specifically to the impurity (*āśauca*) due to birth for a *pūrṇajāti* (one of full caste), and not to that caused by the stage of life (*vayovasthā*), because of the statement of Manu: "But when ten days have passed... As for what Devala says in the *Mādhavīya*:
"Until three fortnights, there shall be three nights; from six months, a night-and-day (*pakṣiṇī*);
beyond that until one year, a single day; after that, one becomes pure by bathing."

Thus it should be understood that this applies when there is no emergency (*anāpadi*). And this refers to death occurring in the same region. However, in the case of another region, there is merely bathing;

for upon hearing of the death of one who has died in a foreign land, or of a eunuch, a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), or an ascetic (*yati*), as well as in the case of a miscarriage, the kinsmen (*gotriṇaḥ*) are purified immediately by bathing alone.
Thus says Vijñāneśvara, citing the words of Parāśara. However, Viṣṇu in the Mādhavīya states:
"Within three fortnights [there is impurity] for three nights; within six months, for a day and night;
and within a year, for one day—even in the case of those who have died in a foreign land."
Thus he said. Here, the determination is made by means of "distress" (āpad) and "non-distress" (anāpad). Regarding "another country" (deśāntara), Bṛhaspati says:
"Where there is a great river between, or a mountain acting as a barrier, and where speech differs—that is called another country. Thus.

Regarding the regional dialects of speech, there are only two positions—that they are either distinct from it or both are residual [of the standard language]—because the word *vā* (or) denotes oneness. However, in all cases, the impurity for parents is full; for even if he is staying far away, a son, upon hearing that his parents have died, shall become subject to birth-impurity (*sutaka*) for ten days starting from that very day.

Thus says Pāraskara. According to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, the same applies between a man and a woman, as well as between co-wives. However, for a stepmother, the impurity lasts three nights. Vyāghra states:
"For all [relatives], it is equal when they are of the same age, and likewise when that age has passed.
The determination regarding the overlapping of periods of impurity (*āśauca*):

In that regard, if during the days of a full period of impurity there occurs another death or birth of the same class—whether equal or less [in duration]—then purification occurs through the remainder of the first period within the six-fold case; however, if a birth or death occurs in the interval, one is purified by the remaining days of the subsequent period.

Thus says Yājñavalkya. This [rule] applies when there is an impurity (*āśauca*) of full duration. However, the Gauḍas maintain that when there is a concurrence of a short impurity of three days or more, only the subsequent one [determines purification]. Haradatta also holds this view. Others, however, state that even in that case, purification occurs through the first [impurity]. But when a birth-impurity coincides with a death-impurity (*śāva*), whether it be equal, less, or greater, only the latter must be observed; there is no purification from the remainder of the first, because of the greater degree of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*). For the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states: "A birth-impurity is purified by a death-impurity, but a birth-impurity does not purify a death-impurity."
"However, in the conjunction of death and birth, death would be more significant," according to the *Kūrma Purāṇa*. But in the *Ṣaḍaśīti*, it is said:
"A woman who naturally has many births, however, purifies [the period] by fewer children."

Thus, the cessation of birth-impurity (*sūti*) by means of death-impurity (*śāva*) has been stated. Aparārka holds that if, during the period of three days or more of death-impurity, a subsequent impurity—whether of the same or a different kind—that lasts for a longer duration occurs, then purification does not take place by the former. However, in the *Śuddhiviveka*, because of the general rule that "birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity," it is stated that even in such a case, purification occurs by the former. That is not correct; for the latter is stronger due to its greater duration, as it is said:
"If, after three nights have passed, one enters a ten-day period of impurity and the impurity recurs, one becomes pure upon the completion of that [second] period."

Thus say Mādhava, Haradatta, the Mitākṣarā, and others, citing the words of Yama. This [rule] is an exception (*bādhaka*) to the statement, "A birth is purified by the impurity of death" (*śāva*), for otherwise that scriptural injunction would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, even when there is purification after three nights during an impurity caused by death due to a birth, the state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) resulting from the cause of death still persists, according to the *Kaumudī*, which states: "Death is more serious [than birth]. Śātātapa states an exception to the purification following the remainder of the previous period:
"If the night remains, purification occurs after two days; if one watch (*yāma*) remains, one becomes pure after three days."

In this context, the word *rātri* refers to a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*), according to the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita: "At the end of the day, [one is purified] by two [days]; at dawn, by three. Furthermore, Baudhāyana states: "If there is a coincidence of two ten-day periods of impurity (*daśarātra*), the first ten-day period lasts until the ninth day; after that, purification occurs in two nights if the dawn has broken, and in three nights otherwise. Thus say the *Parāśara-Mādhava*, the *Hāralatā*, the *Śuddhitattva*, and others. The Gauḍas hold the same view. Vijñāneśvara and others, however, maintain that it refers to when only a single night remains. In this matter, the settlement depends on local custom. The specific details should be known from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. But when there is a coincidence of a three-night period or the like while only a night remains of the previous period, purification occurs by the remainder of the previous period alone. However, if another, longer period of impurity falls within the second or third day already extended by the previous impurity, purification occurs by the longer period alone because the extended duration is shorter. Nor does the extended period constitute a "remainder" of the previous one; for when a night remains, the rule regarding purification by the previous remainder is set aside by the principle of reviving the occasional (*naimittika*) repetition, since the general rule (*utsarga*) applies only in the absence of an exception (*apavāda*). Śaṅkha states another such exception:
If the father dies while there is still impurity due to the mother having died previously, his purification shall be by the remainder of the father's period;
however, he should observe a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) for the mother.

The meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] is that if a mother dies during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for a father, one should observe an additional *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night). This applies when the mother’s death occurs before the tenth day. Some hold that if the mother dies on the tenth night or at dawn on the eleventh day, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the two-day and three-day periods with the *pakṣiṇī*. That is not correct; for by introducing a different number, there would be the consequence of subverting the scriptural injunctions regarding the "three days" and so forth. For this very reason, in the twelfth chapter, the combination was rejected because it would subvert the scriptural numbers such as "one [day] should be given" or "six [days] should be given. However, in the case of a mother following her husband in death (*anvārohaṇa*), there is no *pakṣiṇī*.
When a woman enters the fire out of a desire for her beloved,
then the period of impurity must be observed according to the sequence of the husband's impurity.

Thus, according to the statement of Laghu-Hārīta in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*: [197] there is absolutely no cessation of impurity for a mother, father, or husband due to the impurity of other *sapiṇḍas*, because of the Smṛti text: "From that day onwards, one shall remain in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days. Furthermore, in the case of *anvārohaṇa* (following the husband in death) after his period of impurity has passed, the impurity lasts for three nights.

"When the three-day period of impurity has expired, one obtains the right to perform the *śrāddha* according to the scriptures," as stated by Brāhma in the *Aparārka*. However, in the case of *sahagamana* (dying with the husband), the full period applies; for when following a husband killed in battle, since the impurity is immediate (*sadyaḥśauca*), the *anvārohaṇa* (following the husband) results in a three-night period, according to the statement of Brāhma. For the husband as well, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) occurs after three days. But if they were of one mind [regarding death], there is immediate purification. As stated in the *Ṣaḍaśīti*:
"The same purification that applies to birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) applies through the preceding period of impurity."
Having abandoned the woman who has recently given birth, the one who set fire [to the house], and even the sons of the deceased;

Likewise, Devayājñikas maintain that if a son is born amidst a period of impurity caused by death or other such causes, the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth must indeed be performed; and if the father’s rites, such as the *vṛṣotsarga* on the eleventh day, fall within the mother’s *pakṣiṇī* period of impurity, they must likewise be performed.
[199] Now follows the exceptions to impurity (*aśaucāpavāda*).
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, regarding the principle of purity:
"Immediate purification is declared in times of famine or calamity,
as well as when one is killed by infants, in battle, by lightning, or by kings."

"In the case of an *upadrava* (epidemic), it refers to a situation where there is extreme mortality. Parāśara also states: "Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed even in the event of an *upasarga* (plague);

an *upasarga* is that which causes extreme mortality," according to Śūlapāṇi, Hāralatā, and others. Likewise, there is no impurity regarding the giving of gifts and so forth for one who is about to die.
"Even in times of adversity, the purity of those who are afflicted [by impurity] is ordained.
Thus says Yājñavalkya. Dakṣa also states in the *Śuddhiratnākara*:
"All this is proclaimed as *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) during a time of well-being."
For everyone who has fallen into calamity, there is no impurity even during a birth-impurity.
Pracetas says:
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves,
kings, and royal servants are declared to be immediately pure.
Artisans, cooks, craftsmen, and laundrymen.
Laghuvishnu states:

"In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire offerings (homa), worship, and recitation (japa), there is no impurity (sūtaka) once they have begun; however, if they have not begun, there is impurity."
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the formal selection [of priests]; in the case of a vow or a long sacrificial session (sattra), it is the formal resolve;
in marriage and similar rites, it is the Nāndīmukha ceremony; and in a Śrāddha rite, it is the preparation of the cooked food.
As for Viṣṇu’s statement, “Not for those under a vow during the vow,” that too refers only to those vows already commenced. In the *Triṃśacchlokī*:

“There is no [impurity] regarding gifts, initiation, sacrifice, *śrāddha*, battle, consecration, tonsure, pilgrimage for the sake of sacred sites, recitation, marriage, and other festivals already begun; nor is there impurity for the purpose of these.
By the word “also” (*api*), it is implied that there is no impurity even when listening to the *Mahābhārata*, the *Harivaṃśa*, and so forth.

"Even for one who has undertaken a vow, there shall be no [impurity] from anything else," according to the statement of Brahmā. Jābāli says in the *Candrikā*: "The twilight prayers, the five great sacrifices, the daily rites, and the duties prescribed by the Smṛtis."
If one should omit it during that interval, the rite must be performed again at the end of ten days for those [deceased].

However, during an eclipse, even in the midst of a period of impurity (āśauca), the performance of śrāddha, giving, and so forth must indeed be carried out; for it is stated in the Laiṅga Purāṇa: "Purification occurs only when the release [of the moon or sun] is no longer seen."
[200] Now, regarding the fault of death:
from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* and the *Kaurma-purāṇa*, as cited in the *Hemādri*.
If one should cause his own death by means of fire, water, or other such methods,
for him no period of impurity is prescribed, nor should the water-libation rite be performed.
O Brahmins, in the future, death by one's own will shall occur through horned animals, fanged beasts, and reptiles;
through those of the lowest castes, poison, hanging, or even by self-inflicted blows.
Those who have resorted to heretical sects, as well as those who have committed the great sins,
unchaste women, and likewise those who have fallen from their vows after having ascended [the spiritual path].
For them there is no ritual bathing, no funeral offering (*śrāddha*), and no *sapiṇḍana* rite.
As stated in the *Brāhma*: "He who, being deluded, performs these rites for those who have fallen [from their caste]..."
His purification occurs only through two *taptakṛcchra* penances, and not otherwise.

This [penance] applies when done intentionally; however, if done through ignorance, it is half [the penance]. Regarding touching [an impure object] or shedding tears, if done knowingly, it is a three-night fast; if done unknowingly, it is a single day of fasting—such details are to be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. This [rule] is to be understood as applying when an act is performed out of pride (*darpa*) and with full awareness. But when an act is unintentional or committed through negligence (*pramāda*), everything should be performed [as a penance]; for:

"If someone should die through negligence by means of fire, water, or other causes, the period of impurity (*aśauca*) must be observed for him, and the water-libation rites (*udakakriyā*) must be performed."

Thus it is stated by Aṅgiras. Regarding death due to negligence (*pramāda*), the Gauḍas, such as the author of the *Śuddhitattva*, maintain that there is impurity for three nights; the Southerners (*Dākṣiṇātyas*) maintain it lasts ten days. An exception to this is found in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*: "Whether through negligence or intentionally, one should not fail to perform the worship of the serpent (*nāga*) when death occurs from [the bite of] a snake. The meaning is that it must be performed without exception. In that regard, Śātātapa has prescribed gifts and other rites for the cause of a "bad death" (*duramaraṇa*) occurring through negligence.
When a Brahmin has been killed by a tiger, one should marry off his daughter;
when he has been bitten by a snake, an offering to the Nagas should be given, along with a golden serpent.

This and so forth should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Regarding one bitten by a snake, Vyāsa says: "By fashioning a Nāga out of a bhāra of gold and likewise giving a cow to Vyāsa according to the prescribed rites, he attained freedom from his debt to his father."
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* cited by Hemādri:
"On the fifth lunar day, one should have a golden serpent fashioned from a single piece of gold;
it should be placed upon a vessel of milk and clarified butter, worshipped, and given to a Brahmin."
This expiation for one bitten by a snake has been proclaimed by Śambhu.
In the case of one who dies of pride or from a snakebite other than this, there is a combination of this with the Nārāyaṇa-bali. Likewise, there is no fault even in the death of a physician.
[201] An elder who has lost the memory of ritual purity and whose few remaining rites have been abandoned—
But he who would kill himself by means of Bhṛgu, fire, fasting, or water—
"His period of impurity lasts for three nights;
on the second day, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth day"—thus it was stated by Vṛddhagārgya. In the *Aparārka*, Brahmagarga says:
He who, afflicted by a great disease, is unable to live,
does not incur fault in the next world by performing the "great journey" through fire or water.

And that [immolation] occurs only for the sick in a location distinct from Prayāga; furthermore, even there, it applies only to one who has become an aged forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), according to Vijñāneśvara and others. However, at Prayāga, it applies even to those who are not sick. Specifically, a Śūdra may do so even elsewhere, or a non-Brāhmaṇa may do so out of a desire to attain great fruits such as heaven:
"He may enter the blazing fire, or likewise practice fasting."

Thus, from the Ādi-purāṇa. Although this death of the elderly and others—“The death of the elderly and others likewise occurs through leaping from a precipice or entering fire”—is prohibited in the Kali age according to the statement in the Mādhavīya commentary on the Ādi-purāṇa, nevertheless, it certainly takes place at Prayāga, based on the Vedic revelation: “Those who indeed cast off their bodies [there].”
O dear one, your mind should not be diverted from the prospect of dying at Prayāga, neither by worldly talk nor even by the words of the Vedas.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhārata* and the *Mātsya*:
"O beautiful one, he who gives up his life there at the roots of the banyan trees transcends all worlds and attains my realm."

Thus it is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*. Regarding this, the followers of Bhaṭṭa (*Bhāṭṭas*) maintain that the full period of impurity lasts ten days. However, the three-night period is more appropriate, because of the scriptural statement regarding death by fasting. Divodāsa also holds this view. Furthermore, as for the previously mentioned cases—those killed by lightning, those who have entered fire or water, those who die by leaping from a cliff (*bhṛgu*), those who die in battle, those who die in a foreign land, and those whose teeth have just emerged—the period is three nights, according to the statement of Kāśyapa in the *Śuddhitattva*. As for the prohibition of cremation, impurity, and other rites for those who commit suicide, that applies only at that time; but at the end of a year, one should perform everything [for them], as well as for those killed by cows or Brahmins, and likewise for those who have fallen from their caste (*patitas*).
After one year has passed, one should perform all the funeral rites for the deceased.
Thus, from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* in the *Hemādri*: therein, the expiation for self-killing (*ātmavadha-prāyaścitta*) and the *Nārāyaṇabali* are prescribed. In that very same work:
"Having first performed the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance, the ritual must be carried out according to the rules;
the *Nārāyaṇabali* should be performed by men out of fear of public censure."
Afterwards, one should perform the offerings of rice-balls and water, as well as the rite of releasing a bull and other such acts;
likewise, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
In the *Madanaratna*, however, it is stated in the *Brāhma* [Smṛti]:
"If one, even through negligence, becomes fearless and is suddenly impelled by fate,
and is killed anywhere by Caṇḍālas, Brāhmaṇas, or thieves..."
Since he has not fallen [from his caste], the rites of cremation and so forth must be performed for him;
for his purification, there shall be a Cāndrāyaṇa and two Kṛcchra penances.
Alternatively, one should burn [the body] according to the prescribed rite after performing fifteen *kṛcchra* penances;
however, for deeds committed intentionally, one should perform thirty *kṛcchra* penances.

Thus it has been stated. As for the *nārāyaṇabali*, however, it should be understood from my own work, the *Mitākṣarā*, and the *Nirṇayasindhu*. In the case of one who has died abroad, cremation is performed only if bones are available; in their absence, with *palāśa* leaf-stalks; and in their absence, with *kuśa* grass. Regarding death in a foreign land: "Having brought the bones and anointed them with clarified butter; or, if bones are not obtained, using leaves or wood-shavings according to the prescribed procedure."
One should cremate [the effigy] as many times as there are bones; from that point forward, the period of impurity (sūtaka) begins.
In the *Hemādri*’s commentary on the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, it says:
"One should fashion an effigy of the deceased out of darbha grass using three hundred and sixty kuśa blades."
Or with fuel-sticks of Palāśa wood; and the number is proclaimed to be as follows.
In the *Madanaratna*, Yājñavalkya states:
"One should place fifty [tufts] on the head, ten on the neck,
one hundred and ten on the two arms, and ten on the fingers."
One should strike thirty times on the chest, twenty times on the belly,
twelve and a half times on the testicles, and eight and a half times on the penis itself.
One should give one hundred [pieces] for the thighs, three hundred for the two shanks, and ten for the toes; this is the preparation for the deceased.
One should place a coconut on the head, a gourd likewise on the palate,
the five gems in the mouth, and a plantain fruit on the tongue.
On the two eyes, however, are two *kapardins*; on the nose is the *kālakam*;
on the ears are the *brahmapatras*; and on the hair are the *vaṭaprarohakas*.
One should place the stalks of lotuses in the position of the intestines;
as for the earth-element, the minerals are yellow orpiment and sulphur.
One should apply mercury to the semen, and likewise bile to the feces;
sesame paste should be applied to the joints, and barley flour to the flesh.
Honey should be placed in the position of blood, and deer-skin in the position of the skin;
two guñjaka berries should be placed on the breasts, and a śatapatra flower on the nose.
There should be a lotus at the region of the navel, an eggplant resting upon the testicles,
a red-rooted object on the penis, and a fine silken garment for the lower body.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, fragrance, and all medicinal herbs and so forth [should be used] everywhere; this is stated at the end of the *Gāruḍa-kriyānibandha*:
"The stalk should be placed at the navel, and tin is prescribed for the loincloth."
Pearls upon the breasts and an application of saffron upon the head.

In the case of one who has gone abroad and for whom no news is heard, the father must wait fifteen years; for anyone other than him, the wait is twelve years—thus it is stated in the *Madanaratna*. In that regard, if the wife and son have not yet observed the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prior [to the cremation], they must observe the full period of impurity; if they have already observed it, they observe three nights. After the twelve-year waiting period, if the cremation takes place, the *Kalpataru* states that for all, including the son and others, the impurity lasts three nights. However, regarding the recovery of bones after the cremation with leaf-arrows (*parṇaśara*), the *Brāhma* cited in the *Madanaratna* says: "Now, when the leaf-arrow body has been cremated and the placement of the leaves has been performed..."
When the fires have gone out, whatever remains of that body is found thereafter in some place.
Then, having churned those half-burnt logs, one should burn him;
provided that his own half-burnt log is indeed not obtainable.
Then, that fragment of bone should be cast into great water. Now follows the time for cremating the deceased.

If a death occurs while one is already in a state of impurity (*āśauca*), there is no further purification required. However, if a funeral rite (*saṃskāra*) takes place during a period of impurity, it must be purified upon its conclusion; if that is possible, it should be purified at the end of that period. At the end of the year, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is most auspicious; even then, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is preferred. Furthermore, the following must be strictly avoided: the constellations (*nakṣatra*) of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, the three quarters of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the five following them (Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvā-bhādrapadā, Uttarā-bhādrapadā, Revatī, and Aśvinī); the birth star, the tenth, and the nineteenth stars from the birth star; the fourth, eighth, and twelfth lunar days (*tithi*); the new moon; the *vaighṛti*, *vyatīpāta*, and *parigha* yogas; the *viṣṭi* karana; the *nandā*, *bhadrā*, thirteenth, and fourteenth lunar days; Friday, Tuesday, Saturday; the heliacal setting of Jupiter and Venus; the month of Pauṣa; and the intercalary month (*malamāsa*). On the anniversaries of the Manvantaras, the Yugas, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), and the new moon, nothing should be purified at all. The primary sources and specific details should be sought in the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
Thus ends the determination of impurity (*āśauca-nirṇaya*) in the *Śūdradharma-tattva*, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) of a Śūdra.
Regarding those entitled to perform them, they should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. In the absence of all [other heirs], a son of Dharma (*dharmaputra*) should be appointed;
as it is said: "By one who is childless, a son should be diligently made, regardless of his nature."
For the purpose of performing the rite of offering funeral cakes, and for the establishment of the Dharma.
Thus it is stated by Vyāsa. In the *Divodāsīya*: "When a son, seeing his father standing nearby on the ground with eyes half-closed, causes him to bestow a gift, [that gift is most meritorious]."
That is superior to the *gayāśrāddha* and even to a hundred horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*). As stated in the *Bhārata*:
"During the bright fortnight, by day, on the ground, at the Gaṅgā, and during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*)."
Blessed are they, my dear, who shall die with Janārdana dwelling in their hearts.
In the Hemādri-vārāha:
"The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Saṃkrānti, and likewise an eclipse of the sun—
all these auspicious times [are surpassed] when death has arrived."
On that very point, Vyāsa says:
"A cow with her calf should be given by one whose death is imminent, as previously described;
in its absence, a cow alone is indeed for the sake of crossing over hell."
In the *Madanaratna*, Jātūkarṇya states:
"One should give ten gifts for the deceased, beginning with the gift of departure (*utkrānti*):
namely, a cow, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, and molasses."
They say silver and salt; these are the ten gifts in successive order.
These ten gifts should be performed by men at the time of death or birth for the sake of prosperity, both for the deceased and indeed for oneself in the next world.
In the Brāhma [Kalpa]: "He who gives a copper vessel filled with a *prastha* measure of sesame seeds, along with gold, to a twice-born man according to his faith and wealth [attains the fruit]."
With his soul purified of all evil, he attains the supreme destination.
Having performed the *utkrānti* and *vaitaraṇī* rites, as well as the ten gifts (*daśadāna*),
for that deceased person even while he is still a corpse, one should cremate him according to the rules for the dead.
In the *Gāruḍa-kriyānibandha*, eight gifts are mentioned:
having placed a *tulasī* plant near the presence [of the deity], as well as a *śālagrāma* stone,
sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, and likewise salt.
"Seven kinds of grain, land, and cows— each one is remembered as purifying.
One should cause a vessel of sesame seeds according to one's capacity, and likewise the gift of a bed, to be performed," thus [it is said] in the *Pariśiṣṭa*.
Then, one should whisper meritorious mantras into the ear of the dying person.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa, the offering of madhuparka to one who is about to die is prescribed:
"Indeed, seeing him greatly agitated as he follows the path of Yama..."
At the time of departure, however, a person [should act] according to the mantra and in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
Taking the madhuparka in haste, he should utter this mantra:
"Accept this first madhuparka, which brings about the destruction of saṃsāra and is equal to nectar."
Composed by Nārāyaṇa, this work brings peace to those dear to you and is honored in the world of the gods.
With this very mantra, one should offer the madhuparka;
for a person at the time of death, it brings about happiness in the next world.
It is the same even for one born under a divine asterism.
Now, the ritual application:

A son or other relative, having learned that his father or other elder is near death, should cause him to perform penance for six years, three years, or one and a half years. To this end, he should seat an assembly of twice-born men numbering seven, five, three, or at least one; then, wearing wet clothes, he should set aside gold or silver weighing one *niṣka* (or half a *niṣka*), or four times that amount in the case of a cow or a bull—this being the price of a cow or a bull—and prostrate himself with the eight limbs of his body. When asked by them, "What is your business?", he should say: "For the removal of all my sins—whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, repeatedly or once, physical, verbal, mental, or through contact; whether by touching what is forbidden or not, eating what is forbidden or not, drinking what is forbidden or not, or whether known or unknown—including major sins (*pātaka*), minor sins (*upapātaka*), those causing loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), those causing impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*), those rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), those causing loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*), and miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇapātaka*)—may you show me favor and instruct me in the appropriate penance. Thus he should speak.
O best of the twice-born, may all you protectors who discern the nature of phenomena perform the complete purification of my body.
I have committed a most terrible sin, whether knowingly or unknowingly;
please grant me your favor and bestow upon me the permission for auspiciousness.
May I become purified by these most excellent of the twice-born, who are worthy of worship.

Thus he should recite or listen [to the text]. A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*. He should say, "His sons and so forth," and so on. Then the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*) should prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for him before the reciter (*anuvādaka*), according to his capacity. At that time, the one to be purified (*śodhya*) should perform worship of the book, the members of the assembly, and the reciter with perfumes and other offerings, and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the reciter according to the gravity of the sin. It is the custom to offer the price of a cow to the book as part of the worship of the legal code (*nibandha*). Then the members of the assembly should say three times before the reciter: "By performing this such-and-such expiation, together with its preliminary and concluding parts, or by means of a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) according to your capacity, you shall become pure. The one to be purified, having said, "I accept your favor," should go to a river or similar place, perform ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and, mindful of the place and time, say: "For the purpose of removing [the sin] beginning from my birth... and so on, up to "...for the sake of its removal. Having said, "I shall perform the such-and-such expiation instructed by the members of the assembly, together with its preliminary and concluding parts, by means of the such-and-such substitute at the appropriate time," [he should proceed].
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the murder of a Brahmin, reside in dependence upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair.
Thus, having had his hair, beard, and nails shaved— excluding those of the armpits and the private parts—
he recites: "O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, glory, luster, offspring, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence."

Having thus performed the cleansing of the teeth and bathed silently, one should say, "I shall perform the ash-bath as a constituent part of the expiation. Having said "Salutation to Rudra" and bathed with ash, and likewise having bathed with cow-dung, earth, water, cow's milk, curd, ghee, and kuśa-water, and having put on a washed garment and applied the *tilaka*:
"The fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of the cows;
therefore, may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and in the next."

Having performed the gift of a cow (*godāna*) as described above, and having given cooked rice (*āmānna*) to four or more pairs of Brahmins for the sake of removing sin and pleasing the Great Viṣṇu, one may consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or not. However, the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) is not for a Śūdra. For Jābāli has prescribed a rule regarding the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*): "One should indeed offer two separate oblations with clarified butter alone in the hall-fire (*śālāgni*)," and because there can be no substitute for the sacred fire.
Therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma,
an expiation should be granted that is devoid of recitation and burnt offerings.

And because of this statement by Parāśara, the performance of the *homa* through the mediation of a Brāhmaṇa is refuted. Therefore, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) on that day and having made the gifts of cows at the conclusion of the Viṣṇu-śrāddha as previously described, one should give the ten gifts mentioned before. The mantras for these gifts, however, are to be found in my *Dānakamalākara*.
[210] Now follows the gift of the Vaitaraṇī.

Then follows the gift of the Vaitaraṇī (the river). Having recited: "Remembering the place and time, for the sake of my easy crossing of the river situated at the gate of Yama, and for the attainment of all divine and human happiness, I shall perform the gift of the Vaitaraṇī," one should worship Yama—who is mounted upon a buffalo, holds an iron staff in his right hand and a noose in his left, and is seated upon a heap of cotton measuring one *droṇa* in a copper vessel. There, having tied a boat made of sugarcane with silk thread, one should worship and consecrate (*adhivāsa*) a black cow with her calf, which has horns tipped with gold, hooves with silver, a bronze milking vessel, a pair of black garments, the seven grains, an umbrella, and shoes. On the following day, having chosen and worshipped a recipient, and having taken hold of the tail of the cow while she faces east—provided with clarified butter, milk, *kuśa* grass, gold, and sesame seeds—one should remember the place and time, and after mentioning the aforementioned fruits, recite the mantra: "I give this black cow, together with a golden image of Yama placed upon a heap of cotton measuring one *droṇa*, equipped with gold-tipped horns, silver hooves, a bronze milking vessel, a pair of black garments, grains, an umbrella, shoes, and other accessories—or, if unable [to provide these], the cow alone—to you, O [Name] of such-and-such lineage; it is not mine. Thus saying, he should recite the mantra.
Desiring to cross the terrible river Vaitaraṇī at the most horrific gateway of Yama,
I give this cow Vaitaraṇī to you.
Regarding the acceptance [of the gift], some say this is the mantra:
"O Viṣṇu-form, best of the twice-born, god on earth, purifier of the assembly!
This cow Vaitaraṇī, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), has been given by me to you."
At the most terrible gate of Yama lies that river Vaitaraṇī;
to cross it, I give this cow to you as the Vaitaraṇī.
Having thus given the sacrificial fee and having presented a cow, and having circumambulated Yama and the Brahmin, he should offer everything [to them], saying:
"O little cow, wait for me at the gate of Yama, which is full of great terror;
O Goddess Vaitaraṇī, salutations, salutations to you, as I desire to cross over."
Thus one should follow. This concludes the gift of the Vaitaraṇī river.
Now, other gifts.
In the *Divodāsīya*, other gifts are also mentioned, as follows:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, grant me liberation; O Janārdana, grant me liberation.
By this gift of the cow of liberation, may Mukunda be pleased with me."

Thus, from the *Mokṣadharma*: "Whatever debt I have incurred in this world or the next, and whatever has been accumulated over seven lifetimes— may all that attain purification for me as I give this cow."
Thus ends the section on the debt-cow. O Keśava, may all the evil accumulated since birth through the actions of mind, speech, and body perish by means of this gift of a cow.
Thus one should give the "sin-cow.
Now follows the expiation for an untimely death (*durmaraṇa*). Regarding that:
In the case of death caused by a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste, or death in the air (by hanging), one should perform the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, or *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
likewise upon touching a woman in her menses, a woman recently delivered, or an untouchable (*antyaja*).
And for one killed by a Mleccha, there is a Kṛcchra penance for one year.

In the event of contact with one who has food remnants on the upper body (*ūrdhvocchiṣṭa*), on the lower body (*adharocchiṣṭa*), or on both (*ubhayocchiṣṭa*), or with a *caṇḍāla*, a carnivore (*kravyāda*), or when death occurs on a bed (*khaṭvā*), or when a corpse (*śava*) infested with worms or insects arises, one should perform three, six, or fifteen *kṛcchra* penances, or three *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, and then cremate [the body]. In the case of contact with an outcaste (*antyaja*), one should perform a year-long *kṛcchra*. In the case of falling from a precipice or by poison, nine *kṛcchras* are required. For suicide by means of horns, a Brahmin, weapons, thieves, and so forth, a year-long penance is prescribed. If the corpse has been left overnight (*paryuṣita*), three *kṛcchras* are required. The same applies to death occurring during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). The root source for this should be sought in my own work, the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Thereafter, one should recite or cause others to recite meritorious hymns (*puṇyastotra*) and the names of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. Then, once the departure of the life-breath has occurred, the son, having shaved his head, bathed, put on a portion of a new garment as his lower cloth and another portion as an upper garment (*uttarīya*), should have the deceased’s hair shaved, bathe him, cover him with a cloth, and adorn him with flower garlands and the like. Gālava states thus in the *Madanaratna*:
On the first day, the shaving of the hair and beards of the attendants must be performed; having shaved the hair, beard, and so forth of the deceased, one should then cremate him.
Manu states: "One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern city gate.
Regarding this, six funeral cakes (piṇḍas) are mentioned in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa within the section on ritual procedures (kriyānibandha).
At the time of the departure of the deceased, one should offer six rice-balls in succession:
at the place of death, at the door, and at the crossroads for the sake of Tārkṣya.
There are six [offerings] for resting, for the piling of wood, and likewise for the collection [of the bones].
Likewise: "At the beginning, there are six rice-balls for the gods, and ten rice-balls for the tenth-day rites."
In a place on the path, when half the way has been traversed, at a funeral pyre where a corpse is held in hand.
To the spirits dwelling in cremation grounds, [offerings are made]; likewise, the sixth [offering] is at the time of gathering the bones.
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Having bathed the weak person and having clothed him in clean garments..."
One should have it placed on the ground, covered with sacrificial grass (barhis), with its head toward the south.
Having anointed him with ghee and bathed him, [the performer], wearing a clean garment and sacred thread,
should adorn him— whose entire body is sprinkled with sandalwood paste— with flowers.
Having thrown pieces of gold into its seven openings and then having covered its mouth, his sons and other relatives should carry it out.
The seven apertures are located right there.
"One should place pieces of gold in the ears, the eyes, the mouth, and the nostrils.
Thus it is said elsewhere.
Taking food in an unbaked clay vessel, one person should follow behind the deceased who is preceded by the fire; halfway along the path, he should discard half of it upon the ground.
One should perform the cremation facing upwards, seated and facing the south.
Having slowly bent his left knee and offered a funeral cake (piṇḍa) with sesame seeds,
the son or another relative should then bathe and construct a large pyre of wood.
There, having laid him down supine with his head toward the south, [one should place the fire] in his mouth;

this state of being supine is intended for one who possesses the sacred fires (*sāgni*), because of the injunction regarding the placement of the fire-vessels. A male *śūdra* is to be cremated face-down, while a female is to be cremated supine. This is stated in the *Adipurāṇa*, cited in the *Śuddhitattva* and the *Hāralatā*:
"The corpse, taken by those born of his own lineage, is placed upon the funeral pyre."
Even a man [in this state] has his face turned downward and his feet directed toward the southern quarter.
"But a woman with her body laid supine [should be burned] even by her sapindas and other kinsmen.

This [rule] has been stated by others as pertaining to the *brāhma* rite. The Gauḍas maintain that this also applies to one who is without the sacred fires (*niragni*). However, Madanapāla, in the *Smṛtikaumudī*, states:
"If he is initiated (*upeta*), then for the one who is cremated, the procedure is like that of one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*)."
Because it is stated that even one who has not maintained the sacred fires is to be cremated like one who has maintained them, and regarding that [procedure], Kātyāyana says:
"Having laid him there on his back with his head to the south, [one should place] [fuel] in his mouth."

Because of the statement that [the body] is face-upward (*uttāna*), he says that even for one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*), it is exactly the same. However, it must be considered how instruction (*upadeśa*) is set aside by this extension (*atideśa*). Some, however, say that since the scriptural extension is equal to the original instruction, and because the rule "if he has been initiated" (*upetaś cet*) refers specifically to the twice-born (*dvija*), whereas in the *Brāhma-purāṇa* the word "twice-born" is absent, this [rule] refers only to Śūdras; thus, for the twice-born, there is no such thing as being face-upward. Others, however, say that for the twice-born of the *Chandoga* school there is the face-upward position, while for others there is the face-downward position. Let the discussion regarding the twice-born who maintain no sacred fires rest for now. As for the uninitiated twice-born and Śūdras, their face-downward position and having the head toward the north are beyond dispute. However, the cremation of a Śūdra is performed without mantras. Madanapāla states: "For whomsoever the rite—from conception (*niṣeka*) until the cemetery (*śmaśāna*)—is ordained to be performed with mantras. The truth is that this prohibition applies only to Vedic rites, whereas the Puranic rite certainly does take place. That will be explained in the section on the ritual performance (*prayoga*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"O daughter, such is the procedure for the four castes," so it was said. Pracetās states:
"One should not cremate a naked body; one should give nothing away nor abandon anything."
Yama says: "One should cremate the deceased after he has been bathed, adorned with garlands, and scented with auspicious fragrances.
This is stated in the *Gāruḍa-kriyānibandha*.
The performer, with a water-pot slung over his shoulder, should pour an uninterrupted stream of water clockwise from the base all around the altar.

But Baudhāyana says that when a husband and wife die at the same time, the rites up to the cremation constitute a single ritual procedure (*ekatantra*), while the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*) and the offering of water and rice-balls (*udakapiṇḍadāna*) and so forth are performed separately; this is also the case for *anvārohaṇa* (the widow ascending the funeral pyre). The offering of water is prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa texts.
First, having washed their clothes and being covered by those very garments,
they must perform a bath with their clothes on (sacaila-snāna), which removes all impurities.
Then, on a stone surface, water with sesame seeds should be offered by all;
thirty [libations] should be given to a Śūdra who has gone to the land of the deceased.
The specific details should be understood from the Nirṇayasindhu.
[215] Now follows the ritual procedure (prayoga).

The son or other relative, having performed the *apasavya* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder), and having stated: "Remembering the place and time, for the sake of ending the state of being a *preta* and attaining the highest world for our father of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, the deceased named So-and-so Dāsa, I shall perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*)," [proceeds as follows]. At the site of death, upon *darbha* grass, he says: "O *preta* of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, named So-and-so Dāsa, this is your water for washing (*avanejana*). This is your rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and the water for rinsing (*pratyavanejana*). Having thus offered the rice-ball for raising [the corpse] (*utthāpanapiṇḍa*), and having tied the rice-ball to the *preta’s* garment, he should lead it out through the southern door. Rice-balls should be offered at the door, at a crossroads, at the resting place, and at the funeral pyre (*citā*). Then, in a pure place prepared with the fivefold purification of the earth (*pañcabhūsaṃskāra*), having kindled the fire known as *kravyāda*, and having worshipped it with perfumes and garlands, he should cause the *preta*’s hair to be shaved. Adorned with perfumes and garlands, he places pieces of gold—or in their absence, clarified butter—into the seven openings of the face. Having wrapped [the body] in new cloth and smeared it with ghee, he places the male on the pyre facing downward with his head toward the north, and the female supine. Having offered an oblation of clarified butter either silently or with the mantra "This [is for] the world of the one to be consecrated, svāhā," he should apply fire to the location of the head. The mantra is found in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*.
Having committed an evil deed, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
when a man has come under the power of the time of death and reached the state of the five elements;
May he burn all the limbs of one who is joined with merit and demerit and enveloped by greed and delusion; may he go to the divine worlds.
One should cause a blazing great fire to be placed at the location of the head;
O daughter, such is the arrangement among the four castes.
The mention of the four castes refers to the twice-born who have not yet been initiated. However, in the *Gāruḍa-kriyānibandha*, a different mantra is stated:
"O Creator of beings, O Source of the world! You are the protector of the worlds; you are declared to be the agent of dissolution.
Therefore, lead this deceased person to heaven. Thus it is said.

Then, once a small portion of the cloth has been burnt, they should take the water-pot (*kumbha*), circumambulate it three times from left to right, break the pot with a stone three times, and throw the pot away. Without looking back, led by a child, they go to the water, wash the garment previously worn, put it on again, and stir the water with their left nostril. Then the elders and others bathe, place a stone upon *darbha* grass on the bank, and—holding a handful of straight *darbha* grass filled with sesame seeds—say: "O deceased Dāsa of the Kāśyapa lineage, may this handful of sesame seeds reach you," or "May it reach you. Facing south, everyone offers this once or thrice and bathes again.
