The offering of water (*udakadāna*) is optional for the daughter of one whose bride was carried off by force, a maiden, a sister’s son, a mother-in-law, a father-in-law, a maternal grandfather, his wife, a maternal uncle, and a king; it is not to be performed for a eunuch, a husband who died while pregnant, or those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). Others may perform it for these individuals as well. In this manner, one should offer water every day for thirty, fifteen, or ten days. Each day, the number of offerings should be increased by one, two, or three. Then, led by the child, they emerge from the water, wring out the lower garment, stand at the door of the house, bite three neem leaves, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), touch cow dung, mustard seeds, a bull, water, *durvā* grass, and fire, and place their foot upon a stone before entering the house. The elders should perform rites to dispel public ill-fortune. Thereafter, in two earthen vessels, one should place water for one or three days saying, "O deceased one, bathe here," and milk saying, "Drink this. According to Hemādri, this lasts for ten nights. Every day at mealtime, the performer should mentally resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to offer food upon the ground. Then there is a fast for three days, or alternatively, eating food that has been purchased or obtained. All must sleep on the ground for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts. On the first, third, seventh, and tenth days, they may eat together with their relatives, but only during the day. A lamp should be kept outside, and so forth; such details are to be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*.

[217] Now, the collection of the bones (*asthisaṃcayana*). This should be performed by Śūdras on the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, or ninth day; specifically, on the tenth day. Thereafter, it should be performed on a day excluding Tuesday, Saturday, and Sunday, as well as even lunar days (*tithi*), and those asterisms (*nakṣatra*) that consist of one, two, or three quarters. The performer, having remembered the place and time, and having said, "I shall perform the *śrāddha* for the collection of the bones for the sake of removing the state of being a ghost and attaining the highest world for our deceased father, the preta named so-and-so of the Kāśyapa gotra," and having placed a bundle of *kuśa* grass,
Having abandoned this world, you have gone to the supreme goal;
O Brahmin, I shall now unite myself with you through my mind in the form of the wind.
O such-and-such preta, may this seat be presented to you. Likewise, may the water for the guest-offering (argha), perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and clothing be presented.

Having thus given three offerings of raw rice (*āmānna*) to the flesh-eating deities (*kravyādadevatā*), to the deceased (*preta*), and to his friends, he should sprinkle the funeral pyre with curds, milk, and water. Then, having removed the ashes from the pyre with a *palāśa* branch, he should take the bones from the head, chest, hands, sides, and feet using the thumb and little finger. Having washed them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and Ganges water, honored them with perfumes and other offerings, wrapped them in linen cloth, and placed them in a new jar, he should cover it with a shallow bowl. Having buried it in the ground at the root of a tree in the forest or elsewhere, and having thrown the ashes into a river, he should construct an altar at the site of the pyre. There, having established three jars provided with *avakā* grass, *mīpa* leaves, umbrellas, and banners, and having made an offering to the flesh-eating deities, to the deceased, and to his friends, he should offer funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) into the jars. The mantra is as follows:
Salutation always here to the gods who have the eaters of raw flesh as their chiefs;
these gods dwelling in the cremation ground are proclaimed to be the attendants of corpses.
May food and water, inexhaustible as a jar, attend upon them—
those venerable and eternal deities who may be present here in this cemetery.
May they accept from us this inexhaustible eight-limbed bali offering,
and may they bestow upon this preta eternal and auspicious worlds.
May you grant us long life, health, and happiness for a long time.

Thus, having first given [the offerings] to those dwelling in the cremation grounds, the middle one to the deceased, and those to his friends on its southern side, he should bathe. He should cast the remaining bones into the Gaṅgā. The procedure for that is as follows: having performed the *hema-śrāddha* and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), he should wash the bones with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Having placed gold, pearls, silver, and coral within the bones, he should go to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), bathe, sprinkle [the bones] with *pañcagavya*, worship them with gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, and place them in a lump of clay. Facing south, saying "Homage to Dharma," he should enter the water and cast [the lump] in, saying "May he be pleased with me. Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins, he should again perform the *śrāddha* and the libation. In this context, they perform the ten gifts, the gift of a cow, and so forth. This should not be done during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), during the waning of Venus (*śukrāsta*), and so on; however, there is no fault if it occurs within the ten-day period [of impurity].
[219] Now, the *śrāddha* for provisions on a journey (*pātheya-śrāddha*).

Having said, "For the sake of providing provisions for the deceased belonging to the Kāśyapa lineage, named So-and-so, who has gone from the world of men to the world of *pretas*, I shall perform a *pātheya-śrāddha* (provisions-shrāddha)," one should say at the end of the previously mentioned mantra upon the bundle of *kuśa* grass: "Having abandoned this world, may this seat be presented to you. In the same way, one should say in every instance: "May the *argha*, scents, flowers, incense, lamp, clothing, and uncooked rice be presented. Then: "This is your seat for the *piṇḍa* (rice-ball offering); [may there be] the water for washing the feet (*avanejana*), the *piṇḍa*, the water for washing back the hands (*pratyavanejana*), the worship of the *piṇḍa*, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the procedure for all *śrāddhas* for the *pretas*. In this manner, one should perform the *śrāddha* for covering the naked; herein is the gift of clothing.

Now follows the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-fold funeral rite). It should be performed on odd-numbered days—namely, the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh. [The formula for the purpose is: "For the sake of the deceased [Name]’s liberation from the state of being a *preta* and for his attainment of the highest world, I shall perform the *viṣamaśrāddha* on this first day. Regarding the invitation of the Brahmins here, the mantra is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "You have gone to the divine world by the path ordained by Kṛtānta (Death)."
O Brahmin, I appoint you with my mind, which has become like the wind.
"I shall worship you with enjoyments"—thus one should invite the Brahmin.
The rest is as before. In the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*: "For the nine, seven, and twenty kings, there are nine *śrāddhas* in succession."
Regarding those two castes, the great seers say that there are six [subdivisions].
[220] Now, regarding the funeral balls for the *preta*s:
Halāyudha says they should be made of raw rice alone; others say they should be made of *caru*. Although Hemādri quotes Pāraskara as stating, "For a Śūdra, thirty are prescribed," nevertheless—

"One should offer ten *piṇḍas* to the deceased from all castes (*sarvavarṇa*). Since this was stated by that very [authority], there are indeed ten. Others, however, citing Viṣṇu’s statement, "They should offer water and *piṇḍas* for the deceased as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts," maintain that the number of *piṇḍas* corresponds to the duration of the periods of thirty, twenty, or fifteen nights. In the *Brāhma* section of the *Hemādri*, however, regarding those Brahmins for whom the "ten-*piṇḍa*" option applies, an extension of the *piṇḍas* is mentioned.
But the tenth *piṇḍa* to be offered by kings is on the twelfth day.
For Vaiśyas it is indeed in the fifteenth month, while for Śūdras it is given [at that time].

Regarding immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*): in the case of three-day purification (*tryaha*) and so forth, it is indeed the same there. In the case of immediate purification, all [offerings] should be given simultaneously;
likewise, in the case of three-day purification, only one [offering] should be given on the first day.
On the second day there were four, and on the third there were indeed five.
Śātātapa states: "Even when there is a reduction in the period of impurity (āśauca), one should nevertheless offer exactly ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
A reduction in the period of impurity occurs when the cremation takes place after the [initial] period of impurity has passed, or when it is performed using a leaf-shroud."
In this matter, the identity of place, agent, and substance should be understood;
the very same substance that was used on the first day shall be used for the ten-day period. Where the rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered on the first day, there one should complete everything.
Thus it is stated by Vyāsa in the *Kriyānibandha*. In the *Brāhma*: "He who, being composed in mind, offers food to the deceased on the first day, he indeed offers it even on the other nine days."
"In the *Mitākṣarā* it is stated that 'the one who performs the cremation alone shall observe the ten-day period. This is also found in the *Vāyavīya* section of the *Śuddhitattva*:
'Whether he be of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man, whoever provides the fire for the deceased, he alone shall indeed offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).'"
Regarding the death of the performer [of the rite], Bṛhaspati says in that very context:
"If anyone among those engaged in the performance should perish,
the rite must be performed by his kinsman or by all the collaborators together."
The Gauḍas maintain that the remaining rites should be performed with another [mantra]; others hold that everything should be done from the beginning. As stated in the Ādityapurāṇa:
"One should recite: 'May this piṇḍa attend upon the deceased (preta).
Now, the formal application (prayoga).

Having prepared an altar in the northeast, and having cooked a *caru* (oblation) in either a metallic or earthen vessel, or having made a ball (*piṇḍa*) the size of a wood-apple (*kapittha*) consisting of barley meal mixed with sesame, honey, and ghee, one should state the lunar day and other details, and say: "I shall perform the offering of the first-day body-filling ball for the sake of the formation of the head, eyes, teeth, and limbs of the deceased [Name], of the *Kāśyapa* lineage. For the second day and so forth, one should say "for the second day" and so on. Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu upon a stone and having performed the rites of the *darbha*-seat and the *avanejana* (water-sprinkling), one should say: "O deceased [Name]... for the sake of the formation of the head-limb, may this first-day body-filling ball be presented to you. The *pratyavanejana* (return-sprinkling) consists of *bhṛṅgarāja* and *tulasī* leaves. One should cast the ball into the water. The offering of the joined palms (*añjali*) has already been described. This is done thus for ten days. There is a specific variation in the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for each: On the second day: "For the sake of the completion of the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth-limbs. On the third day: "For the sake of the completion of the throat, arms, and chest," and also the *viṣama-śrāddha*. On the fourth day: "For the sake of the completion of the navel, genitals, and anus. On the fifth day: "For the sake of the purification of the knees, shanks, and feet-limbs," and also the *viṣama-śrāddha*. On the sixth day: "For the sake of the completion of all vital organs and limbs. On the seventh day: "For the sake of the formation of the limbs in the form of marrow, fat, flesh, sinews, and channels," and also the *viṣama-śrāddha*. On the eighth day: "For the sake of the accomplishment of the limbs of teeth, hair, and nails. On the ninth day: "For the sake of the accomplishment of the limb of virility (*vīrya*)," and also the *viṣama-śrāddha*. On the tenth day: "For the sake of the fulfillment of the body, its satisfaction, and the cessation of hunger. Every day, water-pots (*kumbhas*) should be given according to the number of *añjali* offerings. However, if one is unable to do much, it should be understood that food should be offered to the deceased for three days according to the procedure of the *piṇḍa-yajña*. Vyāsa states in the *Aparārka*:

On the final day of the period of impurity (āśauca), one should undergo shaving if the mother or a preceptor (guru) has died. Āpastamba states: “And there is the shaving for those who follow. Regarding this, the *Mitākṣarā*, the *Ratnākara*, and other authorities maintain that “those who follow” (*anubhāvinaḥ*) refers to the younger siblings. The Gauḍas, such as the author of the *Śuddhitattva*, hold that it refers to the shaving of all those who experience the impurity. This is stated in the *Ratnamālā*: “[It is permitted] by the command of the king or of the twice-born...”
Shaving is desired during marriage rites, deaths, and births; likewise,
it is recommended for the release from bondage, at sacrifices, and during initiations, as well as under all [favorable] constellations.
Vyāsa states in the Aparārka:
"The son and the wife should perform the shaving of the head at the conclusion according to the rules;
any other person who is entitled to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) should likewise do so with a concentrated mind."

The collective performance at the beginning and end for the sons should be understood. On the tenth day, having offered the limb-piṇḍas and having constructed a triangular altar (vedī), one should offer three piṇḍas to the friends of the deceased, to the deceased himself, and to Yama. Having presented cakes, banners, umbrellas, and water-jars, and having given the *kākabali* (the offering to crows), the son, the wife, all those who were younger than the deceased, and others should anoint a stone with oil, cast it into the water, and discard the two garments worn by the deceased while touching him. Then, having bathed, they should all offer three handfuls of *dharma-udaka* (water for the dharma) and, having bathed with a paste of mustard seeds, or sesame and *āmalaka* fruits, they should return home. Regarding the occurrence of a new moon (*darśa*) within the ten-day period, Mādhava cites Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
Gautama says that if a new-moon sacrifice (darśa) should occur during a period of impurity for members of any caste, one should complete the rites for the deceased.
Ślokagautama states: If the new moon occurs within ten days [of death], one should complete everything therein;
however, for the parents, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and handfuls of water (jalāñjali) for as long as the period of impurity (āśauca) lasts.

This [rite] also occurs on the new moon day within the three-day period. However, after that, even for the ancestors (pitṛs), the *tantra* must indeed be concluded on the new moon day; but if the new moon day falls during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the parents, one should conclude it then.
Only after those three days would the subsequent *tantra* be finalized.

Thus says Gālava. For others, however, the period may be completed even within three days; this is stated in the *Kālāmṛta* and the *Nirṇayāmṛta*. In the *Madanaratna* and the *Pārijāta*, however, it is said that the rule of Gālava applies to those in distress or to those who are not the biological sons (*anaurasa*) of their parents; for parents, there is no reduction of the period even after three days. The source for this [latter view] must be investigated.
Thus ends the section on the impurity (*āśauca*) of Śūdras and their duties, composed by the venerable Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa in the *Śūdradharma*.
Now, on the eleventh day:
Manu says, "A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya by touching his mount and weapon."
A Vaiśya [should carry] a goad or reins, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties [should carry] a staff.
Devala states in the *Śuddhitattva*:
"When the initial days have passed, having bathed well and performed auspicious rites,
and having caused the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce blessings (*svastivācana*), they are liberated from the impurity."
The learned authorities maintain that this [rite] occurs after the *sapiṇḍana*. Śaṅkha, in the Hemādri, states:
"One may perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day even while impure;
for the performer there is temporary purity, yet he remains impure thereafter."

The same applies to a Śūdra as well. Thus Paiṭhīnasi said: "The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all; however, the period of impurity (sūtaka) for the four castes is distinct for each."
As for that which Marīci stated:
"At the end of the period of impurity, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) is then properly concluded;
the entire śrāddha ceremony should be performed—this is the rule for all castes."
Thus, for all [castes], that [period] lasts ten days at most. As for what is stated in the *Mātsya*:
"On the eleventh day, likewise, a Kṣatriya or others should feed eleven Brahmins; however, at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), one should feed an odd number of twice-born men."
Thus, the *Madanapārijāta* states that this refers specifically to the *śrāddha* for the host of Rudras;

for there is the scriptural injunction: "It should be performed with Rudra in view, as it brings satisfaction to the deceased. However, Śūlapāṇi, Vācaspati, and others in the *Kalpataru*, on the basis of this very statement and because of Viṣṇu’s declaration regarding the cessation of impurity (*āśaucāpagama*), maintain that even for Śūdras and others, the end of the period of impurity occurs precisely at the conclusion of the aforementioned period, since the statements of Śaṅkha and others cited previously are not authoritative [in their view]. Others, however, due to the force of the two types of texts, assert an option (*vikalpa*) depending on local custom (*deśācāra*). Satyavrata says:
Even in the case of immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca), [the rite] must be offered on the eleventh day for the deceased; so says Uśanas:
"Even when the impurity lasts for three days, the first [rite] must be performed on the eleventh day."
Regarding a past object, that [knowledge] is held to occur either immediately or after three days have passed.
Regarding the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, Baudhāyana states in the Hemādri: "The Ekoddiṣṭa should take place on the very next day, or again on the twelfth day;
thereafter, one may perform it on odd-numbered days according to one's capacity."
Whether in half a month, or in a month, or in a season, or even in a year.
[225] Now, the ritual of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
According to the *Mātsya* and *Kaurma* Purāṇas in the *Hemādri*.
That son who does not perform the rite of releasing a bull, nor offers handfuls of water at a sacred ford,
is indeed nothing but the excrement of his father.
It is also written:
"One should desire many sons, so that even one might go to Gayā,
or perform the horse sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If a woman who has sons and a husband dies before her husband,
she should not perform the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), but should instead give a milch cow."
If for a deceased person the *vṛṣotsarga* (release of a bull) is not performed on the eleventh day,
his state as a *preta* remains firmly established, even by means of hundreds of *śrāddha* offerings.
As for that which is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa in the Hemādri: "On the third day of Caitra, or on the twelfth day of Vaiśākha"; and that which is in the Viṣṇudharma:

"And on both equinoxes, as well as on the anniversary of a kinsman's death"—this [rule] is to be understood as applying when the previously mentioned [times] are unavailable. In the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]:
"That which is red in color, but white at the mouth and the tail..."
That bull which is white in its hooves and horns is called *nīla*.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "O auspicious lady, there are four calves, or even two, though they may not be born."
[226] Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

In that regard, for one belonging to the divine class (*devajātīya*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the form of Viṣṇu has been mentioned previously; the source for that must be investigated. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), having recollected the place and time, and having said: "For the purpose of the deceased *dāsa* of the Kāśyapa gotra named so-and-so attaining the world of Rudra—or the worlds of the Vasus and others—by means of the cessation of his state as a *preta*, I shall perform the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*)," [one proceeds].
Nandā, Sumanā, Suśīlā, Payasvinī, and Surabhi as the fifth—these are said to be the mothers of the bull; one should worship them, or else not.

Then, having worshipped Rudra in the pitcher (kumbha) located in the northeast (aiśāna), having established the fire (agni), and having prepared the seat of Brahmā (brahmāsana), one should pour water and milk into two portions of the *praṇītā* vessel, prepare a milk-rice oblation (*pāyasa*) and a flour-oblation (*piṣṭacaru*), and perform six oblations to Agni first—based on the traditional rule, "Six oblations to Agni and then the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*)"—with the mantra *agnaye svāhā*. Then follow the two *āghāra* offerings and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Next, having offered clarified butter to Prajāpati, Indra, Agni, and Soma; then having offered the milk-rice to Agni, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhaga, Mahādeva, and Īśāna; and then having offered the flour-oblation or the rice-oblation with the mantra *pūṣṇe svāhā*; and finally having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for both [oblations] and nine oblations of clarified butter ending with Prajāpati—one should decorate a bull, or four, two, or even one heifer (*vatsatarī*). Regarding this, Madanapāla maintains that for a Śūdra there is no oblation with Vedic mantras. Others, however, say it may be done by name. Then, having circumambulated the bull and the fire four times, and having sprinkled them with the water from the Rudra-pitcher, one should decorate the bull and the cows with perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth. Having given the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), a seat, and perfume to the four Brahmins representing the forms of Rudra, and having given four types of cooked food (*āmānna*) to the Brahmins representing the deceased (*preta*) in the form of Rudra, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the *vṛṣotsarga* Śrāddha. Some say that one should offer funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) at the footprint of the bull. Then, having marked the bull on the left flank with a trident and on the right with a discus (or vice versa), and having taken its tail along with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, gold, and water, one should state the place and time: "For the sake of my father, of such-and-such a deceased person belonging to the Kāśyapa gotra, for the purpose of attaining the world of Rudra by means of liberation from the state of being a *preta*, I release this bull, together with a heifer, dedicated to the deity Rudra, for the deceased of such-and-such a gotra. I give you a husband; roam at will with this husband; through him, may the illustrious Rudra be pleased. Having said this, and taking the water from the tail with sesame seeds while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should recite: "O deceased one of such-and-such a name, may this water from the tails of the bull and the heifer attend upon you. Thus one should recite.
O Dharma, you who take the form of a bull and bring joy to the world;
O eternal one, protect us, for you are the foundation of the eightfold form.
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is proclaimed to be a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion, so that he may lead this deceased one to heaven.
For he has been given by me as the supreme husband for all of you;
and these beautiful women have all been given by me to you as your wives.
"May this bull, given by me, always deliver him.
Having thus offered a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) to the Brahmin and a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) with gold to the preceptor (*ācārya*), he should perform the dedication to the Lord (*īśvarārpaṇa*).
Thus concludes the ritual of the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
[227] Now, the offerings to the Vasu-gaṇas, the Śrāddha rites, and so forth.

Then, having performed the *vasu-śrāddha*—consisting of eight or one Brahmin, dedicated to the eight Vasus beginning with Dhara and Dhruva, just like the *nava-śrāddha*—and likewise the *rudragaṇa-śrāddha* (the "uneven śrāddha") for eleven or one Brahmin; having sipped water (*ācamya*), recalled the place and time, and said: "I shall perform the first śrāddha on the eleventh day according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, for the sake of ending the state of being a *preta* and attaining the form of the Vasus and others for our father, the deceased named so-and-so of the Kāśyapa lineage"; then, having invited eleven or one Brahmin for the first śrāddha, saying: "A moment must be granted in the place of the deceased named so-and-so; may you grant it; I accept," and having invited a *darbha-baṭu* (a student) while saying: "With those who are free from anger and devoted to purity," the entire *nava-śrāddha* should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rules. In that regard, having drawn a circular mandala at the door, sipped water, and worshipped, he gives the water for the feet (*pādya*) saying: "O deceased named so-and-so, may this *pādya* be present for you. Having sipped water again and sat facing north, he says: "O [deceased] of such-and-such lineage, may this perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, clothing, umbrella, ornaments, and so forth, be present for you. After causing [them] to recite "May there be completion," many authorities say there is no *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). However, according to the *Gṛhya-bhāṣya*, it exists. In that case, there is one offering of raw food (*āma*) with the formula: "Svāhā to the deceased named so-and-so. Then: "May the raw food together with a water-pot and accessories be present for the deceased named so-and-so in this first śrāddha. Regarding the scattering of rice (*vikira*), there is an option. Then, having drawn a line on the altar (*vedi*) and for the *ucchiṣṭa-piṇḍa* (the remnant ball), he performs: "This is the seat for the ball," "this is the washing," "this is the ball," "this is the re-washing," and the worship of the ball and the thread. Then, having performed the *suprokṣita* (well-sprinkled) rite and so forth, and having said, "May our lineage increase," he gives the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In the case of the eleven [Brahmins], he should give ornaments, vehicles, and so forth to the first [deceased]. Bṛhaspati says: [text follows].

Having honored with perfumes and garlands the ornaments, garments, and so forth of the deceased, as well as the father’s vehicles and such, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha meal.

Then he should dismiss them with the words, "May you depart happily. The remainder [of the procedure] is like that for a *navashrāddha*. Then he should perform the first monthly *śrāddha*, or the sixteen *śrāddhas* which share the same ritual framework (*tantra*) as it. Some say that the first annual *śrāddha* (*ādyābdika*) should also be performed here. Regarding this, the offering of the "feet" (*padadāna*) is mentioned in the *Devajānīya-Gāruḍa*, beginning from the eleventh day:
"Everything is given on the twelfth day, especially on the thirteenth;
the 'feet' are all things, and there are thirteen of the most excellent ones."
O Vainateya, he who gives here for his own sake while still living— even though the recipient has died—
becomes happy and travels upon the Great Path.
A seat, sandals, an umbrella, a seal-ring,
a water-pot, food, a vessel-stand, and garments— this is the eightfold station.
Likewise:
"By the gift of a vessel and a seat, by food with a ring,
and by clarified butter and a sacred thread, one's state shall reach fulfillment."
One certainly becomes happy through the gift of a buffalo, a chariot, or a cow;
here, there are thirteen steps provided with all necessary accessories.
He who gives here on behalf of the deceased, even while living for his own sake,
goes to the supreme state, freed from great suffering.
On the eleventh day for the deceased, these thirteen items should be given according to one's ability; by that means, he shall be satisfied.
Food, water, sandals, a water-pot,
an umbrella, a garment, a staff, and an iron rod as the eighth.
The fire-vessel, a lamp, sesame seeds,
betel, sandalwood, and the offering of flowers— these are the fourteen gifts.
Whoever bestows a horse, a chariot, or even an elephant upon a Brahmin shall obtain corresponding happiness in accordance with his own greatness.
Regarding this, the specific mantras for each gift should be understood from my *Dānakamalākara*; however, the original source for this must be investigated. Next is the gift of a bed (*śayyādāna*).
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, as cited in the Hemādri: "Therefore, having procured a firm bed made of strong wood,
beautiful, inlaid with ivory filigree, and adorned with golden bands."
Covered with swan-down feathers, provided with beautiful pillows for the head,
furnished with a bedspread, and perfumed with fragrant incense.
Upon it, one should establish a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī;
here, in the place of Hari, one should place the deceased.
At the head of the bed, one should arrange a water-pot filled with ghee.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, that should be known by the wise as the "sleep-pitcher" (nidrākalaśa),
along with betel, powdered saffron, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should devoutly place by the sides a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a seat, and a vessel, as well as the seven grains.
Whatever else is beneficial for one lying on the bed—
such as golden jars and water-pitchers, and a canopy of five colors— is provided.
The mantras,
however, are as follows: "Just as the bed of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean,
so may my bed also be never empty in birth after birth."
Because the bed of Keśava and Śiva is not empty,
that very half [of the offering] belongs to him alone.
Having thus given it all to him and prostrated, one should dismiss him.
On the eleventh day as well, this same procedure is proclaimed.
And listen, O Indra among kings, as I describe the distinction here:
whatever clothing, vehicles, or vessels were used by him, [he gave them away].
Whatever was desired by her, all that one should imagine;
one should always place that very same golden Puruṣa within it.
Having performed the worship, the death-bed (mṛtaśayyā) should be given as prescribed.
In that very same *Padma Purāṇa*:
"On the second day after the end of the impurity, one should give a bed endowed with auspicious characteristics."
In the same way, [one should offer] a golden man, provided with fruit and clothing.
Having honored a brahmin couple adorned with various ornaments and having seated them upon a bed, he should then offer the *madhuparka*.
Having taken a small piece of bone from the forehead with a silver vessel, one should prepare a fine dish of milk-rice mixed with curd and milk.
One should feed a Brahmin couple; this indeed is the eternal rule.
This very rule was observed by the most excellent Brahmins of the Pārvatīya region. Regarding the acceptance of gifts therein, it is stated as follows:
But once she has been taken [as a wife], she indeed requires the rite of consecration again.
In the future,
by the power of the gift of a bed, that living being dwells happily in heaven, in the city of Purandara, and likewise in the abode of the Son of the Sun.
He remains free from all affliction until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus ends the section on the gift of a bed. In another Smṛti, regarding the performance of rites:
"If a second death occurs during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka)..."
One should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) as well as the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga).
One should not perform the rites of the eleventh or twelfth day during a period of birth-impurity;
whether pure or impure, one should simply perform them without hesitation.
[232] Now, the Water-Pot (*udakumbha*).
From the *Haimādri-Smṛtisamuccaya*.
From the eleventh day onwards, sons should daily offer a water-pot filled with water and food for as long as a year.
In the *Madanaratna*, Gautama states:
"One should perform daily the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha that excludes the gods, accompanied by a water-pot and free from [specific] ritual injunctions,
according to the procedure of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), following the annual śrāddha."

Regarding this funeral cake (piṇḍa), there is an option: one should give food and a water-pot to this Brāhmaṇa day after day. According to Pāraskara’s statement cited in the Hemādri, "Some also offer a funeral cake. The specific details should be understood from the Nirṇayasindhu. In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, as quoted in the Devajānīya, it is said: "A lamp should be offered daily on a difficult path for a man, even for as long as a year, with the desire for the welfare of the deceased."
One should perform the rite for Yama’s pleasure, having properly resolved it with the ancestors' [mantras] well-established.
Now, regarding the monthly rites (*māsika*):
the *sapiṇḍana* must be performed only after those have been completed.

According to the Smṛti of Laugākṣi, "One should not perform the Sapiṇḍana rite without having first offered the sixteen Śrāddhas," it follows that for one whose Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed before the completion of a year, the Śrāddhas must be performed again after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
A monthly offering and a water-pot should also be given for him for a year.
Because it has been stated by that very [author]:
"Even those rites performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by being drawn forward [out of their time] are again drawn back,
because of the prohibition against performing them after a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*."

And because of the statement of Gālava: "Those [rites] should be performed before the *sapiṇḍana* according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, but after that according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure," and so forth; this is to be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Kātyāyana states them as follows:
"The twelve monthly rites, the first [anniversary], the two half-yearly rites, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—this constitutes the sixteen *śrāddhas*."
The three fortnightly rites and the annual rite—these are the sixteen śrāddhas.

Thus is the reading of Jātūkarṇya. The first is the *ūnamāsika* (the deficient monthly); the sixth-monthly is the *ūnaṣaṣṭha*; the annual is the *ūnābdika*. Therefore, for the deceased [Name], in order to terminate his state as a *preta* and to attain the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), I shall perform—having drawn them forward on the eleventh or twelfth day—the first monthly, second three-fortnightly, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, *ūnaṣaṣṭha*, seventh, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and *ūnābdika* *śrāddhas*, which are to be performed at their respective times, for the sake of accomplishing the qualification for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Having said this, and having seated sixteen Brahmins or *kuśa*-grass substitutes for the first monthly, saying, "May this moment be present for you," he should perform everything for the first monthly just as in the *navaśrāddha*, and offer sixteen portions of rice and *piṇḍas*.
regarding the *sapiṇḍana*:
in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*.
On the twelfth day, after six months, or after three fortnights, or at the end of three months; or on the eleventh day, or when a full year has passed, or upon the arrival of an auspicious occasion.

Viṣṇu states: “Having performed the Śrāddha for the twelve days as if they were the monthly rites, one should perform it on the thirteenth day. Furthermore, another Smṛti says: “For Śūdras, it is declared that [the rites] should be performed on the twelfth day, excluding the Mantras. This refers specifically to a Śūdra who performs the Darśa-Śrāddha, according to the *Aparārka* and the *Kalpataru*. The meaning is that after the period of impurity (*āśauca*), having performed the twelve monthly Śrāddhas during the twelve days, the Sapiṇḍana rite is performed on the twelfth day; however, if there is an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), it is on the thirteenth. The details should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
[234] Now follows the formal argument.

Having said, "Remembering the place and time, for the sake of ending the state of being a *preta* for my father of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, the deceased named so-and-so, and for the purpose of his attainment of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) such as the Vasus, I shall perform the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha*, which consists of both the *Ekoddiṣṭa* and *Pārvaṇa* forms," he should say, "Please grant your favor by granting a moment [of attention] in the place of my father, the deceased named so-and-so. Then, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), saying "Grant a moment in the place of the Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla," and so forth—two [moments] for the divine portion (*daiva*). Alternatively, the moment may be granted for the *preta* immediately after the divine portion. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), saying "Grant a moment in the place of our father, the servant named so-and-so, who is of the form of the Vasu," and so forth. Likewise, "In the place of our father’s grandfather, the servant named so-and-so, who is of the form of Rudra," and so forth. Likewise, "In the place of our father’s great-grandfather, the servant named so-and-so, who is of the form of Āditya. Thus there are six Brahmins, or *kuśa*-effigies (*kuśabaṭu*). The mantra "Free from anger, devoted to purity" is recited everywhere. In the place of the *preta*, it is like the *Navaśrāddha*; in the ancestral (*pitrya*) portion, it is like the *Pārvaṇa*. Then, on the following day, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and again granted the moments, he should draw a square mandala for the divine portion and to its south, a circle or triangle for the *preta*. Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) in order and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he says: "O Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla, please be seated; be seated. "O *preta*, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, please be seated. Having seated them on their seats, he ties the waist-cloth (*nīvī*) and says, "I shall perform the commenced *Śrāddha* rite. When told, "Do so," he says: "This is the seat for the Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla; it is a comfortable seat. Be seated here; you are Dharma. Let a moment be granted for the divine portion. May I obtain it accordingly. Thus for the second divine portion. Then, having said, "Two *argha* vessels have been prepared," he says, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla into your presence. When told, "Invoke them," he says, "Salutation to Kāma and Kāla; may the illustrious ones come," and having invoked them, he gives the *argha* water to the two Brahmins, saying, "O Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla, this *argha* is for you. Having turned the vessel face down, he offers perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and clothing, and causes the declaration of completion to be recited. With the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he says, "May this seat stand before our father of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, the servant named so-and-so; it is your own seat. May you accept it," and so forth. Then, having offered seats for the father’s father and the others according to the *Pārvaṇa* rite, he prepares four *argha* vessels. In the first [set], there are four purifiers (*pavitra*); in the other three, three each. Then, having given [the *argha*] saying, "O *preta* of the Kāśyapa *gotra, named so-and-so, may this *argha* stand before you," and saying, "I shall unite the *arghya* of the *preta* of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, named so-and-so, with his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather," and being told, "Unite them," he places one purifier in the vessel for the father and pours the *arghya* into that vessel while saying, "O *preta* of the Kāśyapa *gotra*, named so-and-so, having merged with your father, the servant named so-and-so, who is of the form of the Vasu, may you attain union with him. In the same way, he does so with the grandfather of the form of Rudra in the second vessel, and with the great-grandfather of the form of Āditya in the third. Then:
"O fathers, this preta who has followed you, I give him to you.
May it be well for the rest; may they be born long-lived."

Thus he should touch [the vessels]. Madanapāla states that after the *saṃsarga* (reintegration), the offering of *arghya* water is made for the deceased (*preta*). Then, having offered three *arghya* portions to the deceased, the father, and the others according to the *pārvaṇa* rite, and having turned the vessel face down, he should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, clothing, and ornaments to the deceased and to his father and the others. Having caused [them] to recite the words "May there be completion," he should offer an oblation into the hand [of the deceased], saying: "May this oblation reach the deceased, the deceased, and Yama. Or, having performed the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) for the deceased’s father and the others, he should resolve upon the uncooked rice (*āmānna*) for the gods, the deceased, and the deceased’s father and the others. Having given the remnant-rice ball (*ucchiṣṭapiṇḍa*) and the scattered offerings (*vikira*), he should give rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) from the household cooking—either with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or with barley meal (*saktu*)—to the deceased and to his father and the others. [He should say: "Today, etc., for the sake of the liberation of the deceased Amuka-dāsa of the Kāśyapa lineage from the state of being a *preta*, and for the attainment of the world of the Vasus and other ancestors, I shall unite this rice-ball of the deceased with the rice-balls of his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, [all] of the Kāśyapa lineage, [who are] in the form of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. When [the officiant] says, "I unite them," he should divide the *preta*-rice-ball into three parts. Taking one part and honey, he should say: "O deceased of the Kāśyapa lineage, Amuka, I unite your rice-ball with the rice-ball of your father, Amuka-dāsa of such-and-such lineage, who is in the form of the Vasu. This is your rice-ball; for you, *svadhā* and obeisance (*namaḥ*). In the same way, the second part is united with the grandfather in the form of Rudra, and the third part with the great-grandfather in the form of Āditya. Then, having recited the previously mentioned mantra, "This deceased has followed you," and having performed the ritual rinsing (*pratyavanejana*), the worship of the rice-balls, and so forth, he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having performed the ten gifts, including the gift for the Vaitaraṇī river, he should complete the remainder. Then, having performed the *pātheya-śrāddha* (provision-shrāddha), he should perform the daily water-pot *śrāddha* (*udakumbha-śrāddha*) every day until the end of the year, and again perform the monthly *māsika* rites at their proper times.
Thus concludes the section on the ritual for the deceased (*aurdhvadehika-prayoga*) in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by the venerable Kamalākara.
[238] The Section on the Determination of Castes (*jātinirṇaya-prakaraṇa*).
Now, the duties of the Śūdra.
In this regard, twice-born men who have not been initiated are equal to Śūdras;
for they are indeed equal to a Śūdra as long as they do not perform sacrifices with the Veda.

Thus it is stated in the *Manu-smṛti*. This equality [of status] consists merely in the lack of entitlement to perform ritual acts; however, bathing, the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), and so forth do exist [for them], because of Gautama’s statement: "Prior to initiation (*upanayana*), there is freedom in conduct, speech, and eating. But the *śrāddha* rite certainly takes place with mantras, for the *Manu-smṛti* states: "One should not employ the Veda (*brahma*) except when offering the *svadhā* libation. Here, *brahma* means the Veda. Furthermore, this is also stated in the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Padma-purāṇa*.
On the new moon day, on the eighth days, and on the fifteenth days of the dark fortnight,
even one who is uninitiated should perform this [rite] during all the years.
The Śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa bestows the fruit of all desires;
even one separated from his wife, or even while staying abroad, should perform this constantly.
Even a Śūdra, though lacking the sacred mantras, may perform [the rite] according to this procedure, O wise one.

The same applies at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*); however, the specific details should be understood from the section on *śrāddha* rites in the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Now, the duties of women (*strīdharma*).

The same applies to the wives of the twice-born as well. For them too, there is no entitlement [to Vedic study] up to what has been stated—namely, the blessing and the vow of celibacy—because of their inequality, according to the principle of the sixth book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]. However, they certainly do have entitlement to the *śrauta* and *smārta* rites that are accomplished by means of fire. This is because the masculinity mentioned in the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*) is not intended to be significant (is *avivakṣita*) as a qualification of the person addressed, according to the principle of the sixth book; and furthermore, because of the statement of Āpastamba: "For from the taking of the hand [in marriage], there is joint status in ritual acts as well as in the fruits of merit. Also, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, the entitlement of the wives of the twice-born to the practice of *śrauta* knowledge is affirmed.

"Some learned men declare that women are equal to Śūdras," and because of the Smṛti text: "Women and Śūdras share the same dharma. Furthermore, their sacraments (saṃskāras) are likewise silent, like those of the Śūdras;
indeed, this entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without mantras.
Thus it is stated by Manu. Furthermore, because of the statement of Jātūkarṇya: "Therefore, a Śūdra may be entitled to the dharma of *pūrta* (charitable works), but not to the Vedic [dharma]."

And because of the statement by Vyāsa: "Whatever gift is given outside the sacrificial altar (vedī) is declared to be *paurtika*," there is likewise eligibility for Śūdras in the case of the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*) such as the *tulā*, as well as in the consecration of temples and reservoirs; for, according to the rule of the sixth [case], the masculine gender mentioned in the scriptural injunction is not intended to be significant with respect to the fruit. Consequently, married women have eligibility even independently through their husband’s permission, since these acts do not require the mediation of the sacred fire (*agni*). Widows, however, certainly possess eligibility due to their independence. This has been explained in detail by Vijñāneśvara in the section on legal procedure (*vyavahāra-adhyāya*). For this very reason, [the same applies] regarding the *tulā* and other such rites.

"A man shall become like Pradyumna, and a woman shall be equal to Pārvatī"—such is the hearing of the fruits for women. If it is argued that, because this is a duty of Śūdras, the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) would also apply to women, listen:
the injunction for the five sacrifices is that a householder must never neglect them.

Thus, according to the statement of Śaṅkha and others, since the masculine gender is intended to be significant—just as the singular number of the agent is in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta)—there is no application for a woman. Furthermore, there is no scriptural text regarding a compulsory (*nitya*) rite that would allow for the inclusion of a woman by disregarding the masculine gender associated with it; for, due to the impossibility of the rite being compulsory, the absence of sin (*pratyavāya*) would otherwise have to be merely inferred. Only on the basis of an explicit scriptural statement can there be entitlement (*adhikāra*) to a compulsory rite. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa within the *Madanaratna*: "Every day, the libation for the husband must be performed with water, *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds."
A woman who is childless indeed possesses the entitlement even for the *śrāddha* rites— whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—
because of the statement of Śaṅkha: "The husband shall offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband."
A wife who, being childless, maintains her husband’s funeral rites while remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall herself offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive his entire share of the inheritance.

This is because of the statement of Vṛddha-Manu. This has been explained in detail in the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Where there is a scriptural mention of a fruit (*phalaśravaṇa*), as in the case of the worship of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and so forth, there is certainly eligibility (*adhikāra*). The same applies to vows (*vrata*) and other such rites. Therefore, although women are equal to Śūdras, they do not perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). Rather, at the time of eating, one should cast a single mouthful of food soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the fire. As stated by Gobhila in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*: "He whose food would otherwise be purified in their presence shall eat after having first offered it to the fire. This is the general direction; much more is not said here for fear of excessive prolixity. [240]
Now, the duties of women. Manu:
"The procreation of offspring and the protection of those already born..."
The daily course of worldly life is visibly dependent upon women.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her.
And those who become attached to sense-objects must indeed be established under one's own control;
for the father protects her in childhood, and the husband protects her in youth.
But sons have no independence whatsoever when their father is in his old age;
women, moreover, must be protected especially from even the most subtle lapses of heedlessness.
For if they are not protected, they will bring ruin upon two families;
a father who does not give [a daughter] in due time is censurable, and a husband who does not approach her is likewise censurable.
The meaning is "they go away.
Regarding the son when the husband has died, Paiṭhīnasi states in the Kalpataru: "The son should be told [to protect] his mother, for she is unprotected."
Be vigilant and guard this thread;
do not sow the seeds of others in another’s field.
Guard your wife in her youth, fearing the seed of another.
Women are the deities of the household; for them there is no ritual purity, no vow, and no fasting. By serving their husbands, they attain the supreme goal. (Brāhma).
Purity is not to be questioned in the case of women, children, and the sick. Manu says:
"Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, and wandering about..."
Sleeping, and dwelling in another's house—these are indeed the six vices of women.
They do not examine their form, nor is there any regard for their age; whether handsome or ugly, they enjoy a man simply because he is a male.
Manu assigned to women the bed, the seat, ornaments, lust, anger, dishonesty, a malicious disposition, and evil conduct.
It is established as the law that women have no ritual action with mantras;
for it is the settled rule that women are eternally devoid of sensory power and excluded from mantras.
No one is able to guard a woman by force;
rather, one should employ her in the accumulation of wealth and in its expenditure.
In the practice of sexual intercourse with his wife, and in the protection of what has been received.
Manu: Whether by a girl, a young woman, or even an aged woman,
no action whatsoever should be performed independently, even within the home.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or even her son;
for through separation from these, she becomes censured in both families.

Viṣṇu: When her husband is away on a journey, she must not apply cosmetics; she must not visit the houses of others; and she must not stand near the doorway or at the windows. Yājñavalkya: [The same].
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, the three aims of life flourish there.
A father should protect his daughter, a husband his married wife, and sons her in old age.
In their absence, their kinsmen [have authority]; a woman never has independence anywhere, [being subject] to her husband, brothers, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and brother-in-law.
Women should be honored by their kinsmen with ornaments, clothing, and food;
they should keep the household utensils in order, be skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
Devoted to her husband, she should perform the salutation of the feet of both parents-in-law;
the word of the husband must be carried out by women—this is the supreme duty of a woman.
For one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must be awaited until purification;
[he is forbidden] from recreation, bodily adornment, and witnessing social gatherings or festivals.
A woman whose husband is away from home should avoid laughter and traveling to the houses of others;
so says Bṛhaspati: [she should also avoid] adorning herself, dancing and singing, and witnessing social gatherings and festivals.
And one should not indulge in meat or liquor when the master is away on a journey.
In the *Kalpataru*, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"While her husband is away on a journey, she must refrain from swinging, dancing, sporting, viewing curiosities, visiting forest gardens, using vehicles, using artificial beds, consuming superior drinks or foods, playing with balls, and from the use of perfumes, garlands, ornaments, tooth-cleansing sticks, collyrium, mirrors, and other articles of adornment.
In that same *Kalpataru*, the *Bhārata* states:
These women are indeed called "glories" (śriyaḥ) and should be treated with honor by one who desires prosperity;
for when a woman is both charming and restrained, O Bhārata, she becomes true glory (śrī).
Manu says: Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual acts there become fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Therefore, these women—sisters-in-law, daughters-in-law, sisters, and so forth—should be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food. As stated by Dakṣa in the *Kalpataru*:
"Every woman is like a leech [for her husband's wealth] unless she is provided with ornaments, clothing, and food."
For even when constantly well-nourished, it indeed causes a man's downfall.
The leech draws out blood alone, for she is but a poor creature;
but the other [the woman] takes away wealth, property, flesh, virility, strength, and happiness.
Full of apprehension during her childhood, she becomes devoted in her youth;
yet in old age, a woman regards her own husband as mere straw.
"Otherwise, one will later become childless, just as a disease that has been neglected. Manu says:
"A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's maintenance."
For a woman, even one who is steadfast, may become corrupted when emaciated by lack of livelihood.
Yājñavalkya:
When there is another wife who possesses all the [required] wealth, he should have her perform the religious duties;
among wives of equal status, she who is devoted to dharma should do so in accordance with dharma, but not by any other except the eldest.
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"A man with many wives should have service such as tending the sacred fire performed by a wife of the same caste;
if there are many such wives, it should be done by the eldest, provided she is not censurable."
Kātyāyana says: Among these women, one should employ her who has borne sons, who carries out orders, who is skillful, sweet-spoken, and pure.
The *Kalpataru* states:

"If she who is traditionally recognized as the lawful wife is faultless, then there is no fault even if [the husband] has another; however, if she is at fault, another woman endowed with good qualities should be taken."
Manu says:
A husband should wait for a year for a wife who shows him enmity;
after a year has passed, he may take another wife, but he shall not cohabit with her.
If she transgresses [this rule] when he is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease,
she shall be abandoned after three months, along with her ornaments and belongings.

There is no abandonment of one who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, seedless, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there the distribution of his inheritance, provided he is not [the wife] of one she hates.
Manu and Kātyāyana: A husband, even if he is devoid of virtue, acts out of lust, or is lacking in good qualities, must always be served by his wife like a god; for the husband is her deity.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
she who serves her husband is exalted in heaven because of that.
A woman who, while her husband is still living, observes fasts and practices vows,
takes away the longevity of her husband and goes to hell.
Hārīta states in the Kalpataru:
"While her husband is away on a journey, she should not adorn herself, nor should she loosen her braid.
The Skanda Purāṇa states in the Madanaratna:
She should never wake her husband— whether he is asleep, sitting comfortably, or enjoying himself at his own will— even during times of distress.
A woman who has seen blood (a Rajasvalā) must not show her own face for three nights,
nor should she let anyone hear her voice, until she has bathed and become pure.
Having bathed well, she should look at the face of her husband and not that of anyone else;
or else, having meditated upon her husband in her mind, she may gaze at the sun.
Turmeric, saffron, vermilion, and collyrium,
as well as a bodice, betel leaf, and auspicious, beautiful ornaments.
Desiring long life for her husband, a virtuous woman should never, under any circumstances, remove the ornaments from her hair, her braid, or her ears.
She does not form a friendship with an unfortunate woman,
nor should she ever converse with a woman who is hostile toward her husband.
She should never be alone anywhere, nor should she ever bathe naked;
nor should she stand upon a grindstone, a pestle, a broom, or even a mortar.
A woman who, intent on anger, gives a retort when spoken to, should never sit upon a mechanical device, a threshold, or a grinding stone.
She is born as a dog in a village and as a jackal in a desolate forest;
one should not utter slander and should abandon quarreling from afar.
Even in the presence of one's gurus, one should not speak loudly nor laugh;
she who, when struck, desires to strike back is a tigress or a female snake.
"She who abandons her husband and eats sweet food alone shall become a sow or a donkey in a village that eats excrement and filth," according to Yama in the *Kalpataru*.
But a woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband,
shall be proclaimed in the midst of the assembly as a destroyer of the embryo and banished.
Baudhāyana says: Wise men immediately abandon a woman who is disobedient, barren, unchaste, harmful, or one who speaks unpleasantly.
One should abandon a wife who bears no children in the tenth year, one whose children are all daughters in the twelfth year,
one whose children die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.

Vasiṣṭha: "In sexual intercourse, in visiting sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), and in religious duties, one desists; *vyavahā* means transgression, and *tīrtha* means the womb. Hārīta: [Thus it is said.]
One should immediately abandon a woman who causes the depletion of wealth and grain. Nārada says:
"In the case of a woman's infidelity, there shall be shaving of the head and sleeping on the ground."
Bad food, poor clothing, and work that arises from a refuse heap.

Śaṅkha says: She should not go out of the house without being told; she should not go out without an upper garment; she should not walk hurriedly; she should not converse with a stranger; she should not expose her navel; she should wear her lower garment [reaching] down to the ankles; she should not reveal her breasts; she should not laugh with her mouth uncovered; she should not harbor hatred toward her husband or his relatives; and she should not stay in one place with courtesans, rogues, and the like. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
She who, being pleased, delights her beloved—by her the three worlds are delighted;
when he eats, she eats, and while he stands, she stands.
She should remain awake when he sleeps and be the first to awaken;
she should never appear before her husband without being adorned.
When her husband has gone abroad on business, she should avoid all ornaments and must not utter his name;
this leads to the increase of her merit.
Even when reviled, she does not revile in return; even when struck, she does not despond.
She says, "Do as you wish, my lord; let it be considered done."
When summoned, she leaves her household duties and goes quickly;
she herself shall cleanse all the implements for worship in water.
She should attend to the water for ritual purification, the sacred fires, and whatever leaves, flowers, and so forth [are required];
she should consume the remnants of her husband's food, as well as the desired food, fruits, and other such items.
Having said, "Great favor," he accepts what has been returned;
this is stated in the *Kalpataru*.
A householder should always wear ornaments and worship them.
Constantly devoted to her household duties, she should worship and sweep the house.
Having bathed daily, she should worship her braid with flowers and garments;
she should go to a secluded place beforehand, before anyone else has awakened.
She should perform the worship of the deities and offer incense, flowers, and oblations. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Except during festivals, she should not wear perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or discolored garments; nor should she converse with other men, except for merchants, renunciants, and the elderly."
Hārīta says:

Having bathed and put on two white garments, she should enter the temple of the gods, pay homage, and sprinkle food with clarified butter. When that has been offered there to the gods, she should offer oblations in the wedding fire (*udvāhāgni*) to the two wives of the gods and then present the ritual offering (*bali*). Once the service to the gods and guests has been performed, she should satisfy the householders according to their rank; then the wife, having eaten the remainder in a private place, should wash and rinse the vessels. Outside, in the north-eastern direction, she should pour out water with the words, "Homage to Vāstūpati, to Bhūpati, to Rudra. In this same manner, in the evening, after the boiled rice and other foods have been prepared, when everyone has lain down, she should close the door with ashes while saying, "Homage to Bhuvanapati, to Rudra who dwells in the ashes; with ashes I provide protection. She should then move her husband, her sons, and so forth, as well as herself. The meaning is that whatever else requires protection, she should touch it with ashes. Bending low, she should lie down at her husband's feet; she should not remain sitting while he is standing, nor should she sit higher than him. She should not look at him with a distracted gaze, nor in a place where he is deliberating, nor with a haughty look. Having wiped his limbs and massaged them, she should attend to him; in the heat, she should fan him, and she should wipe the rain, sweat, or water from his limbs. If he has entered the village, is burdened by a load, or is lying down, she should lift him up with a cheerful mind and honor him with wealth. Likewise, she should not even mentally covet another's beds, seats, clothes, or ornaments. Similarly, she should avoid sharing a single vessel with him, nor eating wine or meat, nor consuming his leftovers or his floral offerings (*nirmālya*), except in the case of her elders, her husband, or her children.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: A woman seeking the merit of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) should drink the water from her husband’s feet;
for a woman, her husband alone is superior even to Śiva or Viṣṇu.
In the *Paraśurāmapratāpa*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"A woman who offers the *arghya* oblation to the Sun at the time of dawn shall never experience widowhood for seven births."
Having drawn a mandala on the outside, one should constantly worship the Sun there with unbroken rice grains and other offerings; indeed, the deities are pleased with her who does so.
Any woman who, having become pure and composed in mind, worships the threshold at the time of dawn,
attains all her desires.
When a woman does not daily offer a portion of her food to her elder sister according to her ability, she shall go to hell after death.
Women who desire sons, grandsons, and wealth must certainly perform the daily propitiation of the eldest [wife] by means of an offering.
In the *Kalpataru* and the *Bhārata*:
"As soon as a husband learns that his wife is devoted to spells and roots, he should tremble before her, like one who has encountered a snake within his own home."

In that very place, Viṣṇu spoke these words to the Earth regarding women who are eternally pure, devoted to their husbands, and pleasant in speech: [244] "Among women who are eternally pure, devoted to their husbands, and pleasant in speech..."
Among those with open hands, those accompanied by sons,
those whose vessels are well-guarded, and those who delight in offerings.
In women whose dwellings were well-kept, who had conquered their senses, who were free from vice, devoid of greed,
observant of dharma, and endowed with compassion;
I, the creator of the worlds, am eternally established.
Vyāsa says:
Constantly sitting at the doorway, peering through the window,
idle chatter, and laughter— these are the vices of women of good family.
In Bhārata, during the Kali Yuga, the marketplaces will have their stakes for sale, the crossroads will have their stakes for Śiva, and women will have their stakes for hair.
Paraśurāma states its meaning:
"Those who perceive the true essence of the Vedas declare that 'aṭṭa' is food, 'śiva' is the Veda, 'śūla' is indeed sale, and 'keśa' is the female organ."
Manu says: "The husband is a god, the husband is a guru, and he is dharma, the sacred fords, and the vows;
therefore, setting all else aside, she should worship her husband alone."
She who eats when her husband has eaten, sits when he is seated, or sleeps when he has fallen asleep— that woman is to be known as devoted to her husband.
Aṅgiras:

She who is distressed when he is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected when he is away on a journey, and emaciated when he has died— she who would die when her husband dies is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).

The characteristics of a pregnant woman and one who has her menses, as well as the determination and the rules regarding accompanying the husband [in death] (*sahagamana*) and ascending the funeral pyre (*anvārohaṇa*), have been stated by us in the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
Now, the duties of widows (*vidhavā-dharma*):
according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*, as cited in the *Madanaratna* and the *Pārijāta*.
Any woman who, even after her husband has died, maintains her state of widowhood at all times,
attains the heavenly world once again upon regaining her husband.
The binding of a widow’s braid leads to the bondage of her husband;
therefore, a widow should always perform the shaving of her head.
One should always take food only once a day, never a second time;
or one may observe the vow for three nights, five nights, or even for a fortnight.
Or he should perform a month-long fast, or likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa;
or he should perform the Kṛcchra, the Parāka, or even the Taptakṛcchra.
One should sustain one's life by means of barley-food, fruit-diet, vegetable-diet, or milk-vows,
until the vital breath departs of its own accord.
A widow who sleeps on a couch causes her husband to fall;
therefore, she should sleep on the ground out of a desire for her husband's well-being.
A widow must never perform the rubbing of her body with unguents,
nor should she ever personally apply fragrant substances to herself.
Every day, libations (tarpaṇa) should be performed for the husband with water containing kusha grass and sesame seeds;
the same should also be done for his father, preceded by the mention of his name, lineage (gotra), and so forth.
This applies in the absence of sons and other [male heirs].
However, the worship of Viṣṇu must be performed with the recognition that he is her husband, and not otherwise;
she should always meditate upon her husband alone as the supreme bearer of the form of Viṣṇu.
Whatever is most beloved in the world, whatever was previously desired—
that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtue, with the desire to please her husband.
In the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha, one should observe special vows:
performing ritual bathing, giving charity, visiting sacred pilgrimage sites, and repeatedly chanting the name of Viṣṇu.
By offering water-pitchers in Vaiśākha, ghee-lamps in Kārttika,
and gifts of sesame and wealth in Māgha, one is distinguished in the heavenly world.
In the month of Vaiśākha, a water-stall should be constructed and a water-dripping vessel should be offered to the Lord;
likewise, sandals, a fan, an umbrella, fine garments, and sandalwood paste should be given.
"Gifts should be given to the foremost of the twice-born with the thought, 'May my husband be pleased.
In this manner, widows [should conduct themselves] through various rules and vows.
One should pass the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha in this very manner;
one should not mount an ox even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
She should not wear a bodice, nor should she wear discolored clothing;
thus endowed with dharma, even a widow remains devoted to her husband.
She attains the world of her husband and shall never be miserable anywhere.
She should perform the *śrāddha* with six rice-balls (*ṣaṭpiṇḍa*),
likewise for three ancestors beginning with her own husband and for her own paternal ancestors.
A widow should perform the śrāddha at the proper time, without being indolent.
Thus, from the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*, it is stated by Vṛddha-Manu:
"The worlds of those women of virtuous vows are equal to those of their husbands; however, the worlds of unchaste women are those of jackals."
Hārīta: But that virtuous woman devoted to her husband who reaches her final end when her lord has died—
having abandoned all sins, she shall attain the world of her husband.
Bṛhaspati says:
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on self-restraint and charity, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
Manu says: She may indeed emaciate her body with flowers, roots, fruits, and water;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Manu and Yama remained patient, self-restrained, and celibate until death; through dharma alone, they desired the unsurpassed state of being a true husband.
Neither in the Veda nor in the Śāstra is renunciation prescribed for a woman;
for her own duty is indeed procreation from a man of her own caste—this is the established rule.
Eighty-eight thousand sages of the brahmin class, whose vital energy was drawn upward, ascended to heaven without having established a lineage for their families.
A woman who, upon the death of her husband, remains established in celibacy,
goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Devoted solely to her husband, she should not do anything whatsoever without first consulting her sons."
Thus end the duties of widows.
[253] Now, the duties common to Śūdras.
Likewise, the *kuṇḍa* and *gola* are also equal to the *śūdra*. Thus, Devala states in the *Smṛtikaumudī*:
"But he who is begotten by a second father upon a wife of the same caste is to be known as a *savarṇōḍha*; by birth, however, he follows the dharma of the *śūdra*."
"However, those sons who are born of women of the same caste by a man of the same caste, yet are devoid of vows and have not undergone the sacraments,
are excluded as *vrātyas*.
On this very point, Manu says:
Two kinds of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the son born of an adulterer while the husband is alive is a Kuṇḍa; when the husband is dead, he is a Golaka.

But if the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are not Brahmins, how can there be a prohibition against them at a *śrāddha*? For since it is stated that "he is a Brahmin for the sake of the success of the *śrāddha*," when any Brahmin whatsoever is obtained, the purpose [of the prohibition] is to exclude some among them. As Yājñavalkya says:

"The diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, the one-eyed, the son of a remarried woman, likewise the *avakīrṇin*, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, the one with deformed nails, and the one with black teeth."

Thus, since the status of non-Brāhmaṇa does not apply to those two, the prohibition would be redundant. Furthermore, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated that they are to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) in the Brāhma marriage. Some say that the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* born of twice-born men are to be consecrated; however, even that is not tenable.

It is said: Vijñāneśvara (on YDh 1.90) maintains that the prohibition regarding the *śrāddha* ceremony applies to one who has been mistakenly thought to be a Brāhmaṇa based on the rule, "One born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇa mother is a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, Aparārka holds that their eligibility for sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the prohibition against the *śrāddha* refer specifically to the *kṣetraja* son; for such a person is authorized by the scriptures. Since no other [type of son] possesses the status of a Brāhmaṇa, there is no possibility of their inclusion; thus, even when there is a confusion of the substratum (*upādheya*), there is no confusion of the defining attribute (*upādhi*). Kātyāyana states in the *Kalpataru*: "A woman who engages in intercourse for her own pleasure, and not with the desire for her husband's offspring..."
She may indeed give birth to a son, but she is considered blameworthy and sinful.
If a woman, having abandoned the family of her husband, should take refuge with another,
she is censured in the world and is called one who has had a previous husband.
But where a woman has had a previous husband, the lord [the new husband] has no authority over her there;
however, having obtained her for the sake of dharma and wealth according to the proper sequence, he becomes her master.
She may be restrained and even beaten for the offenses of her previous or subsequent paramours,
or when she has fallen into the hands of thieves, due to the force of a river, famine, or civil unrest.
"A woman acquired after crossing a wilderness, one obtained by chance, and one inherited in due order—there is no fault in enjoying these; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures."
A woman given by her husband may be taken back if she is to be given away, but not otherwise;
however, a woman who does not consent to being given away herself should neither be given nor accepted— this is the rule ordained by the wise.
One should not marry a woman who is superior, nor one who is unwilling, nor likewise one who already has sons;
however, such a woman may be taken by paying an appropriate bride-price.
Yama says:
One born of an adulterer from a woman of the same caste is called a Kuṇḍa while the husband is alive;
but if he is dead, he is named a Golaka. Both of these are remembered as being of low birth.
Those sons who are procreated by twice-born men upon women of a different caste,
and upon all the wives of others, are declared in tradition to be *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*.
Their maternal castes have not been declared, nor are their paternal castes recorded;
furthermore, their sons are ineligible for marriage with the kinsmen on either the father’s or the mother’s side.
He himself [must perform penance]:
having killed one born of a mixed womb, he should perform the *sāntapana* penance;
but having killed a *sūta*, a *kuṇḍa*, or a *golaka*, he must perform the *atikṛcchra*.
Manu says: A son born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan by his qualities;
however, it is certain that one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is a non-Aryan.

The meaning is that those born of superior [wives] from inferior [husbands] are to be consecrated, but not those born of inferior [wives] from superior [husbands]. In the *Smṛtikaumudī*, citing the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"Those who are begotten by others even upon wives of the same caste are known as *avaroṭakas*; they are devoid of vows and sacraments."
It is stated in that very same [text]: "Only those born of a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Brāhmaṇa father are to be initiated, and no others. Furthermore:
"The procreation of children by one man for men of all four castes while they are alive is to be known as *kuṇḍa*; if it occurs after they are dead, it is *golaka*."
Devoid of caste, he should cause the mothers to grasp his actions and names; that is to say, their actions and names belong to him.
He should be employed in the city by the king, who is fearful of the intermixture of castes.
In the city of the gods, at the gate of the gods,
there was a brahmin named Kuṇḍa or Golaka, who knew nothing more than the performance of the twilight devotions.

He should recite that [mantra] during bathing, eating, and at the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) before the deities. When addressed as "O Brahmin" (*vipra*), for him alone there is the *saṃdhyā* and initiation (*upanayana*). In the *Mitākṣarā* as well, it is stated: "The *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are to be consecrated according to their respective fitness. Likewise, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, the *Prayogapārijāta*, and the *Brāhma*, it is said:
"In this very manner, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* born of twice-born men are to be consecrated."
