Regarding "snāna" (bath): the meaning is that one should recite these words like a bard at the time of bathing and other such occasions.
Thus ends the section on the Kuṇḍa and Golaka.
Now, the characteristics of the impotent (*klība*):

likewise, even one born of the twice-born who is a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*) is equal to a *śūdra*. This is because, in the injunction for initiation—“One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring”—masculinity is intended as a required qualification, just as it is for the *camasādhvaryu* priest; consequently, like women, such a person is excluded from initiation. Furthermore, although the subject of the statement regarding the eight-year-old is not explicitly specified, since it is a restatement of what is already established, it refers only to a male. Devala also states in the *Mitākṣarā*: “A eunuch is devoid of sexual organs, and he is not at all fit for the sacraments.”
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu states in that same work:
"Having killed a eunuch Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra.
And because of the statement in the Baudhāyana-sūtra and the Smṛtyarthasāra, initiation (upanayana) is prescribed; so too in the Brāhma section of the Prayogapārijāta.
The Vedic revelation states: "One born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇī mother is a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, [this applies] even to those who are eunuchs, deaf, humpbacked, dwarfs, or lame.
Having stated this and more, [it is said]:
"And for these whose masculinity has been destroyed, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should be performed according to their fitness.
This was also stated previously. And that [masculinity] is of seven kinds. Thus says Devala, as cited by Gauḍa:
The *paṇḍaka* born of wind, the *paṇḍa*, the *paṇḍa*, the *klība*, the *napuṃsaka*,
and the *kīlaka*— thus the sevenfold classification of the *klība* is established.
He himself states their essential nature:
"Among them, one who has speech and gestures equal to those of a woman is a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) equal to a woman;
the meaning is that he possesses such qualities as having elevated breasts, a beard, and so forth."
A man, having fashioned the lingas, should likewise break them afterwards;
and a woman, assuming the state of a man, possessing qualities consistent with male conduct.
One known as a *vātaka* would be a eunuch (*paṇḍha*), or perhaps one called a *strīṣaṇḍha*.
One should distinguish and abandon the characteristics of female, male, and neuter;

that is to say, sometimes she is a woman, sometimes a man, and sometimes a eunuch. Furthermore, like a man, a woman may enjoy another woman even without the emission of semen, by the power of wind (vāta); such is the meaning.
Moreover, one who lacks the [proper] characteristic is a eunuch, while a eunuch is one whose penis is flaccid.
A man who eats impure things is a eunuch; one whose semen is lost is a neuter.
One who eats impure substances and consumes the semen of another through oral intercourse is called *āsekya* in medical science (*vaidyaka*). As it is stated in the *Śuśruta*:
"An *āsekya* occurs when a couple has little virility;
he attains erection of the penis by consuming semen, without a doubt."
He is called a "stake" who,
out of impotence, first unites his own fortune with another man and afterwards enjoys that very same fortune himself.
In the Suśruta, however, others are also mentioned:
"He who is born from a putrid womb is known as Saugandhika;
having smelled the fragrance of the womb and the phallus, he gains strength."
But he who, out of lust, behaves like a man toward women by inserting his own penis into his own anus is to be known as a *kumbhīka*; now hear further about the *īrṣyaka*.
One who, having seen the sexual union of others, engages in sexual union himself, should be known as an *īrṣyaka*; now hear about the fifth type of *paṇḍaka*.
He who, out of delusion, behaves toward his wife during her fertile period like a woman,
is born thereafter as one designated a eunuch, possessing the behavior and movements of a woman.

In the *Mādhavīya*, however, fourteen divisions are mentioned; they should be understood from that very source. Among these, all the sacramental rites (*saṃskāras*)—with the exception of the initiation (*upanayana*), the four vows (*vrata*), the return home (*samāvartana*), and marriage—are performed silently. This is because, in passages such as "When a son is born" (*kumāraṃ jātam*), the masculine gender of the person to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is not intended to be restrictive (*avivakṣā*); thus, just as for women, the rite would apply to a eunuch (*paṇḍha*) as well. As Yājñavalkya has stated: "These rites for women are silent, but their marriage is accompanied by mantras."

"And they are proclaimed to possess the characteristics of women, having speech and gestures equal to those of women"—such is the statement of Vṛddha-Manu. This applies even to reservoirs of water, temples, the consecration of deities, great gifts (*mahādāna*), and so forth; for by the logic of the "sixth [case]," the masculinity mentioned in the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*) is not intended to be significant because it resides in the subject (*uddeśya*), and thus women are entitled [to perform these acts] just as men are. This is likewise the case for all types of giving, and because non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and other such duties are common to both. However, there is no entitlement for the father in rites such as the *śrāddha* (ancestral offerings), because Āpastamba states that "he who takes the wealth is the one who gives the *piṇḍas*," thereby specifying that only the taker of wealth offers the *piṇḍas*; and this also excludes the eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*).
Because Manu and others have prohibited the inheritance of property by those who are impotent, outcastes, lame, insane, or mentally deficient; Yājñavalkya also states:
"The impotent and the rest shall not perform the water-libation, nor shall those who are excluded from the *vrātyas* or who are devoid of dharma."
Thus are the eunuchs.
Others also are equal to Śūdras;
this was stated by Yama in the Kalpataru.
Those who have turned back from the going-forth, those who have gone forth in vain,
he who is born of one who has been initiated, and he who has fallen away from the going-forth.
These duties of the Śūdra have been proclaimed by Manu. Yājñavalkya states:
One who has fallen from the life of a wandering mendicant (pravrajyāvasita) is a slave to the king for as long as he lives.
Others also have been declared by Yājñavalkya to be equal to Śūdras:
"One falls immediately through [selling] meat, lac, and salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within a month by selling milk."

Regarding this, the Bhaṭṭācāryas maintain in their Vārttika that these [passages] merely constitute a censure of the Dharma; Vijñāneśvara, however, holds that they are intended to convey the loss of the status of the twice-born. Therefore, they are equal to Śūdras.
Now, as for the Vrātyas:
the same applies to the Vrātyas as well. And so says Manu:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas,
and Vaiśyas who have not undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana) after one year from their respective limits are all traditionally declared to be Śūdras.
Except for the Vrātyastoma sacrifice. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Until the sixteenth, the twentieth, and the twenty-fourth year, respectively, is the final period for the initiation of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya."
From this point onward, these people fall, excluded from all religious duties;
they are outcasts regarding the Sāvitrī, becoming Vrātyas, except through the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
[261] Now, regarding the formal injunction (*niyoga*):
Devala states in the *Kalpataru*:

A husband who has disappeared, one who has renounced the world, one who is impotent, one who has fallen from his caste, one who has committed an offense against the king, or even one who has gone to another world, must be abandoned by his wife.
Whether her husband is dead or alive, a woman may take another husband for the sake of preventing the extinction of the lineage; women possess no independence.
Nārada: A Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for eight years if she is childless;
but if she has given birth, she shall wait four years, and if she has borne twins, two years.
No specific time is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there any transgression of dharma; especially for a woman who has given birth, she may remain [in her father's house] for a year.
This period is prescribed for women whose husbands have not returned;
however, if the husband is heard to be alive, this limit shall be doubled.
In the procreation of offspring, this is the conduct of women ordained by Prajāpati;
therefore, no fault is found in women for approaching another man in this context.
Thus is the injunction.
Now, in order to speak of those equal to Śūdras, the offspring of mixed castes (saṃkaraja) are described by Yājñavalkya:
For from a Brahmin and a Kṣatriya woman is born the Mūrdhāvasikta; from a Vaiśya woman, the Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra woman, the Niṣāda or the Pāraśava.

From a Kṣatriya, however, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman give birth to Māhiṣya and Ugra sons respectively; from a Vaiśya, a Karaṇa is born of a Śūdra woman. This is the rule recorded for marriages with women of lower castes.

Thus, there are six *anuloma* castes—the Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, Pāraśava, Māhiṣya, Ugra, and Karaṇa—who partake of the duties prescribed for the caste of their mothers; these are born of women of lower varṇas. Among them, those born of superior women are *anuloma*, while those born of inferior women are *pratiloma*. Manu says: "From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from a Śūdra woman, the Kṣatriya-born are called Ugros. Yājñavalkya says:

From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born. A Māhiṣya is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; a Karaṇī is born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother; and from her (the Karaṇī) is born the Rathakāra. Vasiṣṭha states their occupations in the Smṛtikaumudī.

For the *mūrdhāvasikta*s, it is the training in elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, and missiles, as well as the wielding of arms. For the *ambaṣṭha*s, it is the protection of living beings by means of gems, spells, and medicinal herbs. For the *māhiṣya*s, it is livelihood through song, dance, and astrology, as well as the protection of crops. For the *pārasava* and *ugrakaraṇa*s, it is service to the twice-born, supervision of wealth, service to the king, and the guarding of forts and the inner apartments. For the *rathakāra*, it is the knowledge of hidden treasures, as well as the management, nourishment, and taming of elephants, horses, and charioteers. Thus says Śaṅkha.

The *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) is one born from a *kṣatriya* father and a *vaiśya* mother in the immediate sequence of castes; for him, the sacraments of study, sacrifice, giving, and initiation are not prohibited. His livelihood consists of studying the science of chariots (*ratha-sūtra*) and architecture (*vāstu-vidyā*). Thus it is stated in the *Jātiviveka*:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should, by any means, mount a Śūdra woman upon his bed..."
By means of the common practice of sexual intercourse, he shall procreate upon her a son of mixed caste (pāraśava).
He is renowned as a Mahāśūdra, slightly superior to other Śūdras;
for him, the goldsmith, bathing here is his purifying rite of cleansing.
All conduct according to dharma is the livelihood of a Śūdra. Likewise:
one who deals in counterfeit gold and a seller of forbidden meat [are both outcastes].
But a Brahmin must be made a king; and he should be made to pay the highest fine.
Uśanas says: One born from the union of a Kṣatriya man and a Brāhmaṇa woman is called a Mūrdhāvasikta;
he is proclaimed to be superior to the Rājanyas in terms of the duties of the Kṣatriyas.
Performing the rites of the Atharvaveda, including the obligatory and occasional ceremonies,
he may indeed drive a horse, a chariot, or an elephant by the king's command.
One may serve as a commander, practice medicine, and maintain a livelihood through various occupations;
one should practice the eightfold Ayurveda taught therein in accordance with the Dharma.
He may practice astrology, mathematics, or even a physical livelihood;
for one born from a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman according to the prescribed rule is called an Ambaṣṭha.
His livelihood shall be agriculture, and likewise he shall be a dancer before others;
the medical treatment of men, horses, elephants, and so forth shall be his means of subsistence.
Vāgbhaṭṭa:
"The right hand of that quack physician who does not know seven, five, or even three *saṃhitās*, should be cut off by the king."
Manu says:
"He who explains penance, medical treatment, astrology,
or the determination of dharma without [relying on] the scripture is called a slayer of Brahman."
This is the physician with the sword (the surgeon).
Born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother, he is a Māhiṣya born in the natural order;
he is devoted to the eight branches of medical administration and is skilled in the sixty-four ancillary arts.
All his activities, such as agriculture and trade, would be successful;
astrology, the science of omens, and the science of sounds would be his means of livelihood.
In the *Viśvaṃbhara-śāstra*:
"But one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is indeed a Karaṇa, a maker of scripts and a scribe.
Yājñavalkya [states]:
An elevation of caste should be known to occur in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of karmas, there is equality, and as before, there is the distinction of higher and lower.

The "elevation of caste" (*jātyutkarṣa*)—the attainment of a superior caste—is to be understood as occurring in the seventh generation from the use of the word "apaśabda," or in the sixth or fifth. This is the meaning: a maiden born of a *śūdra* woman married to a *vipra* gives birth to a son; she too, when married to another, gives birth to a *vipra* in the seventh generation. Similarly, a maiden born of a *vaiśya* woman married to a *vipra* gives birth to a *vipra* in the sixth generation; one born of a *kṣatriya* woman married to a *vipra* gives birth to one in the fifth. A daughter born of a *śūdra* woman by a *kṣatriya* gives birth to a *kṣatriya* in the sixth generation; one born of a *vaiśya* woman gives birth to a *vaiśya* in the fifth. This is the meaning of the first half-verse. Likewise, if a *vipra* lives by the occupation of a *kṣatriya*, his progeny reaches the fifth generation as a *kṣatriya*; if he lives by the occupation of a *vaiśya*, the sixth generation is a *vaiśya*; if he lives by the occupation of a *śūdra*, the seventh is a *śūdra*. If a *kṣatriya* lives by the occupation of a *vaiśya*, the fifth generation is a *vaiśya*; if he lives by the occupation of a *śūdra*, the sixth is a *śūdra*. If a *vaiśya* lives by the occupation of a *śūdra*, the fifth generation is a *śūdra*.
[265] Now, regarding those born in the inverse order (pratilomaja),
Kātyāyana states in the Kalpataru:
One should effect procreation through appointment (*niyoga*) as prescribed for the sake of its purification;
this is the law regarding the wives of the twice-born, while for a Śūdra, this [method] should always be the case.

The meaning is that there is no appointment (*niyoga*) among *śūdras*. Bṛhaspati says: "Niyoga was indeed mentioned by Manu, but he himself prohibited it; because of the decline of the age, mortals are incapable of performing it according to the prescribed rule."
The sons who were produced in manifold ways by the ancient seers cannot be produced now by those of this age who lack such power.
On that very point, Hārīta states: "The wanton woman, the remarried woman, the one who bears seed, the one who acts according to her own will,
and the one who eats all things— these five are to be known as those born of Śūdra origin."
Whatever offspring may ever be born of these women, one should not seat them in the rows [of guests]; they are traditionally held to be unworthy of the row.
A *kuṇḍa* woman is one who conceives by [another man], while a *māta* woman is one who acts according to her own desire, approaching more than four men. A *sarvabhakṣā* woman is a drinker of liquor.
Yājñavalkya says:
From a Kṣatriya father on a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya father, a Vaidehaka.
But one born from a Śūdra woman is a Caṇḍāla, excluded from all religious duties.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Māgadha was born; and from a Śūdra father, she likewise gave birth to a son called a Kṣattṛ.
Furthermore, from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother, she produced a son known as an Āyogava.
The Māgadha is the Bandī; the Kṣattṛ is well known as the Niṣāda and the Bhilla; the Āyogava is the Pulkasa. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"Upon a Kṣatriya woman, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra beget the Bandī and the Niṣāda respectively; upon a Vaiśya woman, the Śūdra begets the Pulkasas. Vyāsa also says:
From a Śūdra [man] and a Kṣatriyā woman, through transgression, a Niṣāda is born who is a fisherman;

by that [rule], there are two types of Niṣādas: one previously mentioned as an *anuloma* (born in the natural order), and this one [the other]. In the *Jātiviveka*: "From the union of a Śūdra with a Kṣatriyā woman, he shall procreate a son called a Kṣattṛ."
He is known as a Niṣāda, excluded from all social classes.
Devoid of the conduct befitting a Śūdra and always intent on evil thoughts,
he held snares and nooses in his hands and was skilled in trapping deer.
A forest-dweller who is the destroyer of various species of wild animals,
he always lives by that very livelihood of meat, filled with anger.
One should employ a bell that brings about the destruction of evil; it produces wonder at night.
And here, hunting is said to be of two kinds: that of those who move through the sky and that of those who move upon the earth.
One desiring wealth for the sake of prosperity should engage in the sale of honey.
Yama, however, states that there is a different designation for the Māgadha and Niṣāda;
from a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, one named Mucupa is born.
Where a Kṣatriya woman is deluded, a Madgu bird is born from a Śūdra.
Delusion is sexual intercourse. In another Smṛti: "A Kṣatriya woman gave birth to a son from a Māgadha Vaiśya;
he is called a Bandījana, being devoid of the binding of vows."
His livelihood is said to be somewhat superior to that of Śūdras;
he is capable in the arts and proficient in the six languages, including poetry, rhetoric, and prose.
The prose and verse compositions of kings are varied and contradictory.

[266] A son born to a Kṣatriya woman from a Vaiśya father shall be a Kṣattṛ, a bearer of the staff. As stated in the *Laghujātiviveka*: "Those Sūtas are they who always recite the ancient accounts of kings."
And those Māgadhas who praise heroes who have been dead for only a short time.
Those who describe contemporary kings who have successfully performed the deeds of war through literary compositions are proclaimed as *bandhin* (binders).
Manu states: "From a Niṣāda, however, a Vaidehī gives birth to a Kārāvara, who is a leather-worker.
The term "Vaidehī" is to be understood as the subject remaining from the previous context.
From a Vaidehaka are born the Andhra and the Meda, both of whom have their dwellings outside the village.

From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Vaideha; from him, on a Kārāvarī woman, an Andhra is born; and from a Niṣādī woman, a Meda—thus says Medhātithi. However, Aṅgiras has mentioned other types of Caṇḍālas as well: "He who is born of a Prāvrajikā and a Brāhmaṇī, he who is born of a Śūdra woman, and the son of one who has married a woman of the same *gotra*—these three are declared to be Caṇḍālas."
Manu also spoke regarding the Pulkasa:
"One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Pulkasa by birth;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is indeed known as a Kukkuṭaka."
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is called a Śvapāka;
one produced by a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is called a Vena.

From a Śūdra and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kṣattṛ; from a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman, an Ugra; from these two, a Śvapāka. From a Vaiśya and a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaideha; from a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha; from her (the Ambaṣṭha woman), a Vena. Vasiṣṭha states their occupations as follows:

For Sūtas, [the occupations are] serving as ministers, scribes, women-livelihoods, and tailoring; for ministers, the office of scribe and the knowledge of truth (or principles); for Vaidehakas, the profession of actors and appearing on the stage; for Venas, cutting wood, whetstone-work, and boring gems, pearls, and corals—*bhrama* here meaning a whetstone; for Āyogavas, the manufacture and joining of copper, iron, tin, lead, and weapons, as well as the construction of towns; for Sairandhrīs, the production and sale of *surā*, *madya*, and *sīdhu* liquors, and the sale of flowers, fruits, and vegetables; [these are stated] in the Viśvaṃbhara-śāstra.
The son born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Kṣatriya is called a Sūta; he is an elephant trainer and should make the taming of horses his primary livelihood.
From a king, through marriage with a Brāhmaṇa girl, one born of such union is designated as a Sūta; he is a twice-born according to the rules for the inverse order (pratiloma).

Regarding the context of marriage, the meaning is "when a Brāhmaṇa girl has been wed. Furthermore, one who is unworthy of the Vedas and likewise a teacher of their duties— such a son born of a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Vaiśya father is known as a Vaidehaka.
The craft of working with stone and wood is his excellent means of livelihood.
Manu says: For Sūtas, the management of horses and chariots; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, service to women; and for Māgadhas, the way of trade.

The duty of women is the protection of the inner apartments (*antapura*). The merchant’s path is the royal highway; its protection is their duty. The catching of fish is the duty of the *niṣādas*, and carpentry is that of the *āyogava*.
Carpentry means the carving of wood; the term *vardhaki* has this meaning. However, according to Uśanas:
From the union of a Vaiśya with a Nṛpī woman, one known as an Āyogava is born;
these become weavers, subsisting on cotton and bell-metal.
Some Śīlikas here subsist on clothing made from living beings;
while for the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pulkasas, their livelihood consists of dwelling in holes and the killing and binding [of animals].

"Those who dwell in holes" refers to snakes and the like. Here, "ugra" (the fierce) refers to one born of a reverse-order union (*pratilomaja*), because he is listed among them; thus it is stated in the *Smṛtimañjarī*.
For those of the four castes, the work is leathercraft; for the *venas*, it is the playing of musical instruments (*bhāṇḍa*).
"Musical instrument" (*bhāṇḍa*) refers to the *muraja* drum, the *paṭaha* drum, and so forth.
At sacred shrines, under trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves.
These known persons shall live together, subsisting by their own occupations;
"known" means marked with the signs of their kin.
But the dwelling place for Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village.
They should be made outcastes, their wealth being dogs and donkeys;

they should live outside the village, in a place devoid of a village. "Outcaste" (avapātra) means one with a broken vessel, or alternatively, one who is deprived of cooking vessels and the like—as he will state later: "Their food shall be dependent on others. Or rather, food and other items should not be given into a vessel held in their hands, but rather onto the ground.
Their clothing shall be the rags of the dead, and their meal shall be eaten from a broken dish.
An ornament of black iron and wandering are his constant lot; wandering means not staying in one place. A man practicing the Dharma should not seek association with them.
Their mutual dealings and marriages shall be with their own equals;
their food, moreover, should be given by others from a separate vessel.
They should not wander through villages or cities at night;
or, if they must wander for the sake of business, they should do so marked by royal insignia.
It is the established rule that they shall carry out the funeral of a corpse even if it has no kinsmen;
and they shall always execute those deserving of death according to the scriptures by the king's command.
They should take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to death;
and for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, the abandonment of one's body without seeking reward is meritorious.
Medhātithi states that freedom from greed for wealth and other such things is "non-attachment" (*anupaskara*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause of success for the strong in the protection of women and children," the connection is that when women, children, and others are in distress, the abandonment of one's own body is [the means]; "success" (*siddhi*) here means the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Thus says Uśanas.
Their head-ornament shall be made of iron or even black metal;
having bound a leather thong around their necks or a small drum (jhallarī) at their side.
They should perform the removal of impurities and the purification in the forenoon;
they must remain gathered together, otherwise they are especially liable to be executed.
[271] Likewise, those born of *vrātyas* are equal to *śūdras*. Regarding them, Manu says:
From a Vrātya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, and the Puṣpaśekhara.
From a *viprā* woman, a *vrātyavipra* father begets a *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka*;

Medhātithi states that *āvantya* and the others are merely designations for this very same person. Others, however, say that from a *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka* and a *viprā* woman is born an *āvantya*, from him on her [the *viprā*] is born a *vāṭadhāna*, and from him a *puṣpaśekhara*. The same applies to those who follow. Having mentioned these in relation to the *viśvaṃbharas*, [it is said]:
"By means of these, however, the worship of Viṣṇu and other deities must be performed for the sake of livelihood."
The playing of dance, song, instrumental music, conchs, lutes, and so forth.
From a Vratya of the royal caste (rājanya) are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Viccibira;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khaṃsa, and the Dramiḍa.

These are born from a *vrātya* father and a *kṣatriya* mother; this is another *karaṇa* caste born in the direct order (*anuloma*). Furthermore, from a *vrātya* father and a *vaiśya* mother are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kārūṣa, the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
[This occurs] only with respect to a Vaiśya woman. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
From a Brāhmaṇa who is a Vrātya, a Mṛjjakaṇṭaka is born of a Brāhmaṇī woman;
as well as the Āvantya, Vāṭadhāna, and Puṣpaśekhara castes.
In this context, the rite of malevolent magic (*ābhicārika*) consists of consuming *bhṛjjakaṇṭakinī* seeds,
except for the purpose of bringing [the enemy] face-to-face through mantras, medicinal herbs, and weapons.
For they act for kings; therefore, being unaltered by others, they remain unaltered—meaning they are exempt from punishment. *Saṃmukhīkaraṇa* means bringing under control.
From a Kṣatriya who has become a *vrātya*, there arise among queens the *jhalla*, *malla*, *naṭa*, and *jhaṣa* castes.
There are numerous Karanas known as Āvitthibīkas and Dramiḍas;
by the king's command, affairs concerning foreign kingdoms are to be conducted by them.
The Khasas and Mallas likewise arose from such conduct, as did the state of being friends and enemies; furthermore, from a Vaiśya who is a Vratya, a Kāruṣaka is born through Vaiśya women.
At a crossroads and in a cremation ground, he should be a member of the circle of friends (*mitramaṇḍala*);
the meaning is that there, by the king's command, he should be one who knows the ways of the world. In the reading *mātṛmaṇḍana*, he is a worshiper of the Goddess.
Furthermore, Sudhanvan the teacher should be a worshiper of Rudra.
And the third is called Vijanman, who honors the lying-in chamber;
his wife shall be Sāmbikā—this is the meaning.
And he should worship the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas by royal decree.
The fourth is the worshipper of the Sādhyas, who is friendly toward the Caityas and so forth;
the fifth is named Sātvata, the worshipper of the abode of Viṣṇu.

From the mutual intermixture of these, those of low status are born. Regarding this, Manu says: "Just as a Śūdra begets an outcast being upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, so too does an outcast beget an internal outcast within the four castes."
Manu states the distinctions regarding the mutual intermixture of the castes:

"When those outside [the caste system] behave in a contrary manner, they produce further outsiders—both intermediate and lower—from those who are already low; thus, there are exactly fifteen such castes."

The "outcasts" (*bāhya*) are those such as the *caṇḍālas* and others. Those who have intercourse with women of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) in the inverse order (*pratikūlam*) produce low-born offspring from both their own and other [caste] lineages. These, in turn, when they have intercourse with women of higher or lower status, give birth to those who are inferior or non-inferior. The term *varṇa* here refers to the castes (*jāti*). The meaning is as follows: from a Brāhmaṇa (*vipra*), there are only those born in the direct order (*anuloma*); from a Śūdra, only those in the inverse order (*pratiloma*); and from the two middle castes (Kṣatriya and Vaiśya), there are both. For the Kṣatriya, there are two in the direct order and one in the inverse; for the Vaiśya, one in the direct order and two in the inverse. In this regard, from a Śūdra, by intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya woman respectively, three are born: the *caṇḍāla*, the *kṣatta*, and the *āyogava*. From a *caṇḍāla*, by intercourse with women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, four are born. Thus, from the *kṣatta* and the *āyogava* respectively, there are twelve; and including these three themselves, there are fifteen. Likewise, from a Vaiśya, by intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, a *māgadha* is born; with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a *vaidehaka*; and with a Śūdra woman, a *karaṇa*—these are the direct-order offspring (*anuloma*). By these [Vaiśyas], when procreated upon women of the four castes, four are produced for each, totaling twelve; and including these three themselves, there are fifteen. Similarly, from a Kṣatriya, by intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, a *māhiṣya* is born; with a Śūdra woman, an *ugra*; and with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a *sūta*—this last being the inverse-order offspring (*pratiloma*). From these, by intercourse with women of the four castes, four are produced for each, totaling twelve; and including these three themselves, there are fifteen. Thus, from a Brāhmaṇa, three in the direct order—the *mūrdhāvasikta*, the *ambaṣṭha*, and the *pāraśava*—each produce four by intercourse with women of the four castes, totaling twelve; and including these three themselves, there are fifteen. Altogether, these number sixty. Including the four castes themselves which are considered "corrupt," there are sixty-four. However, in the *Jātiviveka*, it is stated otherwise.
Six types of men are proclaimed according to the direct order of the castes;
those same six exist according to the inverse order, thus making twelve divisions in total.
These twelve mixed [castes], being further intermingled with the four [primary] varṇas,
along with the eight divisions that exist, constitute sixty-two when added to the twelve.
"Those numerous divisions of mixed castes (*saṃkarajāti*), numbering thirty-six hundred and sixty, have been destroyed; beyond these, there would be many others.
These [latter] are equal to Śūdras.
For it is stated by Manu: "All those born of degradation (apadhvaṃsaja) are remembered as having the same dharma as Śūdras. Those born of degradation are those born of illicit union (vyabhicāra).
The nature and functions of those born from intermixture (*saṃkara*) have been described;
their nature and functions are also stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"A *Mūrdhāvasikta* is one who is born from a Brahmin father and a Kṣatriya mother."
He provides medical treatment even for those among humans who are afflicted by disease.
By the force of the word "also," the duty of a Kṣatriya is likewise included.
From a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra maiden is born a Pāraśava;
he, by the king's command, always performed the killing of fish.
From a Brāhmaṇa and a woman of the Ugra caste, one named Ambaṣṭha is born;
he performs medical treatment for humans who are afflicted by disease.
The two Ambaṣṭhas are those born from a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa and from a Śūdra woman by a Kṣatriya.
Likewise, an Ābhīra son is born to a Brāhmaṇa by an Ambaṣṭha woman;
he tends cattle, goats, and sheep, even in royal palaces.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and an Āyogavī mother is born a man known as a Dhigvaṇa.
An Āyogavī is a woman born to a Śūdra from a Vaiśya woman;
he is to be understood as a leather-worker, a despised one who lives by working with hides.

These six—Mūrdhāvasikta, Pāraśava, Ambaṣṭha, Ābhīra, Carmakāra, and Avaroṭa, as previously mentioned—are of the same nature as their mothers and not [of the nature] of their fathers' sons. Furthermore, there are three others: Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, and Niṣāda.
By approaching women of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes here,
each [of these men] produces four kinds of sons respectively.
These twelve exist together with the primary natures (mūlaprakṛtis);
thus, O Brahmin, they become fifteen, and [the soul] becomes the sixteenth.

From a *mūrdhāvasikta* man and a *viprā* woman, a *pratiloma* is born; from a *kṣatra* man and women of the other castes, there are four *anulomas*. Thus, including the *ambaṣṭha* and the *niṣāda*, there are twelve. These three themselves make fifteen. Including the *vrātya* Brāhmaṇa or the *avaroṭa*, there are sixteen. These are known as *dasyus*, performing tasks like those of their mothers.
From a king and a Brāhmaṇa maiden, however, the *sūta* caste is born.
He constantly served as the charioteer for kings, being both skillful and ever-present;
yet another Sūta was Prajāpati himself, Janārdana in the form of illusion.

He is remembered as the speaker of the Vedas and other scriptures, as well as the Purāṇas; he is called "Sūta" by name alone, but not by birth—this is the meaning. He is like those with names such as Ugra and others. [Thus it is said: "The son of a Sūta is Ugraśravas, the Sauti, the reciter of the Purāṇas. Likewise:
"From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya maiden, one named Māhiṣya is born."
He was skilled in the songs and dances of the constellations and was a protector of riches.
From a king and a Śūdra woman is born one named Ugra;
his duties are the protection of the fort, the harem, and the treasury, as well as the recitation [of sacred texts] for Brahmins.
There is also another, fierce and wicked, among the dasyus;
moreover, the three [classes] beginning with the Sūta, Māhiṣya, and Ugra arise from the four varṇas.
Each one indeed gives birth to four sons;
together with herself and the king, there are sixteen of them there.

Devala says: Whatever wealth has been acquired by gods, Brahmins, children, women, the destitute, the blind, and the miserable, it belongs to them; indeed, by the abandonment of such wealth, robbers [arise].
Now, from a Vaiśya with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one named Vaideha is born;
these twelve, together with the root-natures (mūlaprakṛti), exist.
A Brahmin indeed becomes fifteen-fold, and he becomes sixteen-fold when devoted to his livelihood as a protector of royal fortresses.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, one named Mucuka is born;
he provides protection upon whatever path exists, whether on water or on land.
A royal messenger or one who lives by music may be a *kīrtiprakāśaka* (proclaimer of fame);
he is indeed a *bandī*.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, there is the *karaṇa* caste; he is one who performs [various crafts].
He should provide for the protection of the forts, the inner apartments, and the treasuries, as well as the gathering together of Brahmins.
According to the *Amara-kośa*, "gañjā" means a liquor-house; "saṃgraha" means protection. These three—the Vaideha, the Māgadha, and the Karaṇa—are [the types of spies].
Deluded, they procreate sons from the castes as before;
and these sixteen are born together with the primary natures (mūlaprakṛtis).
Those bandits even perform the wicked occupations of Vaiśyas;
furthermore, from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a loathsome Caṇḍāla is born.
He performed the cleaning of the royal highways and other such base deeds;
and from a Śūdra man with a king’s wife, a Kṣattṛ and a Mainda were born.
He then made the hunting of porcupines and iguanas his means of livelihood;
moreover, that Āyogava is born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother.

The carpenter (*takṣā*) and the master builder (*sthapati*) are said to be those who always construct the dwellings of kings. A wood-cutter is a *takṣā*, while a stone-cutter is a *sthapati*; these two are distinct categories.
Likewise, the *āyogava*, the *kṣattṛ*, and the *caṇḍāla*—these three are also [distinct].
Then, as before, they procreate sons upon women of the four castes;
together with those born of Śūdra fathers, they number sixteen.
Even those bandits commit such wicked deeds;
these are to be known as Brahmins and others among the sixty-four classes of beings.

They produce similar and mixed offspring in other wombs; here, among those distinct [classes], there are one hundred and twenty-six varieties produced by them in those [wombs] or produced by those [beings] in them. When these are multiplied by sixty-four, they become eight thousand and sixty-four. Due to the mutual mixing of these through the blending of colors and castes, their number becomes infinite; it is not stated here for fear of excessive prolixity. Manu says:
"But through the gradual neglect of ritual duties, these Kṣatriya lineages..."
And by transgressing against Brahmins, they have fallen to the state of outcasts in this world.
Through adultery, through a man knowing a woman who should not be known,
through improper attachment, and through the abandonment of dharma, the intermixture of castes arises.
"Association" (*saṅga*) refers to association with low-born people such as Mlecchas and others. Regarding some of these, Manu says:
"An Ayogavī bears a Dasyu [son] who knows how to adorn and attend to others, who is not a slave yet lives by the life of a slave, and who subsists by means of nets."
[276] From a Vaiśya woman, a Śūdra father begets an Āyogava; from a Dasyu, he procreates those born of the intermixture of castes. And those Dasyus are enumerated by Manu:
the Pauṇḍrakas, the Coṇḍras, the Dramiḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, and likewise the Daradas.
Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, the arms, and the thighs—
whether they speak the language of the Mlecchas or the language of the Yavanas— all of them are recorded as Dasyus.

These are the various types of Mlecchas. *Prasādhana* means adornment; *upacāra* refers to massaging the limbs and so forth. Vasiṣṭha, however, mentions another means of livelihood: "For Sairandhrīs, it is the preparation of spirituous liquor, wine, and *sīdhu*, as well as their sale, and the sale of flowers, fruits, and vegetables. Thus says Manu.
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka,
who praises men incessantly by ringing a bell at the break of dawn.

"These [castes] arise among the *āyogava*s," according to the statement of Manu; thus, from a *vaideha*—born of a *vaiśya* father and a *śūdra* mother, who is an *āyogavī*—one born of a *vipra* woman bears a *maitreya*. He is the same as the *mādhūka*.
A *niṣāda* begets a *mārgara*, a *dāśa* who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a *kaivarta*.
The meaning is that there are ten [sons] born from a Niṣāda father and an Āyogavī mother previously mentioned, when she is of Kṣatriya descent.
This follows from the continued application of the phrase "from a Brāhmaṇa" [in the previous rule]. Manu says:
"An Ābhīra is born from an Ambaṣṭha woman, but a Dhigvaṇa is born from an Āyogavī."

From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Yogavī; from her, by a Brāhmaṇa father, is born a Dhigvaṇa. From a Vaiśya mother and a Brāhmaṇa father is born an Ambaṣṭhī; from her, by a Brāhmaṇa father, is born an Ābhīra. This [Ābhīra] is mentioned here incidentally as one who follows the lineage of cowherds. Regarding the *Jātiviveka*: "Those seeking wealth should maintain cattle, buffaloes, and the like with grass and water, and sell their milk, curd, ghee, and buttermilk."
[279] Now, those whose food may be eaten.
Yājñavalkya states the fact of his being one whose food may be eaten:
Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares the plow is fit to be eaten, as is that of a barber and of one who offers himself [as a servant].
Regarding the eating of the food of a Śūdra, Manu says:
"The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame."
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
but if eaten intentionally, as well as semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.
As for that which Śaṅkha stated:
"A Brāhmaṇa, having eaten the food of a Śūdra, or likewise of a stage-player,
a cruel physician, or one who lives off women or hunting animals..."
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, a king, one who lives by forbidden means, a universal beggar, a vintner, or a woman recently delivered, one should observe a vow for one month.

The vow consists of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*). This applies to repeated practice; however, if it concerns raw grain (*āmānna*), the penance is one-third of that. Regarding the food of a *caṇḍāla*, Viṣṇu has stated in the *Mādhavīya*: "Having eaten the food of a *caṇḍāla*, one should fast for three nights; having eaten cooked food (*siddhānna*), one should perform the *parāka* penance. Here, "the food of a *caṇḍāla*" refers to raw food. But in times of distress (*āpad*), Parāśara says: "If a Brahmin eats in the house of a Śūdra during a time of distress, he may be purified by mental remorse and by reciting the *Drupadā* verses a hundred times."
This refers primarily to raw grain:
a learned twice-born man should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha);
he may accept from him only raw grain for his subsistence, and that only for a single night.
Thus says Manu. As for what Yājñavalkya stated:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, the sharecropper, the barber, and he who offers himself [as a servant], are those whose food may be eaten."
Thus says Devala:
"A personal slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a farmer—
these five born of Śūdra wombs may have their food eaten even by Brāhmaṇas."

Thus, here the word *anna* refers to food in general and not specifically to boiled rice (*odana*). As for what is stated in the *Bhaviṣya*: "If a twice-born man cooks the food of a Śūdra by means of the act of offering it [into the fire], that food becomes unfit to be eaten, as does that Brāhmaṇa who acts as his domestic priest (*purohita*)."

"The *Kalpataru* states that 'offering' (*upakṣepaṇa*) means the entrusting of one's own food to a Śūdra in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of cooking. This refers to cases other than those involving a personal attendant (*śuśrūṣaka*). Furthermore, O fair-faced one, cooked food must be prepared by members of the [other] three castes, as well as by Śūdras who have entered into service."

Thus it is stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*. Consequently, the *Gaṅgāvākyāvalī* states that even the food offering (*naivedya*) for the gods should be cooked. It is stated in the *Śuddhitattva* that "all [these rules] refer to times other than the Kali age. Regarding the specific case of food that has been defiled by contact with a *śūdra*, Sumantu says in the *Aparārka* and the *Śūlapāṇi*:
"One may eat milk products, roasted flour (*saktu*), oil, oil-cakes (*piṇyāka*), cakes (*apūpa*), and whatever else is prepared with milk, even from a *śūdra*."

The cooking [of milk-rice] is performed with milk that has not been mixed [with water], and without [the addition of] water. Therefore, there is indeed a fault in *pāyasa* (milk-rice), because the instrumental case in the word *payasā* (with milk) conveys independence [from other liquids], and because a fault is stated regarding the water of a Śūdra. As for the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and whatever," it implies that this applies only to cakes (*apūpa*) made with milk; thus, the meaning is that there is indeed a fault in *polikā* and similar items made with water. Herein lies the essential point: the twice-born (*dvija*) is of two kinds—those devoted to the food of a Śūdra and those who have desisted from it. For the former, the aforementioned food of a Śūdra is to be eaten. For this very reason, Hārīta is cited in the *Aparārka* and by Śūlapāṇi.
Manu has declared that those who eat the food of Śūdras may consume milk-rice cooked with raw sugar, milk-rice cooked with clarified butter, milk-rice, curd, and barley-meal.

“Even those things prepared in the house of a Śūdra may be eaten by the twice-born,” so says the latter half of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* in the *Śuddhitattva*. Regarding milk-rice (*pāyasa*), it is said in the *Smṛti* of Śātātapa: “Milk-rice made with milk without cooking is raw; the cooked food of a Śūdra is called ‘raw,’ while his leavings are called ‘cooked. Furthermore, because it was previously stated, “and whatever else is made with milk,” this is fit to be eaten even from the house of a Śūdra. This is stated in the *Brāhma Purāṇa* as cited by Śūlapāṇi.

"One may eat at the festival of kings, at the auspicious occasion of Vaiśyas, or at the [festival] of cows; likewise, one may eat food in the house of a virtuous Śūdra consisting of clothing, land, jewels, gold, and grain. This too is to be avoided in the Kali age.
Among Śūdras, the householder may eat the food of cowherds, family friends, and those who till half the land; however, he must stay very far away from their sacred fords.

"Even for a Śūdra, there may be the performance of actions such as cooking [food] for Brāhmaṇas and others," so it is stated in the *Mādhavīya*, the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*, and the *Ādityapurāṇa*. Regarding one who has desisted from the food of a Śūdra, Aṅgiras says in the *Śūlapāṇi*:
"Food coming from a Śūdra to one's own home may be accepted if it has been placed in another vessel."
If a Brahmin [accepts] milk or even curd in the house of a Śūdra,
One who has returned from a journey must not eat the food of a Śūdra; this too is recorded in the Smṛti.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa it is said:
"Having sprinkled it with water, one may accept the food of a Śūdra that has come to one's house."

As for Yājñavalkya’s statement, “One should enter the water with one's clothes on after touching *śūdras* or twice-born men engaged in improper occupations,” which prescribes bathing upon touching a *śūdra*, that refers to *śūdras* other than servants and the like; otherwise, [it would be inconsistent].
Wage-earners, Śūdras, female slaves,
and male slaves likewise are not defiled when engaged in bathing, personal grooming, or household chores.

Because of contradictions such as: "A *garbhadāsa* (slave born in the house) is purified by immediate contact; a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) is pure after three days," and so forth; and because Manu says:
"Having eaten the food of those whose food is unfit to be eaten, or even the leavings of women and Śūdras..."
Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
In the case of knowledge, it is double;
thus says the Viśvambhara-śāstra.
From a twice-born man and a Māhiṣyā woman is born an Ābhīra, a seller of milk;
from a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaidehī woman, through illicit union, is born a son called an Udavāha.
He should carry an umbrella and likewise engage in the trade of men.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is born the Māhiṣya; from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born the Vaideha. He who is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Niṣāda woman is the Pauṣṭika, a carrier on the shoulders.
From a Brahmin father and a Śūdra mother is born a Niṣāda; from a twice-born father and an Ambaṣṭha mother is born a son who performs the work of a bell-metal smith.
For his livelihood, he should fashion various beautiful vessels of bell-metal.
His station is prescribed everywhere according to the dharma of a Śūdra.
He who is born from a twice-born man by an Ugrā woman is called a Kumbhakāra (potter).

He is excluded from the dharma of a Śūdra; he should fashion vessels of clay. According to the *Jātiviveka*: "A Vrātya born of a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman performs the duties prescribed for a Śūdra."
He should provide wealth for the princes and train them to be skilled in weapons and missiles.
Having received from them what is necessary for his own livelihood, he should observe his own duty—
the royal preceptor. From him, a son named Malla was born through an illicit union with a Kṣatriya woman.
Having aroused the curiosity of kings, one should acquire wealth through wrestling.
Furthermore, one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother who is an Ambaṣṭhī is called a Vaitālika.
A son born from a Kṣatriya man and a Pārasavī woman makes his living by means of the science of erotics, by praise, or by the work of a panegyrist; he is a professional actor and a copper-smith.
From a merchant (vaṇij) father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born the Antaḥpurapālaka;
from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born he who is named Vaidehaka.
For he should indeed make the inner apartments of kings pure and beyond compare;
common women are to be supported, and they are their primary means of livelihood.
He should form associations with courtesans and kings according to their wishes;
among those who live by their beauty, the *viṭa* should especially remain unattached.
He alone is the lord of their life, and no other, not even their husband;
the sixty-four arts and the science of love are merely the means of subsistence for them.
The sixty-four arts (*kalās*) have been described by Bharata:

the Vedāṅgas, the Āgamas, the sciences of craftsmanship (*śilpa*), poetry, eloquence, the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*), gambling, weaponry, marvelous discourse, the composition of soups, painting, and medicine.
Knowledge of various jewels, ancient inscriptions, men, women, donors, languages, scripts, wisdom, drama, play, elephants, horses, and the science of physiognomy (sāmudrika).
Knowledge of beds, food, battle, massage, ornaments, binding, and all bodily gestures;

skill in rope-work, boats, arts, and the construction of chariots; intelligence regarding the eight enjoyments of pleasure; protection from water, poison, fire, and enemies; and mastery over chariots, horses, limbs, and the head—[these are the results].
That which consists of difficult groves, the slaughter of animals, the utterance of the syllable "et," and the worship of Śiva and so forth.
Fragrance, a woman, clothing, song, betel, food, a bed, and adornment— these are declared to be the eightfold enjoyment.
He who is born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is known in the Smṛti as a Vaṇigjana; and he who is born from a Māhiṣya father and a Pārasavī mother is called a Mālākāra.
One should cause flowers and vegetables to grow for the increase of wealth;
for he who is deficient in the duties of a Śūdra is a master over the assembly at Padmaka.
But one born from a Sūta by a Vaidehī becomes a Sūtakāra;
however, from a Karaṇa by an Āyogavī, he is born as a Sairandhra, a performer of tasks related to perfumes.
His livelihood consists of flowers, sandalwood, merchandise, and other articles of adornment;
he performs the washing of feet and the decoration of the private parts.
The massaging of every limb, the anointing with sandalwood paste,
the application of musk in union with camphor, and the creation of a new amorous adornment.
Her livelihood is said to be that [of a maidservant]; she is known as a *sairandhrī*. In the *Viśambhara-śāstra*, it is proclaimed:
"One who is highly skilled in the art of adornment is called a *sairandhrī*."
If some Śaiva or Pāśupata who has ascended [to a high state] should fall;
He is known as Jaṅgama.
Born from him upon the wife of a Śūdra, his son is remembered as Bhasmāṅkura.
His duty is the worship of Śiva, and his livelihood is through gifts from devotees of Śiva.
Wearing matted hair and ashes, he should worship the Śiva-liṅga;
[he should offer] betel, unbroken rice grains, wealth, cows, fields, and a cowrie shell.
Whatever else has been given with devotion by living beings for the sake of Śiva—
known on earth as Caṇḍīśa— it is by means of that that his livelihood here is sustained.

From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Vaidehī mother is born a Kuśīlava, who performs dancing and other such arts; this is stated in the *Jātiviveka*. Furthermore, from a Māhiṣya father and a Māgadhī mother is born one known as a Śuddhamārgaka.
He too, being devoid of the duties of a Śūdra, would beget a son.
For the sake of his livelihood, he should practice the fourfold song and instrumental music according to the science of music (*saṅgītaśāstra*).
In that regard, first there are three kinds of song and also four kinds of instrumental music.
The fourteen types of dance, preceded by song, [were performed] by the learned.

Amarasiṃha has stated that musical instruments are of four kinds: "Stringed instruments are the lute (*vīṇā*) and so forth; percussion instruments are the drum (*muraja*) and so forth; wind instruments are the flute (*vaṃśa*) and so forth; and solid instruments are the bronze cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*) and so forth."
This man is a drummer;
born of a low-caste Ābhīra family, he fashions arrow-fletching.
His livelihood consists of crafting arrows with the feathers of birds.
Born from Ugrā in Māgadha, he was one who performed the work of trimming hair and beard;
he is called a barber (nāpita), the performer of the rites of shaving.

From a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra; from a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Māgadha. Skilled in shaving the beard and expert in clipping the nails, he shall live in the midst of the village by this occupation as a servant among the social classes.
Among men, the barber is considered a rogue and is remembered as being superior even to Śūdras. Vṛddha Manu says:
"One born from a Śūdra girl but consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa..."
Another is called a barber; he is even superior to one whose duty is that of a Śūdra.
Yājñavalkya, however, has stated that the barber is indeed a Śūdra:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, the sharecropper, and the barber— these are those whose food may be eaten."

However, Śaṅkha has stated that this one is born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). As for the twofold classification mentioned in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*—namely, the *ūrdhvanāpita* and the *adhonāpita*—that should be understood as being contextually determined (*vyavasthita*).
[287] Now follows the origin of the Kāyastha.

In the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Padmapurāṇa*: At the beginning of creation, for the sake of making living beings aware of their good and evil deeds, the Creator remained absorbed in meditation for a moment; from his entire body, [the personified Dharma] emerged.
A man of divine form, holding an ink-pot and a pen in his hand,
known as Citragupta, stands in the presence of Dharmarāja.
Appointed by Brahmā to record the good and evil deeds of living beings,
he is a knower of supersensuous knowledge, the foremost of gods, and the eternal enjoyer of sacrifice.
And because food is always offered as an oblation by the twice-born from that [source],
and since he is born from the body of Brahmā, the one established in the body (kāyastha) is called a caste (jāti).
Indeed, there are many lineages of Kāyasthas descended from him on this earth.
As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Reṇukāmāhātmya*:
"Having thus slain Arjuna, Rāma fixed sharp arrows [to his bow]."
He pursued all those distressed kings in order to slay them.
Some took refuge in the dense forest, while others entered the netherworld;
the pregnant wife of Candrasena went to the hermitage of Dālbhya.
Then Rāma arrived at the unsurpassed hermitage of Dālbhya;
indeed, Rāma was honored by the sage with offerings of water for his hands, water for his feet, a seat, and other such honors.
At the time of midday, he respectfully gave him food;
Rāma, however, requested the desire dwelling in his heart.
The great sage Dālbhya requested a boon from Rāma,
and then the two of them, being exceedingly pleased, joyfully partook of a meal.
After the meal, Dālbhya questioned Bhārgava:
"O Lord, you ought to explain that reality which was requested by you."
Rāma said:
"O highly fortunate one, a pregnant woman has arrived at your hermitage;
she belongs to the high-souled royal sage Candrasena, a Kṣatriya."
"Therefore, O great sage, grant me that which I have requested; otherwise, I shall harm her. Then Dālbhya replied, "I give you what you desire."
"O King, you ought to grant me that which I have requested.
Then the sage summoned the wife of Candrasena.
He gave the frightened woman to Rāma, and Rāma became pleased in his mind.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, that which was requested by you previously at the time of the meal—"
Tell me that, O illustrious one; I shall grant you whatever you desire.
Dālbhya said:
"Women have conceived this child; you ought to give him back to me.
Then Rāma said to Dālbhya: "That for which I have come here—"
I am the destroyer of Kṣatriyas, yet you have entreated me;
and being thus petitioned by you, O Brahmin, this supreme embryo has been placed within your body.
Therefore, the auspicious name Kāyastha shall belong to this child;
for he was born from a Kṣatriya father upon a Kṣatriyā mother, and thus he is called Kāyastha.
By Rāma’s command, he was excluded from the duties of a Kṣatriya by Dālbhya;
the duty of a Kāyastha, as traditionally remembered for Citragupta, was bestowed upon him.
And from them arose the Kāyasthas of the Dālbhya lineage;
they were indeed teachers of the Dālbhya tradition, most righteous and speakers of truth.
Constantly devoted to virtuous conduct, they were always intent on the worship of Hari and Hara;
indeed, they were the worshippers of the gods, the brahmins, the ancestors, and guests.
A woman of the Māhiṣya caste gives birth to a son from a Vaideha;
he is called a Kāyastha, and his duty is prescribed as follows.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother, a Māhiṣya is born; from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, a Vai-deha is born. He should practice the writing of scripts produced in various regions, as well as the diverse art of calculation, according to the different divisions of arithmetic and algebra (*bīja*).
He is inferior even to the Śūdra caste, for he possesses only five sacraments;
indeed, his service to the four castes consists of the means of writing and engraving.
Diligence in craftwork is declared to be their means of livelihood;
they should [immerse] their topknot, sacred thread, and reddish garment in water.
And he who avoids the touch of deities while they reside within his body— he is called "kāyastha.
Now begins the section on miscellaneous topics.
A person born from a Mālākāra father and a Lāvadyā mother is called Maṇirandhrakṛt,
Maṇihāra, and Mañju.
In Kunālī, Śālmala Mañju is the seller of nāgavalī.
His livelihood here consists of goods obtained through the purchase of betel;
from a florist, he is born as a Śilīndhra by a Kṣatriya woman, whose occupation is massaging.
Excluded from the duties of a Śūdra, his livelihood consists of massaging limbs;
and from a Śilīndhra father and a Kṣatriya mother, one named Kolhāṭi is born.
[290] Bahurūpin was a man of great vigor.
From a Vaiśya father and a Karaṇī mother was born Gocārī, the keeper of calves;
he begot a son named Chagalaka from Dhaṭadhānā.
In this world, Mañjubhāryā’s son was known as Ajapāla; likewise,
he who was born from Puṣpaśekhara by the wife of Karmacaṇḍāla.
He was indeed named Maṇḍalaka, the feeder of a pack of dogs.
The king should employ him to catch pairs of dogs;
for one born to a widow from an ascetic is called a *karmacaṇḍāla*.
Furthermore, one who performs the work of digging earth for ponds, wells, and the like, is indeed untouchable.
As stated in the *Jātiviveka*: "A son born from an Ambaṣṭha father and a Vaidehī mother is a Kuśīlava."
One who knows music and performs dance should travel from one country to another.
From an Āyogava father and a Māgadha mother, a Bhr̥kuṃsa is born;
he stands outside the [social] castes, yet among religious duties he is skilled in correctly chanting the hymns.
One should teach beloved women the art of dance and *lāsya* in the dance hall.
Regarding the entry onto the stage, Bharata has stated:
"It is indeed fourfold: physical (*kāyika*), vocal (*vācika*), external (*āhārya*), and internal (*sāttvika*)."
Four types of dramatic representation (abhinaya) have been proclaimed by those who are masters of the Nāṭyaśāstra.
In the treatise on music (*saṃgītaśāstra*):
"Singing, instrumental music, and dance—these three are called *saṃgīta*.
However, the word *saṃgīta* is used exclusively for dance."
The wise know *lāsya* to be delicate and *tāṇḍava* to be exuberant;
*tāṇḍava* arises from foot-strikes and the like, while *lāsya* is endowed with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Through glances, gestures, speech, and the like, as well as by means of bees, rays of light, and so forth,
and by the casting of glances at their breasts, arms, and thighs— that [deception] of young women is truly marvelous.
The son who is born to a female scribe by her union with a garland-maker is known as a Śālakya.
Fashioning ornaments from elephant tusks in the wilderness,
that wretched man would always craft jewels for those of the Śūdra caste.
One should work with crystal, jujube fruits, and the like, making a livelihood from those materials. Born from a Vaideha man and a Śūdra maiden is the one called Āndhasika.
He should prepare various foods and eatables, preserving them for the purpose of sale;
whatever wealth he obtains from that selling shall be his means of livelihood.
He is known as the *kāndū*.
Born from the union of a *karaṇī* woman and a Vaiśya, he is designated by the name Vatsaka.
Being inferior even to the duties of a Śūdra, he should tend cattle on grassy meadows.
From union with a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra man, there is one known as an Āyogava;
he is excluded from the duties of a Śūdra and is an artisan of stone and brickwork.
He should prepare a paved floor, and his livelihood shall be by means of powder;
the son whom a Niṣāda woman bears from union with a Śūdra [is known as a Māhiṣya].
He is called Krodhaka and Kukkuṭa, known by these two names;
he is the maker of coins everywhere in the mints.
He who was born from a Māgadhī woman and a Kṣatriya man, known by the name Ulmuka, should live by the work of iron; he is the highest among the outcaste classes.
Known as a blacksmith, his livelihood consists of ironwork;
having understood the combination of their qualities, he is the fashioner of weapons.
In the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇakāṇḍa*): A weapon measuring six [units] plus one *aṅgula* is called "the cutter of seven" (*saptahṛcchedaka*).
There is enmity between the owner of the weapon and the lord; otherwise, it brings death, but [if measured differently], it is auspicious.
Thus ends the Smṛti on the blacksmith. As long as the sound of oil-pressing machines continues, one should not perform work in the vicinity of Śūdras or those of the lowest castes.
In this world, Kukkutī became united with Kumbhakāra;
her son was clearly renowned as Kuruvinda.
He may manufacture silk garments for his own livelihood;
he is equal to those of the lowest castes, yet he must observe his own specific duty.
He was known as Sāli.
When his mother, Venavanitā, had united with a fisherman in secret, this son, popular among the people, was born to her; he was named Śāmbarika.
He is inferior even to the outcaste castes; he is a weaver who provides clean clothing. He who is born from an Ābhīrī woman and a cock is known by the name of Akhira.
He who makes garments for his own livelihood from the fibers of silk-worms is so called; however, one who produces them by the opposite method is called a *nīlīkartṛ* (a dyer using indigo).
He who was born of Mārgaṇāpita and is known by the name Sākhilya is inferior among the Guhyakeśas; he shall perform the shaving with a blade.

One should employ leeches, *tumbī*, and horns for the purpose of bloodletting. In the case of *jāndhikā* (a type of tumor), one should use the white variety of *maitreyaka* (*jāta*) that has grown spontaneously.
This one known as Bandhula is the lowest among all castes;
he sees gold and other such things in the dust of a goldsmith’s shop.
From union with a Niṣāda woman, he shall procreate a son who brings prosperity;
he is indeed known as a Pāṃsula, the maker of hemp-thread.
He is the maker of secondary silk cloths, and that is his livelihood and wealth;
from a Pulkasa woman, a Pāṃsulaka begets a son known as a Vāsika.
He should provide fodder for horses and other animals with young grass alone; as for the horse named Medas,
he should be fed in secret with the marrow from the body of a woman.
She gave birth to a Yavana son, who is celebrated as a Turuṣka;
he is well-known in the Mleccha country, where his livelihood consists of the slaughter of cows.
Born from the union of a *bandinī* and a *śūdra*, he is known as a *spandālika*;
excluded from the four castes, he is a dyer of madder.
With those pigments, one should always fashion variegated garments and diverse hand-paintings; thus, the means for producing paintings are twofold.
He alone is known as the Śucika, who buys scissors and needles;
born from a Kṣatriya father and a Māgadhī mother, he is the Ulmuka, a worker in iron.
From Ugra was born the son Pārāśava, who was a barber on earth;
he was inferior in caste as a washerman, and he is the foremost among the outcaste (antyaja) groups.
One may perform the washing of clothes solely for the purpose of one's own livelihood;
however, they know Mañjūṣa, born from a Ugra father and a Vaidehī mother, to be a washerman.

From a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra; from a Vaiśya with a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Vaideha. He shall operate an oil-press; he is the highest among the lowest castes. Sin arises from the noise of the oil-press, from violence, and from the extraction [of oil].
Therefore, Maukalika must always be banished outside the city;
for that daughter of the chariot-maker has united with a Yaugandhara.
He who procreates a son is also called a *sūtradhāra*;
he is a *jāyājīva*, a *śailūṣa*, and one who is proficient in the *nāṭya-śāstra*.
From Āvartaka, born of a Veṇī woman, came the Cāra, the weaver of thread;
and from Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, the Chāgalī gave birth to the Aurabhra, the shepherd.
He should have them make variegated woolen cloths and the tending of sheep;
from Kṣemaka, the son of Āvarttaka’s wife, he [obtained] a camel-herder.
From a Malla man and a Rauma woman is born the Deśika, who is engaged in the work of salt-making;
from a Dvija man and an Āyogavī woman is born the Dhigvaṇa, who makes armor and other such items.
He should fashion the horse’s saddle-cloth from leather according to its beauty;
this is known as the *mocis*.
And the Āyogavī woman bore a son called the Kaivarta through a man of another caste.
Excluded from all castes, he always takes up a net and kills fish and other aquatic creatures for his own livelihood.
One may cause boat-work or oars to be carried on a river during the rainy season;
one may help people cross the river, and likewise accept wealth from them.
From a Niṣāda and a Dhigvaṇī is born one who is known as a leather-worker;
his livelihood consists of the hides of cows and buffaloes.
An Ābhīra woman may obtain from a Veṇa a son known as a Śauṇḍika;
having prepared and sold liquor, he shall make his livelihood by that means.
Vaidehī obtained from Karmacaṇḍāla a son named Pāṇḍuśopaka,
who belonged to the Baruda caste and was a constant destroyer of his lineage.
"From a Niṣāda father and a Vaidehī mother was born Gāruḍī, the best of Ḍiṇḍibhas," and so forth. Thus says Manu.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍuśopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍaka. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī.

From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Vaideha; he is a bamboo-worker (tvaksāra), living by the craft of cutting bamboo and so forth. This [caste] is called Baruda, and is likewise born from a Vaideha woman. From a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Niṣāda; this is the Āhiṇḍaka, a bamboo-worker and dog-cooker (śvapāka). Furthermore, from a Caṇḍāla father and a Pulkasī mother is born a Sopāka, who lives by the occupation of root-digging and is always censured by virtuous people.

The root cause is the primary calamity: separation from one's life and being put to death; that indeed is their livelihood. From a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman is born a Niṣāda; from him and a Śūdra woman is born a Pulkasa, who is well known as a Kasāra. But a Niṣāda woman bears to a Caṇḍāla a son called an Antyāvasāyin, who dwells in cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system.
Some are also mentioned in the Ādipurāṇa:
"Now, from a Niṣāda woman by a Śūdra, a Kukkuṭa is born;
he wields the discus, the tomara-weapon, the trident, the sword, the club, the spear, and the tomara."
He was a striker of the wheels, the masses of weapons, and the *bhiṇḍipāla* missiles of kings; he was a fighter of cocks and an expert in the sport of royal cocks.
From a Vaideha father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is born a Vena;
he beats a large drum, proclaiming the king’s commands even among the subjects.
The Pulkasa, the Kukkuṭa, and the Vena—these three are forest-dwellers;
and from an Āyogava woman by a Dasyu father, one named Sairandhra is born.
The Dasyu, such as the Pauṇḍraka and others, has been mentioned previously;
he who lives by killing deer and other animals through constant snaring,
and he who guards the doors of royal women and those in childbirth.
From a Niṣāda father and an Āyogavī mother, one known as a Dhīvara is born;
he is the maker of boats for rivers and shall always ply them.
From a Niṣāda father and a Vaidehī mother, he becomes a Kārāvara;
he constantly performs the cutting of hides, their sewing, and their buying and selling.
Now, from a Niṣāda father and a Vaidehī mother is born the Candramecaka;
he always carries out the slaughter of wild animals.
From intercourse with his wife, the Kṣattṛ shall procreate a son who is a Śvapāka—
a forest-dweller who eats dog-flesh and lives by means of a wicker basket for catching game.
From a Caṇḍāla, indeed, by a Vaihya woman, one known as a Pāṇḍusopāka is born;
he indeed carries out the sale of sandals, leather, and bamboo.
An Āhiṇḍaka is born from a Niṣāda and a Vaideha;
he is one who provides protection for robbers who are condemned to death.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Niṣāda woman is born a man known as an Antyāvasāyin;
he dwells in cremation grounds, follows their livelihood, and is despised even among the Caṇḍālas.
They even carry away the helpless, the naked, and the child far from home;
by the king's command, they take the beds, ornaments, and garments of those condemned to death.
Having imposed the prescribed penalty of execution, they constantly seize [the property];
and they perform marriages and other rites among those of the same caste, even when there is an intermixture of castes.
Those who die for the sake of cows or Brahmins may sometimes cross over [to higher realms].

Vasiṣṭha says: The livelihood of Niṣādas is by means of boats; that of Kaivartas is the killing of wild animals, cattle, and birds, as well as the sale of meat; that of Āvṛtas is the management of elephants and horses; that of Ābhīras is the protection of cows, goats, and sheep; that of Dhigvaṇas is the working with leather and living by its sale; and that of Kārāvaras is the cutting of leather, the maintenance of lamps and seats, the carrying of umbrellas, and the carrying of men on their backs.

This *kahāra* is well known as a *bhoī*. Their occupations include weaving, cutting trees, and planting them. For the Andhra-Medas, their livelihood consists of cleaning house doors, impure places, and refuse heaps; touching private parts; clearing away food remnants, feces, and urine; and working as oil-pressers (*cakravṛttitā*). Regarding "touching private parts," the *Smṛtimañjarī* states that it refers either to performing purification or to acting as a barber for the lower class.
The *Smṛtimañjarī* further explains that *cakravṛttitā* means being an oil-presser.

For Madhūkas, there is the description of reciting praises of kings at dawn, which serves as an awakening from sleep; for those who have reached the end of their life as renunciants, a lifelong state of servitude; and for Pulkasas, subsistence by roots and the making of winnowing baskets. "Root" refers to the roots of trees, medicinal herbs, and the like. For Caṇḍālas and Antyāvasāyins, there is the guarding of forests and cremation grounds, as well as the application of poisons, fire, and toxins. For women, there is service to their husbands, the preparation of food, condiments, and drinks, and the study of dance, song, and the *Kāmasūtra*. Whatever tasks such as preparing food and condiments are for men, those same tasks apply to women; however, for women such as performers (*cāraṇa*), there is specifically dance and the like. All these [outcaste groups] are outsiders, excluded from all religious duties (*dharma*).
Except for the protection of living beings, the dharma consisting of non-violence and so forth is equal for all:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
generosity, self-control, compassion, and tranquility— these are the means of dharma for everyone."

Thus, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya. It was stated previously that at the annual anniversary (ābdika) for the parents, one should provide food for those of the same caste and give gifts such as clothing, gold, and so forth. However, Śaṅkha has stated otherwise:

The duties of the *sūtas* consist of the grooming of the limbs, the shaving of hair, beard, body hair, and nails, bathing, anointing, ornamentation, breaking in horses, and feeding and nourishing them;

"suitable food" refers to fodder and the like. The duties of the *kṣattṛ* consist of guarding the entrance, protection, and messengership. The duties of the *māgadhas* consist of playing the *mṛdaṅga*, lute, and flute; dancing, singing, and instrumental music; performing rites for success (*siddhi*) and appeasement (*upa-sthāna*); reciting verses (*gāthā*); and awakening at dawn.
At the time of anger, one should recite the verse that pacifies it, beginning with "Siddhiḥ. The meaning of the word *siddhi* is the sound "japa-jīva" (live by chanting).

For the Ambaṣṭhas, the ritual activities (*karmāṇi*) consist of extracting bodily arrows and probes, and the treatment and nourishment of those suffering from insanity, impotence, fever, and epilepsy.
"Bodily arrows" refers to the probes, which are the veins (*sirā*); their extraction means their opening or piercing.

The duties of the *vaidehakas* are cutting, sewing, dyeing, washing, and cleaning clothes, as well as drawing water from wells and tanks, maintaining pleasure gardens, and clearing away refuse. The duties of the *ugras* are capturing elephants, holding the royal parasol, guarding the city, and the confinement of prisoners in the jail. The duties of the *venas* are leaping, swimming, wrestling, fighting, sorcery, *śambara*, and *indrajāla*.
Wrestling (*niyuddha*) refers to hand-to-hand combat. Sorcery (*māyāśambara*) is the transformation of objects through agility. *Indrajāla* is the manifestation of non-existent things and the like.
The cock-fighters' equipment consists of weapons such as the discus, the javelin, the slingshot, the spear, the sword, the axe, the club, and the iron netting.
"Weapon" (praharaṇa) means an armament; "iron netting" (lohajālikā) refers to armor.

The occupations of the Āyogavas are working with iron, carpentry, pottery, and dealing in gold, silver, iron, swords, and leather. The occupations of the Pulkasas are guarding the city streets, keeping watch, carrying out the corpses of those who have no relatives, cutting out paintings and documents, killing bees, extracting honey, digging tunnels, and excavating wells and the like. The occupations of the Cāṇḍālas are guarding cremation grounds, impaling criminals, shaving the condemned, and executing those sentenced to death; these same [occupations] belong to the Śvapacas as well. In this regard, for a single individual, there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) of these various occupations. Others are to be understood according to the distinctions of caste (*jāti*); such is the summary.
But is it not stated in the ninth book of the Bhāgavata that the absence of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas occurs in the Kali age?
[It says: "This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall end with Sumitra;
for upon reaching that king, it will indeed reach its conclusion in the Kali age."
"Devāpi, having resorted to yoga, will take refuge in Kalāpa village;
when the Lunar dynasty has perished in the Kali age, he will re-establish it at the beginning of the Kṛta age.
Thus [it is said] in the twelfth [chapter] as well.
Of these high-souled men, whose names and characteristics remain as mere narratives, only their fame persists upon the earth.
Devāpi, the brother of Śantanu, and Maru, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
both endowed with the power of great yoga, resided at Kalāpagrāma.
Having come here at the end of the Kali age, those two, instructed by Vāsudeva,
shall propagate the dharma consisting of the [four] castes and [four] stages of life, just as it was before.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well: "Devāpi, the Paurava king, and Maru, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage— these two indeed came here at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga to initiate the Kṣatriya order."
Likewise: "A certain Nanda, the lord of Mahāpadma, was the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas;
and this Nanda was born at the beginning of the Kali age, immediately after Parikṣit."
From the time of your birth until the consecration of Nanda,
this period consists of one thousand one hundred and fifteen years.
Also in another Purāṇa:
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—these are the four castes; the first three are twice-born.
They all exist in every age, but in the Kali age, they remain only at the beginning and the end."
Therefore, how can those born from the intermixture of the twice-born be so described? Do not say so. For in the Kali age, some who possess the seeds [of the higher castes] remain upon the earth;
likewise, Devāpi and Puru are currently established [as such].
Thus, from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who were present here for the sake of the seed—
indeed, in the Kṛta Yuga, they existed together with them [the gods] without distinction."

And because of this statement by Mātṛdatta, our venerable father [held that] there certainly exist in some places Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who have fallen from their own duties and whose forms are concealed.
He is the helmsman of the deep ocean of the Bhaṭṭa system and the piercer of the vital points in all other scriptures as well.
May the virtuous Budharāmakṛṣṇa be pleased by this labor which Kamalākara has indeed undertaken here.

Thus ends the section on the nature of those born of *saṃkara* unions who are equal to Śūdras, in the *Śūdradharmatattva* composed by Kamalākara, the younger brother of Dinakara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, grandson of the illustrious Jagadguru Mīmāṃsaka Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa Sūri.
